The gradient is attenuated among mothers with adverse early birth experiences and among those informed about complications during antenatal care, consistent with belief updating. However, it cannot be fully explained by differences in biomedical risk. Exploiting plausibly exogenous improvements in road connectivity and financial access, we show that credit and supply constraints can amplify the gradient, and improved infrastructure attenuates it.

title: How institutional quality configurations shape national innovation: a configurational moderation approach
authors: Fernando Manuel Pereira de Oliveira Carvalho

title: Structure over intensity: decomposing interdisciplinarity as a diagnostic for technology transfer complexity in academic spin-offs
Gain or loss? The effect of leader risk taking on team effectiveness based on collective regulatory mechanisms
Exploring Emotional Solidarity Through Gap-Generational Travel: Social Interactions Between Chinese Grandparents and Their Grandchildren
abstract: This study explores the social interactions between Chinese grandparents and their grandchildren during travel through the theoretical lens of emotional solidarity. Gap-generational travel is a growing trend in the tourism and leisure industry and has gained increasing attention from both academic and practical perspectives. However, existing literature provides limited insight into the dynamics between grandparents and grandchildren in the context of family travel and leisure. Chinese grandparents remain marginalized in tourism scholarship, as studies related to family tourism mostly focus on parent–child dyads and emphasize family travel decision making, the benefits of travel, and family travel experiences. This study contributes to family tourism scholarship by applying the theory of emotional solidarity to interpret gap-generational travel from a non-Western perspective, highlighting the need for more inclusive theoretical frameworks, particularly regarding disadvantaged family members in tourism. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 80 Chinese grandparents, and the data were analyzed thematically. Four main themes emerged: communal joy; the creation of new memories and experiences; compensation for (un)available resources; and the celebration of shared lives between grandparents and grandchildren. The results also showed that Chinese gap-generational travel is shaped by a patrilineal family system embedded in Confucian ethics, in which family lineage follows the male line. The findings call for inclusive policies and socio-culturally oriented practices that enhance the well-being of both grandparents and grandchildren. Furthermore, the study highlights the need for approaches to elderly travel that transcends market segmentation by recognizing older adults as embedded within family relationships where emotional solidarity is both produced and sustained.

title: Towards a theory of public-sector organizations with targeted mandates: a case study of New Zealand’s Māori Health Authority
Does level of government and messaging influence public evacuations? Examining public compliance and agency trust
abstract: Extreme weather events are increasing globally, yet research on how public leadership messaging and the level of government delivering crisis communications influence public compliance and institutional trust remains limited. Drawing on public leadership theory and federalism research, we employ a 2 × 3 survey experiment embedded in the 2023 US Cooperative Election Study (N = 409) to examine how messaging style (authoritarian versus democratic) and the level of government agency (federal, state, or local) influence evacuation intent and agency trust. We find that messaging from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) increases evacuation intent, despite local governments being legally responsible for issuing evacuation orders. Democratic, or collective, messaging is associated with greater trust in agency. However, trust is more strongly associated with pre-existing individual orientations, public service motivation, and political ideology, than with one-time communication cues. Findings have implications for crisis communication strategy, public leadership, and intergovernmental coordination in emergency management.

title: Associations Between Psychosocial Factors and Pre-exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) Adherence Among Black Men Who Have Sex with Men in Ending the HIV Epidemic Jurisdictions: Findings from Project Adhere
Marketing Tactics for Nonprofit Disaster Management: A 7T Framework for Community Resilience
abstract: Disaster management, a critical issue for human life, significantly influences production, consumption, and social resilience. This research proposes a nonprofit disaster management adaptation of marketing mix logic through a 7T framework. Drawing from the marketing mix concept, a 7T framework is developed grounded in community resilience, victim-centered value creation, and the public good, and criteria were analyzed with the Best-Worst Method. The findings show that the priorities in disaster management are primarily basic goods and services followed by distribution and rapid communication. The study provides a practical roadmap for nonprofit sector in terms of building public trust in disaster processes. Ultimately, the transformative role of marketing discipline in going beyond commercial objectives to generate social good and resilience is emphasized.

title: Legal form or financial behaviour? Explaining variation in excess returns in municipal waste management in Finland
Life cycle and techno-economic assessment of anion exchange membrane electrolysis: Cradle-to-gate supply chain emissions and scale-dependent cost analysis
abstract: This study presents an integrated assessment of anion exchange membrane electrolysis that combines experimentally validated lifecycle inventory data, comprehensive cradle-to-gate greenhouse gas accounting, and probabilistic techno-economic analysis under scale-dependent conditions. The results demonstrate that under a realistic Net Zero 2050 grid scenario, the total carbon footprint is estimated at 2.53 kgCO 2 eq/kgH 2 , with electricity consumption dominating the environmental impact. However, evaluating the system under an ideal zero‑carbon electricity supply reveals a baseline footprint of 0.44 kgCO 2 eq/kgH 2 , demonstrating that upstream material production and component manufacturing impose an irreducible minimum emission threshold. Economically, the levelized cost of hydrogen decreases from $8.16/kgH 2 at a production scale of 1,000 kgH 2 /day to $5.05/kgH 2 at 50,000 kgH 2 /day, driven primarily by economies of scale. Notably, the two-parameter interaction analysis reveals that system availability and electrochemical efficiency act as primary co-optimization drivers, exhibiting a pronounced synergistic interaction for global warming potential while delivering additive economic benefits for hydrogen production cost. Furthermore, increasing system scale not only lowers costs but also progressively narrows economic uncertainty. These findings highlight that the sustainability of green hydrogen cannot be accurately evaluated without incorporating upstream supply chain impacts alongside operational metrics. The study provides an evidence-based framework for evaluating emerging electrolysis technologies and informing rigorous carbon certification standards.

title: More-efficient water splitting utilizing heated-cooled active pure water with reduced hydrogen bonds
abstract: Within the realm of renewable energy technologies—particularly those centered on hydrogen evolution reactions (HERs) and oxygen evolution reactions (OERs)—noble metals have long been regarded as the archetypal catalytic materials. In recent years, however, research efforts have pivoted toward earth-abundant, cost-effective catalysts featuring diverse compositional and structural motifs. A seminal development occurred in 2014 with the introduction of plasmon-activated water (PAW), an innovative system engineered through hot electron transfer (HET) from gold nanoparticles (AuNPs). In this review based on our published papers, we put forward an alternative paradigm aimed at enhancing HER and OER efficiencies by redirecting the focus onto water itself—specifically, a condensed water derived from Au-free processing of heated PAW containing trace amounts of Au. Relative to active PAW, this condensed form exhibits a diminished electron-doping character alongside more-pronounced disruption of hydrogen-bonding networks. Notably, its emergent properties are critically governed by the heating rate applied during PAW boiling. Analogous behaviors were observed in cooled active water, where the cooling rate during post-boiling treatment of deionized water (DIW) played a similarly decisive role. Remarkably, when employed in HER and OER applications, the heated-cooled active pure water—whether derived from PAW or DIW—consistently outperformed pristine DIW, a fact attributable to its distinctive features: reduced hydrogen-bond connectivity and a modified electron-doping state. Moreover, the latter property conferred upon the prepared active water a pronounced capacity for scavenging 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) free radicals. Even after several days of aging, both the unique physicochemical characteristics and the corresponding electrochemical activities showed only marginal attenuation, underscoring its viability for real-world deployment. Collectively, our findings establish this stable active water as a promising green solvent platform capable of enabling more-efficient HERs and OERs in electrochemical systems.

title: Fibrous fabric-derived solar interfacial evaporators for renewable water production: A review on material tuning, structural design, and applications
abstract: Growing global freshwater scarcity has motivated solar-driven interfacial water evaporation (SIWE) to emerge as a sustainable and carbon-neutral strategy for desalination and wastewater remediation. Compared with conventional rigid porous substrates or swollen hydrogels, fibrous fabrics offer distinctive advantages owing to their intrinsic multiscale porosity, flexible mechanical properties, and tunable capillary action. These hierarchical micro/nanofiber networks enable effective regulation of water supply, vapor escape, and localized thermal confinement. Although recent reviews have examined solar-driven interfacial evaporation and textile-based evaporators, the integrated relationships among fiber properties, textile architecture, fabrication, and interfacial transport remain insufficiently explored. Accordingly, this review adopts a structure-property perspective for fibrous fabric-derived solar interfacial evaporators, emphasizing the coupled transport of light, heat, water, vapor, and salt. The characteristics of natural and synthetic fibers are correlated with multiscale textile architectures and their impacts on light absorption, thermal localization, capillary water supply, vapor diffusion, and salt migration. The effects of fabrication strategies and textile structures on evaporation performance, durability, and stability are discussed. Multifunctional applications, including desalination, wastewater purification, energy generation, atmospheric water harvesting, and photocatalysis, are reviewed. Rather than identifying an optimal material or structure, this review highlights the trade-offs among material properties, textile design, fabrication strategies, and application requirements. Finally, remaining challenges and future perspectives for fabric-based solar evaporators are discussed.

title: How can prospective life cycle assessment support the eco-design of an innovative battery-grade lithium carbonate production process?
abstract: The transition to low-carbon energy systems drives increasing lithium demand, making alternative recovery technologies essential for long-term supply resilience. This study shows how eco-design principles guide the identification of the most environmentally-friendly configuration, supporting future mitigation-oriented design choices. Three innovative lithium recovery routes, distinguished by their concentration-stage configurations, are assessed: Route A uses reverse osmosis with impurity removal, Route B excludes membrane technology, and Route C applies nanofiltration without prior impurity removal. Life cycle assessments are conducted considering decarbonised background systems and process circularity, including resource and energy efficiency in the foreground system. The most effective eco-design strategy delivers potential reductions in climate-change impacts of ∼21% through foreground improvements, ∼60% through background improvements, and up to ∼68% when combined from the current to the optimised future scenario. Residual impacts further highlight the need for additional eco-design strategies. Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses evaluate key factors, including ore-grade variability and data quality.

title: The politics of forest biomass co-firing in Indonesia: Explaining policy implementation through the Actor–Network–Interest (ANI) framework
abstract: Biomass co-firing in coal-fired power plants has been promoted as a transitional strategy for increasing the share of renewable energy in Indonesia's electricity sector to support the national goal of net-zero emission. This paper analyses actor's behaviour to shed light on why the implementation of biomass co-firing policy has yet to reach the target level required to achieve national targets. To do so, this paper develops a novel Actor–Network–Interest (ANI) Framework that predicts actors' implementation behaviour based on the interaction between their structural positions within policy networks and the consistency of their formal and informal interests. It employs a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) of 65 actors with in-depth interviews and qualitative stakeholder analysis. SNA was used to identify influential actors through degree and betweenness centrality, while qualitative analysis explored the formal and informal interests underlying actors' policy responses. The results reveal a cross-sectoral network dominated by actors from the energy and forestry sectors, with limited participation from market and civil society organisations. Perhutani and PLN Energi Primer Indonesia (PLN EPI) occupy the most central positions due to their strategic roles in biomass supply and electricity system integration. The interaction between network position and interest finds three dominant implementation patterns: 1) selective–pragmatic, 2) administrative–selective, and 3) compliant–administrative. These findings support the explanatory and predictive value of the proposed framework. At the same time, brokerage functions remain weak, indicating limited capacity to coordinate interests across sectors. Consequently, biomass co-firing has been implemented largely as an incremental adjustment compatible with existing coal-based electricity systems rather than as a transformative energy transition strategy. The findings highlight the importance of stronger brokerage mechanisms, better-aligned incentives, and more effective cross-sectoral coordination to accelerate renewable energy transitions.

title: Cyclic energy storage performance and particle evolution in a directly irradiated fluidized reactor for calcium looping thermochemical energy storage
abstract: Calcium looping thermochemical energy storage (CaL-TCES) integrated with directly irradiated fluidized reactor (DIFR) is promising for large-scale and long-duration energy storage. However, the thermochemical behavior and cyclic particle evolution in DIFR remain unclear. In this study, energy storage performance of CaL-TCES composite particles in DIFR is investigated, with a fixed bed irradiation test used as a reference to clarify the necessity of fluidization. In the fixed bed, high-flux and nonuniform irradiation causes a serious mismatch between localized solar heating and bed-scale calcination, leading to severe particle structural degradation. After fluidization is introduced, bed temperature uniformity is effectively improved. During calcination under simulated concentrated solar irradiation, the temperature plateau in irradiated zone shifts to higher temperatures and becomes shorter, while reaction rate remains near its peak when irradiation is stopped. The fixed irradiation duration becomes less matched with calcination behavior in later cycles. The irradiation-to-particle energy conversion efficiency stabilized at 40–42%, with the energy distribution shifting from chemical energy toward particle sensible energy. After 10 cycles, energy storage density remained 1035 kJ/kg, with a retention of 79.6%. The particle size distribution shifts toward smaller sizes, while the external surface becomes denser and the internal porous morphology is largely retained. Average solar absorptance increased from 64.5% for fresh particles to 83.1% after cycling. These findings provide guidance for matching irradiation duration with calcination behavior and improving particle stability in DIFR.

title: Digging into disclosure: Mapping site-level publicly disclosed VSS engagement in lithium and cobalt mining
abstract: The growing importance of critical minerals such as lithium and cobalt in the energy transition has intensified scrutiny over environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices in mining supply chains. While Voluntary Sustainability Standards (VSS) are increasingly used to signal responsible sourcing, publicly disclosed engagement with these standards at the mine-site level remains poorly documented. This study systematically maps publicly disclosed engagement with VSS across industrial lithium and cobalt mining operations and examines how these patterns vary geographically and by ownership structure. A global dataset of 117 industrial mining sites was compiled using 2023 production data from S&P Global Market Intelligence, company disclosures, official VSS databases (including IRMA and TSM), publicly available audit documentation, and other mine-site sources. Sites were analysed based on publicly disclosed VSS engagement, mine-site references to sustainability initiatives, and ownership structure using the headquarters country of the largest shareholder as a proxy for the geographical distribution of ownership. The results reveal a structural asymmetry in publicly disclosed VSS engagement: engagement is concentrated among a limited number of high-output sites, while most mine sites report no publicly disclosed VSS engagement. Lithium production is highly concentrated around IRMA, whereas cobalt exhibits a more fragmented governance landscape and substantially lower mine-site VSS engagement when supply-chain and smelter/refiner-level initiatives are excluded. These findings provide new empirical evidence on the uneven coverage of publicly disclosed VSS engagement and highlight the limitations of VSS as comprehensive governance tools in critical mineral supply chains. The results have implications for emerging due diligence regulations and highlight the need for improved transparency tools to support policy implementation.

title: WiFi sensing for urban analytics: An open-source R toolkit
abstract: WiFi sensing passively captures the WiFi packets that smartphones broadcast, offering continuous, low-cost pedestrian monitoring. The technique has been applied to footfall estimation, transit analysis, and public space studies. However, existing implementations remain tied to individual deployments, and the complete processing pipeline is rarely available as reusable code together with sample data. This paper presents an open-source R toolkit that processes raw WiFi data into five urban analytics metrics: Location, Count, Track, Revisits, and Activities. The toolkit spans the full pipeline from sensor assembly to metric extraction and is documented as an online book with executable code. Demonstrations on a university campus (24 sensors, 26 days) and in a commercial district (17 sensors, 9 days) show how the metrics describe temporal rhythms, origin–destination flows, observed visit frequency, and differences in inferred stays between street types. The five-metric framework offers a common foundation for pedestrian measurement that can carry over to other urban sensing technologies. All code and approximately 20.5 million pseudonymized WiFi observations from the two field deployments are archived in a publicly accessible repository, providing a methodological framework for future pedestrian sensing research even as MAC address randomization becomes increasingly widespread.
journal_name: Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science

title: How land retirement programs affect crop production: Evidence from China's Grain for Green Program
abstract: Abstract This paper evaluates the impact of one of the world's largest land conservation programs—China's Grain for Green Program—on crop production, and examines whether land retirement policies can balance ecological goals with food security objectives. By combining detailed county‐level crop production data with remote sensing data, our difference‐in‐differences estimates suggest that the program significantly reduced total cropland area but increased total crop production. This unexpected increase in production can be explained by the program's significant increase in labor input, fertilizer use, and multiple cropping on the remaining cropland. More importantly, we find that the program improved the local microclimate and substantially alleviated the damage of weather stress on crop production. Our findings suggest that, under certain institutional conditions, it is possible to adopt land‐use policy to protect the ecosystem without compromising food security.

title: From Individual Advancement to Structural Conditions: Reframing Leadership Development
abstract: ABSTRACT Low‐wage workers represent a significant segment of the organizational workforce, yet they remain largely absent from leadership development research and practice. These workers routinely face barriers such as limited access to development opportunities and occupational stigma. However, leadership development research has primarily emphasized individual readiness and human capital, paying too little attention to how leadership systems shape access to development. Drawing on Scarcity Theory and Pierre Bourdieu's Theory, we argue that leadership development operates as a classed system influenced by both material constraints and cultural expectations. These dynamics disadvantage low‐wage workers whose everyday leadership contributions often go unrecognized. We contribute to human resource management scholarship by integrating social class and scarcity into leadership development research by showing how economic precarity and class‐based norms jointly shape limited access to leadership development for the low‐wage worker. The proposed conceptual model reframes leadership development as a more inclusive talent management practice capable of leveraging a broader range of organizational expertise. We conclude by outlining future research directions on how HR systems can reduce structural barriers and expand leadership pathways for low‐wage workers.

title: Invisible Scaling and Resource Efficiency: Decoupling Market Reach From Organizational Growth in Digital Small and Medium Enterprises
abstract: ABSTRACT This study introduces invisible scaling, a digitally mediated growth configuration in which entrepreneurial firms expand market reach without proportionate growth in internal employment and organizational infrastructure. Using an exploratory secondary‐data design, it examines 24 purposively selected digital SMEs across four countries and sectors. The analysis identifies variation in reach‐size decoupling and suggests two preliminary configurations: platform‐automated firms relying mainly on digital infrastructure and algorithmic market access, and partner‐orchestrated firms coordinating broader networks of external providers. An organizational decoupling index provides a preliminary representation of market reach relative to internal employment, although the study does not establish causality or the prevalence of the phenomenon. The findings distinguish invisible scaling from its possible mechanisms and show why organizational leanness should not be treated as environmental performance. As energy use, emissions, materials, logistics, and external labor are not measured directly, the environmental implications remain exploratory and concern the appropriate boundary of assessment.

title: Climate Change Disclosure and Sustainability Awards: Does Assurance Add Value? Evidence From the European Context
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainability awards have become an increasingly visible mechanism for recognising firms' environmental and social performance. This paper examines the individual and combined effects of climate change disclosure and the external assurance of sustainability reports on firms' likelihood of receiving awards for sustainability performance. Using a sample of 600 European companies for the period 2015–2022, we estimate linear and logistic regression models with both fixed and random effects. The findings show that sustainability assurance significantly enhances the comprehensiveness of climate change disclosure. Both climate disclosure and independent assurance increase the probability of winning sustainability awards. Moreover, assurance strengthens the signalling value of climate disclosure, thereby further increasing the likelihood of award recognition. However, the characteristics of the assurance provider do not influence these effects, although assurance tenure positively affects the probability of receiving sustainability awards. Robustness checks corroborate the stability of the results under different methodological specifications.

title: Micro-delight and anticipatory anxiety in mobile travel reviews: shaping tourist satisfaction
abstract: Purpose Mobile travel reviews contain fine-grained emotions that aggregate sentiment misses. This study aims to examine how discrete emotional cues – micro-delight (joy + surprise) and anticipatory anxiety (fear + sadness) – shape tourist satisfaction, and whether tour type (guided vs self-guided) moderates these effects. Design/methodology/approach A total of 3,678 English reviews were collected from guided (GetYourGuide, Viator) and self-guided (VoiceMap, GPSmyCity) platforms. BERT-based emotion extraction quantified discrete emotions, PCA on sentence embeddings controlled for latent semantic content and ordinal logistic regression tested the hypotheses, supported by robustness checks and model diagnostics. Findings Micro-delight positively predicts satisfaction (ß = 2.115, p < 0.001), while anticipatory anxiety negatively predicts satisfaction (ß = −1.006, p < 0.001). Tour type moderation was limited: including tour-type interaction terms improved model fit (χ2(2) = 19.49, p < 0.001), but only the micro-delight × tour type interaction was statistically significant, whereas the anxiety × tour type interaction was not (p = 0.479). Tour type was significant as a control (ß = −0.692, p < 0.001), indicating lower baseline satisfaction for self-guided tours. Practical implications Hospitality managers should prioritize reducing anticipatory anxiety as a universal strategy, while investing in delight-inducing features that yield comparable returns across guided and self-guided tour formats. For self-guided tour operators, reducing wayfinding anxiety and amplifying delight through personalized content offer a clear path to improve satisfaction. Originality/value The study provides large-scale evidence that discrete emotional cues predict satisfaction beyond aggregate sentiment, supporting emotional granularity in mobile review contexts. The findings provide limited evidence that tour type alters the relationship between discrete emotions and satisfaction, suggesting that emotional management strategies may be applied broadly across tour formats. The methodological pipeline demonstrates how BERT-based emotion extraction can be aligned with theory-driven hypothesis testing in tourism research.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Peer Accounting Comparability and Focal Firms’ Earnings Management: A Perspective of Accounting Discretion
abstract: This study investigates how firms manage earnings through accounting discretion when industry peers produce more comparable accounting information. Utilizing data from Chinese A‐share listed firms, we find that peer accounting comparability inhibits focal firms’ accruals‐based earnings management. We identify two possible mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. First, peer accounting comparability helps to establish generally accepted accounting practices that induce focal firms to align. Second, peer accounting comparability contributes to mitigating outsiders’ information asymmetry, thus improving external monitoring. Cross‐sectional analysis indicates that the effect of peer accounting comparability holds across varying levels of focal firms’ internal and external governance mechanisms. Furthermore, we find that manipulating accruals when peer accounting comparability is high causes lower cumulative abnormal returns during the earnings announcement window and a higher cost of equity. Finally, we show that when focal firms cannot manage earnings through accounting discretion because of high peer accounting comparability, they turn to real earnings management.

title: Managing Innovation in the Entrepreneurial Family Galaxy: Toward a New Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Innovation management is central to the long‐run competitiveness and renewal of entrepreneurial families, and prior research has documented how socioemotional wealth preservation, risk preferences, long‐term orientation, and idiosyncratic endowments shape their innovative behavior. We welcomed contributions that deepened our understanding of how family involvement shapes innovation inputs, processes, and outcomes; moved beyond R&D intensity and patenting; and extended the analysis to the diversity of actors, governance arrangements, and organizational forms through which entrepreneurial families innovate. The nine featured articles answer that call across multiple levels of analysis, from board and top management team composition, through succession and intra‐family relational dynamics, to firms' embeddedness in local knowledge ecosystems. These studies show that the predominant unit of analysis remains the single operating firm, systematically underestimating the transgenerational and multientity character of innovation in entrepreneurial families that today operate across a multitude of firms, family offices, foundations, holding companies, academies, and trust companies. To organize these contributions and chart the next wave of research, in this article we draw on and extend the entrepreneurial family galaxy perspective, combining its five dimensions (shape, mass, luminosity, distance from the center, and regeneration rate) with the input–process–outcome framework. Drawing on our examination, we have developed an agenda for future research on innovation in the entrepreneurial family galaxy. Managerial Summary Innovation management is decisive for the long‐run competitiveness and renewal of entrepreneurial families that own and govern their businesses. Family firms, the dominant organizational form worldwide, generate a substantial share of global GDP and employment, so how they innovate matters not only to the firms themselves but also to society at large. Existing research and practice have accumulated a rich understanding of how families' emotional attachment to the business, risk preferences, long‐term horizon, and unique resources drive or constrain innovation. Yet most current thinking still treats the family firm as an isolated entity, whereas today entrepreneurial families increasingly operate across a galaxy of organizations—operating companies, family offices, philanthropic and artistic foundations, holding companies, new ventures, and trust companies—through which innovation emerges, evolves, and accumulates over generations. This work extends current understanding across multiple levels: how boards and top management teams shape innovation intentions, how succession redesigns innovation trajectories, how families balance financial and socioemotional goals in their innovation choices, how tradition can serve as a springboard for international product innovation, how absorptive capacity turns emotional commitment into green innovation, and how local knowledge ecosystems support the transition to sustainability‐driven innovation. We introduce the entrepreneurial family galaxy as a practical lens for understanding innovation management in this ecosystem. For families and their advisors, the galaxy's five dimensions—shape, mass, luminosity, distance from the center, and regeneration rate—provide a tool for assessing and strengthening the innovation inputs, processes, and outcomes of the entire entrepreneurial ecosystem across generations.

title: Corporate Governance and Evolving Corporate Disclosures: A Commentary and Reflections
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This editorial introduces the Special Issue on “Corporate Governance and Evolving Corporate Disclosures” and advances a framework for understanding how governance structures and disclosure practices co‐evolve in response to regulatory reforms, stakeholder pressures, and technological change. We conceptualize disclosure not only as an outcome of governance but also as a mechanism that reshapes monitoring and accountability. Research Findings/Insights The contributions demonstrate that disclosure outcomes depend on stakeholder salience, institutional context, and technological advances. While low‐power stakeholder interventions may have limited effects on reporting practices, improvements in disclosure readability can reduce governance‐related shareholder proposals. Technological tools enhance monitoring capacity but also introduce risks of selective information design, information overload, and new power asymmetries. Decentralized infrastructures redistribute rather than eliminate governance challenges. Theoretical/Academic Implications The Special Issue advances governance research by highlighting bidirectional relationships between governance and disclosure and by integrating implications of emerging technological tools and digital platforms into governance theory. It calls for greater attention to stakeholder heterogeneity, power redistribution, and causal identification strategies. Practitioner/Policy Implications Regulators and boards should complement disclosure mandates and technological adoption with safeguards that enhance interpretability, oversight capacity, and accountability in increasingly complex information environments.

title: Spatializing Ageism in Commercial Spaces: Discursive Justifications and Lived Experiences of Age-Based Exclusion
abstract: Abstract This study examines how age-based exclusion is materially organized, discursively justified, and experienced within everyday commercial environments. Drawing on marketing systems theory and critical spatial theory, it conceptualizes commercial space as moral infrastructure through which market participation is organized. Using topic modeling of public discourse and in-depth interviews with older consumers, the study examines the discursive, material, and lived dimensions of age-based exclusion. Public discourse legitimates exclusion through five recurring justificatory themes: moral generalization, economic rationalization, youth-centered normalization, behavioral stigmatization, and institutional normalization. Interview accounts illustrate how material and operational arrangements, including kiosks, service practices, and youth-oriented spatial design, can shape older consumers’ participation and how participants experience and negotiate these conditions through discomfort, anticipatory withdrawal, behavioral self-regulation, and the internalization of market expectations. The findings suggest a spatial mechanism through which public discourse can legitimate exclusion, material arrangements can organize participation, and lived experience can shape expectations of belonging and non-belonging. The study contributes to business ethics by showing how age-based exclusion can be understood as a form of structural injustice reproduced through routine market coordination within marketing systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Bureaucratic Discretion, and Democratic Administration
abstract: ABSTRACT Since the start of the COVID ‐19 pandemic, many countries have been using artificial intelligence ( AI ) to replace civil service personnel. We argue that this practice undermines core democratic values. Using the public values framework, we identify four clusters of values that are threatened when bureaucratic discretion is transferred to algorithms: accountability, fairness and equity, individual consideration, and reason‐giving. Each of these values is incompatible with how algorithms render decisions. Because algorithms produce outputs based on statistical regularities, they diffuse responsibility across multiple parties, fail to make accurate predictions about anomalous cases, and attenuate citizens' claims to individualized consideration. Thus, this article frames AI adoption as a constitutional question about which decisions can be automated, and which should remain under human control because they implicate democratic values. We propose a centaur model in which AI supports rather than replaces human officials, which can preserve efficiency while protecting democratic governance.

title: Patterns of Drug Use Across Social and Sexual Contexts in Spain: Insights From the European Web Survey on Drugs 2024
abstract: Abstract Drug use is a global public health issue. Sexualized drug use (SDU) involves intentionally using substances to enhance sexual activity across diverse contexts, but it lacks a unified definition. Chemsex is a specific SDU subset that features stimulant use (methamphetamine, GHB/GBL, mephedrone) in prolonged sex group sessions, predominantly among men who have sex with men (MSM). We analyzed data from 6,399 valid participants residing in Spain who completed the European Web Survey on Drugs. Our focus was on sex-related drug use, including chemsex. Recreational use was the most common reason for drug consumption (78.01%). Cannabis and heroin were frequently used to relax or manage stress (49.73% and 30.14%, respectively), improve sleep (26.66%), and cope with anxiety and/or depression (26.35%). Drug use to enhance sexual performance and pleasure was reported by 13.66% of participants, while chemsex use was lower at 3.31%. Though historically associated with MSM, chemsex use is increasingly reported among women. Methamphetamine, cannabis, and MDMA were more frequently used by men to enhance sexual experiences, with methamphetamine and new psychoactive substances being primarily linked to chemsex parties. Illicit drug use in Spain is predominantly recreational and typically occurs at home, festivals, or nightlife venues. Chemsex, particularly among MSM, is an emerging issue associated with sexual, physical, and mental health risks. Addressing this requires targeted prevention strategies, including health education, harm reduction, inclusive care services, and professional training to reduce associated harms and improve health outcomes.

Direct aqueous mineral carbonation of cementitious fines derived from hardened ready-mix concrete waste: Process performance and carbon accounting
abstract: The growing need to mitigate anthropogenic CO 2 emissions is driving the development of low-energy carbon capture and utilization technologies. Hardened ready-mix concrete waste represents an underexplored alkaline feedstock for direct aqueous mineral carbonation, offering opportunities for simultaneous CO 2 sequestration and waste valorisation. This study investigates direct aqueous mineral carbonation of concrete fines derived from hardened ready-mix concrete waste under ambient conditions using a CO 2 gas blend representative of cement plant flue gas. The influence of solid-to-liquid (S/L) ratio on dissolved Ca evolution, CO 2 uptake, CaCO 3 production, and degree of carbonation was evaluated, while a gate-to-gate carbon accounting framework assessed the environmental performance of the process. Geochemical equilibrium modelling was used to elucidate the mechanisms governing dissolved Ca evolution during carbonation. Feedstock and carbonation products were characterised. Surface morphology, thermogravimetric, and phase analyses confirmed successful carbonation and the formation of crystalline calcite. An S/L ratio of 1:10 achieved the highest total CO 2 uptake of 100.9 g-CO 2 /kg-concrete fines (20.2 g CO 2 per 2 L batch), with 84.5 g-CO 2 /kg-concrete fines permanently fixed as crystalline calcite. The modelling attributed the observed Ca rebound to continued decalcification of Ca-bearing phases coupled with evolving carbonate speciation. Carbon accounting indicated a net-positive footprint under laboratory conditions; however, substituting technical gases with industrial waste flue gas shifted the process toward a near net-zero carbon footprint. These findings establish hardened ready-mix concrete waste as a promising feedstock for direct aqueous mineral carbonation and highlight process integration with industrial flue gas and product valorisation as key pathways towards industrial implementation.

title: Land Degradation Pathways of Open‐Pit and Underground Mining in Karst Regions: A Spatial Indicator Assessment
abstract: ABSTRACT Mining in the karst regions of southwest China threatens ecosystem stability and accelerates land degradation. Regional evaluation rarely distinguishes between degradation pathways in open‐pit and underground operations, due to spatial heterogeneity and geomorphological confounding effects. Using land use/land cover data from the China Land Cover Dataset (CLCD) for 2010, 2015, 2020 and 2025, we examined 4318 mines in Guizhou with a multiscale (0–4 km) distance‐decay model that applies local topological constraints to separate mining footprint changes from background landscape changes. We found that these two types of mining represent two distinct spatial disturbance regimes. For open‐pit operations, localized physical degradation was pronounced, with surficial stripping expansion peaking at a 2.0‐km radius and maintaining a sustained degradation footprint. Underground mining displayed a diffuse spatial signature. Rather than a sharp distance‐decay gradient, surrounding forest cover showed a uniform decline of 18.0 percentage points below the control baseline across the 4.0‐km study area. This non‐gradient degradation pattern implies a landscape‐scale response to alterations in subsurface hydrology rather than direct surface disturbances. These results emphasize the inadequacy of uniform buffer zones for managing regional environmental impacts. We recommend a 2.0‐km core management zone for prioritizing open‐pit mine rehabilitation, while addressing the impacts of underground mining requires transitioning from static spatial boundaries to broader landscape‐level hydro‐ecological management.

title: Linking Ecosystem Risk, Health, Services to Ecological Security Assessment in the Yellow River Basin: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Nonlinear Driving Characteristics
abstract: ABSTRACT A scientific assessment of ecological security (ES) and its nonlinear mechanism for key driving factors in the Yellow River Basin (YRB) is of great significance for ecological protection and sustainable development. This study proposes an ES assessment framework, which links ecosystem risk (ER), ecosystem health (EH), and ecosystem services (ESS). We applied this framework to reveal the YRB's ES characteristics from 2000 to 2023, and explored the reliability of the assessment results. By coupling the XGBoost‐SHAP model, we identified the dominant driving factors of ES and quantified their nonlinear response relationships as well as key thresholds. The results indicated that under the comprehensive effect of significant decline in ER, overall improvement in EH and ESS in the YRB, the ES level showed a steady upward trend, with a stable pattern of high in the south and low in the north, and significant spatial positive correlation characteristics. The forest and grassland proportion, precipitation, vegetation coverage, and the construction land proportion are the dominant driving factors affecting ES, and each driving factor exhibited clear threshold characteristics in its impact on ES. Among them, the beneficial effects of the forest and grassland proportion, precipitation, and vegetation coverage on ES significantly increased when exceeding the thresholds of 49.6%, 512.2 mm, and 67.2%, respectively. The ecological impact of construction land proportion becomes negative when exceeding the threshold of 10.5%, showing a coercing effect. Our research not only provides key control objects and threshold basis for the ES management in the YRB, but also provides a robust framework for other similar regional ES research.

Stephen Hawking biography explores an ‘exceptionally clear, uncluttered mind’
Old hearts age backwards: transplanted organs adjust to host's biological age
China now leads the world in trials for next-gen CAR-T therapies
An IV Hazard Model of Loan Default with an Application to Subprime Mortgage Cohorts
abstract: ABSTRACT I develop a control function methodology robust to endogenous or mismeasured regressors in hazard models. Applying the estimator to the subprime mortgage crisis, I quantify what caused the foreclosure rate to triple across the 2003 to 2007 subprime cohorts. To identify the elasticity of default to housing prices, I use various home price instruments including historical variation in home price cyclicality. Loose credit played a significant role in the crisis, but much of the increase in defaults across cohorts was caused by price declines unrelated to lending standards, with a 10% price decline increasing subprime mortgage default rates by 50%.

title: Deadwood Labor? The Effects of Eliminating Employment Protection for Older Workers
abstract: We analyze mandatory retirement in Sweden, which eliminates employment protection at age 67. Employment falls by about 10 percent and total average earnings by about 20 percent immediately at age 67. Eight percent of jobs separate immediately due to loss of protection, with effects stemming from jobs with stronger initial employment protection (long tenure, firms subject to “last in, first out” rules), and those in the public sector. We examine the effects on continuing jobs. While wages appear rigid, we uncover novel, sizable intensive-margin hours reductions, resulting in an 8 percent drop in earnings conditional on staying on the job. (JEL J14, J22, J26, J31, J63, K31)

title: Who Gets a Family? The Consequences of Family and Congregate Care Allocation for Child Outcomes
abstract: Hundreds of thousands of children grow up in the US foster care system every year and are at high risk of experiencing negative outcomes such as incarceration and homelessness. This paper documents how the placement of foster children into families rather than congregate care improves their outcomes, using the exits of other children from families as an instrument for their placement setting. Policies that change which children are matched to families can achieve a large percentage of the gains from policies that add families to the foster care system due to heterogeneity in treatment effects. (JEL J12, J13, J18, K42)

title: Money, Time, and Grant Design
abstract: We conduct survey experiments to test how the design of scientific grants—the money and time awarded—can be used to manage researchers. On average, researchers are relatively unwilling to trade off money for time when choosing among grants. However, there is significant heterogeneity in researchers' preferences. Conditional on receiving a grant, different designs cause only minor changes in researchers' plans for how they would use the funding. Marginal changes in grant design are more relevant for selection effects (funders' ability to attract certain researchers) than treatment effects (funders' ability to change researchers' strategies). (JEL C83, I23, O31)

title: Do Workfare Programs Live Up to Their Promises? Experimental Evidence from Côte d'Ivoire
abstract: We study contemporaneous and post-program impacts of a public works program which provides urban youth seven months of employment at the formal minimum wage with complementary training in entrepreneurship or job search. During the program, the employment rate only increases slightly, but we find a shift toward wage jobs, higher earnings and savings, as well as positive changes in work habits, behaviors, and well-being. After the program, we find no lasting impact on employment or behaviors, with only limited gains in earnings stemming from independent activities. Using machine learning to analyze heterogeneity, we show that alternative targeting approaches can substantially improve welfare. (JEL C45, G51, H53, I38, J13, J64, O15)

title: Detection of Collusive Networks in Multistage Auctions
abstract: We develop a method for detecting cartels in multistage auctions. Our approach allows firms to act collusively against cartel members yet competitively otherwise. In these auctions, bidders submit initial bids and can later revise them downward. As initial bids are shaded, close initial bids indicate similar costs and thus create strong incentives to undercut rivals. We classify firm pairs as collusive if they ignore this incentive by failing to update bids against each other, relative to other pairs with similarly close initial bids. Our algorithm predicts Ukraine's Antimonopoly Committee sanctions: Classified pairs are nine times more likely to be sanctioned. (JEL D22, D44, H57, K21, L12, P31, P35)

title: From Access to Achievement: The Primary School-Age Impacts of an At-Scale Preschool Construction Program in Highly Deprived Communities
abstract: We evaluate a large-scale public preschool construction program in deprived rural communities in Mozambique using a randomized controlled trial. The program increased preschool enrollment from 2 to 75 percent, improved primary school enrollment and progression, and led treated children to score higher in cognitive and social-emotional skills tests. Impacts were strongest among children of illiterate parents, in less poor households, and living near preschools. We provide evidence that preschool construction mediates later educational success at primary school age. We also detect increased parental investment in children and higher preschool enrollment for younger siblings. Finally, we estimate the program was implemented cost-effectively. (JEL I21, I26, I32, J13, O15, O18)

title: Globalization, Capital Taxation, and Development: Evidence from a Macrohistorical Database
abstract: This paper builds and analyzes a new global macrohistorical database of effective tax rates on capital and labor in 154 countries. We establish a new stylized fact: While effective capital tax rates fell in developed countries between 1965 and 2018, they rose in developing countries after 1990. Multiple country-, sector-, and firm-level research designs suggest that trade openness contributed to this rise by increasing the share of output produced in corporations and larger firms, where effective capital taxation is higher. In contrast to a common view, globalization appears in many countries to have supported governments' ability to tax capital. (JEL F41, F62, H24, H25, O19, O23)

title: Early Grade Retention Harms Adult Earnings
abstract: This paper provides new causal evidence on the effects of grade retention on educational attainment, behavioral outcomes, and labor market performance by analyzing Texas's reading test–based retention policy. Using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, I find that third-grade retention significantly reduces annual earnings at age 26 by $3,477 (19 percent). While temporarily improving test scores, retention increases absenteeism, violent behavior, and juvenile crime, and reduces the likelihood of high school graduation. Moreover, retained students exhibit higher community college enrollment but lower public university attendance, though neither estimate is statistically significant. (JEL D91, H75, I21, I26, I28, J31)

title: The Long-Term Effects of Cash Assistance
abstract: We investigate the long-term effects of cash assistance on beneficiaries and their children among participants in the Seattle-Denver Income Maintenance Experiment. Treated families in this randomized experiment received thousands of dollars in extra government benefits for three or five years in the 1970s. We match experimental records to Social Security Administration data using a novel algorithm, finding that treatment decreased adults' postexperimental annual earnings by $1,800 and increased their disability benefit applications. Effects were strongest around retirement age; evidence suggests possible occupational mechanisms. In contrast, children experienced no significant effects on earnings or interaction with the disability system. (JEL G51, H55, H75, I32, I38, J12, J14)

title: Designing Incentives for Impatient People: An RCT Promoting Exercise to Manage Diabetes
University as a Melting Pot: Long-Term Effects of Internationalization
abstract: This paper provides the first evidence on the impact of exposure to international students on the long-term outcomes of native students. I combine unique survey and administrative data from the Netherlands covering one million students across three decades and employ an across-cohort design. I find that exposure to international students leads natives to (i) form social ties with nonnatives, (ii) hold more positive attitudes towards migration and learning about other cultures, and (iii) seek opportunities abroad. Notably, I find precisely estimated zero effects on employment, income, entrepreneurship, and the share of international coworkers up to 25 years after university entry. (JEL F22, I23, I26, J15, Z13)

title: Who Profits from Amateurism? Rent Sharing in Modern College Sports
abstract: Intercollegiate amateur athletics in the United States have historically prevented student-athletes from receiving market wages, creating substantial economic rents that are primarily generated by men's football and basketball programs. Using financial data from college athletic departments, we estimate rent-sharing elasticities to measure how rents flow to women's sports and other men's sports and lead to increased spending on athletic facilities and coaches' salaries. Using player-level data, we find that the rent-sharing transfers spending away from students who are more likely to be Black and come from poor neighborhoods toward students more likely to be White and come from higher-income neighborhoods. (JEL I23, J15, J16, J31, L83, Z21, Z22)

title: Disastrous Displacement: The Long-Run Impacts of Landslides
abstract: Natural disasters displace millions of people a year, but their economic impacts are difficult to study when the affected population becomes dispersed. This paper estimates the long-run impacts of six landslides in Uganda on nearly the full affected population. The analysis exploits the sharp boundaries between households residing along a landslide path and those on the same slopes but outside the path. Years after the landslides, affected households earn 50 percent less income and are 18 percentage points less likely to report being satisfied with their lives. Further analysis points to social capital as a determinant of successful post-disaster recovery. (JEL H84, J11, O12, O13, Q54, R23, Z13)

title: Innovation through Inventor Mobility: Evidence from Noncompete Agreements
abstract: Proponents of labor mobility restrictions argue that innovation incentives more than offset harm to workers. Yet the causal effect of such policies on innovation is an open empirical question. Leveraging plausibly exogenous state-level changes in the enforceability of noncompete agreements (NCAs), we find a significant negative effect on innovation. This effect is even larger for the most novel and innovative patents and firms. Further analysis shows these negative effects on innovation cannot be explained by entry alone and instead likely result from reduced knowledge flows. Our findings suggest that labor mobility plays a crucial role in spreading knowledge across firms. (JEL E24, J08, J21, K31, O31, O33)

title: All Roads Lead to Rome: Global Air Connectivity and Bilateral Trade
Treatment evaluation at the intensive and extensive margins
abstract: This paper provides a solution to the evaluation of treatment effects in selective samples when neither instruments nor parametric assumptions are available. We provide sharp bounds for average treatment effects under a conditional monotonicity assumption for all principal strata, i.e. units characterizing the complete intensive and extensive margins. Most importantly, we allow for a large share of units whose selection is indifferent to treatment, e.g. due to non-compliance. The existence of such a population is crucially tied to the regularity of sharp population bounds and thus conventional asymptotic inference for methods such as Lee bounds can be misleading. This problem can be solved using smoothed outer identification regions for inference. We provide semiparametrically efficient debiased machine learning estimators for both regular and smooth bounds that can accommodate high-dimensional covariates and flexible functional forms. Our study of active labor market policy reveals the empirical prevalence of the aforementioned indifference population and supports results from previous impact analyses under much weaker assumptions.

title: Correction to ‘The Announcement Volatility Risk Premium in Agricultural Markets: Evidence From USDA Report Releases’
abstract: He, X, and S. Bian. 2025. “ The Announcement Volatility Risk Premium in Agricultural Markets: Evidence From USDA Report Releases.” Journal of Agricultural Economics 76, no. 3: 651–665. https://doi.org/10.1111/1477-9552.12647. The funding statement read: ‘This work was supported by Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, 2662022JGQD004, 2662022JGQD005; National Natural Science Foundation of China, 72303075.’ It should have read: ‘This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China, 72303075; Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, 2662022JGQD004, 2662022JGQD005.’ We apologize for this error.

How the cryptocurrency market is connected to the financial market
