title: A critical political economy of syndemics: HIV in Ukraine amid war, reform, and COVID-19
abstract: The spread of complex viral epidemics and pandemics worldwide has become more dangerous, and researchers, policymakers, and health organisations have focused on the biological determinants and sequelae of these conditions. This paper explores the concept of a syndemic from the public health literature, infused with a critical political economy framework, to understand an intractable and dangerous viral emergency: that of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in Ukraine during violent conflict. The syndemic paradigm combines a concern with both biological and social factors in understanding disease emergence, progression, and outcomes, but the literature using this framework has so far elided the structuring logics and social relations of multi-scalar political economies that this paper argues are vital to study epidemics. Using HIV in Ukraine during war as a case study, the paper explores how the virus has emerged from being practically unknown in Ukraine during the 1990s to become one of Europe’s worst syndemics. Individualised, biological factors only explain a very small part of the story, this piece argues, and the ongoing HIV emergency in Ukraine is intimately interrelated with state failure, the collapse of social services, healthcare reform, decentralisation, war, mass displacement, COVID-19, and Russia’s formal invasion in 2022.

title: FOMC Announcements and Household Expectations
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the impact of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcements on household expectations by comparing responses to the Survey of Consumer Expectations before and after Federal Open Market Committee meetings, over the period 2013–2019. We find that Fed decisions strongly affect expectations of interest rates on savings accounts, but the impact on the expectations of other variables, notably inflation, is muted. We explore three possible factors that can rationalise our results: (i) Lack of information, that is, the signals sent by the Federal Reserve on its actions via the media are not sufficiently strong to reach a sufficiently large share of the households; (ii) lack of understanding, that is, not enough households grasp the transmission of monetary policy to real activity and/or inflation; and (iii) lack of attention, that is, most households neglect monetary policy news as they focus on issues that are perceived as affecting them more closely. We provide evidence that these explanations partly contribute to the results, but none of them fully accounts for the insensitivity of household inflation expectations.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Multi-stakeholder market shaping for sustainability: effort types and enactment pathways in B2B markets
abstract: Abstract Marketing scholarship has primarily focused on influencing consumer behavior towards sustainability, yet many sustainability challenges require market-level changes across multiple stakeholders. Addressing this gap, we examine how heterogeneous stakeholders collectively shape markets for sustainability. We conduct a multi-case study of B2B markets whose impact on climate change and biodiversity is actively contested. Drawing on institutional field theory, we conceptualize market shaping for sustainability as linked to issue fields where diverse stakeholders engage to influence market trajectories. Our abductive analysis identifies four types of multi-stakeholder market-shaping efforts pursuing markedly different—at times opposing—market-level outcomes: status quo maintenance, targeted reform, infrastructure reform, and market contraction. To explain this variation, we delineate four pathways through which stakeholders enact sustainability-related issues—two for challengers and two for incumbents. By linking these pathways to intended market-level outcomes, we advance theory on market-based sustainability interventions and offer actionable insights for navigating multi-stakeholder market-shaping processes.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Commentary on Han et al.’s meta-analytic work on high-investment human resource practices: through the 3P lens for workforce management
abstract: Abstract Han, Kang, Allen and Pan’s (2026) meta-analysis integrates human capital resources (HCR) theory and institutional theory to examine how educational systems and labor market institutions jointly influence the effectiveness of high-investment human resource practices (HIHRPs). Contrary to their theoretical prediction, low–low educational system and labor market configurations relate to firm performance as positively as high–high configurations do, and that puzzle remains unresolved. This combination describes the institutional profile of many host economies, which makes it an international business problem: should multinational enterprises transfer their HIHRPs abroad or adapt to local practice? This commentary outlines substitution effects, drawn from the institutional voids literature and organizational support theory, as an alternative mechanism that may better account for its effect. We reflect that theoretical parsimony, while elegant, could oversimplify and obscure complex phenomena that span multiple levels of analysis, the types of topics that strategic international human resource management (SIHRM) aims to research. We then propose a people–places–practices (3P) lens to note the theoretical directions Han et al.’s work addresses and those it leaves for future work. The commentary illustrates how deliberate theory integration, guided by the specific research question and institutional context, can enhance explanatory power in SIHRM research.

title: Appearance-Based Legitimate Distinctiveness: Founder Attractiveness, Gender, and Venture Evaluations
abstract: This study proposes a way to reconcile the beauty premium and beauty-is-beastly arguments by suggesting that founder appearance is processed through two separable and countervailing channels: perceived legitimacy and perceived distinctiveness. We further theorize that in startups, the relationship is gendered, because women do not fit the entrepreneurial prototype, limiting their perceived legitimacy. A field study of 359 founders supports our theorizing that male founders are evaluated best when moderately attractive, while female founders see no significant attractiveness effects. A preregistered experiment with 771 participants, using AI-manipulated attractiveness, does not confirm these patterns but supports our theorizing about both mediators.

title: Correction to “Revisiting Zuckerman's (1999) categorical imperative: An application of epistemic maps for replication”
Designing for unanticipated uses: How product attributes shape community‐led exaptation
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Users often discover new uses for products that firms may later commercialize, which we call community‐led exaptation. We examine how product attributes shape users' discovery of new functions versus new functionalities. Using 1925 IKEA product hacks, we find that modularity increases the likelihood of new functions. This effect strengthens when product components are compatible across product lines but weakens when esthetic product variants exist. Visual simplicity, conversely, increases the likelihood of new functionalities. These findings suggest that firms can structure the opportunity space for discovery through product design. Exploratory analysis of archival data and interviews further illustrates how IKEA responds to these discoveries. We contribute to exaptation, user innovation, and design research by showing how product attributes shape the types of new uses communities discover. Managerial Summary How can firms design products to facilitate community‐led exaptation? We find that product attributes can shape what users discover. Modular products enable users to find new functions (i.e., applications), while visually simple products enable users to find new functionalities (i.e., new product capabilities). Firms' decisions to offer components that are compatible across product lines and esthetic product variants can influence the likelihood of new functions. Additionally, firms can capitalize on these new uses by showcasing promising community‐discovered functions on official channels or incorporate them as complements to existing product lines. However, functional modifications can raise safety concerns and may require additional development. Firms should therefore design for intended use, and for the kinds of new uses they are willing to seed and commercialize.

title: CEO Tax Lock-In and Share Pledging
The Issuance and Design of Sustainability-Linked Loans
How Awareness of Media Slant Affects Reaction to News: Field and Experimental Evidence from Microblog Users
abstract: This paper investigates whether news consumers react strategically to media slant. Using data from Microblog users and an online experiment that varies whether sources and stances are disclosed, we find that users are more likely to repost news consistent with their own attitudes, yet they also exhibit a higher propensity to repost news inconsistent with the reporting outlet’s general stance. Evidence suggests that this latter behavior reflects strategic inference: users recognize the outlet’s tradeoff between popularity and stance, and thus infer greater popularity for inconsistent news. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that users with stronger Bayesian updating and level-k reasoning abilities display larger strategic reactions. Finally, we show that simply reminding users of media slant can serve as an effective nudge to foster more strategic responses. This paper was accepted by John Beshears, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72225002, 72394393, 72225001, 72192843, 72531001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07339 .

title: Who Directs the Control Tower? Customer vs. Supplier-Managed Inventory in Supply Chains
abstract: Information distortion and incentive misalignment often undermine supply chain performance. In response, many firms adopt a “control tower” approach, whereby one party assumes responsibility for replenishment decisions across the supply chain. Industry examples showed that this role may be assigned to the customer, Customer-Managed Inventory (CMI), or to the supplier, Supplier-Managed Inventory (SMI). This paper investigates when one governance structure is preferable. We study a two-echelon, one-to-many supply chain consisting of a single supplier and a customer operating multiple warehouses. We characterize optimal base-stock policies and equilibrium holding-cost-sharing parameters under CMI and SMI and benchmark them against decentralized operations and a fully centralized system. Two primary forces shape the choice between CMI and SMI: the relative shortage penalty costs of the two parties and the structure of the customer’s distribution network. Specifically, CMI is preferred when the customer faces relatively higher shortage penalties and operates in a more asymmetric environment—for example, when demand is concentrated in a subset of its warehouses or when replenishment lead times vary substantially across these locations. In contrast, SMI is favored under opposite conditions. We further examine how intertemporal and interspatial demand correlations affect this comparison. A key finding is that, although neither CMI nor SMI achieves the first-best outcome, their efficiency loss relative to full centralization is typically small. Calibrated numerical studies based on four industry cases disentangle the incremental value of information sharing, decision-right transfer, and cost sharing, showing that most performance gains stem from decision-right transfer supported by appropriate holding-cost sharing. This paper was accepted by Jayashankar Swaminathan, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02137 .

title: Estimating the Private Value of Financial Statement Statistics
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a method for estimating the private value of knowing the future realization of some financial statistics, and then we apply the measure to the familiar ratios from the DuPont decomposition of return on equity. The estimation is grounded in the standard rational expectations model, adapted to accommodate relative risk aversion, and determines an investor's willingness to pay for information denominated in units of a riskless asset (e.g., money). The method can accommodate different levels of investable wealth, multiple assets, and any information system regarding those assets. We use this method to document several interesting contrasts. An investor with $1 million in wealth who already knows all the current DuPont ratios, as well as the most recent analyst forecast, would be willing to pay $2861 to know all of next year's ratios. This amount increases to $3158 for firms below the median size. We find that the value of financial information is higher in periods of high sentiment and for firms that are hard to value or hard to arbitrage (i.e., firms with high sentiment exposure). In practical terms, this suggests investors prioritize their information search to small, young, loss‐making, high‐growth, low book‐to‐market, non‐dividend‐paying, and illiquid firms. In terms of the DuPont components, we find that knowing next year's operating profit margin alone is worth $1226, whereas knowing next year's leverage is worth only $170 and knowing next year's sales growth is worth only $184. In practical terms, this suggests that investors allocate more attention to forecasting profitability and less attention to forecasting sales growth. Finally, we demonstrate that the estimated value of financial statistics increases substantially when we assume the investor can trade in the firm asset and can also hedge using an industry exchange‐traded fund (ETF). This result suggests that professional investors integrate their information search with their hedging behavior.

title: Interdisciplinary Theorizing I Tell You Folks, It's Harder Than It Looks
abstract: Abstract Calls for interdisciplinary scholarship are ubiquitous, but what that means and why/how it is done are more often assumed than explained. Clarifying what it takes to theorize across disciplines, why it is important and how to set the conditions for success is the point of this essay. Authors, reviewers and readers should know what interdisciplinary theorizing is, and why/how to establish its value.

title: The Effect of Lead Directors on Corporate Social Responsibility
abstract: Abstract Drawing on insights from the compromise board leadership structure theory, which posits that the presence of a lead independent director on corporate boards enables management to maintain unity of command through consolidated leadership and autonomy while also ensuring effective oversight, we theorize that this balance creates an equilibrium in which the firm is more likely to achieve stronger corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance. We further propose that improved financial flexibility serves as the economic mechanism through which the main effect operates. We also posit that these collaborative efforts are expected to contribute to superior long‐term firm performance. Additionally, we argue that women in the influential role of lead independent director bring distinctive qualities to the board that further enhance firm outcomes in this context. Our findings, robust to potential endogeneity concerns, are consistent with these propositions, underscoring the significant impact of board structure and female leadership in a key position on advancing CSR performance and firm profitability.

title: ‘If I Don't Get That Belonging Among Us It All Falls Down’: How Middle Managers Experience Belonging Through Self and Others
abstract: Abstract Belonging at work is a fundamental yet complex experience, associated with acceptance, inclusion and recognition, and underpinned by relational dynamics in organizations. Despite increasing interest, little is known about how belonging is experienced by middle managers, a group positioned between hierarchical levels and responsible for others. Drawing on 22 semi‐structured interviews and two focus groups, this paper explores this issue. The findings show that managerial belonging is structured through two interrelated orientations: self‐focused and other‐orientated. Self‐focused belonging reflects managers’ experience through organizational alignment, role legitimacy and interpersonal relationships. Other‐orientated belonging captures how managers’ own sense of belonging is shaped through their perceptions of whether those they manage belong. Rather than operating separately, these orientations are mutually constitutive, producing a recursive dynamic in which managers evaluate their own belonging through the perceived belonging of their teams. This extends the notion of double‐relationality by showing how managers’ intermediary positioning can have recursive consequences for their own belonging. The paper contributes empirically by foregrounding middle managers as a distinct group within belonging research and conceptually by showing how managerial belonging can be recursively evaluated through managers’ perceptions of the belonging of those for whom they hold responsibility.

title: Reversed conspicuousness: turning conspicuousness upside-down in luxury brands' extended services
abstract: Purpose Conspicuousness is a core concept in luxury but has hitherto been studied primarily as a signal of underlying exclusivity and quality for luxury goods. This article introduces reversed conspicuousness in extended luxury services, a process through which conspicuousness can cease to signal exclusivity and quality and instead becomes a substitute for them. Design/methodology/approach We triangulate the findings of an ethnographic study combining 33 on-site observations, a netnography of 26 sites, and 11 accompanied visits and interviews with luxury consumers of luxury brands' extended services. Findings Our findings show how conspicuousness becomes the core offering in extended services whereby an ostentatious service experience is shaped by social media, but often at the expense of exclusivity and service quality. We further identify that when conspicuousness is perceived as compensatory rather than rooted in luxury, consumers view the service as inconsistent with the luxury brand. Practical implications We identify that extended services relying on reversed conspicuousness constitute a risk for luxury brands whereby such service extensions may weaken luxury consumers' perceptions of the overall luxury brand behind the extended service. Originality/value This article extends the luxury service literature by introducing the concept of reversed conspicuousness, showing how conspicuousness shifts from signaling luxury characteristics to substituting for them in luxury brands' extended services.

title: Uncovering affordances for mutualistic value co-creation between humans and nonhuman actors: the ecocentric service ecosystems framework
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop an ecocentric perspective of service ecosystems by building on affordance theory to understand value co-creation among human and nonhuman actors and how their interactions can foster ecosystem well-being. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a qualitative approach based on the Gioia Methodology, involving 67 interviews with actors (forest and agricultural landowners, NGOs, industry, and academia representatives) related to a forest service ecosystem. Findings Study results enabled the uncovering of forest ecosystem-related affordances, revealing latent possibilities for action that enable value co-creation interactions between human and nonhuman actors, and their valence for each actor. By exploring the valence from interactions between actors, this research identifies whether these interactions are parasitic or mutualistic and systematizes four potential service ecosystem trajectories over time: thriving, recovery, decline and collapse. Originality/value Building upon study results, an Ecocentric Service Ecosystem Framework, where human and nonhuman actors are considered equal, is proposed. Using the Affordance Theory lens, this framework seeks to identify and promote mutualistic interactions between human and nonhuman actors.

title: Institutional employment protection and entrepreneurial entry: evidence from a natural experiment
Multinational dynamic capabilities: How multinational, how dynamic, how capable?
Making Sense of Change: Supervisors’ ICSR Communication as a Sensemaking Cue in Organizational Change
abstract: In contexts of continuous organizational change, employees must make sense of ambiguous and disruptive developments. Drawing on sensemaking theory, we conceptualize supervisors’ communication about internal corporate social responsibility (ICSR) as an interpretive cue that shapes employees’ perceptions of change appropriateness and, in turn, their extra-role behavior. We further argue that this process depends on three sensegiving conditions: sensegiver relationship quality, sensegiving consistency, and sensegiver motive orientation. Using multilevel data from 176 employees nested within 42 teams in a German hospital undergoing restructuring, we find that supervisors’ ICSR communication enhances employees’ perceptions of change appropriateness, which subsequently promotes extra-role behavior. Moreover, this indirect effect varies systematically across the three sensegiving conditions. By positioning ICSR communication as an interpretive cue in employees’ sensemaking of change, this study contributes to sensemaking, organizational change, and CSR research by explaining how socially responsible practices become meaningful through supervisory interactions.

title: The Many Lives of Law in the Commons: How Legislation Shapes Collaborative Engagement
abstract: While commons research has traditionally emphasized bottom-up, self-organized governance, many commons are increasingly subject to top-down institutional pressures, such as legislation. How these external pressures shape commons governance, however, remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we examine the role of legislation in infrastructure commons, where value depends not only on physical assets but also on how interdependent resources are collectively used and governed across organizational boundaries. Drawing on a qualitative case study of infrastructure commons in Australia, we identify three interrelated pathways of legislative engagement: compliance-driven, reciprocity-driven, and stewardship-driven. We theorize legislation as an enabling framework for commons governance that structures collaboration and activates multiple, co-existing engagement pathways, rather than merely constraining collective action. In doing so, we develop a mechanism-based account of how legal mandates shape collaboration in the commons, showing that legislatively driven commons governance is layered, contingent, and unevenly enacted across actors.

title: When chatbots speak local: cultural understanding as a driver of value co-creation
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how chatbot cultural understanding shapes consumer responses in online retail, focusing on perceived brand localness, consumer–brand identification and value co-creation behaviors. Guided by social identity theory, the study also examines the moderating role of consumer ethnocentrism. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a sequential mixed-methods design. Study 1 involves 15 semi-structured interviews that explore consumer perceptions of culturally intelligent chatbots. Study 2 tests the proposed model through a field study of 303 consumers recruited online and analyzed the data using structural equation modeling. Findings Chatbot cultural understanding enhances perceived brand localness, which leads to consumer–brand identification and, in turn, value co-creation behaviors. Consumer ethnocentrism does not moderate associations between chatbot cultural understanding and perceived brand localness and indirectly with value co-creation behaviors. Originality/value This research extends social identity theory to conversational AI, highlighting how culturally attuned chatbots act as cultural insiders that strengthen consumer identification and co-creation. It contributes to international marketing by demonstrating the role of cultural alignment in driving value co-creation in digital service encounters. These contributions are bounded to encounters in which international retailers actively localize chatbot communication, and the evidence is drawn from a single cross-border e-retailer operating in one collectivist emerging market.

title: The dark side of diversity management: lived experiences and everyday practices in organizations
abstract: Diversity management holds a central place in human resource management theory and practice, where it refers to the organizational handling of individual and group differences together with the structural inequality, normatively loaded discourses and legal conditions attached to it. Approaches vary in their objectives, ranging from affirmative action and human resource strategy to controlling, policy making, and marketing; and they vary in direction between a business case and a justice case. This conceptual breadth produces ambivalent effects, contradictory findings, and limited knowledge about what such practices mean for the people who work under them. Drawing on a qualitative design, this study reconstructs the meaning of diversity management from the first-person perspective. The analysis relies on forty-five in-depth interviews with stakeholders across hierarchical levels and career stages from different types and sizes of organizations. The findings show how diversity management appears either as an alienating practice drained of meaning or as a threat, and it is understood by participants to sustain the inequalities it addresses. Between the status groups, negatively biased mental representations, attribution and projection, externalization and defensiveness solidify the reverse outcomes, building up to a negative circuit; diversity management then settles into a unitarist logic that subordinates its normative objective to economic interest and undermines its original goal. The findings support a radical reassessment of current approaches, and argue for integrative and contextualized perspectives, new theorizing, and structural change.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Complementary and compensatory job resources for work engagement and innovative work behaviour
abstract: This study investigates the interplay between job resources and Information Technology (IT) employees’ work engagement and innovative work behaviour under varying levels of workload and ethical climate. Using the Differentiated Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model as a theoretical framework, the research examines how these resources interact to influence engagement, focusing on complementary and compensatory relationships. Data were collected from 377 IT professionals in India through a structured survey instrument, and hypotheses were tested using hierarchical regression analysis. The findings reveal that transformational leadership and psychological capital are positively associated with work engagement. High workloads amplify these effects, emphasising their role as challenging demands. While ethical climate amplifies the relationship between psychological capital and work engagement, it weakens the relationship between transformational leadership and work engagement. Importantly, ethical climate enhances the positive association between engagement and innovative work behaviour. Our study contributes novel insights by exploring boundary conditions that affect engagement outcomes, enriching the JD-R framework. Practically, it highlights strategies for IT managers to foster engagement through tailored resource allocation, emphasising the synergy of complementary resources and the buffering effect of compensatory ones. These findings underscore the importance of designing supportive work environments to sustain innovation at IT workplaces.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Illuminating the dark corners: a multi-level integrated framework of high-performance work systems, interpersonal deviance, and organizational deviance in the healthcare sector
abstract: The existing human resource management scholarship on deviant behavior indicates that high-performance work systems (HPWS) may inadvertently correlate with adverse employee outcomes, such as increased workloads and breaches of psychological contracts. These outcomes can subsequently fuel deviant behavior. Nevertheless, there is a paucity of multilevel insights regarding the mechanisms by which HPWS affect both interpersonal and organizational deviance. The current multilevel research is based on data from 345 medical staff nested within 226 hospitals in healthcare organizations (hospitals), which suggests that psychological contract breach and work intensification serve as mediators between HPWS and interpersonal deviance. Furthermore, the progression of interpersonal deviance to organizational deviance is moderated by servant leadership, which diminishes the upward trajectory of deviant actions inside the organization.

title: Does international collaborative R&D expand the boundaries of regional low-carbon innovation?
abstract: Amid intense market competition, this study examines how international collaborative R&D influences the boundaries of regional low-carbon innovation. Using the “Behavior-Capability-Outcome” analytical framework and provincial panel data for China’s manufacturing industry from 2012 to 2023, it further investigates the roles of regional absorptive capacity, digital industrial geographic agglomeration, and digital industrial virtual agglomeration. The results show that international collaborative R&D has an inverted U-shaped relationship with regional low-carbon innovation boundaries. Regional absorptive capacity partially mediates this relationship, while digital industrial geographic agglomeration and digital industrial virtual agglomeration flatten the inverted U-shaped curve. The effects also vary across geographic divisions and levels of environmental regulation. These findings clarify the nonlinear relationship and underlying mechanisms between international collaborative R&D and regional low-carbon innovation boundaries, providing targeted policy insights for expanding such boundaries across regions.

title: The Long and Short of It: A Warmth‐Based Explanation of the Effects of Brand Name Length on Brand Equity
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite a consensus that shorter (vs. longer) brand names positively influence consumer mindset metrics, the mechanisms driving this influence remain unclear, as does the effect of brand name length on brands' financial performance. This article helps fill these literature gaps. Drawing on four focal experiments, a follow‐up experiment, and two data sets covering 7775 real brands, the authors propose and demonstrate that shorter (vs. longer) brand names convey stronger impressions of warmth, which lead to higher brand equity, reflected in more favorable brand evaluations and stronger purchase intentions. Shorter names are also associated with more funds raised through crowdfunding. These effects emerge across various industries (e.g., clothing, food), product types (e.g., hedonic, utilitarian), brand types (e.g., unfamiliar, established), brand name types (e.g., meaningful, meaningless), and languages that use Latin or non‐Latin scripts (e.g., English, Amharic). The findings further clarify that shorter names are not necessarily more fluent; thus, ease of processing cannot always account for the positive effects of shorter brand names. The findings also show no empirical support for several additional alternative explanations, such as perceived name memorability and distinctiveness. In addition to advancing understanding of brand name length effects, this article provides guidance for crafting effective brand names.

title: EXPRESS: Forced Choices without Resolutions: A Dialectical View of Strategic Change in an Endgame Industry
abstract: Endgame industries confront firms with intensifying contradictions. Yet little is known about how such conditions shape strategic change over time. Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Software Corp., a leader in the shrinking output management industry, we develop a dialectical process model of strategic change in endgames. Using multi year field data, interviews, and internal documents, we show how firms face apories - individually plausible yet incompatible commitments - that escalate into conflicts and prompt provisional settlements. These recursive cycles of contradiction, conflict, and temporary resolution can explain how endgame strategies evolve as external positioning pressures combine with internal resource reallocation decisions. We contribute to research on declining industries by conceptualizing endgame strategy making as iterative and conflict-driven rather than fit-based. We also extend dialectical theorizing by advancing an aporetic account of strategic change that highlights the provisional and cyclical nature of action in structurally constrained contexts.

title: EXPRESS: Sustaining collective strategy through cross-level leadership: Microdynamics of managing paradoxical tensions in coopetition projects
abstract: Coopetition is a form of collective strategy in which firms collaborate to create value while competing to capture it, generating paradoxical tensions that may escalate over time. While prior research emphasizes firm-level mechanisms, it offers limited insight into how leaders across organizational levels manage these tensions. Drawing on five years of qualitative longitudinal data from innovation clusters, this study develops a model of how strategic and operational leaders manage paradoxical tensions in coopetitive projects. Under manageable tensions, top managers adopt a paradox mindset while aware of emotional ambivalence, whereas project managers adopt a paradox-separating mindset, prioritizing problem solving while blurring ambivalence. As tensions escalate, project managers elevate issues beyond their mandate, prompting top-manager engagement. Through their interplay, leaders recalibrate collaboration, enabling firm participation and sustaining collective strategy over time. These findings advance research on the microdynamics of cross-level leadership in coopetitive collective strategies while offering insights for managing coopetitive projects.

title: TikTok as a stage: How short video creators’ identity performance drives engagement with tourism experiences
abstract: Destinations are increasingly collaborating with short-form video creators to engage consumers. Through Goffman's dramaturgical lens, this study explores how creators' performed identities in travel videos relate to audience responses. Combining machine learning and AI-powered analyses of over 10k short-form videos and 176k viewer comments with a controlled experiment, we identified four identities that creators performed in these videos (the “showman,” “diarist,” “docent,” and “photographer”) and classified them at scale. Results showed that identity performance is associated with distinct configurations of audiences' behavioral engagement. The “docent” generated more audience engagement than other identities, including audiences' learning, endorsing, and intending to participate dimensions. Guided by the knowledge gap theory, a subsequent experiment showed that the “docent” identity increased engagement by sparking curiosity. These findings guide content creators in adopting effective identity performance strategies, destinations in partnering with well-aligned content creators, and platforms in using algorithmic curation to achieve desired marketing outcomes.

title: Navigating Algorithmic Fallibility: Evaluating Implementation and Guidance Strategies in AI-Augmented Service Frontlines
abstract: Despite substantial investments in collaborative human–artificial intelligence (C-AI), implementation outcomes remain mixed due to people- and leadership-based hurdles. Thematic qualitative analyses of frontline employees and their managers reveal two implementation strategies related to frontline employee empowerment and AI use guidance. Drawing on agency and cognitive evaluation theories, we conceptualize C-AI implementation as a governance design challenge. We examine how empowerment and AI use guidance shape frontline AI compliance decision-making, especially when AI fallibility manifests through incorrect recommendations. Across a large-scale experimental chat simulation involving 730 frontline employees and 6,500+ decisions in AI-assisted customer service and using hierarchical mixed-effects models, we demonstrate that outcome-control-oriented empowerment increases customer-centric decisions and reduces compliance with erroneous AI recommendations. Prescriptive guidance improves baseline decision quality by clarifying evaluative criteria but can attenuate empowerment’s protective effect by reinforcing procedural conformity. Importantly, exposure to incorrect AI recommendations significantly reduces subsequent customer-centric decisions, suggesting that algorithmic fallibility destabilizes trust and disrupts frontline employee decision calibration. Empowerment partially buffers this post-error decline, whereas prescriptive guidance exacerbates it. Collectively, the findings highlight that effective C-AI implementation requires balancing algorithmic monitoring with calibrated frontline employee discretion to sustain customer-centric outcomes.

title: Customer Relationship Management in the AI Era: A Framework for Intelligent and Ethical Service Management Systems
abstract: Customer relationship management (CRM) has progressed from a transactional, data-storage tool to a strategic, service-oriented capability for creating long-term customer value. As artificial intelligence (AI) accelerates the transformation of service systems, CRM is entering a new phase. This paper develops an integrative framework for CRM in the AI era, showing how advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), and more recently generative models (GM) and foundation models (FM), are reshaping the data, analytical, interactional, and governance foundations of CRM. We first trace CRM’s pre-AI evolution, showing how database technologies and analytical tools enabled firms to personalize marketing and manage customer equity. We then analyze how advances in ML/DL and GM/FM have reshaped four core CRM dimensions. Whereas ML/DL enhances prediction, automation, and pattern recognition, GM/FM mark a substantial shift by enabling multimodal reasoning, generative simulation, and adaptive, human-centered interaction at scale. These developments shift CRM toward an intelligent, co-creative system that learns continuously, collaborates with humans, and embeds ethical governance into its core operations. The paper concludes by outlining theoretical, methodological, and managerial implications for building AI-enabled CRM architectures that enhance empathy, transparency, trust, and responsible value co-creation, laying the foundation for future service innovation.

title: Field Philosophy: A Methodological Approach to Organizational Philosophy-in-Practice
abstract: Organizational research methods have increasingly been concerned with the relation between scholarship and practice, as part of an impact-oriented, responsible management literature. These concerns find an unexpected ally in recent developments within the field of philosophy, in which a distant and abstract relation to the field is replaced by a practice-oriented, collaboratively intense form of engagement referred to as “field philosophy.” Considered as an organizational research method, field philosophy emphasizes exchange, knowledge from below, and insider–outsider collaboration. The current article develops field philosophy for the study of organizational phenomena, illustrating this method with an empirical illustration from a field study of a carbon credit project in the Brazilian Amazon, and drawing out implications for the design and application of field philosophical methods for studying organizations.

title: When Does Digital Capability Enable Innovation Capability for Competitive Performance in an Emerging Economy? An Examination of Two Institutional Forces
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Despite growing interest in digital transformation in emerging economies, the relationships among digital capability, product innovation capability (product IC), process innovation capability (process IC), and firm performance remain insufficiently understood, especially under varying institutional conditions. The authors draw on the IT‐enabled organizational capabilities perspective, grounded in the lens of dynamic capabilities, to first develop a chain model, showing how digital capability enables product IC and process IC, two higher‐level organizational capabilities for a firm's competitive performance. The authors then integrate institutional theory to examine the roles that dysfunctional competition and government support, two institutional forces prominent in emerging economies, play in the chain model. Based on data from 241 firms in China, the findings reveal that digital capability enables product IC and process IC for stronger competitive performance. However, this chain effect is contingent on institutional context: dysfunctional competition and government support showcase distinct moderating effects on different links in the chain model. The authors discuss the results and their implications for theory and practice toward the end. Managerial Summary Firms should view digital transformation as more than a technology investment. Managers need to develop digital capability that can support innovation capability. However, the benefits of establishing and leveraging both digital and innovation capabilities are not universal. Two institutional forces, that is, dysfunctional competition and government support, common in emerging economies affect how digital capability translates into innovation capability and performance. Their effects differ across product and process innovation capabilities, suggesting that managers should consider the broader institutional context when building and leveraging different types of organizational capabilities.

title: Can Traveling Change Your Life? Testing Claims of Durable Transformation With the T-Index
abstract: Whether travel can change a person’s life is one of tourism’s oldest promises and one of its least tested claims. Research on transformative travel has relied on retrospective self-reports, which cannot distinguish durable change from the short-lived mood lift that follows any vacation. The T-index addresses this gap: built on the Day Reconstruction Method, it measures everyday quality of life before and after a travel experience, against a randomized control group in a difference-in-differences design. Applied to a 5-week itinerant nature-based physical activity journey across the Canary Islands, designed with transformative intent, it detects wellbeing improvements that persist 4 months after return, accounted for mainly by changed emotional experience within unchanged routines. For researchers, it tests transformation claims against a counterfactual; for program designers and destination managers, it offers a comparable metric separating durable impact from pleasant holidays and flagging facilitation-focused design as a hypothesis, not a lever.

title: Employment protection and firms' reliance on trade credit: international evidence
abstract: Purpose Employment protection legislation (EPL) constitutes a salient institutional source of labor adjustment rigidity, yet firms' financing responses within the supply chain remain underexplored. Drawing on financing advantage theory and operations–finance research on transaction-embedded supplier financing, this paper examines how firms' reliance on trade credit varies with major changes in EPL strictness in a large international sample. It further investigates the operational, financing, and informational mechanisms underlying this association, as well as firm- and country-level boundary conditions that moderate its strength. Design/methodology/approach Based on 315,625 firm-year observations across 29 countries during 1991–2019, this study constructs a reform-based country-year measure of major changes in EPL strictness and estimates fixed-effects panel models. The analysis further examines three mechanisms – operational rigidity, financial constraints, and information asymmetry – and investigates how firm-level characteristics and country-level institutional environments condition the association between EPL reforms and firms' reliance on trade credit. Findings The results suggest that (1) stricter EPL is associated with firms' greater reliance on trade credit; (2) this effect is intensified under greater operational rigidity, tighter financial constraints, and more severe information asymmetry; (3) at the firm level, the association is stronger for firms with weaker market power and greater growth opportunities; (4) at the country level, the association is more pronounced in countries with weaker creditor protection, higher labor unionization, lower political risk, and greater social embeddedness. Originality/value This research advances the literature on the operations–finance interface, trade credit, and employment protection by linking national labor-market regulation to firms' use of transaction-embedded supplier financing. By showing that supplier-provided trade credit becomes more salient under EPL-related labor adjustment rigidity, the study highlights an interfirm financing channel through which firms respond to labor-market institutions.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: The Effect of Ethnic Stereotypes and Evaluators’ Ethnic Identity on Funding-Worthiness: Evidence About Latinx Entrepreneurs in the United States
abstract: Abstract Despite the growing importance of entrepreneurship as a pathway to economic mobility, ethnic minority entrepreneurs continue to face persistent disadvantages in access to capital, particularly following business failure. This study examines how ethnic stereotypes and evaluators’ ethnic identity shape perceptions of funding-worthiness for Latinx entrepreneurs relative to White non-Latinx entrepreneurs in the United States. Using a full-profile conjoint experiment comprising 12,496 evaluations from 781 evaluators, we provide evidence of systematic ethnicity-based disparities in post-failure funding assessments. Latinx entrepreneurs are evaluated as less funding-worthy than White entrepreneurs, even when objective financial indicators such as the level of debt indicate comparable or lower financial risk. These findings suggest that favorable financial attributes do not fully offset ethnicity-based disadvantages in evaluations. We further show that the ethnic identity of evaluators conditions these evaluations. Shared ethnic identity does not mitigate ethnicity-based disparities in perceived funding-worthiness. Instead, Latinx evaluators evaluate Latinx entrepreneurs less favorably than White evaluators. Together, these findings show how post-failure funding evaluations are shaped by embedded ethnic hierarchies, reproducing inequality in entrepreneurial finance. By identifying how ethnic stereotypes and ethnic identity jointly influence funding assessments, this study advances research on ethnic minority entrepreneurship and contributes to business ethics scholarship by clarifying mechanisms through which systemic inequality is sustained in evaluative decision-making.

title: Does Operating Flexibility Improve Firm Investment Efficiency? Evidence from China
abstract: Employing a sample of listed Chinese firms, this study investigates whether operating flexibility improves investment efficiency. The findings indicate that greater operating flexibility improves investment efficiency. Moderation analyses further indicate that this effect is more pronounced for firms facing higher financing costs, higher credit risk, and greater environmental uncertainty. Additional tests further reveal that the efficiency gains associated with flexibility are concentrated among firms with weaker implicit government guarantees and firms headquartered in more economically developed regions. Overall, the findings identify operating flexibility as an important internal adjustment capability that helps firms improve capital allocation in emerging markets.

title: From Assemblies to Institutions and Back Again? Cycles of Democracy and Representation in the Spanish Labour Movement
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing interest in union renewal, worker voice and new forms of labour organisation, industrial relations scholarship has paid limited attention to assemblies as an organisational form in their own right. This article argues that assemblies constitute a historically recurring democratic repertoire through which workers negotiate the relationship between participation and representation, rather than a residual or transitional stage in the development of trade unionism. Drawing on a historiographical analysis of the Spanish labour movement from the early 20th century to the present, the article examines the changing role of asamblearismo (assembly‐based decision‐making) across successive political and institutional contexts. The analysis traces the evolution of assemblies from the anarcho‐syndicalist tradition of the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT), through their reconfiguration within clandestine workers' commissions under Francoism and their displacement following the institutionalisation of trade unionism after democratisation. It then examines their persistence within radical unions and social movements and their renewed prominence in labour struggles among precarious workers, where assemblies coexist with selective engagement with trade unions and formal institutions in hybrid forms of representation. The article makes three contributions to industrial relations scholarship. First, it conceptualises assemblies as workers’ organisational repertoire whose historical evolution has remained largely absent from debates on union democracy, worker representation and labour revitalisation. Second, it demonstrates that the relationship between assemblies and institutional representation is cyclical rather than linear, with participatory practices repeatedly re‐emerging when institutional arrangements struggle to accommodate new worker subjectivities and forms of employment. Third, it shows how historiographical analysis can enrich industrial relations theory by revealing the historical continuity of organisational forms frequently presented as contemporary innovations. The Spanish case, therefore, offers broader insights into the democratic foundations of worker representation under conditions of institutional change and labour market fragmentation.

title: Problem and Solution Framing in Senate Tweets: Scaling Expert Interpretation With Machine Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT Central to theories of agenda setting is the distinction between problems and solutions. Kingdon's multiple streams framework argues these processes are rhetorical and have distinct logics and incentives, yet empirical research struggles to measure them separately in digital, elite communication. Legislators bridge the multiple streams through their representational styles and legislative behavior, yet we lack scalable tools for identifying when elites frame issues as problems and when they promote solutions. This research note introduces a machine learning approach for classifying elite communication according to this core agenda‐setting distinction. We develop and validate a supervised model for 1.68 million tweets from U.S. Senators that categorizes messages into problem and solution frames, demonstrating that the problem/solution distinction can be reliably automated. This methodological research note establishes that the distinction is empirically measurable at scale and offers a validated, dataset‐specific measurement approach and theoretical foundation for classifying senatorial Twitter communication as problems or solutions.

title: Beyond Evidence: How Framing Shapes Public Health Policies During Health Crises
abstract: ABSTRACT Does the level of evidence that accompanies policy action depend on how a problem is framed, and on who frames it? This article examines these questions in the context of health crises. Bridging sociological and equivalence framing theories, it treats frames as preexisting interpretive schemes shared within communities of actors, whose downstream influence depends on the information available. Using a comprehensive textual database of COVID‐19 press conferences held in Quebec, where political decision‐makers held greater authority, and in Sweden, where scientists enjoyed more autonomy, the study combines natural language processing, OLS regressions, and Granger causality tests to analyze how frames and disclosed evidence were articulated with suppression and mitigation policies. Findings show that in Quebec, framing the pandemic as an imminent danger was associated with far‐reaching suppression measures even at low levels of disclosed evidence, while the moderate frame's association with mitigation strengthened as evidence increased. In Sweden, no relationship between framing and suppression policies appeared in public communications; framing instead operated jointly with evidence, the dangerous frame being associated with fewer mitigation references mainly at high levels of disclosed evidence. These results suggest that the relevant question is not how much evidence policy action requires, but by whom that evidence is required, and under what conditions. The evidentiary threshold attached to a frame appears to be a property of the community that carries it, with direct implications for how democratic institutions allocate influence between accountability and expertise.

title: “Clean” Meat? Regulatory Entrepreneurship and Jurisdictional Contestation in a Nascent Industry
abstract: In nascent industries, uncertainty about which regulatory agency has jurisdiction is often a major challenge for pioneering ventures. Yet, much of the literature on new ventures’ nonmarket strategy takes for granted the existence of a designated regulator. How do ventures manage regulatory jurisdictional uncertainty? We conduct an inductive, multi-case research study on how entrepreneurial organizations pioneering the nascent cell-cultivated-meat industry navigated such uncertainty in the United States between 2015 and 2019. Drawing on extensive semi-structured interviews and archival data, we uncover stratagems and processes that organizations employ across three phases of regulatory jurisdictional uncertainty: jurisdictional void, contestation, and convergence. Our resulting theoretical framework distinguishes two overarching strategies— complementary and oppositional —and unpacks their underlying mechanisms, theorizing how they enable organizations to influence jurisdictional uncertainty. Our study uniquely elucidates the rich dynamics among the disparate actors that compose nascent technology-enabled industries: new ventures, nonprofits, incumbents, investors, and regulators. More broadly, it provides a fresh perspective on how entrepreneurial organizations shape the regulatory architecture of the industries they are striving to create.

title: Unveiling the intangible: a systemic perspective for creativity and innovation in public organizations
abstract: This study examines how systemic creativity manifests empirically in the public sector using Csikszentmihalyi’s systemic model operationalized through 15 empirically grounded categories. By analyzing 60 Brazilian cases from the OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation, findings reveal that the most decisive enabling conditions are intangible: trust, psychological safety, shared purpose, and relational dynamics. A consistent pattern of frugal innovation emerges, with resource scarcity activating systemic mechanisms that substitute material resources. Theoretically, the study operationalizes an abstract model of creativity in organizational contexts. Empirically, it expands insights beyond Global North settings. Practically, it offers public managers a lens for rendering visible innovation's invisible infrastructure.

title: Strategic planning for digital technology adoption: drivers and mechanisms in the public sector
abstract: While strategic planning facilitates public sector digital transformation, it remains unclear why public sectors engage in shaping strategic plans for digital adoption. This study employs the 3Ps framework (People–Process–Plan) to construct an adapted explanatory model of these driving factors. Adopting a longitudinal case study (2019–2024), it investigates a Chinese local government’s digital anti-corruption strategizing based on 28 interviews. Findings extend the 3Ps framework by conceptualizing People as multiple stakeholders, differentiating Process into mutually evolving constructive and conflictual processes, revealing the moderating role of resource accessibility, and demonstrating the feedback effect of implementation outcomes on ongoing Strategic Plans, ultimately advancing digital strategizing from static compliance to a purposeful, dynamic closed-loop system.

title: modelscompete4 : An R Package for Comparing Nested and Non-nested Structural Equation Models
abstract: modelscompete4 is an R package for comparing nested and non-nested structural equation models (SEM). It streamlines the entire workflow by fitting a named list of model syntax strings, automatically detecting nesting relationships using parameter names and free-parameter counts, and applying the appropriate statistical test—likelihood ratio test for nested pairs and Vuong test for non-nested pairs. Unlike existing tools, it natively supports latent variables, handles any number of models simultaneously, and returns a comprehensive structured output including fit indices and a pairwise comparison matrix. Bootstrapped standard errors and parallel processing are also supported. The package is freely available on GitHub and CRAN.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Labor Market Outcomes Under State Paid Family Leave: A Multistate Analysis
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: The 150‐Year‐Old Hybrid Organization: A Historical View on Municipally Owned Corporations ( MOC ) in Sweden
abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents a 150‐year longitudinal analysis of the development of municipally owned corporations (MOCs) in Sweden, tracing their emergence in the mid‐nineteenth century, their expansion during the growth of the welfare state, and their transformation in the era of market‐oriented public sector reform. While MOCs are commonly discussed in relation to New Public Management (NPM) and contemporary forms of hybrid governance, this perspective overlooks their much longer historical trajectory. Drawing on three major Swedish government inquiries (1924, 1965, and 1982), complemented by secondary historical sources, we examine how MOCs have evolved across changing political, economic, and administrative contexts. The article conceptualizes MOCs as constitutional hybrids, organizations that combine elements of public authority and corporate governance by design, and employs insights from institutional theory and historical institutionalism to analyze their long‐term development. The findings identify three historical phases characterized by changing functions, governance rationales, and institutional expectations. Across these periods, MOCs were repeatedly reinterpreted and adapted to new circumstances while maintaining their basic organizational form. The study contributes to the literature on hybridity by demonstrating that hybridity should be understood not merely as a contemporary consequence of public sector reform, but as a historically evolving institutional condition. We argue that the enduring presence of MOCs reflects the adaptive capacity of hybrid organizational forms, whose flexibility allows them to accommodate shifting demands for efficiency, legitimacy, accountability, and public value. By historicizing hybridity, the article offers a new perspective on institutional resilience, and the long‐term evolution of public governance.

title: A Replication of “Your Money, Your Life, or Your Freedom? A Discrete Choice Experiment on Trade‐Offs During a Public Health Crisis”
abstract: ABSTRACT A prior experiment conducted in Italy examined how individuals navigate trade‐offs among money, life, and freedom during government‐mandated lockdowns. This study replicates that experiment across three Confucian societies: Shanghai (China), Singapore, and Taipei (Taiwan). The findings indicate that, in the aggregate sample, the preference pattern of “money > life > freedom” mirrors that reported in the original study. However, when analyzed separately, residents of Taipei show stronger preferences for income and freedom than their counterparts in Singapore and Shanghai. Conversely, Singaporeans demonstrate heightened concern regarding the loss of life. In addition to replicating previous findings, this study contributes to the field of comparative public administration by highlighting the importance of considering contextual nuances in the formulation of crisis‐management practices by public managers.

title: Taking artificial intelligence from the ‘priesthood’ and providing it as a service: a media-genealogical perspective on big tech’s AI platformisation
abstract: Recently, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google have been positioning artificial intelligence as a utility that should be accessible to everyone. At the same time, they promote their cloud platforms as a means of ‘democratizing’ AI as they distribute easy-to-use AI services at scale. In this article, I propose a media-genealogical approach to situate this claim of ‘democratization’ within a broader development in the infrastructuralisation and platformisation of computing. I focus on three historic moments: (1) the invention of time-sharing and the idea of a ‘computer utility’ in the 1960s; (2) the introduction of abstraction to facilitate software development in the 1970s; and (3) the rise of digital platforms and the provision of user-friendly internet services in the 2000s. I demonstrate how each of these moments of ‘democratization’ is marked by a certain duality: on the one hand, they have expanded access to information technologies through the large-scale distribution of resources and the simplification of complex technologies into services. On the other hand, they have introduced new avenues for the centralisation of power. By means of a critical discourse analysis of Google’s cloud AI platform, I show how cloud companies leverage this duality to forward a process of platformisation, where they establish themselves as the central intermediaries and transform AI technologies into services to be provided at scale. This allows them to increase dependency on their infrastructures and to exert control over technological design. The media-genealogical analysis, finally, points to alternative paths that the democratisation of AI could take.

title: Correction to : Impact of quitline services on tobacco cessation: an application of modern epidemiologic methods
Effects conditional on post-treatment events generated by independent mechanisms
abstract: In both observational studies and randomized trials, post-treatment events such as dropout, nonadherence, and truncation by death occur frequently. In some studies, conditioning on post-treatment variables is a deliberate strategy to isolate particular treatment effects on the outcome. However, naive comparisons of outcomes conditional on posttreatment events generally lack a causal interpretation, even when treatment is randomly assigned. There exist causal estimands that account for post-treatment events, including survivor average causal effects and conditional separable effects, but identification usually requires measurement of common causes of the post-treatment event and the outcome. In this article, we show that such measurements are not always necessary. Conceptually, what we require is that the treatment and other unmeasured causes of the outcome generate the post-treatment event through “independent mechanisms”. Then, conditional separable effects and survivor average causal effects can be identified without adjustment for common causes of the post-treatment event and the outcome. We illustrate the results in studies with truncating events, differential nonadherence, and the birth weight paradox.

title: Wounds that parent: Emotion regulation difficulties as pathways for the intergenerational continuity of harsh discipline
abstract: Background Harsh discipline (HD) remains common across cultural contexts and is often transmitted intergenerationally. However, the mechanisms underlying this continuity remain underexplored in non-Western contexts. Objective This study examined whether parents' recollections of maternal and paternal HD predict HD with their children, and whether emotion regulation difficulties mediate these associations. Participants and setting The sample included 467 Egyptian parents aged 23–62 years ( M = 37.76, SD = 5.78), and each reported on one child aged 2 to 12.4 years ( M = 7.73, SD = 2.95). Methods Participants completed the Recollection of Parental Harsh Discipline Scale (PHDS), Child Harsh Discipline Scale (CHDS), and Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS-16). Mediation analyses examined both the DERS-16 total score and individual DERS subscale scores using PROCESS (Model 4) with 5000 bootstrapped samples, controlling for parent age, gender, child age, and intention to parent differently from one's parents. Results The DERS-16 total score partially mediated both associations (maternal indirect effect = 0.04, 95% CI [0.02, 0.07]; paternal indirect effect = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.06]). In parallel mediation models, only impulse control difficulties, a DERS subdimension, significantly mediated the maternal HD-child HD association (indirect effect = 0.02, 95% CI [0.002, 0.05]); all other subdimension effects, including those in the paternal model, were nonsignificant. Conclusions Findings identify overall emotion regulation difficulties and impulse control difficulties as pathways through which HD may be transmitted across generations, highlighting the need for culturally informed interventions targeting caregiver regulatory capacity.

title: Poverty, Neglect, and Socioemotional Outcomes: An Examination of Child Care as a Promotive and Protective Factor
abstract: According to the family stress model (FSM), poverty increases parent's psychological distress and maladaptive parenting behaviors, which contribute to children's behavioral difficulties. Poverty is one of the strongest predictors of neglect, but there is less evidence of neglect as a mediator in the FSM. Most families in poverty do not engage in neglect and some children exposed to poverty demonstrate adaptive socioemotional outcomes. One way to enable child and family well-being could be access to child care, but there remain questions regarding its benefits. This study examined associations between poverty and children's socioemotional development via parental psychological distress and neglect and the promotive and protective effects of child care. Lower income-to-needs at birth was associated with more depressive symptoms at year 1. Depressive symptoms and parenting stress at year 1 were related to more neglect at year 3, which was differentially related to socioemotional outcomes at year 5. We found promotive effects of child care at year 1 with lower levels of neglect and protective effects of child care at year 3 for socioemotional development. Our findings suggest the importance of neglect prevention and increasing child care access (e.g., universal preK or means-tested programs) for supporting families impacted by poverty.

title: Urban–Rural Workforce Study in Pennsylvania Child Welfare
abstract: Using data from a statewide cross-sectional survey of Pennsylvania child welfare caseworkers, this study examined job demands, job resources, and intent to leave across rural and urban contexts. Guided by the Job Demands-Resources framework, analyses focused on caseloads, workload, service capacity, organizational resources, flexibility, court-related work, recognition, salary/benefits satisfaction, and turnover intention. A total of 712 caseworkers initiated the survey; rural/urban agency classification was available for 670 respondents. Rural and urban respondents did not differ significantly in caseload or intent to leave, but rural respondents reported higher satisfaction with flexibility and court-related work. In rural/urban correlation analyses, service capacity was negatively associated with intent to leave among rural caseworkers but not among urban caseworkers. Benefits satisfaction was negatively associated with intent to leave in both groups, with a stronger negative association among rural respondents. In the adjusted logistic regression model, workload satisfaction and organizational resources were negatively associated with having considered leaving, while public county employment was associated with higher odds of having considered leaving compared with private provider employment. Findings suggest both shared and context-specific workforce concerns: retention strategies should strengthen workload manageability and organizational resources across settings while attending to rural-specific concerns related to service capacity and benefits.

title: Shanghai Mundane: Survival and Revival of Bourgeois Sentiments under Chinese Socialism Lei Ping. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2025. 336 pp. £95.00 ISBN 9781666951387
From human touch to aI-based self-service: antecedents of business users’ switching intention in government-to-business services
abstract: Governments are increasingly deploying AI-based self-service technologies (AI-based SSTs) to improve government-to-business (G2B) services, yet little is known about why business users switch from human-assisted G2B services to AI-based SSTs. Drawing on the push–pull–mooring (PPM) framework, this study examines how negative incumbent service experiences, perceived benefits of AI-based SSTs, and status quo biases jointly shape switching intention. Using survey data from 461 business users in Chinese government service agencies and PLS-SEM, we find that perceived intelligence, shaped by responsiveness, personalization, and autonomy, together with physical attractiveness, procedural fairness, and structural assurance, generates pull effects toward AI-based SSTs. Switching costs, habit, and desire for human interaction strengthen inertia, which directly reduces switching intention and weakens the effects of both push and pull factors. The study extends the PPM framework to digital government service delivery and offers guidance for reducing inertia and promoting migration to AI-enabled self-service channels.

title: Merit, autonomy, and corruption: the moderating role of anti-corruption institutions in Africa
abstract: This study examines how merit appointments and bureaucratic autonomy influence corruption in African governments, and whether the independence and capability of anti-corruption institutions condition these relationships. Using two-way fixed effects regression to analyze a panel of 486 African countries from 2013–2021, we find that bureaucratic autonomy is negatively associated with corruption, while the relationship between merit appointments and corruption depends on the capability of anti-corruption institutions: where such institutions lack the capability to hold politicians and bureaucrats accountable, merit appointments are positively associated with corruption; as the capability of anti-corruption institutions increases, this relationship weakens and can eventually reverse. Neither the independence nor the capability of anti-corruption institutions is independently associated with corruption. These findings suggest that professionalizing civil service hiring without corresponding investments to bolster the capability of anti-corruption institutions can backfire and point to the conditions under which anti-corruption reforms are likely to succeed.

title: Building tolerance through experience: administrative engagement and burden tolerance across four countries
abstract: Research on burden tolerance suggests that people who previously faced burdens tend to be less accepting of administrative burdens more generally. However, the empirical focus has been on program-specific burdens and in particular social welfare programs. Thus, it remains an open question whether and how more general, everyday engagement with administrative tasks—and the emotional experiences involved—may influence burden tolerance. To better understand the relationship between administrative engagement, emotions, and burden tolerance, we survey residents in the United States, Mexico, the United Kingdom, and Denmark. We find that frequent engagement with administrative tasks is positively associated with burden tolerance in all countries, except Denmark, and that residents with more positive emotional experiences tend to be more tolerant of burdens. While correlational, we interpret these findings as suggesting that engagement with everyday administrative tasks builds capability for managing administrative burdens, which in turn fosters burden tolerance.

title: Assessing the global viability of solid gravity storage in decentralized hybrid microgrids
Deliverability matters? Modeling capacity and energy market equilibrium under PJM-inspired framework
Computational design of water splitting electrocatalysts: From d-band center to machine learning descriptors
Corridor-scale coupling of stochastic passenger EV charging demand and photovoltaic power supply at expressway service areas
abstract: Expressway service areas have become corridor-scale hotspots of passenger electric vehicle (EV) charging demand under transport electrification, while their coordination with distributed photovoltaic (PV) supply remains insufficiently quantified at the corridor level. This study develops a coupled assessment framework that integrates stochastic passenger EV charging demand with PV power supply across consecutive expressway service areas. A Monte Carlo-implemented Markov state-transition framework is used to simulate passenger EV state evolution and charging decisions, with key behavioral parameters informed by 102 valid questionnaire responses from passenger EV users. PV deployment potential is evaluated under rooftop, parking-area, and roadside deployment configurations. A case study of 26 service areas along the Gansu section of the G30 Lianhuo Expressway is conducted. The results reveal distinct corridor-scale heterogeneity in passenger EV charging demand. Under the baseline scenario, charging probability ranges from 0.08 to 0.29 in the east-to-west direction and from 0.07 to 0.26 in the west-to-east direction, while the average energy replenished per charging vehicle remains relatively stable within 46.89–54.81 kWh. Daily charging demand varies from 27.5 to 56.2 MWh/day across service areas and is strongly associated with the cumulative distance to adjacent service areas ( R 2 = 0.799, p < 0.001). Sensitivity analysis identifies the maximum available driving range ( R max ) as the dominant parameter affecting corridor-scale charging behavior. Optimal tilt-angle PV deployment reduces the required installed capacity to 4.94–11.67 MW, with an average capacity reduction of 14.5% compared with horizontal-angle deployment. However, rooftop and parking-area PV resources alone are constrained by available built-environment space, requiring supplementary roadside PV deployment of 168–837 m at several service areas. Economic and carbon-reduction assessments show that optimal tilt-angle deployment yields average annual return ratios of 5.09%–9.50% and cumulative CO₂ emission reductions of 137–281 kt over a 25-year lifecycle. The proposed framework provides quantitative support for coordinating passenger EV charging infrastructure with distributed PV deployment at expressway service areas.

title: A comprehensive review on accurate numerical simulation of proton exchange membrane fuel cell
abstract: PEMFCs involve strongly coupled electrochemical reactions and transport processes of gas, water, charge, and heat. Numerical simulation is therefore an important tool for understanding internal transport phenomena, predicting performance, and supporting PEMFC design and operation. This structured narrative review synthesizes representative PEMFC numerical-simulation studies identified primarily through topic-specific manual searches of the Web of Science database. While many earlier reviews focus on individual processes, components, scales, or modeling routes, the present review connects numerical models from the MEA to macro-scale and multi-scale single-cell models, stack models, operational-process models, system temperature-control models, and efficient-study models based on artificial intelligence and similarity theory. The principal modeling approaches are compared in terms of their physical descriptions, applicable scales, computational costs, validation approaches, and suitable applications. The review shows multi-physics and multiscale models are essential for resolving coupled internal processes, but their effectiveness is constrained by uncertain transport and kinetic parameters, coupling methodology between scales, limited validation data for local physical fields, and high computational cost for large stacks. AI-assisted and reduced-order approaches can improve computational efficiency, but their prediction capability and applicable scale require further development. The review provides a structured summary and outlooks for selecting and improving PEMFC numerical models.

title: A transient equivalent circuit model of lithium-ion batteries for the external short circuit fault in BESS
abstract: The external short circuit (ESC) fault can cause large current within a short period of time, potentially resulting in serious accidents in battery energy storage stations (BESS). However, the transient behavior of BESS under ESC faults remain insufficiently understood, which hinders the development of precise protection strategies.
