These findings are often interpreted as evidence of sentiment‐driven mispricing, but such conclusions depend on assumptions about how investors form, process, and revise beliefs. This survey re‐evaluates the literature through a mechanism‐based framework that distinguishes between competing channels of belief formation, including non‐fundamental demand, biased beliefs, rational information aggregation, attention and salience, and feedback effects. We show that similar empirical regularities can arise from fundamentally different economic mechanisms and therefore require careful theoretical interpretation. The survey clarifies the role of machine‐learning‐based sentiment measures, highlights the limits of interpreting predictability as market inefficiency, and provides a framework for linking sentiment evidence to coherent asset‐pricing models.

title: Shock spillovers and international financial (dis)integration
abstract: Global shocks - ranging from climate-related disasters and geopolitical conáicts to pandemics - transmit rapidly across borders and shape Önancial market co-movements. This paper develops a two-country general equilibrium model to study how cross-border shock spillovers a§ect optimal international portfolio holdings and the degree of Önancial (dis)integration. The analysis highlights that both the magnitude and heterogeneity of spillovers across income sources (capital versus labour income) play a central role in determining international risk-sharing opportunities. When spillovers mainly a§ect capital income, countries reduce their foreign asset positions and markets become more segmented. By contrast, when labour-income spillovers dominate, Önancial integration strengthens. The model generates empirical implications regarding the relation between global shocks, international portfolio rebalancing, and time-varying degrees of Önancial integration, providing a structural framework that can help interpret recent episodes of global Önancial fragmentation.
journal_name: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money

title: Not all apples fall close to the tree: survival of pushed spin-offs from Danish shipyards
abstract: This exploratory study investigates the survival and exit of pushed spin-offs created during industrial decline. Drawing on the resource-based view, we examine how configurations of VRIO resources and diversification relative to the parent firm’s main activity shape the survival of incumbent-created and employee-created spin-offs. Using unique, hand-collected, multi-source data on pushed spin-offs from the Danish shipbuilding industry from 1980 to 2015, we analyse survival paths through crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (csQCA). We find that incumbent-created spin-offs survive when they diversify away from the parent’s main activity, regardless of whether they possess VRIO resources. In contrast, employee-created spin-offs survive when they combine diversification with VRIO resources. We conclude that diversification is a central driver of pushed spin-offs’ survival, but that its effect depends on the founding actors and inherited resources. The study shows that pushed spin-offs are heterogeneous and survive through different configurations of founding actors, inherited resources, and diversification strategies.

title: ‘Save the banks or save the planet?’: governing through strategic ambiguity in EU sustainability-related banking regulation
abstract: The literature remains divided on whether sustainability-related financial ­governance has shifted from a narrow risk-based approach to a stronger focus on transition pathways, and whether the currently dominant approach has the potential to redirect credit away from high-carbon investments toward greener sectors. Building on a strategic-relational approach and the concept of ­strategic ambiguity, as well as insights from 30 expert interviews, documentary analysis, and three public consultations, we argue that the introduction of the current sustainability-related financial policy approach in the EU was conditioned on an ambiguously framed risk narrative. By reconstructing the policy process, we suggest that while strategic ambiguity initially helped to preserve an element of credit steering, it ultimately hampered its full institutionalization. Thus, we conclude that the current policy approach neither constitutes a simple ­continuation of existing prudential approaches nor marks a substantial ­divergence from them, i.e., allocative policies. While we contend that the ­dominant approach has shifted toward a stronger focus on transition ­pathways, we suggest that it represents an unbalanced mediation of stakeholders’ ­interests, which also limits its allocative potential.

title: Buying cooperation: financial inducements and the reconstruction of relations between major powers
abstract: Creditor states have used financial inducements in an attempt to influence the security and foreign policies of their indebted peers for centuries. We examine when inducements are effective and whether they can promote cooperation. Analysis of three cases involving major powers – the United Kingdom’s use of cheap capital to help secure a favorable peace treaty with the United States (1871–1872), the United States’ unsuccessful offer of a reconstruction loan to the Soviet Union (1943–1946), and West Germany’s offers of loans to the Soviet Union to enhance post-Cold War cooperation (1989–1990) – illuminates the viability and relational effects of financial inducements. We argue that success depended on the confluence of facilitating conditions – target states facing serious financial challenges that require external financing, the absence of other suitable creditors, and a low risk of future conflict and cheating. Our research also highlights the importance of second order effects. Financial inducements can help to facilitate the reconstruction of major power relations in more cooperative terms.

title: Economic theory and political action: “labour is the source of all wealth” in chartist thought
abstract: This paper explores the intellectual sources and uses of the idea that “labour is the source of all wealth” during the Chartist movement. Having established the centrality of the idea (and its various manifestations) within the language of Chartism, the paper finds that reformers often turned to Locke, Smith, J.R. McCulloch and, to a lesser extent, Ricardo for intellectual validation – using their ideas in ways not originally intended by the theorists they cited. Interestingly, reformers used the idea both as a coherent statement of working-class consciousness to unite labourers against their employers; and as a continuation of the radical position that separated the “industrious” (both labourers and their employers) from the “idlers” (landowners and political elites). “Labour is the source of all wealth” provided a versatile rhetorical framework that accommodated diverse interests within a movement characterised by complexity, internal tensions, and ideological heterogeneity.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: How Can We Research Social Mobility in Entrepreneurship?
abstract: Social mobility is a central concern in contemporary societies, yet its dynamics within entrepreneurship remain insufficiently understood. This paper’s purpose is to facilitate research on entrepreneurial social mobility by making three key contributions: first, we examine the distinct conceptual and methodological challenges related to capturing social mobility in entrepreneurship and provide strategies for solving them; second, we introduce multidimensional social mobility measures that move beyond the predominant focus on income-based metrics in existing quantitative research; third, we demonstrate how alternative quantitative and qualitative methods can produce more holistic evidence for understanding social mobility among entrepreneurs.

title: Between Play and Reason: Integrating Sensible Foolishness Into Strategy‐Making Workshops
abstract: Abstract Sensible foolishness through play can offer a valuable escape from prevailing dogmas and rational models of intelligence, affording actors freedom to explore, imagine, and create without constraint. Yet the value of sensible foolishness, and the vital interplay between play and reason, remains underexplored in strategy scholarship. Drawing on a qualitative experimental study of three SMEs, we examine how high‐stakes strategic challenges can be addressed through sensible foolishness. Our analysis shows how the interplay between play and reason gains generative momentum during strategy‐making workshops, as actors co‐create playful atmospheres and shift into more expressive, embodied ways of being. We identify three transitional modes – deliberate , dialectical , and dwelling – through which actors integrate play and reason and co‐produce moments of strategic insight and value. We develop a process theory of integrating sensible foolishness into strategy‐making, showing how attuned facilitation and atmospheric shifts enable its enactment as a collective, affectively sustained mode of strategizing. This extends debates in strategy and serious play scholarship by advancing a practice‐based view of sensible foolishness as a complementary instrument of collective strategic intelligence.

title: Startup multihoming in enterprise software ecosystems: The role of skill breadth and organizational learning
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We investigate startup decisions to multihome to another platform. We develop a theory that shows startup engagement with the initial platform leads first to exploratory learning and later a shift toward exploitation, leading to an inverted U‐shape relationship between duration of platform partnership and the likelihood of multihoming. This tradeoff is shaped by the breadth of the startup's skill base. Startups with a broader set of skills initially face slower learning, but over time skill breadth provides greater adaptability that better positions them for multihoming. We test our theory using a novel dataset on SAP partners' multihoming decisions, examining the implications of Oracle acquisitions that increased the expected benefits of multihoming. Our empirical findings are consistent with our hypotheses. Managerial Summary The growth phase forms an important part of any startup's evolution, particularly when engaging with digital platform ecosystems, where expansion often depends on the ability to multihome. Startups' accumulated experience with a platform shapes how they respond when opportunities to expand to another platform arise. Startups with moderate levels of prior platform experience are most likely to expand, while longer relationships can create dependencies that reduce flexibility. Importantly, the breadth of a startup's skill base changes this trajectory. Startups with diverse skills are better able to avoid lock‐in and remain flexible, even after long partnerships. Evidence from the enterprise software ecosystem shows managers should see platform partnerships as both opportunity and risk, investing in broad skill sets to balance deep collaboration with the ability to grow across platforms.

title: Partisanship, Information, and Punishment for Misconduct at Work
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether firms apply partisan standards when responding to employee financial misconduct. Using detailed individual‐level data on financial advisers, we find that advisers who are in the political minority at their firm (political minority advisers) are no different from their colleagues at the same firm and time in the incidence and severity of misconduct, yet following misconduct, they are significantly more likely to depart—a pattern we term “partisan punishment standards.” This pattern is especially pronounced at firms with lower internal information quality (IIQ), proxied with (1) lower external reporting quality (for public firms only), (2) private firms (relative to public firms), and (3) not hiring an independent public accountant to create an internal control report (for both public and private firms). We also document “partisan reporting standards”: Firms are more likely to publicly disclose misconduct by political minority advisers while remaining relatively silent in other cases. Firms that exhibit partisan punishment practices subsequently experience slower growth.

title: Impact of Short-Form Videos on Screentime and Sleep: Evidence from TikTok
abstract: Short-form video platforms have become central to debates about digital overuse and sleep disruption, yet causal evidence on their behavioral impacts remains limited. We study the effects of adopting short-form video in the context of TikTok, which pioneered the format and accounts for a large share of global short-form video consumption. Using granular smartphone touchstream data from a large opt-in panel of U.S. Android users, we track app usage, screen time, and inferred sleep behavior before and after TikTok adoption. We employ a difference-in-differences framework leveraging a high-frequency app usage data set from nearly 7,000 TikTok adopters. Our findings reveal a significant increase in overall screen time—averaging 221 minutes per week for heavy TikTok users—following TikTok adoption, alongside notable declines in usage of other social media and gaming apps, suggesting a strong substitution effect. The screen time effects are highest during late night hours. We also observe shifts in sleep patterns, including delayed bedtimes and a moderate reduction in sleep duration, among high-intensity users. We observe no effects for low-intensity users, who engage minimally with TikTok postadoption. Our findings show that short-form video adoption expands total digital attention rather than merely reallocating it, with important implications for platform design, regulation, and digital well-being. As a side result, our analysis provides clear evidence of substitutability between TikTok and traditional social media platforms, which has important implications for competition policy. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08260 .

title: Data-Driven Population Tracking in Service Systems
abstract: Motivated by an application at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport, we consider a service system in which a manager aims to track the number of people in the system based only on noisy observations of arrivals and departures over a time horizon. We study two tracking problems in this context. In the busyness tracking problem, the manager seeks to determine whether the system is busy or not, whereas in the population tracking problem, the manager tracks the number of people in the system and accumulates losses as squared errors. We characterize the cumulative losses of various policies in an asymptotic regime in which the time horizon grows large. We prove general lower bounds on the cumulative loss of any policy and propose relatively simple policies that achieve these lower bounds, up to logarithmic terms. These policies outperform naive tracking policies in many instances. Finally, we characterize the impact of having the ability to periodically inspect the system at a cost. We find that effective population tracking policies take opportunities to reset the population count to accurate estimates to stop the accumulation of error. Without inspections, this is achieved by resetting the population count to zero when a near-empty system is detected based on observing the departure stream. Inspections, although coming at a cost, allow for greater flexibility in the timing of corrections and, hence, improved performance. We demonstrate the performance of our policies using real-world data we collected by installing people-counting sensors at the airport. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: Financial support from the Triangle Impact Challenge 2021 is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05152 .

title: Growing sentimental value through object usage
abstract: Abstract Consumers often protect their sentimentally valuable possessions by storing them away, which precludes them from being used. Across five studies, we show that usage of sentimentally valuable objects increases their sentimental value. Process evidence suggests one reason this happens: Repeatedly using a sentimentally valuable object makes the association held by the object (i.e., the source of its sentimental value) salient more frequently. This leads one to believe that such an association is more closely integrated into their self‐concept, which cyclically enhances the sentimental value of the object. We conclude by discussing the contribution of these findings to the literature, providing recommendations to marketers and consumers, and elaborating on directions for future research.

title: Turning Participation into Durable Organizational Capability
abstract: Leaders increasingly open strategy processes to employees, yet many participatory initiatives fail to change how work gets done. This study examines how a bounded open-strategy intervention contributes to capability renewal during strategic transitions. Drawing on a three-year case study of a European SaaS scale-up, we identify three mechanisms through which participation becomes consequential: cross-functional triangulation, authorship legitimacy, and distributed translation. Together, these mechanisms explain how participation reshapes coordination beyond the intervention itself and how capability renewal is accomplished in practice through a designed participatory process rather than top-down redesign alone. We translate these findings into RESET, a practical framework for designing open-strategy interventions that build capability rather than symbolic engagement. Discipline strategy (18)

title: Bridging Open Strategy Research and Managerial Practice
abstract: Open strategy has grown from an initial empirical observation of more participatory and transparent strategy making into a thriving stream of research. However, academic insights are rarely translated into concrete managerial guidance. The articles in this special issue of CMR bridge research on open strategy and managerial practice. They focus on deepening and broadening existing academic debates, while providing managerial guidance. In this introduction, we distill their contributions into a 5P framework—purpose, parameters, people, processing, and proof—offering managers key practical questions for designing and managing open strategy processes.

title: Beyond Transparency: Governing Visibility–Opacity Tensions in Circular Supply Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT Circular supply chains are widely promoted as mechanisms of environmental regeneration, yet they generate a fundamental and underexplored operational tension: The same processes that require high levels of material transparency also create strong incentives for strategic information concealment. Circular supply chain research has predominantly emphasized the benefits of transparency and traceability, while adjacent research on alliances, coopetition, and knowledge protection recognizes that firms must also protect commercially sensitive information. What remains insufficiently explained is how this sharing–protection tension becomes embedded in circular supply chain operations, where the same lifecycle and recovery information can be simultaneously necessary for coordination and commercially appropriate. To address this gap, this study examines how firms manage the visibility–opacity tension through operational supply chain management (OSCM) processes. Drawing on a qualitative multiple‐case study of 32 US manufacturing firms and approximately 80 semistructured interviews, we identify three distinct tension‐management logics. Selective disclosure sequencing governs the timing and recipients of information across the partner lifecycle. Boundary‐anchored opacity recurrently reproduces comparatively stable information boundaries through institutionalized access restrictions. Adaptive transparency recalibration involves ongoing adjustment of disclosure practices in response to changing market and regulatory conditions. Collectively, these logics reveal distinct operational implications and trade‐offs that informants associate with different forms of visibility–opacity governance, particularly regarding coordination, protection of commercially sensitive knowledge, and responsiveness to changing conditions. These implications are interpreted as perceived process‐level consequences rather than independently measured performance effects. The study reconceptualizes transparency not as a governance target to be maximized, but as a boundary to be actively managed. For managers, the findings provide guidance on configuring disclosure practices to balance coordination needs with competitive protection. By theorizing disclosure as a processually governed boundary rather than a transparency outcome, this study shifts the information governance problem in circular supply chains from visibility maximization to boundary management.

title: Sustainability Tensions in Food Q‐Commerce Logistics: A Paradox Theory Perspective From a Developing Country
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates key barriers to the environmental, social, and economic sustainability of food quick commerce (Q‐commerce) logistics, using Iran as a representative emerging economy. This study is timely because it examines a rapidly evolving form of urban logistics in which speed, convenience, and sustainability are increasingly in tension, particularly in emerging‐market contexts where these trade‐offs remain insufficiently understood. We adopt a multi‐method approach: first, synthesizing a comprehensive set of challenges across the triple bottom line (TBL) through a literature review and expert consultations; second, applying the content validity ratio (CVR) to screen and retain the most critical factors; and third, using a hybrid stepwise weight assessment ratio analysis (SWARA)–importance–performance analysis (IPA) framework to prioritize 23 barriers based on their perceived importance and current performance. The analysis highlights six “Concentrate here” barriers: shortage of sustainable delivery vehicles; inequitable delivery access; reliance on single‐use packaging; weak enforcement of consumer protection laws; inefficient, frequent small‐quantity deliveries; and precarious gig‐worker conditions. Interpreted through a paradox theory lens, these barriers reflect persistent and interdependent tensions rather than isolated operational gaps, suggesting that sustainability in Q‐commerce requires differentiated and coordinated responses rather than one‐size‐fits‐all solutions. We propose targeted interventions and outline how these insights can inform sustainable Q‐commerce models in other emerging markets.

title: When employees bully their managers: upward bullying victimization in hotels workplaces
abstract: Purpose Upward bullying victimization remains a relatively underexplored phenomenon within the hotel sector. This study aims to investigate the experiences of upward bullying victimization directed at hotel managers and the factors contributing to this phenomenon. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on face-to-face semi-structured qualitative interviews with 21 hotel managers from 14 four- or five-star hotels, the authors identify manifestations and factors of upward bullying victimization. Organizational justice theory (OJT) and affective events theory (AET) serve as complementary lenses. Findings The analysis identifies seven key factors associated with upward bullying episodes among hotel managers: organizational change, leadership transition, unmet employee demands, managerial style, leader favouritism, career envy and unresolved employee trauma. Furthermore, the findings reveal that employees engage in observable behaviours (e.g. coalition-forming, gossiping, service withdrawal) against managers, suggesting that managers may be constrained from disciplining employees without risking service failure − thus potentially reframing traditional power dynamics within an upward bullying paradigm. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of enhancing awareness of the upward bullying phenomenon among hospitality practitioners and HR professionals. These findings can inform the development of confidential reporting channels, policies, training, operational support, transparent procedures and managerial onboarding. Originality/value This study develops a context-specific framework to understand upward bullying dynamics in hotels, highlighting managers as potential targets. Its originality lies in distinguishing key factors from observable manifestations and integrating OJT and AET to interpret hotel managers’ accounts.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Framing sustainability in luxury hotels: impact or commitment?
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how luxury hotels should frame sustainability narratives by comparing achieved environmental impact with future sustainability commitments. This study examines their effects on willingness to stay (WTS), with perceived hedonic value (HV) and hotel integrity (HI) as mediators and message abstraction and greenwashing risk as moderators. Design/methodology/approach Two online experiments using scenarios describing a fictitious luxury hotel were conducted. Study 1 (n = 329) used a 2 × 2 design with sustainability message framing (achieved impact vs future commitment) and message type (concrete vs abstract) manipulated. HV and HI were examined as mediating mechanism. Study 2 (n = 233) examined the moderating role of greenwashing risk (high vs low) on the effects of message framing through HI. Findings Study 1 showed that impact-based framing increased WTS through higher HV, particularly when the message was abstract. Message type did not influence the HI pathway. Study 2 showed that when greenwashing risk was high, impact framing strengthened HI and, in turn, WTS. Practical implications Luxury hotels should focus on verifiable outcomes already achieved when communicating their sustainability efforts. This becomes particularly important when greenwashing risk is salient. Impact-based framing helps preserve anticipated HV. Also, evidence of achieved outcomes can strengthen perceptions of HI when sustainability claims are questioned. Originality/value This study extends attribution theory and construal level theory by showing that sustainability messages influence consumers through distinct psychological mechanisms.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Cosmopolitanism in the digital age: cultural capital and digital contestation in the Mexican context
abstract: Purpose This study examines consumer cosmopolitanism as a socially enacted performance to explore how privileged Mexican consumers, commonly referred to as whitexicans, perform cosmopolitanism as cultural capital and how these performances are contested within the digital community Cosas de Whitexicans. Design/methodology/approach A non-participatory netnography was conducted on 184 selected posts and approximately 2,200 comments from the Facebook community Cosas de Whitexicans (July 2023–June 2025). The data were analyzed using thematic analysis based on cultural capital and symbolic boundary frameworks. Findings The findings identify two interrelated dimensions structuring cosmopolitan consumption in digital contexts: the level of cultural capital mobilization (surface-level and immersive cosmopolitanism) and the intensity of symbolic boundary contestation (mocking and criticizing). These dynamics demonstrate that cosmopolitanism serves as both a resource for distinction and a contested identity within digitally mediated fields. Originality/value The study advances international marketing research by repositioning consumer cosmopolitanism as a relational and performative phenomenon embedded in cultural capital. By integrating symbolic boundary theory and digital mediation, it shows how claims to cosmopolitan status are publicly evaluated and challenged in emerging-market contexts marked by historical inequalities.

title: Cultural dynamics in expatriate psychological contracts: unpacking spillover effects in the breach-violation relationship
abstract: Expatriates work in multi-party settings with concurrent psychological contracts with both home and host organizations. Prior research indicates that a psychological contract breach by one party can lead to a negative emotional response toward the other. The present study builds on the sensemaking perspective in psychological contract theory to theorize that such spillover is not universal. Instead, we propose that it depends on the interaction between the degree of cultural difference between the home and host organization and expatriates’ cultural intelligence, i.e., their ability to interpret and make sense of these cultural differences. Drawing on primary data from a two-wave study with 221 expatriates, we find that cultural distance moderates the spillover effect of psychological contract breach by the host organization on the psychological contract violation toward the home organization. We find that high cultural distance neutralizes this spillover effect. Moreover, this neutralizing effect of cultural distance is stronger among expatriates with low cultural intelligence. As such, under conditions of high cultural distance, psychological contract breach by the host organization is less likely to translate into psychological contract violation toward the home organization when cultural intelligence is low (a three-way interaction). Our findings have important implications for PC theory and the management of expatriate assignments.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Crowded home: Competitive positioning, internationalization, and firm performance
abstract: Prior literature has long established that firm performance depends on competitive positioning. While plausible, most studies on competitive positioning conceptualize that firms compete within a single, bounded marketspace (e.g., a country or industry). This approach, however, downplays firms' heterogeneous market expansion, which can largely reshape the returns to competitive positioning. To underscore the important role of market expansion, we specifically examine how firms' international expansion moderates the relationship between competitive similarity and performance. Analyzing a large sample of US firms from 1997 to 2017, we find support for our core claim: The adverse impact of competitive similarity on firm performance is alleviated when a firm has a greater level of international presence. We further observe that the negative impact is mitigated (albeit more marginally) when a firm's competitors are more international. These findings make important contributions to research on competitive positioning and international business.

title: Reputational spillovers within audit firm networks – evidence from the Wirecard scandal
abstract: This study examines whether reputational damage from a large-scale accounting scandal spills over within international audit firm networks. Prior research mainly studies reputational losses for the national audit firm. We extend this literature by examining whether reputational damage also affects network affiliates in other countries, whether proximity to the scandal matters, and whether affected affiliates respond through reputation repair. Using EY Germany’s involvement in the Wirecard scandal, we find negative stock market reactions for EY clients not only in Germany but also in other European countries. We also document audit market effects: EY Germany loses clients and gains no new listed clients after the scandal, while EY’s other European affiliates face difficulties attracting new clients, especially in countries bordering Germany. Finally, we find evidence consistent with reputation repair among EY’s European affiliates after the scandal. Overall, our findings show that legal independence does not fully shield audit firm network affiliates from cross-border reputational spillovers.

title: Cognitive processing of nonverbal cues in earnings conference calls: The association between CEO vocal emotion and stock market reactions
abstract: As important nonverbal cues, CEO vocal emotion in earnings conference calls conveys incremental information about firms. This study investigates the association between CEO vocal emotion and stock market reactions from the perspective of investor cognitive processing. Particularly, speech emotion recognition techniques are applied to measure CEO vocal valence and arousal in the two-dimensional emotion space and determine the dynamic emotion reversals. Based on a large panel dataset, we conduct various empirical tests and robustness checks to find that CEO vocal valence in earnings conference calls is positively associated with corporate cumulative abnormal returns over the next two trading days. CEO vocal arousal nonlinearly moderates this association, which is strongest at medium levels of arousal. Furthermore, a high frequency of emotion reversals strengthens the main association. This study provides in-depth insights into the role of CEO vocal emotion in market, and the validation of boundary conditions sheds light on mechanism exploration.

title: Product social currency: Conceptualization, measurement and nomological validity
abstract: The marketplace increasingly values products that function as social currency, yet the existing literature lacks a blueprint for understanding the attributes that characterize these products. Product social currency (PSC) refers to a socially constructed symbolic resource derived from consumers’ perceptions that a product’s concrete attributes and consumption experiences provide conversational value and facilitate self-expression and social expression. Using a mixed-methods approach, we first identified these three dimensions through qualitative research guided by grounded theory and then developed and validated a 12-item Product Social Currency Scale across diverse samples (N = 2,672). The scale demonstrated strong reliability, construct, and predictive and incremental validity for consumer brand engagement, purchase intention, and satisfaction. PSC also predicted word-of-mouth within a broader nomological network. These findings clarify social currency at the product level, distinguish PSC from brand social currency, and provide a practical tool for product development and marketing strategy.

title: From transient shocks to unexpected outcomes: Disruptive drivers in scenario pathways
abstract: Scenario pathways (e.g. for the energy transition) often use a single trajectory or a band. That is not sufficient when one needs to understand why outcomes differ and under what stress or uncertainty they arise. Doing so requires tracking disequilibrium along pathways, comparing runs across "worlds" or storylines, and surfacing outcomes that are unlikely under a central view but plausible when how factors interact is uncertain. Cross-Impact Balance (CIB) is a well-established method for generating pathways. This paper extends CIB to formalise and implement these dimensions in pathway runs, and defines four run types that respectively emphasise one-off shocks, extremes under alternative regimes, influence-structure uncertainty that widens over time, and exogenous shocks as a baseline for comparison. The approach is applied to a socio-technical decarbonisation pathway for illustration. Together, the extensions support stress-testing, comparison across storyline or regime assumptions, and exploration of rare or surprising futures, and help analysts distinguish results that are stable across those assumptions from those that depend on structural uncertainty about the influence table.

title: Beyond Pain: The Impact of Physical Pain on Conformity
abstract: ABSTRACT Physical pain is a pervasive feature of everyday life, yet little is known about how it shapes consumer decision‐making in socially influenced contexts, i.e., consumer decisions that are shaped, at least in part, by information about the preferences, judgments, or behaviors of others. The present research examines whether experiencing physical pain influences consumers' reliance on social proof in choice contexts. Across a pilot field study, one laboratory experiment, and two preregistered online studies, we find evidence that physical pain heightens conformity to majority‐endorsed options, even when the majority option is less desirable. Findings are consistent with the conclusion that pain increases consumers' likelihood of selecting socially validated options. Importantly, this pattern emerged even in a context in which the majority‐endorsed option was objectively less desirable. The discussion outlines possible mechanisms and leaves their empirical adjudication to future research.

title: Linking Leader Overqualification to Employee Organizational Citizenship Behaviors Toward the Leader: A Personal Identification Process Model
abstract: ABSTRACT Overqualification has important implications not only for the overqualified but also those who work under the overqualified. Leaders are an influential source of self‐identity for followers and employee‐perceived leader overqualification impacts how followers view themselves and behave to the overqualified leader. Perceived leader overqualification, however, has both positive and negative impacts on followers. Yet, research on effects of follower perceived leader overqualification is limited. From an identification construction perspective, and drawing on personal identification (PI) process model, we theorize that perceiving a leader as overqualified can strengthen followers' identification with that leader and, in turn, their organizational citizenship behavior directed toward the leader (OCBL). Because identification depends on how followers construe a leader's attributes in relation to their own self‐concept, we position follower narcissism as a boundary condition. We argue that narcissistic admiration strengthens the positive link between perceived leader overqualification and leader identification, whereas narcissistic rivalry weakens it, producing divergent indirect effects on OCBL. Results from one vignette‐based experiment in the United States and two multi‐wave, multi‐source surveys in China consistently support this moderated‐mediation model. The findings reposition overqualification as a relationally consequential leader attribute and clarify when, and for whom, it elicits rather than undermines supportive follower behavior.

title: Intergenerational Transmission
abstract: There has been recent and rapid growth in management and organizational research dedicated to the phenomenon of intergenerational transmission—the process through which organizations and other social systems reproduce and reconstitute themselves across long periods of time. This growth has resulted in several different research communities dedicated to understanding how organizational life transcends the involvement, tenure, and lifetimes of individuals. Yet, while assumptions about the nature of intergenerational transmission processes are coherent within research communities, such assumptions also diverge widely across such communities, resulting in contradictions and conceptual challenges. In this manuscript we identify four latent conceptualizations of the process of intergenerational transmission: taken-for-granted persistence, effortful maintenance, incremental adaptation, and discontinuous reinvention. We theorize that these processes represent different modes of what we term sociotemporal transcendence—different ways through which organizational life extends through time beyond the involvement or lifetimes of individuals. Based on these insights, we identify future research directions for a transcendence-based view of organizational life.

title: Toward a Framework of Social Marginalization: An Integrative Review and Research Agenda
abstract: Despite a growing body of research on social marginalization in organizations, this scholarship remains fragmented across identity groups and disciplinary silos. As a result, organizational scholars lack a coherent framework to explain how marginalization persists and evolves across contexts. In this integrative review, we synthesize research from management, psychology, and sociology to develop a multilevel framework that conceptualizes marginalization as a recursive cycle between symbolic disadvantage (e.g., stereotyping, stigma, delegitimization) and material disadvantage (e.g., restricted access to jobs, resources, and institutional protections). We identify recurring mechanisms that operate across micro, meso, and macro levels, demonstrating how these dynamics mutually reinforce one another over time. Our framework also explains why interventions that target only one dimension of disadvantage often fall short or produce unintended consequences. We conclude by outlining a research agenda that advances theoretical development and empirical investigation of marginalization, including approaches to multilevel dynamics, temporal change, and measurement, as well as implications for designing more effective organizational interventions. Together, this integrative framework provides a unifying lens for understanding and addressing the cyclical dynamics of marginalization in organizations.

title: Forgive Us Our Sins—Experimental Evidence on Arrears Forgiveness and Bill Payment From Nairobi, Kenya
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Event-time regression discontinuity for biomedical data: LATT estimation and covariate distribution tests
abstract: Estimating causal effects of drugs on clinical biomarkers is often infeasible through randomized trials, while observational data require designs that approximate experimental conditions. Using linked UK Biobank records collected during 2006-2013, we develop an event-time regression discontinuity (RD) framework for settings in which prescription records are longitudinal but biomarkers are measured cross-sectionally. A surrogate running variable aligns individuals by the interval between biomarker measurement and the first recorded prescription, comparing eventual users measured shortly before versus after that date. Under continuity assumptions, this identifies a local average treatment effect among the treated. We apply distributional covariate-balance diagnostics, robust bias-corrected inference, and parsimonious covariate adjustment. Statin analyses show a local downward LDL discontinuity around the first recorded prescription date, with direction and statistical significance robust across bias-corrected inference, bandwidths, and donut specifications. However, the running-variable density test is significant and donut estimates vary from - 1.00 to - 1.72 mmol/L, indicating residual uncertainty about local comparability. The metformin-HbA1c example is less stable: a sizeable parametric local-linear reduction is not corroborated under robust bias-corrected inference. Event-time RD offers potential for pharmacovigilance and real-world causal inference in linked health databases, but conclusions depend on explicit local timing-exogeneity and continuity assumptions.

title: Prediction-Based Adaptive Designs for Reducing Wave Nonresponse Rates and Bias in Panel Surveys
abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based nonresponse prediction in panel surveys enables selective interventions. However, the optimal use of ML predictions in Adaptive Survey Design (ASD) remains uncertain. We propose a method that integrates field experiment results on incentives, questionnaire length, and questionnaire content with ML-based propensity models to simulate ASD strategies ex-post with minimal assumptions. Using German panel data, we show that treating 15 percent of panelists, selected through ML-based predictions and R-indicator analysis, with increased cash incentives or a survey module on the respondents’ preferred topic can reduce nonresponse rates by up to 2 percentage points. These strategies also reduced bias in selected variables. We present our method as a framework for survey researchers to evaluate the expected outcomes of multiple ASD regimes simultaneously in a realistic setting. The framework helps identify both the criteria for allocating treatments to specific participant groups and the most effective modifications to the survey protocol.

title: How Model Choice and Memory Shape Preference Consistency in Large Language Models
abstract: When a language model answers a sequence of questions, researchers report the model and temperature but rarely what or how it was told about its own earlier answers. I show that this underreported setting behaves as a mode effect. Testing four large language model (LLM) families with revealed preference theory (GARP) across moral, economic, and social tasks ( N = 5,926 ), I find that how prior choices re-enter the prompt, the memory condition , moves the share of internally consistent subjects by up to 48 percentage points, mostly where that share starts lowest. Memory also influences which preferences the models express and, in a silicon-sampling extension, it brings the answers closer to the human distribution. Nonetheless, gains in consistency and surface fidelity do not necessarily translate into representativeness: a consistent, human-looking model may not represent any human population. For LLMs as social-science instruments, this study offers promise, caution, and a method for testing the stability of sequential outputs.

title: Dynamics of Local Clustering in Temporal Social Networks
abstract: While the local clustering coefficient is central to network analysis, it is typically treated as a static property. We introduce delta clustering to quantify changes in an individual's local clustering across adjacent time points in undirected networks. To address structural constraints, we develop a density-based decomposition expressing clustering as a weighted combination of subgraph-specific densities, clarifying how ego-network size and composition bound clustering change. We identify six triadic components distinguishing reconfiguration among persisting contacts from the integration and loss of ties. Using high-resolution university communication networks, we estimate fixed effects models accounting for network size interactions. Variation in delta clustering is driven primarily by density changes among persisting contacts, followed by the integration of new contacts, with magnitudes conditioned by ego-network size and baseline density. We further demonstrate the measure's explanatory power by linking daily clustering changes to individual behavioral outcomes. These results establish delta clustering as a size-aware, temporally grounded measure of local structural change in dynamic social networks.

title: The Cognitive Housework Inventory: Developing Survey Questions to Measure the Division of Cognitive Housework
abstract: Housework is unequally shared in different-gender couples, leading to negative consequences for women and lowering couples’ relationship quality. Although qualitative research identifies cognitive housework as an important type of household labor, we lack validated measures of cognitive housework to use in survey settings, barring quantitative research on its division in broader populations and its effects on household members. We use an open-ended survey and cognitive interviews to develop the Cognitive Housework Inventory (CHI), a seven-item survey instrument to measure the division of cognitive housework among partnered individuals. We then validate the CHI using data from an online survey, along with pairwise correlations, exploratory factor analysis, and bivariate analyses by gender. Regression analyses estimating its associations with stress, burnout, and relationship satisfaction demonstrate how to use the CHI in empirical settings. Results indicate the CHI is a valid and parsimonious instrument that can be incorporated into larger surveys to ultimately generate additional quantitative data on the distribution of housework.

title: A Replication Framework for Observational Research: From Specification Restriction to Specification Expansion
abstract: Sociology has remained relatively insulated from debates about the “replication crisis.” Heeding calls to consider replication more deeply, we introduce a distinction between two types of research reforms that have emerged in the wake of the crisis: specification-restricting and specification-expanding reforms. Specification restriction is often promoted as a way to increase the repeatability of research findings by controlling false positives. We argue that this statistical justification is less compelling in observational contexts—where the assumptions licensing false-positive control are harder to sustain and rigid ex ante analytical commitments can instead enshrine fragile specifications—than in experimental contexts. We further argue that apparently low replication rates do not necessarily imply a high prevalence of false positive findings. Instead, we propose a replication framework centered on specification-expanding reforms, stronger incentives for confirmatory research, and meta-analysis. This approach equips sociologists to assess the repeatability of findings and build a more cumulative discipline.

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Related Digital Skills and Employment Outcomes for Underrepresented Women
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether signaling AI‐related digital skills improves employment outcomes for women from underrepresented groups defined by race, age, sexual orientation and autism‐spectrum disclosure in England. The findings indicate that underrepresented women receive fewer interview invitations and are invited to lower‐paid vacancies relative to majority‐group women. Signaling AI‐related digital skills improves interview invitations for underrepresented women in the pooled analysis, although their disadvantage is not removed. The observed uplift is consistent with AI Capital and productivity‐signaling frameworks, yet such credentials remain insufficient to eliminate disadvantage. AI training should therefore be complemented by stronger equality enforcement.
journal_name: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: State Aid Cuts, First‐Round Cutback Management, and Organizational Performance: Evidence From School Districts
abstract: ABSTRACT Cuts in state aid impose fiscal stress on local governments and require cutback management strategies whose short‐run fiscal and performance implications remain uncertain. This study examines the school districts' first‐round fiscal and performance responses to the elimination of adjustment aid for 126 New Jersey school districts during the 2018–19 school year. Using a panel data set of 2,190 district‐year observations from 2013–14 to 2018–19 and a differences‐in‐differences research design, the study finds that the elimination of adjustment aid is associated with reductions in fund balance and modest reductions in current expenditures, but no evidence of an increase in local revenues. The findings also suggest that districts experiencing the loss of adjustment aid increased student‐to‐teacher ratios, while showing no practically significant changes in standardized test scores. Overall, the findings suggest that districts responded to the elimination of adjustment aid through short‐run fiscal buffering strategies while maintaining district‐wide student achievement during the study period.

title: Single-source domain generalization for ultrasonic state-of-charge estimation of lithium-ion batteries via supervised contrastive learning
Reshaping building cooling in hot and humid climates with a decentralized personal cooling system
Surrogate modeling of interconnector flows: A machine learning alternative to full-scale power system simulations with application to cross-border electricity exchange
abstract: Cross-border electricity exchanges are crucial for operating and planning highly renewable power systems. Many studies reduce spatial granularity to keep the models tractable and prescribe cross-border exchanges exogenously, often by reusing historical import/export time series. Such assumptions become inconsistent as renewable penetration changes the magnitude and timing of flows. This paper proposes a machine-learning (ML) surrogate framework that maps available nodal time series data (e.g., hourly demand and renewable generation) to synthetic, interconnector-level flow time series. The goal is to provide consistent flow profiles that are used as fixed boundary conditions in reduced power system optimization models (PSOMs). To improve downstream feasibility when surrogate flows are imposed in optimization, we further introduce a custom loss for the neural-network surrogate that penalizes physically impossible flow patterns. We demonstrate the framework on a pan-European single-node per country DC optimal power flow setting using the open-source LEGO PSOM with ENTSO-E TYNDP 2024 National Trends assumptions for 2030. We assess two model classes: k-nearest neighbors (KNN) and feedforward neural networks (SQU), using both full and reduced feature sets. The SQU models generalize more robustly than KNN to unseen climate years and substantially improve upon scaled historical benchmarks in terms of predictive accuracy. When imposed as fixed boundary flows in single-node PSOMs, the ML-generated profiles produce outcomes that closely match the results of the full European simulation, while delivering substantial runtime reductions (up to ~500x). These results indicate that ML-based flow surrogates can provide decision-relevant interconnector flows for tractable reduced studies in high-renewable systems.

title: Data-driven modeling and optimization of anode-side structural, transport and electrochemical properties in PEM water electrolyzers
abstract: Proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers are intricate multiphysics systems, whose commercial scale up and viability depend on optimizing the structural/material design of their cell components. Some of these structural properties also influence reactivity of the catalyst layers. The sluggish kinetics on anode side is of particular interest as the main water splitting reaction occurs on this part of the electrolyzer. Unlike PEM fuel cells, the public availability of experimental datasets is still limited. Therefore, in this work we undertake a data-driven approach using synthetic data generated from physics-based numerical model to investigate the effects of important structural, transport and electrochemical properties on cell performance. To facilitate model training through dimensionality reduction, Shapley additive explanations based feature selection procedure is adapted. Two separate artificial neural network models were trained on the reduced dataset to predict cell performance and voltage losses. Parametric analysis shows that based on the selected input properties, the ionomer volume fraction and absolute permeability of the porous transport layer are the important structural properties which influence cell performance. Voltage loss decomposition analysis corroborates these observations. Finally, the surrogate model was employed as the objective function within the genetic algorithm to determine the optimal input feature values. The optimized structural, transport and electrochemical properties demonstrated an improved cell performance when compared to the selected baseline values.

title: Seasonal index-based corn insurance design for Brazil: Insights from Safra and Safrinha
abstract: Index insurance is promoted for climate risk management, but basis risk limits scalability. This article develops an ex ante, multi-hazard weather-yield index framework for corn in Paraná, Brazil, tailored to the state’s dual-season system (Safra and Safrinha) and the distinct priorities of farmers and insurers. We combine municipality-level yield panels with climate extreme indicators spanning temperature, precipitation, humidity, radiation, wind, and evaporative demand, and evaluate mean- and tail-focused econometric specifications alongside penalised alternatives to guard against overfitting. Basis risk is treated as two-sided and designable by explicitly trading off false negatives (uncompensated losses) and false positives (unnecessary payouts) through a stakeholder-weighted objective, implemented within clustered municipal zones and season-specific windows. Our framework delivers a transparent mapping from alternative basis risk priorities to contract design choices, offering a practical blueprint for piloting credible index insurance where products are not yet established.

title: Battery industrialisation and the energy transition: Policy coordination and industrial path in Morocco
abstract: The global energy transition is accelerating battery production, creating policy challenges for countries seeking to join low-carbon supply chains. Research on industrial upgrading and global value chains explains integration into production networks. In contrast, research on the development of green industrial paths establishes the importance of regional preconditions, asset modification, and firm- and system-level agency. Less is known, however, about how system-level actors coordinate these elements in structurally constrained and globally interdependent contexts. This paper examines Morocco's EV battery industry and identifies a mechanism and a boundary condition. Drawing on interviews, policy documents, corporate disclosures and secondary data, it identifies policy-mediated cross-path asset alignment: system-level actors translate external regulatory and market pressures into domestic interventions connecting automotive, logistics, mineral-processing and renewable-energy assets with non-local technology and capital. The resulting pathway combines the renewal of phosphate- and cobalt-related activities with diversification into battery-material production and the prospective importation of cell manufacturing. Although this alignment reduces input, logistics, compliance and market-access constraints and may elicit investment commitments, uneven implementation shows that such commitments do not necessarily produce operational capacity, domestic linkages, capability formation, or durable regional value capture. For energy policy, the findings demonstrate both the importance and limits of coordinating industrial, energy and resource policies under external dependence.

title: Inkjet-printable inks for electrochemical energy devices: A review of materials, formulation, and functional-layer engineering
Sustainable utilization of peanut shells: Global trends, technologies, and future perspectives
abstract: Peanut shells are an abundant lignocellulosic by-product generated in large quantities by the global peanut processing industry and are increasingly recognized as a valuable secondary resource. This review provides a system-oriented assessment of their sustainable utilization, including physicochemical properties, processing routes, environmental applications, and high-value material and energy uses within circular bioeconomy frameworks. Peanut shells show strong potential as precursors for adsorbents, biochar, activated carbon, biocomposites, biochemicals, and bioenergy products, particularly in contaminant removal, carbon material production, and lightweight construction materials. Recent advances in nanotechnology, biotechnology, and digital process optimization further expand their applicability toward multifunctional materials and integrated valorization pathways. However, large-scale implementation remains limited by feedstock variability, lack of process standardization, incomplete techno-economic validation, and insufficient assessment of long-term environmental performance and technology readiness, which currently restrict the transition from laboratory-scale studies toward reliable industrial implementation. The review indicates that integrated valorization strategies represent a long-term development direction with high theoretical potential; however, their industrial implementation remains limited by insufficient demonstration-scale validation, techno-economic evidence, and process integration studies. Overall, peanut shells represent a versatile biomass resource with growing relevance for sustainable materials engineering, environmental technologies, integrated biorefinery concepts, and future circular bioeconomy systems.

title: The Energy System Ontology: A conceptual framework for energy transition research
abstract: The energy transition is characterized by the increasing complexity and interdependence of technological, economic, policy, environmental, and social dimensions. While a large and rapidly growing body of literature addresses these aspects, differences in terminology, conceptual scope, and analytical focus hinder the integration of findings across studies and the alignment of diverse modeling approaches. This paper presents the Energy System Ontology (ESO), a comprehensive conceptual framework developed to bridge these gaps and support the structured organization and synthesis of knowledge related to energy systems and energy transition. ESO is constructed through a systematic, multidisciplinary review of the energy transition literature combined with ontology engineering principles to ensure robustness. The framework identifies and formalizes core relationships across energy technologies, markets, policies, and environmental contexts, enabling a consistent representation of the energy nexus while preserving vital disciplinary distinctions. The resulting ontology provides a domain-wide reference that supports comparative analysis, semantic interoperability across heterogeneous energy-system representations, and the systematic exploration of transition pathways. The current evaluation provides requirements-based verification and application-oriented evidence rather than independent external validation. By offering an explicit and extensible structure, ESO contributes to greater transparency and provides a robust framework for the analysis of socio-technical systems within the energy transition.

title: A framework for multi-objective design of Oyster shell powder–Calcined Clay–Cement (OC3) mortar considering chloride-related durability, cost, and carbon pricing: A case study
abstract: Multi-objective optimization has been widely applied to low-carbon mortar mix design, but comparatively few studies have simultaneously incorporated an experimentally measured chloride-related durability indicator and explicit carbon-pricing scenarios into cementitious binder optimization. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework for oyster shell powder–calcined clay–cement (OC³) mortar based on a simplex-centroid design. Mechanical properties, hydration heat, ultrasonic pulse velocity, and surface electrical resistivity (SER) were experimentally measured and fitted as response models. SER was used as a comparative durability indicator, and carbon pricing was incorporated into the total cost function. Results show that adding durability as an objective markedly increases the optimized calcined clay content, accompanied by higher SER. Higher carbon prices further reduce cement content and carbon emissions per unit volume. This framework provides a practical approach for designing durable, low-carbon cementitious materials under carbon pricing scenarios.

title: Structure-Based Prediction and Ranking of PFAS Groundwater Mobility for EU Drinking Water Regulation
abstract: Abstract The EU Drinking Water Directive (2020/2184) mandates monitoring of 20 priority per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from January 2026, yet predicting which PFAS structures pose the greatest groundwater contamination risk remains challenging. We present a machine learning framework that simultaneously predicts the three physicochemical properties governing PFAS subsurface mobility─soil sorption (log KOC, R2 = 0.90), water solubility (log Sw, R2 = 0.90), and ionization class (93% accuracy)─from molecular structure alone. The models were trained on 122 PFAS spanning 37 subclasses using 44 molecular descriptors, including nine that encode the segmentation of the fluorinated backbone by ether linkages, and were validated by cross-validation, external test sets, leave-one-subclass-out analysis, Y-randomization, and a formal applicability domain. SHAP analysis indicates that ether-linkage descriptors are associated with lower predicted soil retention, providing a model-based explanation for the high mobility of GenX-type replacements. A composite Groundwater Mobility Index integrating the three end points identifies PFBA, PFPeA, and PFPeS as the most mobile EU-regulated compounds, consistent with field monitoring evidence, and flags several nonregulated PFAS with comparable mobility. An open-access prediction tool with applicability-domain screening accompanies this work.

title: Anthropogenic and Geogenic Factors Affecting Groundwater Arsenic and Potential Drinking Water Exposure in the San Luis Valley, Colorado
abstract: Abstract Groundwater arsenic is a serious health threat in many regions with limited surface water drinking supplies. In the San Luis Valley, Colorado, USA, where most residents rely on groundwater for drinking water, elevated groundwater arsenic concentrations (≥5 μg/L) were observed in 19.8% of private wells. Many recent studies have leveraged data science methods to estimate the spatial variability of arsenic at local, regional, and global scales. These studies typically predict depth-independent arsenic concentrations due to limited well depth information. However, arsenic concentrations may vary greatly with depth due to heterogeneous aquifer geochemistry, including redox potential, pH, and biogeochemical conditions. In this study, we apply random forest modeling to predict elevated groundwater arsenic concentrations (≥5 μg/L) over space and depth continuously across the San Luis Valley using a community-driven data set of 435 groundwater measurements of major ions and trace metals. Our model reveals the influence of several known or hypothesized drivers or proxy drivers of arsenic in groundwater, including surface elevation, fraction of fine-grained aquifer sediments, well depth, soil pH, long-term subsidence, and geothermal influences. Elevation, percentage of fine-grained sediments, and elemental indicators of geothermal fluid influence are some of the most important predictors of arsenic, while long-term subsidence is found to have a weak but positive relationship with arsenic. The model has a specificity of 0.82 and a sensitivity of 0.81 on held-out test data sets. In addition to improving understanding of drivers of arsenic in the region, this model produces pseudo-3D estimates of groundwater arsenic. The model can also be used to assess the time-dependent exposure to arsenic as the depth of domestic wells changes over time.

title: Sustained Fe3+/Fe2+ Cycling Enables Photochemical Defluorination of Perfluoroalkyl Carboxylic Acids via Ligand-to-Metal Charge Transfer
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are widespread persistent pollutants that threaten environmental and human health. Although Fe3+-mediated ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) has been shown to promote PFAS photochemical defluorination, existing systems rely predominantly on high-energy UV irradiation, often achieve incomplete defluorination, and generally exhibit poor performance toward short-chain and ultrashort-chain PFASs. Herein, we report a near-UV- to visible-light-driven photodefluorination strategy for perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) using commercial Fe3+ salts in acetonitrile under 405 nm irradiation, which achieved complete defluorination of long-chain perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) within 420 min and ultrashort-chain trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) within 240 min. Mechanistic studies combining density functional theory calculations and experimental evidence revealed that LMCT initiated decarboxylation, generating perfluoroalkyl radicals that subsequently degraded through oxidative chain-shortening reactions. The Fe3+/Fe2+ redox cycle was sustained by molecular oxygen, with hydroxyl and superoxide radicals playing auxiliary roles in reoxidizing Fe2+ and oxidizing intermediates rather than directly attacking intact PFOA. This strategy is broadly applicable to C2–C9 PFCAs, where the degradation rates are inversely correlated with chain length and are effective against perfluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acids. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for Fe3+-mediated PFAS photodefluorination in nonaqueous media and clarify the fundamental chemistry governing this process.

title: High-Throughput Identification of PPARγ-Active Chemicals in Riverine Drinking Water Sources: Discover a Novel DEHP Biodegradation Product
abstract: Abstract While exposure to PPAR active compounds can lead to various adverse health effects, studies on the environmental contaminants and their transformation products with PPAR activity remain limited. This study employed PPARγ protein affinity selection-mass spectrometry (AS-MS) to comprehensively identify and prioritize PPARγ-active contaminants in the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers, key drinking water sources in China. From wastewater treatment plant effluents, river, and source water samples, 61 PPARγ ligands were identified, including 18 antagonists not reported previously. Notably, a novel biodegradation product of di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP), phthalic acid 1-(2-ethylhexyl) 2-(2-ethyl-5-carboxypentyl) ester (5CX-DEHP), was discovered and characterized as a potent PPARγ antagonist (IC50 = 8.5 μM). Semi-quantification revealed total concentrations of 61 chemicals ranging from 965.2 to 5748 ng/L in source waters, with priority agonistic chemicals such as 4-dodecylbenzenesulfonic acid and priority antagonistic chemicals such as 2-amino-6-methylmercaptopurine and 5CX-DEHP posing high ranking. This study comprehensively revealed the widespread occurrence of PPARγ agonistic and antagonistic chemicals in the water samples and identified a previously overlooked transformation product of DEHP as a relatively strong PPARγ antagonist.

title: Urban Nitrogen Policy Should Follow Pathways, Not the Calendar
abstract: E ach summer, many Florida communities prohibit applying fertilizers containing nitrogen (N) or phosphorus to urban landscapes.Nearly 20 million Floridians�91.5% of the state's population�lived in urban areas in 2020.As of 2023, at least 36 counties and 98 additional municipalities had adopted fertilizer ordinances; 18 of these counties impose summer blackout periods. 1 The rationale is intuitive: the Tampa Bay region receives about 1,300 mm of rain annually, two-thirds of it between June and September, 2 raising runoff and leaching risk, so wet-season restrictions are a visible, easily administered response to eutrophication and harmful algal blooms.Yet a calendar date is an imperfect proxy for N export.The waterquality benefit depends on how much recently applied fertilizer contributes to bioavailable N loads relative to other sources.Across urban landscapes, N from multiple sources is stored, transformed, and remobilized in soils, streets, storm drains, and ponds; effective policy should therefore address the sources, forms, storage pools, transformations, and pathways controlling N export to receiving waters (Figure 1).

title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead
Breaking the “Measure-Model-Optimize” Bottleneck: A High-Resolution Spatial Framework for Reliable Wastewater Greenhouse Gas Management
abstract: Abstract Non-CO2 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from urban wastewater resource recovery facilities (WRRFs) are spatially heterogeneous at the meter scale, introducing large uncertainties in national inventories and process-level control. We establish SMART-GHG (Spatially explicit Monitoring, Assessment, and Reduction Technology for Greenhouse Gas management), combining unmanned-aerial-vehicle (UAV) concentration mapping with floating-chamber flux measurements to reconstruct continuous CH4 and N2O emission fields. The framework quantifies sampling requirements and validates an activated-sludge model as a facility-specific digital twin. At a full-scale anaerobic/anoxic/oxic WRRF (300,000 m3 d–1), seasonal surveys of the monitored basin in one of four parallel treatment trains yielded CH4 emissions of 3.15–13.08 kg d–1, dominated by influent stripping, and N2O emissions of 4.74–28.64 kg d–1, with mid-train peaks corresponding to aeration transitions. Numerical sub-sampling indicated that stable emission estimates required approximately 30 measurement points per lane (5 m spacing) in this basin; sparser sampling induced errors up to ±30%. Validation against longitudinal dissolved-oxygen and nitrogen profiles yielded mean absolute percentage errors of 3.6–17.5%. Model-guided optimization of zoned dissolved-oxygen set points predicted approximately 12% lower N2O emissions and 9% lower aeration energy use than a simulated conventional-aeration baseline, while maintaining effluent compliance in the model. SMART-GHG supports spatially explicit emission inventories and model-based aeration optimization in WRRFs.

title: Cellulose Reshapes Microbial C–S–Fe Coupling to Suppress Direct and Fe(III)-Mediated Pyrite Oxidation
abstract: Abstract Pyrite oxidation generates sulfate and acidity in sulfide-bearing mine soils, but how structural carbon suppresses this process remains unresolved. We combined a 56-day pyrite-amended soil microcosm with geochemical measurements, qPCR, metagenomics, DNA stable isotope probing (DNA-SIP), genome-resolved analysis, and apparent kinetic modeling. Cellulose decreased NaOH-extractable sulfate by 72.71% and HCl-extractable Fe(III) by 55.13% at day 56. DNA-SIP showed that cellulose-derived carbon entered a phylogenetically distributed assimilating guild with genomic potential for oxidative-hydrolytic cellulose deconstruction, Fe(III) reduction, sulfate uptake, and assimilatory sulfate reduction. Enriched metagenome-assembled genomes collocated these C, Fe, and S functions within individual populations, whereas time-series metagenomes showed sustained cellulose-deconstruction and sulfur-assimilation potential without broad enrichment of Fe-reduction genes. Thus, functionally important assimilators could reshape Fe–S cycling without consistently dominating bulk community abundance. Consistent with these genomic and geochemical patterns, the apparent model indicated weaker O2-driven direct oxidation, Fe(II) oxidation/Fe(III) regeneration, and effective reactivity of extractable Fe(III). These results identify a microbial mechanism whereby cellulose utilization redirects C–S–Fe coupling toward more reductive and assimilatory transformations, suppressing pyrite oxidation without detectable mineral-surface coating.

title: Multimatrix Biomonitoring and Transplacental Transfer of Legacy and Emerging PFAS in Korean Pregnant Women
abstract: Abstract Maternal–fetal exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) cannot be adequately characterized using single biological matrices because compound-specific distribution patterns vary according to physicochemical properties and elimination pathways. We measured 33 legacy, precursor, and emerging PFAS in maternal serum, plasma, urine, and cord serum from Korean singleton pregnancies (n = 151) to characterize matrix-specific exposure profiles, transplacental transfer, and associations with maternal and neonatal factors. Matrix-specific detection patterns distinguished predominantly protein-bound PFAS detected in blood matrices from short-chain, renally excreted PFAS prevalent in urine at the population level. Notably, the precursor 6:2 diPAP showed a relatively high estimated maternal–cord concentration ratio, whereas the alternative PFAS 9Cl-PF3ONS was consistently detected in maternal blood and cord serum, suggesting compound-specific distribution patterns compared with regulated legacy PFAS. Associations with fetal growth indicators were modest, matrix- and sex-specific, and interpreted as exploratory. Overall, these findings suggest that multimatrix biomonitoring can reveal matrix-specific PFAS detection and distribution patterns that may not be captured by single-matrix approaches. However, maternal–cord comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because maternal samples were collected during pregnancy rather than at delivery.

title: Effects of Meteorology, Emissions, and Regional Transport on Atmospheric Nr Deposition in Lake Taihu, China
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric deposition has played an increasingly important role of reactive nitrogen (Nr) loading in Chinese eutrophic lakes, while its major influencing factors and sources remained insufficiently understood. Here, we applied WRF-CMAQ and its source apportionment module to investigate the interannual change and main drivers of atmospheric Nr deposition by species and form over Lake Taihu during 2017–2020. The annual average of Nr deposition was estimated at 6.55 ± 0.18 Gg N yr–1, and reduced nitrogen (RDN) accounted for 70% resulting from abundant NH3 emissions from agricultural activities and continuous NOx controls in the Basin. Meteorological factors played a greater role than emission abatement in driving the interannual variability of Nr deposition for both summer and winter. Long-range transport from outside of the basin became an increasingly important contributor to oxidized nitrogen (OXN) deposition, partly offsetting the benefits of local NOx controls. Upwind cities were identified with greater contributions to Nr deposition in winter, whereas the circulation pattern strongly affected the contributions of cities in summer. This study advances our understanding of Nr inputs from the atmosphere to aquatic ecosystems and provides scientific evidence for the management of external nitrogen to eutrophic lakes.

title: When does Remanufacturing versus new product manufacture pay off? Derivation of a commercial ReMan formula and decision logic based on empirical ratio analyses across multi company production data
Feasibility study of stabilizing soft soil in the Jianghan Plain using one-part alkali-activated materials developed by iron and steel slags
From data-driven analysis to system development: A framework for developing an ease-of-disassembly evaluation system based on experimental data and multi-source text
abstract: Existing ease-of-disassembly evaluation systems are increasingly challenged by the high integration and multi-layered structural characteristics of electronic products, such as smartphones and tablets. Many existing approaches rely heavily on expert judgement and outcome-oriented metrics, whilst lacking sufficient support from disassembly process data, which limits their interpretability and applicability.
