Rebuilding belonging: the role of organizational support in repatriates’ socio-professional reintegration amid global volatility
abstract: Drawing on Organizational Support Theory (OST), this study examines how perceived organizational support shapes repatriates’ socio-professional reintegration amid global volatility, including geopolitical crises and COVID-19. Although support is central to successful repatriation, limited research captures how repatriates themselves interpret it under unstable return conditions. Based on semi-structured interviews with 35 repatriates across industries and focus groups with HR professionals, the study develops a Two-Level Reintegration Support Model. The model distinguishes career-function support—career continuity, knowledge recontextualization, and structured reintegration practices—from identity-belonging support—recognition, managerial empathy, and peer-network inclusion. Findings show that repatriates returning during disruption were particularly sensitive to support gaps and discrepancies between organizational promises and lived reintegration experiences. These discrepancies affected well-being, organizational commitment, and retention intentions. Rather than identifying entirely new support dimensions, the study demonstrates the close interdependence of career-function and identity-belonging support and shows how their relative salience shifts under volatile conditions. The study extends OST by contextualizing perceived support within global volatility and contributes to international HRM by integrating environmental disruption into repatriation theorizing. It also offers guidance for MNCs seeking to rebuild belonging, leverage international experience, and retain globally competent talent during and after disruption.

title: Bad news travels fast: comment letters, investor trading behavior, and stock liquidity
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the effect of real-time disclosed regulatory comment letters on corporate stock liquidity and explores the underlying driving factors, using a unique sample from the Chinese stock market. Leveraging the timely nature of comment letter issuance and the subsequent reply mechanism in China, the paper aims to unambiguously identify the market consequences of comment letters and the associated mechanisms. Specifically, we focus on the role of different investor groups' trading behaviors, particularly retail net-sells and investor sentiment, in mediating the liquidity changes. Ultimately, this research provides new insights into the market monitoring effect of comment letters and regulatory enforcement in emerging markets. Design/methodology/approach We manually collected a sample of comment letters and their real-time replies issued by the Shenzhen Stock Exchange (SZSE) from 2014 to 2018. We employ event study methodology and Difference-in-Differences (DiD) models to analyze the changes in inquired firms' stock liquidity, measured by the Quoted Spread (QS) and Effective Spread (ES), following the comment letter disclosure. We proxy retail investor trading behavior using net sell volumes of small transactions and examine the driving role of retail net-sells and negative retail sentiment in the observed liquidity decline. This design leverages the unique institutional setting of real-time disclosure in the Chinese market. Findings The findings demonstrate that the stock liquidity of inquired firms significantly declines immediately after the comment letter disclosure. However, this decline does not significantly recover after the firms issue their subsequent replies. The short-term deterioration in liquidity is mainly driven by intense retail net-selling activities and heightened negative retail sentiment. Furthermore, the liquidity exhibits only a partial recovery over a longer period, extending up to 60 days post-disclosure. Finally, the negative effect of comment letters on stock liquidity is more pronounced for firms characterized by higher information uncertainty and greater corporate governance deficiencies. Originality/value This study uses the real-time disclosure mechanism of comment letters in the Chinese market to examine their impact on the trading behavior of different investor groups, particularly retail investors, thus mitigating concerns about insider trading. It confirms a significant regulatory effect of comment letters as a non-punitive regulatory tool in the capital market, filling a gap in the literature regarding their efficacy. By focusing on the unique emerging market context of China, this research enriches the global understanding of comment letters' impact and offers important practical implications for improving regulatory instruments worldwide.

title: Finding green start-ups at scale: Automating selection through Natural Language Processing algorithms
abstract: Research and policy interest in green entrepreneurship is growing, but identifying green start-ups remains a major challenge because the concept of “green” is inconsistently defined across studies, and existing identification strategies often rely on costly, non-scalable, or discretionary procedures. This paper develops an automated procedure to identify start-ups with an explicit environmental orientation using Natural Language Processing (NLP) with minimal human intervention. To ground the approach conceptually, we derive a green classification framework from Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets specifically related to environmental sustainability and use it to map start-up activities into a common set of green topics. We then apply the framework to the websites of more than 10,000 Italian innovative start-ups founded between 2009 and 2023, implementing three complementary NLP pipelines based on an ML dictionary, LDA, and BERTopic approach, to detect firms with environmentally oriented products, services, or processes. The results show that automated text-based identification can capture a broad and policy-relevant landscape of green start-ups while preserving thematic heterogeneity across environmental domains. To illustrate the analytical value of the framework, we compare the resulting distribution of these green start-ups across topics with Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan investments and with SDG performance indicators. This application reveals both areas of alignment and mismatch between entrepreneurial emergence, policy priorities, and environmental sustainability challenges. By offering a transparent, scalable, and SDG-grounded procedure for identifying green start-ups, the paper contributes to the measurement of green entrepreneurship and provides a useful tool for technological forecasting and policy planning.

Strategic Actions to Reduce Corporate Greenhouse Gas Emissions: Pairing Internal Climate Oversight with Science-Based Targets
abstract: What strategic actions help firms achieve credible reductions in greenhouse gas emissions? We examine the sequencing and effectiveness of internal governance mechanisms and external standards, distinguishing actions associated with real progress from symbolic claims. We analyze changes in scope 1 and scope 2 emissions for 146 of the world’s largest multinational enterprises (MNEs) from 2012 to 2023 to assess what strategic actions are associated with climate change mitigation. Widely adopted climate oversight mechanisms—including a climate strategy, board responsibility, internal targets, and verification—do not distinguish firms that reduce emissions from those that increase them. By contrast, having science-based targets externally validated by the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) in place for more years is consistently associated with faster emission reductions. Among MNEs adopting SBTi-validated targets, all had previously established internal climate oversight, suggesting a sequence from internal preparation to external validation. Assigning responsibility to the CEO and linking CEO compensation to climate goals is associated with higher emissions in our sample.

title: The influence of natural disasters on supply chain concentration: the moderating role of digital capability
abstract: Purpose Natural disasters impose substantial operational and strategic challenges on firms. Drawing on Resource Dependence Theory (RDT), this study examines how natural disasters (specifically, typhoons and earthquakes) affect firms' supply chain concentration and investigates the moderating role of digital capability in this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Using a panel of A-share-listed firms on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges from 2010 to 2023, comprising 27,578 firm-year observations, we exploit a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) design to identify the causal effect of natural disasters on firms' supply chain concentration. Findings We find that firms exposed to natural disasters significantly reduce both supplier and customer concentration. Moreover, higher levels of digital capability strengthen the negative effect of natural disasters on supply chain concentration, suggesting that digital capabilities enhance firms' ability to reconfigure their supply chains in response to environmental shocks. These findings are robust to a series of robustness checks. Heterogeneity analyses further show that the effects vary systematically with key firm characteristics, including industry pollution intensity, ownership structure, financial constraints, and managerial optimism. Finally, analyses by disaster type reveal that typhoons significantly reduce both supplier and customer concentration, whereas earthquakes have no significant effect. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by identifying natural disasters (typhoons vs. earthquakes) as an important environmental determinant of supply chain concentration and by highlighting digital capability as a key capability that enables firms to strategically reconfigure supply chain relationships in response to external disruptions.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Institutional Cross‐Ownership and Asset–Liability Maturity Mismatches: Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This paper examines whether cross‐ownership, where institutional investors hold equity stakes in two or more firms within the same industry, affects asset–liability maturity mismatches that occur when cross‐owned firms use short‐term debt to finance long‐term assets. Research Findings/Insights Using a sample of Chinese listed firms for the 2007–2022 period, results suggest that firms with institutional cross‐owners increase asset–liability maturity mismatches since they use more short‐term debt, less long‐term debt, and allocate more resources to research and development (R&D) expenditures because of cross‐ownership. Increase in mismatches because of institutional cross‐ownership is more pronounced for firms with similar technological profiles, for firms facing intense product market competition, for firms experiencing severe agency conflicts, and for cross‐listed firms. Theoretical/Academic Implications We extend the anticompetitive perspective by showing that portfolio‐wide wealth maximization may harm individual portfolio firms through greater maturity mismatches. Moreover, we extend agency and information asymmetry theories by identifying institutional cross‐ownership as an important mechanism through which agency conflicts and information frictions translate into greater maturity mismatches. Overall, our findings shed new light on the “dark side” of institutional cross‐ownership. Practitioner/Policy Implications Managers of institutionally cross‐held firms should avoid excessive reliance on short‐term debt when financing long‐term investments such as R&D expenditures. We advise regulators to monitor the potential adverse financing consequences of institutional cross‐ownership, particularly for firms facing intense product market competition, greater agency conflicts, or higher information asymmetry. Investors and creditors should incorporate cross‐ownership–related maturity mismatch risk into their investment and lending decisions.

title: Stakeholder Integration Through Moral Insight: How a Lay Constructivist Ethics Enables Paradox Cognition
CEO Inherited Altruism, Firm Corporate Social Responsibility, and Shareholder Returns
abstract: Abstract We examine the impact of CEOs’ inherited altruistic inclination on firm corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance and shareholder returns. Specifically, we look at U.S. CEOs’ altruism as an inherited value of the CEOs’ ancestral cultural origin that shapes their moral behavior and influences firm commitment to altruistic and genuine CSR. We find that firms led by CEOs with stronger inherited altruistic preferences have better CSR performance after controlling for firm financial and corporate governance attributes and other leadership characteristics. The impact of CEO inherited altruism on CSR is higher when CEOs operate under lower cash flow pressure. Consistent with a view of ethical leadership which protects the interests of both stakeholders and shareholders, we find that CEOs who inherit altruistic preferences are not significantly associated with firms’ stock returns under normal circumstances, while they protect shareholder returns during times of financial crisis and recessions. The results survive several robustness and endogeneity checks.

title: Of Prometheus and Pixels: The Ethical and Existential Costs of AI-Assisted Entrepreneurship
When Bad Leaders Create Worse Followers: How Toxic Leadership Breeds Employee Unethical Loyalty Through Stigma-by-Association Dynamics
Moving Toward, Moving Away, or Stuck in Conceptual Limbo? Rethinking Approach, Avoidance, and Inhibition in Organizational Research
abstract: Understanding when employees move toward opportunities, away from threats, or pause to balance competing concerns is central for predicting workplace behavior. Organizational scholars routinely apply approach–avoidance logic to explain psychological constructs (e.g., motivation, goals, emotions), behaviors, and performance outcomes. Systematically reviewing 268 papers that apply such logic, we document three usages, from classifying single constructs to organizing entire domains. Across these usages, scholars draw primarily on two foundational approach–avoidance models with distinct foci, often treating them interchangeably. Integrating the two foundational models, we clarify the distinct affective, cognitive, and behavioral constructs related to the approach and avoidance systems as well as a distinct, often-overlooked inhibition system. We identify three meta-concerns where the field’s application is misaligned with what the integration of the foundational models specifies: (1) key constructs are confounded, (2) inhibition responses to goal conflict are omitted or misclassified as avoidance, and (3) approach responses are implicitly treated as functional whereas avoidance and inhibition responses are treated as dysfunctional. Applying the shared vocabulary and resulting integrative model to three exemplar research streams (power, voice and silence, and proactivity), we discuss alternative explanations for empirical inconsistencies and offer diagnostic tools for more precise organizational theorizing.

title: Awe as a Transformative Emotion: An Integrative Review, Metamorphosis Model, and Research Agenda
abstract: Awe has attracted substantial scholarly attention but its implications for management remains fragmented across different accounts of what awe is and why it matters. In this review, we first show that the literature has developed around three dominant perspectives—collective self, epistemic, and well-being—each offering a distinct account of awe’s primary function. To integrate these perspectives, we advance a Metamorphosis Model of Awe, which explains how awe first breaks down self- and non-self-schemata before building them back up again, producing an expansion of mind and self. We then organize the diverse elicitors of awe into cognitive, physical, social, and technological sources, clarifying the conditions under which awe is likely to arise. Through this model, we portray awe as a transformative emotion that influences identity, cognition, and behavior, with implications for core organizational processes such as leadership, work design, organizational change, sensemaking, and innovation. We conclude by charting a forward-looking research agenda calling for greater examination of awe’s role at the individual, team, and organizational levels.

title: Enacting Open Science values in qualitative leadership research: Existing practices and future directions
The Price of power: Politics and longevity
The dance of leadership: How behavioral interaction scripts enable leadership among strangers
Closing the autonomic gap in neuroleadership: How polyvagal theory specifies a physiological mechanism of leadership influence
Caught in the middle: Dual role orientations as a potential source of leader and follower development
At what Price? A Meta-analysis of experiments assessing the impact of leader pay on employees and stakeholders
Citizens' Expectations vs. Recruitment Signals: Are Public Administrations Trying to Attract the Ideal Public Servant?
abstract: ABSTRACT Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.
