Mobile internet connectivity and climate change literacy in Africa
abstract: Addressing climate change requires individual behavioral shifts and a deep understanding of its impacts, yet the role of information and communication technologies (ICT), a powerful driver of social movements and cultural shifts, in shaping climate change literacy remains underexplored. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how ICT, particularly mobile Internet connectivity, influences climate change literacy in Africa. I provide the first systematic evidence on the impact of mobile Internet connectivity on climate change literacy by exploiting variations in peer-based Internet connectivity in an instrumental variable strategy. Using newly georeferenced individual-level data on climate change literacy from over 42,000 respondents across 31 African countries, I show that mobile Internet connectivity has a modest yet robust effect on climate literacy, raising it by approximately 0.57 points for a typical adopter. Heterogeneity analysis shows that mobile Internet access primarily enhances the knowledge-based dimensions of climate literacy, particularly climate awareness and understanding, while also improving risk perceptions to a lesser extent. This suggests that mobile Internet contributes to climate literacy mainly by expanding access to factual information and knowledge about climate change. Suggestive evidence reveals that Internet connectivity can help close climate-related information gaps, among socio-economically disadvantaged groups, such as women, farmers, and those without formal education. Although Internet connectivity increases the frequency of using Internet and social media for news, there is no strong evidence that these platforms serve as channels linking Internet connectivity to climate literacy.

title: Early-life adversity and long-term outcomes: evidence from the cocoa swollen shoot virus outbreak in the Gold Coast
abstract: How do early-life economic shocks that do not directly affect human biology shape long-term development outcomes? While a large body of work documents persistent effects of early-life exposure to health crises, famines, and natural disasters, much less is known about shocks that operate through economic disruption. This study addresses this gap by examining the long-term effects of the Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus Disease (CSSVD), an agricultural epidemic that devastated cocoa production in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) during the 1940s. Combining historical data on climatically suitable cocoa-growing areas with georeferenced household survey data, I exploit variation in exposure across birth timing and space to estimate the epidemic’s long-term effects. The results show that exposure during early childhood and school-going years led to substantial and persistent human capital deficits. Individuals exposed during early childhood lost about one year of schooling and were 8.5 percentage points (pp) less likely to obtain formal education, while those exposed during school-going years lost about 0.8 years of schooling and were 7.0 pp less likely to obtain formal education. Exposure is also associated with worse health outcomes, increasing morbidity by 6.2–8.5 pp and disability by 5–7.5 pp. In contrast, there is no systematic evidence of long-term effects on employment type or labor supply. Evidence on potential mechanisms points to both educational and occupational channels. Conditional on ever attending school, exposed individuals completed fewer years of schooling and were more likely to have incomplete primary education, indicating disruptions to both school progression and initial access to schooling. In addition, exposed individuals are more likely to work in the agricultural sector in adulthood, consistent with reduced educational attainment having narrowed their occupational options. These findings demonstrate that industry-specific economic shocks can generate long-term human capital deficits, even in the absence of direct biological exposure.

title: Spatial perspective on perceived fairness of climate-related fuel tax increases
abstract: We explore the perceived fairness of fuel tax increases from a spatial perspective. Actions in transport sector are needed to meet climate change mitigation targets, but such policies may disproportionately impact rural and urban residents, leading to spatially varying experiences of injustice. Perceived fairness is the most important determinant of public opinion towards mitigation policies, but perceived fairness of these policies itself has been understudied. We combine our inquiry of perceived fairness regarding fuel tax increases with considerations of spatial justice. We explore, whether residential area type, region, and variables such as climate concern, trust in climate policies, political orientation and use of fossil-fuelled car, are associated with perceived fairness of increasing fuel tax, and whether there are regional differences in these variables. Data were collected via a survey in June 2022 in three regions with different characteristics in Finland: Helsinki, Finland Proper, and Northern Ostrobothnia. Our results reveal that residents in rural areas and sparsely populated regions perceive fuel tax increases as less fair. Climate concern, trust and political orientation were found to influence fairness perceptions. Moreover, climate concern and trust were lower in sparsely populated regions. Considerations of fairness perceptions are important for successful climate mitigation policy.

title: Beyond productivity: Does ICT agglomeration drive regional eco-efficiency?
Park-targeted greening on firm productivity and emissions: Evidence from China’s national eco-industrial park program
The Evolution of Quantitative Equity Investing: Half a Century of Alpha Research and Institutional Adaptation
abstract: ABSTRACT This survey interprets the evolution of quantitative equity investing as a history of changing constraints rather than a succession of increasingly complicated forecasting models. Portfolio theory made diversification calculable; characteristic‐based investing converted value, momentum, profitability, and low‐risk effects into scalable processes; alternative data shifted competition toward information engineering; machine learning expanded the admissible class of return functions; and large language models and agentic systems are beginning to reorganize research itself. Yet each advance has exposed a new implementation boundary. A predictor must survive point‐in‐time reconstruction, model selection, portfolio translation, turnover, transaction costs, shorting frictions, capacity, latency, regime change, and institutional governance before it becomes alpha. The survey develops alpha decay as the mechanism linking these generations and gives particular attention to the limited transfer of machine‐learning research into production. It argues that artificial intelligence will accelerate both discovery and commoditization. Sustainable advantage is therefore unlikely to reside in a generic model class. It is more likely to arise from proprietary information transformation, economic structure, cost‐aware portfolio construction, execution, organizational memory, and tightly controlled human–machine systems.

title: Policy-induced environmental technology and innovation: a retrospective
abstract: The debate on the relationship between environmental protection and competitiveness has become one of the defining economic policy discussions in Europe and beyond. Critics argue that stricter environmental standards inevitably raise production costs and reduce profitability, with consequences for maintaining competitiveness. Supporters of ambitious climate goals and environmental policy, by contrast, argue that regulation and taxes can stimulate and redirect innovation, improve resource efficiency, and create new markets for clean technologies. In our 2015 study titled ‘Policy-induced environmental technology and inventive efforts: is there a crowding out?’, we aimed to contribute empirical evidence to this discussion by examining under what conditions potential trade-offs between compliance and innovation efforts arise, which types of firms they affect the most, and what policy can do to mitigate potential side-effects. A decade later, the topic is still high on the agenda of academics and policymakers. In this retrospective, we briefly present our initial findings, analyse how the literature has developed since then, and what newer data can tell us. Finally, we discuss implications and routes for future research.

title: Creation After Destruction? Financial Intermediation and Firm Entry After Bank Cleanups
Leadership and the shaping of a field: a study of presidents of the International Association for Feminist Economics
abstract: This article studies the history of feminist economics by focusing on the work of the first 26 presidents of the International Association for Feminist Economists (IAFFE). We combine different types of materials and mix qualitative and bibliometric methods to capture how this group of women helped to shape the field and measure their intellectual links. This group of women does not represent the entire field of feminist economics. Nevertheless, their research and administrative responsibilities, their intellectual interactions and the way they embody a willingness to diversify the association’s leadership and membership are key pieces in the history of feminist economics.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: Words that move markets: ECB presidential tone and euro area bank CDS spreads
Co-founder selection from a marriage market perspective: How the dark triad shapes judgments of interpersonal attraction, resources, and equity demand
abstract: Co-founder selection is a pivotal decision in new venture formation, yet how lead founders evaluate potential partners remains underexplored. Drawing on insights from marriage market theory, we conceptualize co-founder selection as an act of individuated judgment guided by cooperative logic and associated joint utility projection, wherein lead founders assess co-founder candidates based on social-emotional, instrumental, and distributive considerations reflected in interpersonal attraction, resource contributions, and equity demand. We further propose that lead founders' dark triad shifts this judgmental process from joint utility logic to personal utility maximization. Using a conjoint experiment with 206 entrepreneurs making 3296 co-founder selection decisions, we find that interpersonal attraction and resource contributions positively influence willingness to select a co-founder candidate, whereas higher equity demand reduces candidate attractiveness. Critically, lead founders higher in the dark triad display distinct patterns: they discount interpersonal attraction and display heightened sensitivity to equity dilution—assessments that indicate their prioritization of personal over joint value creation. Taken together, these findings reveal how dispositional tendencies influence the judgments underlying co-founder selection, indicating a shift away from the cooperative logic assumed in marriage market theory and co-founder selection toward greater emphasis on personal utility considerations. We discuss theoretical implications of these findings and offer practical guidance for navigating the complexities of co-founder selection.

title: Re‐thinking academic entrepreneurship: Micro, meso, and macro perspectives
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We summarize and synthesize the papers contained in the special issue and use these studies to illustrate key micro, meso, and macro dimensions of academic entrepreneurship, where micro focuses on the scientist, meso is concerned with the university ecosystem, and macro refers to the broader entrepreneurial ecosystem. A key finding from our special issue is that routines, pivots, and intellectual property, which determine venture viability, emerge from granular individual action, including identity formation and evolution. We also find that macro instruments such as public funding/grants and institutional governance appear to steer resources toward viable science‐based ventures. Our essay concludes by presenting numerous additional micro, meso, and macro research questions to motivate future research on the managerial and public policy implications of academic entrepreneurship. Managerial Summary There are several key managerial implications of our essay and this special issue. “Managers” and those who supervise academic entrepreneurs need to develop and support their scientists entrepreneurial identity formation and evolution. Managers also need to enhance incentives for academic entrepreneurship and foster a culture within their academic departments, schools, and colleges that support these activities. Policymakers need to design entrepreneurial training for scientists with both “micro” and “macro” issues in mind.

title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. When the platform raises the fee-per-lead for a customer-type, those customers—conditional on receiving the same number of provider quotes—are quoted lower prices. However, if the fee is sufficiently high, providers purchase fewer of these leads, which can reduce the number of quotes and diminish customer surplus. To maximize social welfare, a simple policy that sets a market-clearing fee-per-lead for each customer-type guarantees at least [Formula: see text] of the first-best welfare and at least [Formula: see text] of the welfare under the welfare-optimal fees. The first-best outcome can be achieved by subsidizing providers for each job well done, so that experienced providers with cheaper sources of leads do not exit the platform. Understanding these welfare trade-offs can help platforms design policies that support balanced marketplace growth and preserve a sustainable revenue stream. This paper was accepted by Srikanth Jagabathula, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07399 .

title: Early Environmental Shocks and Organizational Reconfiguration in High-Growth Ventures
abstract: We study whether shocks from local natural disasters can leave durable organizational traces in young high-growth ventures. In principle, such firms may be relatively resilient to localized disruption because they are designed to scale beyond local markets and rely heavily on knowledge-based assets. We examine this possibility using a panel of 19,984 U.S. startups founded between 1985 and 2010 that subsequently received venture financing. We identify ventures whose founding counties experience natural disasters within 12 months of founding using FEMA Major Disaster Declarations. Ventures exposed to disasters at an early stage exhibit higher subsequent failure hazards and no general advantage in follow-on financing, yet show higher IPO hazards in favorable market windows, a pattern consistent with greater responsiveness to opportunities requiring substantial organizational reconfiguration. Descriptive employee-level evidence further documents differences in organizational structure and composition consistent with greater retained fluidity among exposed ventures. Drawing on organization design and imprinting theory, we interpret these patterns as consistent with the possibility that disasters function as forcing environments that entrench early-stage coordination features such as flatness, role fluidity, and broader expertise that would otherwise attenuate as ventures mature. These durable organizational traces may, in turn, shape ventures’ subsequent capacity for reconfiguration. We discuss implications for organizational adaptation, imprinting, entrepreneurial geography, and organizational responses to crises.

title: Visual Plant Imagery and Property Valuation: A Descriptive Analysis
abstract: Online home profiles with more plant imagery are associated with higher property valuations, even after accounting for extensive property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors.

title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
Digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing: the mediating role of supply chain complexity in technology-driven operations
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing firms, with particular attention to the statistical mediating role of supply chain complexity. It addresses the limited understanding of how digital technologies, including AI, IoT, and cybersecurity, operate collectively rather than in isolation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability view (DCV), the study employs a quantitative research design using survey data from 732 managerial and supervisory respondents working in manufacturing firms in Mississippi, West Virginia, and Arkansas. Structural equation modeling (SEM) using AMOS is applied to test the proposed relationships. Findings The results indicate that digital ecosystems are positively associated with supply chain resilience, with cybersecurity exhibiting the strongest association with the Digital Ecosystem construct. Supply chain complexity shows a positive but comparatively smaller association with resilience and the statistically significant indirect relationship is consistent with partial mediation. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to manufacturing firms in selected U.S. states, which may affect generalizability. Future research could explore cross-industry and cross-country contexts and examine additional mediating or moderating mechanisms. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should consider investing in integrated digital infrastructure, prioritizing cybersecurity capabilities and using data-driven technologies while proactively managing the complexity of digital transformation. Originality/value This study advances a systems-level understanding of digital ecosystems in supply chains by showing that integrated digital capabilities, rather than isolated technologies, are positively associated with resilience in complex operational environments.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: Navigating Unknown Unknowns in Megaprojects: Insights from the Immersed Tunnel Section of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge Project
How customer incivility reduces employees’ compassionate service behaviors: the exacerbating role of leader–member exchange
abstract: Purpose Grounded in uncertainty reduction theory and conservation of resources theory, this study investigates the relationship between customer incivility and compassionate service behavior among frontline employees. In particular, it examines whether workplace uncertainty mediates this relationship and whether, and to what extent, leader–member exchange (LMX) amplifies the negative effect of workplace uncertainty on compassionate service behavior, thereby moderating the indirect effect of customer incivility on compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach This study employed a four-wave, time-lagged survey design using a sample of 316 customer-facing service employees in the United States, recruited through Prolific. The hypothesized moderated mediation model was tested using the PROCESS macro in IBM SPSS. Findings Results indicated a significant negative indirect effect of customer incivility on compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty. Furthermore, both the relationship between workplace uncertainty and compassionate service behavior as well as the indirect relationship between customer incivility and compassionate service behavior through workplace uncertainty were stronger for employees who reported higher LMX compared to those with weaker LMX. Originality/value This study contributes to the growing literature on the consequences of customer incivility by uncovering workplace uncertainty as a key mediating mechanism. It also challenges the conventional view of LMX as uniformly beneficial, showing that, under conditions of heightened uncertainty, employees in high-quality LMX relationships may experience stronger constraints on compassionate service behavior because uncertainty represents a greater disruption to their typical experience of relational clarity and predictability.

title: A bibliometric assessment of hidden champions research: Mapping an evolving field
Promotion and prevention focus on playful work design: the role of inclusive leadership in the relationship between employee thriving and job burnout
abstract: In the rapidly evolving workplace, employees need to adopt proactive strategies to thrive and avert job burnout. Playful work design (PWD) offers promising avenues for achieving these outcomes. Yet empirical evidence and its underlying psychological processes warrant further investigation. Building on regulatory focus theory (RFT), we hypothesize that PWD might impact employee thriving at work and job burnout through promotion and prevention focus under the boundary conditions of inclusive leadership. We collected three-wave data from full-time employees (N = 468) in Pakistan. Our results showed that promotion focus mediated the positive relationship between PWD and thriving at work, whereas prevention focus mediated the negative relationship between PWD and job burnout. Inclusive leadership moderated the positive indirect relationship between PWD and thriving at work via promotion focus. It also moderated the negative indirect relationship between PWD and job burnout via prevention focus. The findings of our study contribute to the applications of RFT by suggesting that PWD may function as a proactive self-regulatory process, while also offering actionable insights for managers and practitioners.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Paradoxical effect of exploitative leadership on employee performance
abstract: Based on paradox theory, this study aims to investigate the paradoxical consequences of exploitative leadership on employee work outcomes. From the perspective of the ‘performing–learning’ lens, we hypothesize that exploitative leaders boost employee task performance but inhibit employee creative performance. In a three-wave time-lagged field study with 106 leaders and 249 subordinates, the results confirm our hypotheses. We also find the mediating effects of performance pressure and intrinsic motivation, as well as the moderating effect of traditional values. Facing exploitative leaders, employees with high traditionality show high task performance out of performance pressure, whereas those low in traditionality display worse creative performance because of poor intrinsic motivation. The findings contribute to the exploitative leadership literature, emphasizing the distinct influences of exploitative leadership on different aspects of performance, and have implications for practice.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Closing the opportunity gap: Exploring micro-enterprises' behavioral intention to integrate with digital platforms for a broader agri-food system
abstract: Digital agriculture platforms offer marginalized micro-enterprises a vital pathway to bridge the opportunity gap and overcome structural dependencies on focal companies. However, mainstream literature's focal-firm bias leaves the adoption logic of these grassroots operators underexplored. Addressing this gap, we operationalize an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) framework. Using PLS-SEM on data from 167 micro-enterprises, this study investigates their platform integration behaviors. Results reveal distinct adoption pathways: a platform's operational simplicity cannot trigger adoption without first cultivating a favorable organizational mindset (full mediation). Conversely, its tangible strategic benefits—unexpectedly anchored in macro-systemic food safety guarantees and ecological conservation rather than mere short-term profits—motivate integration both directly and indirectly (partial mediation). Socio-psychologically, although micro-enterprises clearly perceive external pressures like government mandates and peer emulation, these fail to translate into adoption intent—a recognition-action gap that leaves adoption strongly conditioned by financial affordability and technical readiness instead. Ultimately, these dynamics reframe the presumed myopic rationality of micro-enterprises: viewed through the lens of push-pull theory, the strategic draw of sustainable platform value is offset by baseline capability constraints, such that this value becomes actionable only when matched by sufficient capability. Theoretically, this demonstrates that cultivating truly inclusive digital ecosystems necessitates shifting the analytical focus from top-down focal designs to bottom-up grassroots decision-making. Practically, it advises policymakers and platform sponsors to move beyond normative persuasion toward tangible capability empowerment and value-driven platform architectures.

title: When Does Mindfulness Translate Into Consumer Well‐Being? The Role of Mindful Consumption and Meditation Regularity
abstract: ABSTRACT Mindfulness correlates with higher life satisfaction, yet consumer wellbeing research rarely specifies the behavioral route through which this relationship emerges. Drawing on self‐regulation theory, the research proposes mindful consumption as that route and, drawing on self‐determination theory, evaluates meditation regularity as a boundary condition. Meditation regularity is selected over other candidate moderators given that meditation practice is the primary activity through which mindfulness is cultivated, so the regularity of that practice should govern how far mindful awareness has been internalized and, in turn, whether wellbeing gains run through consumption behavior or through a direct psychological pathway. Two studies test a moderated mediation model. Study 1, a controlled experiment with postgraduate students, provides the experimental benchmark, given that a 2‐month guided meditation intervention raised mindfulness and mindful consumption relative to a control condition, whereas the postintervention associations among mindfulness, mindful consumption, and life satisfaction supply explanatory evidence of mediation. Study 2, a survey of 503 consumers (74% nonstudents), supports the mediation and clarifies heterogeneity by meditation regularity, which strengthens both the mindfulness to mindful consumption association and the direct mindfulness to life satisfaction association, whereas the indirect effect through mindful consumption is significant among new meditators and non‐significant among regular meditators. The findings position self‐reported mindful consumption as a relevant behavioral mechanism that links mindfulness with consumer wellbeing and identify meditation regularity as a boundary condition that governs both the mindfulness to mindful consumption association and the direct pathway to life satisfaction. Implications emerge for interventions and marketing programs that promote consumer wellbeing through more intentional, consequence‐aware, value‐aligned consumption.

title: From Conversational Agents Back to Human Agents? Drivers and Inhibitors of Customer Switching Intention and Behavior
abstract: ABSTRACT In customer service, companies increasingly replace human agents (HAs) with AI‐powered conversational agents (CAs) because they provide efficiency gains, instant responses, and constant availability. Yet customer service still requires HAs, as customers continue to seek their assistance for different reasons. Against this background, we conducted a two‐wave longitudinal online study of European customers to examine which factors determine switching from CAs to HAs, capturing switching intention in study 1 ( N = 468) and self‐reported switching behavior 2 months later among recontacted participants in study 2 ( N = 237). The pull factor, driven by perceived usefulness of HAs, increases switching intention, whereas the mooring factor, driven by inertia and habit, inhibits both intention and behavior. The push factor reduces switching intention, suggesting that negative CA experiences may lead customers to disengage from customer service rather than switching to a HA. Task difficulty intensifies the push and pull factors while weakening the mooring factor. Switching intention positively influences subsequent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that HAs are particularly valuable for difficult service tasks that CAs struggle to handle. Firms should therefore identify difficult or unresolved requests and provide customers with a visible and straightforward option to switch to a HA before they disengage from customer service.

title: Paying for Pain: How Healthcare Costs Influence Physical Pain Predictions
abstract: ABSTRACT As healthcare costs continue to rise in the United States, consumers increasingly encounter financial burdens that impact their economic well‐being along with their psychological experiences surrounding medical care. This research examines how the pain of paying, a well‐established concept in marketing, shapes consumers' predictions of physical pain associated with healthcare procedures. Across three experimental studies, we find that higher out‐of‐pocket costs increase anticipated physical pain through pain of paying and financial anxiety. Study 1 demonstrates that out‐of‐pocket costs heighten anticipated physical pain via a sequential pathway of pain of paying and financial anxiety. Study 2 shows that cost‐induced financial discomfort extends to behavioral intentions, reducing willingness to schedule a procedure. Study 3 identifies general financial stress as a moderator, such that effects on scheduling intentions are strongest among financially stressed consumers. These findings extend pain of paying theory into the healthcare domain by demonstrating how financial cues spillover into perceptual and affective judgments under medical uncertainty. The results offer implications for healthcare patients, marketers, providers, and policymakers by illustrating how payment structures and cost communication may inadvertently shape patients' expectations and intentions, particularly among financially vulnerable populations.

title: The Algorithmic Well‐Being Paradox: When AI Decision Delegation Helps and Hurts Consumer Well‐Being
abstract: ABSTRACT As generative AI increasingly shapes consumer decision‐making, its implications for consumer well‐being remain unclear. Existing research largely focuses on the trade‐off between algorithmic efficiency and autonomy loss. This research advances understanding by proposing the algorithmic well‐being paradox, whereby the same AI delegation can enhance or diminish well‐being depending on the consumption context. Integrating Savoring Theory and Self‐Determination Theory, we develop a framework that explains when and why these divergent outcomes occur. To test the proposed relationships, four studies were conducted with 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiments ( N = 1427) spanning multiple consumption domains, including cameras, guided tours, ergonomic chairs, glamping trips, smartphones, Arctic expeditions, and smart‐home systems. Study 1 demonstrates that the effects of algorithmic delegation differ between experiential and material consumption. Studies 2 and 3 identify anticipatory savoring and autonomy frustration as the underlying mechanisms, while Study 4 confirms the proposed dual‐mediation process in a high‐complexity context. Results show that consumption type shapes how consumers respond to AI delegation. In experiential consumption, AI delegation increases well‐being by enhancing anticipatory savoring, with these benefits outweighing autonomy concerns. In material consumption, AI delegation reduces well‐being by increasing autonomy frustration, which diminishes the benefits of convenience. These findings advance human‐AI interaction research by demonstrating that the impact of algorithmic delegation depends on consumers' underlying consumption goals and provide guidance for designing more human‐centered AI decision‐support systems.

title: Mixed methods research: Critical review and guidelines for stronger design, integration, and contribution
abstract: Mixed methods research has a prominent place in tourism and hospitality scholarship, yet adoption has advanced faster than methodological selectivity, which leaves many studies combining qualitative and quantitative strands without explaining why both strands were necessary, how the strands were related, or what integrated inference their combination alone made possible. Drawing on a critical review of 222 mixed methods studies published in leading tourism and hospitality journals, this article identifies dominant patterns, strengths and weaknesses, and underused possibilities. In response, the article offers a stage-based guide that links problem formulation, purpose selection, design fit, sampling bridges, strand roles, integration, divergence handling, reporting architecture, and contribution development. In doing so, the article advances a more demanding standard for mixed methods scholarship and argues that the next phase of tourism and hospitality research should shift from routine method combination toward integrated inferences that are conceptually sharper, methodologically clearer, and practically more useful.

title: Digital Search Disruption and Corporate Governance: Evidence From Google's Withdrawal and Executive Gender Diversity in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines whether disruptions to digital information infrastructure influence corporate governance outcomes. Specifically, it investigates how Google's 2010 withdrawal from mainland China affected executive gender diversity by altering firms' external visibility within global information networks. Research Findings/Insights Using a difference‐in‐differences framework, the study finds that firms with greater prewithdrawal exposure to Google experienced a significant decline in executive gender diversity after the withdrawal. The results remain robust across alternative specifications and identification tests. Mechanism analyses suggest that reductions in foreign media visibility and weakened foreign investor monitoring are important channels, which reduce external governance pressures. Further analyses reveal that the effect is stronger in regions with less supportive gender‐norm environments and greater information‐accessibility constraints, with gender norms showing a more robust moderating role. Theoretical/Academic Implications This study extends corporate governance research by identifying digital information infrastructure as an important governance‐relevant information intermediary. The findings broaden existing perspectives beyond traditional disclosure and monitoring mechanisms by showing that governance outcomes are also shaped by the infrastructures that determine firms' visibility and accessibility to external stakeholders. The study further demonstrates that executive gender diversity responds not only to internal organizational choices but also to changes in firms' external informational environments. Practitioner/Policy Implications The findings highlight the importance of maintaining reliable and accessible digital information infrastructures that support external accountability mechanisms. Firms should treat digital visibility as a strategic governance resource and develop diversified channels to maintain stakeholder connections when key information infrastructures are disrupted.

title: Ethical Foundations of Social Entrepreneurship Competencies: A Systematic Review and Integrative Framework
abstract: Social entrepreneurship education is flourishing. However, research on social entrepreneurship competencies remains highly fragmented. Without a coherent understanding of these competencies and their ethical underpinnings, researchers cannot explore how they affect the social impact and financial viability of social entrepreneurship, nor can educators determine learning outcomes. We conduct a systematic review of 147 social entrepreneurship articles and identify 12 distinct social entrepreneurship competencies. Guided by deontological, utilitarian, and care ethics, we group these into normative , pragmatic , and relational competencies. We furthermore identify and discuss their relationships, antecedents, and outcomes, resulting in propositions. Our paper enables research on how competencies help social entrepreneurs navigate ethical dilemmas, whether education effectively cultivates them, and whether their acquisition leads to desired outcomes and social impact. We hope this review stimulates more systematic empirical research on the effects of social entrepreneurial competencies and longitudinal studies on how to develop them. In particular, we argue that new outcome variables (beyond mere intention) must be investigated, especially individual behaviour, team dynamics, organisational performance, and social impact.

title: The Relevance and Materiality of Illegal Acts: Examining Auditor and Investor Judgments
abstract: Abstract The audit expectation gap exists and persists due to changing “…social, economic, and political developments of the time.” (Sikka, et al., 1998) Like stakeholders’ demands for and the profession’s response to fraud detection in the 2000s, investors are increasingly interested in C-suite employees’ and entity’s illegal acts, finding them both relevant and material (Cline, Walkling & Yore, 2018). This study identifies a gap between auditors’ and investors’ relevance and materiality judgments of a CEO’s illegal act. Varying role (auditor vs. investor) and using experience as a control (audit vs no audit), results show that non-auditor investors rate a CEO’s illegal act as significantly more relevant and material than do auditors placed in either role, while auditors in an investor role find a CEO’s illegal act significantly more material than auditors in an auditor role. Qualitative comments indicate that investors see managers’ personal misconduct as indicative of their lack of personal integrity and lose trust in them across personal to work situations. Auditors do not make the same connection. Our findings highlight challenges for the audit profession in meeting investors’ expectations in the context of managers’ illegal acts.

title: Distressed firms and loan guarantee programmes during the COVID-19 crisis
Towards mission theory: A systematic literature review of its critiques and avenues for progress (2010–2025)
abstract: During the last 15 years, researchers and practitioners alike showed a newfound interest in the potential of ‘mission-oriented’ innovation policy to tackle current societal challenges. In this period, the approach prompted multiple reflections and critiques from orthodox and heterodox scholars alike. However, a structured appraisal of this debate has been missing. Untangling its analytical complexity, this paper presents a systematic literature review of 224 articles and book chapters published between 2010 and 2025 to appraise the state-of-the-art debate within ‘mission theory’. Using the PRISMA Protocol and abductive thematic analysis, the paper identifies 18 themes mapped across two analytical dimensions: positioning (identifying either ‘external’ challenges or ‘internal’ gaps within mission theory); and layering (identifying challenges and gaps based on a ‘foundational’, ‘theoretical’, or ‘empirical’ ground). Building on the findings, the paper reflects on the sociological conditions preventing the progress of mission theory in contemporary research efforts – ultimately calling for greater epistemological reflexivity in the strategies adopted by researchers and practitioners to develop avenues for its further progress.

title: From impact to legitimacy: Communicative responsibility and the governance of research impact
abstract: Universities face growing pressure to make clearer the public value of research, yet documented impact does not automatically translate into public recognition or legitimacy. This paper develops the concept of Communicative Responsibility, the institutional and ethical obligation to communicate research outcomes in ways that are legible, accessible, and resonant beyond specialist assessment contexts. Drawing on responsible research literatures, including Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) and Responsible Research in Business and Management (RRBM), we argue that communication should be treated as a core component of research governance and legitimacy. Empirically, we use the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021 Impact Database to examine the communicative strengths and limitations of existing impact evidence. REF impact case studies are not the only way to understand research impact, nor are they primarily written for public audiences. However, they offer a useful proxy for examining how impact might be perceived and how it could be shared more effectively. Using mixed methods, we combine qualitative content analysis of 119 purposively sampled Business and Management cases with quantitative text analysis of all 504 non-redacted cases in the field. Findings show diverse impacts generated through collaboration, interdisciplinarity, and international partnerships, but also substantial variation in communicability. Cases that identify beneficiaries, pathways to change, and accessible dissemination routes are better positioned to reduce the impact-recognition gap. We contribute to theorizing Communicative Responsibility as a governance-relevant extension of responsible research. Our findings have wider implications for how universities communicate impact beyond assessment systems.

title: The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)
When women lead: local political representation and pro-women institutions
abstract: Whether women in office govern differently from men is well documented; whether they govern differently for women is not. The latter is the crux of active representation theory, which expects representatives to act for those they mirror: does electing women change what governments do for women? We investigate the relationship between electing female mayors and councilors and the existence of Pro-Women Institutions across all 5,565 cities of Brazil during four election cycles (2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020). Our results partially support the active representation relationship. While female mayors’ presence increases the likelihood of pro-women institutions, local councilors either do not or are negatively linked to them. Robustness checks through a regression discontinuity design corroborate these findings, and heterogeneous treatment effects on race paint a wider picture about intersectionality. Our findings highlight how female elected representatives might achieve substantial change for their female constituents in local government.

title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
abstract: There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

title: Whose voices and which effects? A scoping review of migration and social media effects
abstract: Social media plays a central role in shaping migration experiences and public perceptions of migration. However, despite growing research activity, no systematic overview exists on how social media effects are examined across host and migrant populations. This scoping review synthesizes 65 empirical studies on social media effects in the context of migration published between 2020 and 2025. Guided by the differential susceptibility to media effects model, the analysis focuses on content types, sample characteristics, the conceptualization of social media, effect types, and mediating and moderating factors. The findings reveal two largely disconnected strands of research: quantitative, host-focused studies that emphasize negative attitudinal effects, and qualitative, migrant-centered studies that focus on empowerment. Framing effects, platform affordances, producer perspectives, and individual, structural, and social factors remain largely neglected. Overall, the review highlights the need for integrative research that bridges the perspectives of both hosts and migrants and pays greater attention to how migrants themselves perceive, interpret, and respond to social media portrayals and migration-related content.

title: A response to Francis and Wesselink’s “measuring structural racism in neighborhoods”
Estimation of the relative effectiveness and waning of the monovalent third dose of COVID-19 vaccine against hospital admission in France: a novel self-controlled case series analysis
Correction: Effects of two community violence interruption programs on firearm violence in Washington, DC
Structure–behavior integrated risk prediction of vehicle groups using Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Accurate identification of vehicle-group-level traffic risk is important for intelligent transportation safety management. Existing risk-prediction studies have mainly focused on individual vehicles, pairwise interactions, or aggregated surrogate safety indicators, while the role of group-level structure–behavior coupling remains insufficiently examined. To address this issue, this paper proposes a leakage-aware structure–behavior graph learning framework for Vehicle Group (VG) risk modeling. First, time-resolved VG graphs are constructed from high-frequency MAGIC trajectory data using an impact-induced grouping strategy with controlled supplementary spatial adjacency. Second, node-level surrogate risk states are defined using inverse Time-to-Collision (iTTC) and activated Post-Encroachment Time (PET), and then aggregated into VG-level surrogate risk labels through a group-risk ratio. Third, structural descriptors and behavioral features are integrated within a Graph Attention Network (GAT) for VG-level risk classification. To improve methodological transparency, the revised framework explicitly justifies the surrogate-labeling thresholds using empirical distributions, threshold tradeoff curves, and sensitivity analyses. It also includes leakage-audit experiments to examine whether model performance is driven by label-proximal surrogate quantities. Experiments on the MAGIC dataset show that the proposed model achieves strong and stable performance under repeated random seeds, with F1-score = 0.960 ± 0.002, ROC-AUC = 0.949 ± 0.008, PR-AUC = 0.991 ± 0.001, and Brier score = 0.058 ± 0.002. Compared with linear, neural, tree-based, and graph-based baselines, the proposed model provides competitive risk-identification performance, particularly in recall, false-negative control, and positive-class ranking. Additional robustness, prospective-prediction, and interpretability analyses indicate that the learned structure–behavior representation remains informative under temporal and sampling-frequency shifts and can highlight risk-relevant vehicles within VGs. The findings should be interpreted as evidence of structure-aware predictive association under a surrogate-labeling framework, rather than as proof that VG risk is inherently structural or that the model is deployment-ready. Overall, this study provides a more transparent and auditable graph-learning approach for VG-level surrogate risk modeling, offering decision-support insights for future CAV-oriented traffic safety management subject to external validation and deployment-oriented computational testing.

title: Measuring Automatic Cognitive Responses to Erotic Stimuli Using Implicit Association Tests: Reliability and Validity Aspects
abstract: Recently, implicit associations have been forwarded as relevant cognitive determinants of sexual desire and arousal. In the present study, using a cross-sectional design, implicit association tests (IAT) were used to measure the strength of automatic associations of erotic stimuli with positive versus negative valence (liking IAT) and with wanting versus not wanting (wanting IAT). The internal consistency and temporal stability, and the construct and criterion validity of the IATs were investigated. Additionally, the effects of stimulus mode on the psychometric properties of these IATs were examined. For this purpose, picture-and-word and full-picture IAT versions of the liking and wanting IATs were compared. Sexual function was measured using the Female Sexual Function Index for women and the International Index of Erectile Function for men. To examine the construct and criterion validity of the IATs, the Sexual Opinion Survey (SOS) and the Sexual Thoughts Questionnaire (STQ) were administered. A community sample was examined (N = 335 total; 234 women). The internal consistency and temporal stability of all IATs were found satisfactory to excellent. The criterion validity of the IATs demonstrated only a few small-size correlations with explicit sexual attitudes. Contrary to similar previous research, the IATs did not predict sexual function level. Speculative explanations for these unexpected findings are presented.

title: Use of Post-Coital Strategies to Prevent Pregnancy: Findings from a National Sample of Adolescents and Young Adults in the United States
abstract: In the context of increasing restrictions on sexual and reproductive health care, inadequate sex education, and increasing antihormonal contraceptive sentiment, we examined post-coital pregnancy prevention behavior among a nationally representative sample of U.S. adolescents and young adults (AYA). We developed a novel measure of post-coital contraceptive strategies (i.e., actions taken after sexual intercourse with the intent of reducing the likelihood of pregnancy) and fielded this measure for the first time as part of a 2025 online, population-based survey of English-speaking 15–29-year-olds assigned female at birth (n = 1,259). Of the 633 AYA who reported having ever had penile-vaginal sex and were not currently pregnant, 25.0% used at least one post-coital strategy to prevent pregnancy the last time they had sex. While methods with established effectiveness (i.e., emergency contraception and copper intrauterine device) were used by 8.9% respondents, 16.1% reported using a non-medically evidenced post-coital strategy, the most common being praying (9.4%). Post-coital strategy use varied by age, race and ethnicity, and number of contraceptive methods used. In multivariable analyses, contraceptive knowledge was negatively associated with post-coital strategy use. Regardless of effectiveness, post-coital strategies are common enough to warrant inclusion in behavioral surveillance and attention in health education and clinical practice.

title: The Relationship Between Cognitive Processes, Self-Stigma, and Internalizing Psychopathology in Individuals with Sexual Interests in Minors
Being a Partner or a Mother: Breastfeeding Mothers’ Perceptions and Experiences of Breast Milk and Sexuality in the Postpartum Period
abstract: Abstract This study aimed to explore breastfeeding mothers’ perceptions and experiences related to breast milk and sexuality between the third and sixth months postpartum. A descriptive qualitative design was employed. The sample consisted of 10 mothers, including primiparous ( n = 4) and multiparous ( n = 6) women, with a mean age of 29 years. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews. Thematic analysis was used to analyze the data. Three main themes emerged from the analysis: avoidance of sexuality, maintaining sexuality as a responsibility, and coping with the effects of breastfeeding on sexuality. Six subthemes were identified within these main themes: physical changes in sexual dynamics; psychological changes in sexual dynamics; religious, social, and cultural influences on sexuality; fulfillment of the female role; changing perceptions of breasts; and various coping strategies. The findings suggest that breastfeeding and postpartum physiological and sociocultural factors shape mothers’ sexual experiences, with sexuality often being perceived as inappropriate during this period due to cultural and religious norms, while participants’ perceptions related to breast milk also contribute to these experiences. Mothers attempt to balance breastfeeding with maintaining their sexual relationships, which frequently leads to emotional distress. It is recommended that healthcare professionals address breastfeeding, breast milk, and sexuality within breastfeeding education programs and provide individualized, culturally sensitive guidance for couples.

title: Burnout Market Feminism: Urban Chinese Businesswomen in the Internet Age Ling Tang. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2026. 208 pp. $50.00 (pbk). ISBN 9780262051880
Multi-electrolyzer system energy management strategy incorporating cold-hot start for improving green hydrogen production and electrolyzer lifespan
Decarbonization dispatch for AI computing center parks considering task-level carbon traceability
abstract: The decarbonization dispatch of AI computing centers should not stop at controlling total park-level carbon emissions; it should also trace the energy sources, carbon-emission responsibility, and low-carbon labels of individual AI tasks. To address the limitation that existing studies mainly adopt park-average accounting and therefore cannot support task-level accounting, this paper proposes a decarbonization dispatch optimization method for AI computing center parks considering task-level carbon traceability. Taking the task execution trajectory as the main line, the proposed method links resource-pool startup and shutdown, IT power consumption, thermally inertial cooling, network storage, and energy-storage operation, thereby forming a closed relationship among the task ledger, energy-consumption ledger, and low-carbon ledger. Meanwhile, a unique low-carbon electricity claim and a label-violation CVaR constraint are introduced to control the risk of label failure under uncertain scenarios. Rolling-dispatch results on the Chenggong, Yunnan, China and the modified IEEE 118-bus system show that the proposed method can significantly improve task-level low-carbon performance with only a small increase in low-carbon attribute procurement and energy-storage throughput. In the Chenggong park case, the operating cost is reduced by 6.6%, and market-based park carbon emissions are reduced by 11.3%. The method provides a dispatch modeling basis for shifting low-carbon computing services from park-average accounting to task-level verification.

title: Exploiting dynamics of electricity–hydrogen–carbon markets using adaptive operating rules for hybrid energy systems
abstract: Electricity markets have traditionally shaped the operating strategies of hybrid energy systems (HESs) integrating hydropower, wind, and photovoltaic resources. Meanwhile, the rapid emergence of hydrogen and carbon markets is transforming system operation by linking electricity supply, hydrogen production, and carbon-related revenues. However, existing electricity–hydrogen operating rules do not account for how pathway-dependent carbon values alter the allocation of renewable electricity between grid delivery and hydrogen production. This study embeds pathway-dependent carbon valuation into the shared energy-allocation decision, allowing the carbon signal to reshape the relative benefits of grid delivery and hydrogen production and propagate into hybrid system operation and operating-rule parameters. An operation-mediated price-feedback framework is incorporated into the long-term operation model to maximize operating benefit and supply assurance. The optimized results are then synthesized into adaptive operating rules through a parameterization–simulation–optimization framework. A case study of the Ertan hydro–hydrogen–wind–photovoltaic system shows that the reservoir release is the key decision variable in rule formulation. The derived optimal operating rules achieve 616.03 million USD in operating benefit and a 98.96% assurance rate, improving conventional rules by 14.94% and 10.79%. These results demonstrate that adaptive operating rules can effectively exploit electricity–hydrogen–carbon market dynamics, thereby enhancing the energy use efficiency of HESs.

title: A two-stage restoration model for power distribution systems with integrated satellite-terrestrial communication networks
abstract: With the development of the satellite internet, the low Earth orbit (LEO)-based satellite communication network (SCN) is gradually applied to power grids to meet the emergency communication requirements. By the advantages of SCN, this paper proposes a two-stage restoration framework for power distribution systems (PDSs) with an integrated satellite-terrestrial communication network (STCN). In Stage 1, a multi-time period operation simulation model for LEO satellite constellation is established to derive the available satellite communication links during restoration. Then, a MILP restoration model is developed that considers the operation constraints of PDSs and STCNs in Stage 2 to obtain the optimal PDS restoration strategy under cyber-physical interaction. The STCN includes an SCN and a terrestrial communication network (TCN), which are coordinated to transmit the operation information of PDSs. Finally, the effectiveness of the optimal restoration strategy is verified by constructing a constellation with 1000 LEO satellites for the PDSs in a practical area. Also, the influences of LEO satellite operation parameters are analyzed in the case studies.

title: Evaluating the global economy-wide impact of energy efficiency policies in buildings
Thermoelectric energy harvesting for sustainable urban infrastructures: Opportunities, challenges, and deployment pathways
Hydrogen valleys: Advancing the hydrogen economy through decarbonization, energy flexibility, and sector coupling
Household infrastructure expansion without spatial convergence during urbanization: Evidence from Chinese cities
abstract: Infrastructure provision underpins basic needs and socioeconomic development, yet systematic city-level evidence on how household infrastructure service provision and its spatial inequalities evolve during the rapid urbanization remains limited. Using official statistics for 295 prefecture-level cities in China from 2006 to 2022, we assess household access to water and energy services. To account for fuel substitution, natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas are treated as substitutable energy carriers, with the higher of their supply rates representing household energy provision. We construct a two-dimensional infrastructure provision index ( IP ), quantify population-weighted inequality across cities and provinces, decompose inequality changes into mean-provision and spatial-dispersion effects, and classify provincial trajectories of within-province inequality. The population-weighted mean IP increased from 0.21 to 0.51, and provision improved in 289 of the 295 cities. Despite this broad expansion, between-city inequality increased from 0.29 to 0.42, while between-province inequality increased from 0.23 to 0.28. Decomposition shows that rising average provision exerted an inequality-reducing effect, but this was more than offset by increasing spatial dispersion. Within-province trajectories were heterogeneous, ranging from decline or reversal to strong increase, with differences primarily associated with the magnitude and timing of dispersion growth. Socioeconomic development and urbanization were positively associated with provision in descriptive comparisons, but these relationships were not stable across panel specifications. These results show that broad improvements in household infrastructure provision do not necessarily lead to spatial convergence, underscoring the need to evaluate both the overall expansion and spatial distribution of infrastructure services.

title: Needs for more integrated, inclusive, and policy-Relevant modeling of food system transitions: Insights from a systematic review
Insufficient Environmental Protection by the European Regulatory Framework for Pesticides
abstract: Abstract Schriever et al. (2025) argue that environmental risk assessment of pesticides in the European Union is sufficiently protective and that regulatory thresholds are rarely exceeded. Here, we reexamine these claims based on existing evidence from monitoring, systematic reviews, and different types of field studies. The available evidence indicates that measured pesticide concentrations frequently exceed predicted concentrations and regulatory thresholds and are associated with adverse ecological impacts. The mechanisms driving this result include the joint action of pesticides applied in temporal and spatial proximity, varied environmental conditions, interactive effects of pesticides with additional stressors, and indirect ecological effects that propagate within biological communities. These neglected intricacies explain why current single-substance prospective assessments tend to underpredict real-world pesticide exposure and impact in field settings. The corollary is that the current regulatory framework in Europe proves to be insufficient to protect biodiversity and ecosystems. Priority regulatory reforms include strengthening postregistration monitoring, refining predictive exposure models, and explicitly considering landscape context, indirect and mixture effects, and interactions with nonchemical stressors.

title: Ebullition-Enhanced Release of Microplastics from Aquatic Sediment to Overlying Water: An Overlooked Transport Pathway
abstract: Abstract Microplastics (MPs) in aquatic systems are typically attributed to wastewater, runoff and atmospheric inputs, whereas the remobilization of sediment-associated MPs by benthic gas ebullition remains poorly understood. Here, we show that air-purged ebullition mobilized four common MPs, polyethylene (PE), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), and polylactic acid (PLA), from sediments into the overlying water, with release ratios of 8.9%–12.1% over 9 d. Suspended MP concentrations in the overlying water increased rapidly during the first 48 h, followed by slower release and eventual plateauing, with the decelerating release behavior empirically described by a power-law model. Theoretical calculations suggest that aggregation with suspended sediment can reduce the flotation velocities of MPs from 9.38–9.99 cm·s–1 to 8.64–9.95 cm·s–1. Combined experimental observations and theoretical analyses support a coupled flotation mechanism involving MPs attachment to rising bubbles, bubble-driven flow that counteracts gravitational settling, and transient pressure gradients. These processes could convert sediments from a long-term sink into a secondary source of MPs during ebullition. Overall, this study identifies benthic gas ebullition as an underappreciated pathway for MP remobilization and provides a mechanistic framework for understanding the fate and transport of sediment-associated MPs in aquatic environments.

title: High Sewage Sludge Loading Drives N2O-Dominated Warming Potential and Destabilizes Soil Microbial Networks during Ryegrass Cultivation
abstract: Abstract The application of sludge as a fertilizer contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, but the associated microbial and geochemical mechanisms across sludge application rates remain unclear. A field experiment evaluated three sludge application rates (0, 3, and 30 kg/m2) under seedling transplanting (T0, T3, and T30), with an additional direct-seeding treatment (S30) at 30 kg/m2 (wet-weight basis). The results indicated that higher sludge rates elevated cumulative CO2 and N2O emissions, with N2O contributing 69.26–97.74% to the total global warming potential. In contrast, sludge application shifted cumulative CH4 fluxes from net emission in T0 to net uptake in all sludge-amended treatments. S30 produced 1.14 and 2.94 times more CO2 and N2O, respectively, than did T30. The K-edge XANES of calcium revealed dynamic shifts in soil calcium speciation associated with GHG variations, with CaC2O4 (14–23%) peaking at maximum GHG emissions and Cax(C6H8O6)y increasing to 32.8% at later stages, consistent with a calcium pump effect. High sludge application altered microbial diversity, co-occurrence patterns, and network stability. Functional gene analysis indicated an enhanced incomplete denitrification potential through increased norC abundance and reduced N2O reduction capacity. Overall, the sludge application rate was the primary driver of N2O-dominated warming potential, while the planting method exerted additional effects under high sludge loading.

title: Inhalation of Environmentally Simulated PET Nanoplastics Induces Demyelinating Disorders via the CXCL12/CXCR4 Axis
abstract: Abstract The health threat from airborne nanoplastics (NPs) remains unclear, as despite inhalation being a more direct brain entry route than ingestion, current understanding relies on oral exposure and commercial particle models that obscure realistic risks. Here, by integrating environmentally simulated polyethylene terephthalate (PET)-NPs with an aerosol inhalation model that mirrors real-world human exposure (0.1, 1, and 10 mg/m3), we demonstrate that chronic NP inhalation translocated to the brain and induced demyelination, neuroinflammation, and cognitive deficits. The most pronounced effects were observed at the highest exposure dose (10 mg/m3), which is relevant to the occupational settings. Mechanistically, NP exposure triggered astrocytic CXCL12 release, leading to CXCR4-dependent microglial activation and cytokine network dysregulation. In vitro, blockade of CXCR4 with AMD3100 attenuated NP-induced microglial migration and oligodendrocytic myelin basic protein reduction. Our study thus definitively links realistic airborne NP exposure to the key neuropathological features of demyelinating disorders and pinpoints a modifiable molecular pathway that could inform exposure-based preventive strategies. These findings underscore the need for further assessment of airborne NP risks, particularly in occupational settings.

title: Rising food production and persistent inequality over global border areas: A conflict between growth and distribution
Optimal strategy selection for green logistics and decarbonization for sustainable household plastic waste logistics networks
Topographic constraints and economic centrality jointly condition building material stock distribution: high-resolution evidence from the Sichuan-Chongqing region
A scenario-based evaluation framework for renewable capacity scale and photovoltaic capacity ratio in a hydro–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage hybrid energy system
abstract: Renewable-capacity planning in hydro–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage hybrid energy systems is jointly affected by wind–photovoltaic output, inflow, renewable capacity, and photovoltaic capacity ratio, yet their coupled effects on operation and capacity preference remain unclear. This study develops a scenario-based resource–operation–capacity evaluation framework for a cascade hydropower–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage system. Five cumulative-probability levels of wind–photovoltaic joint output and five hydrological exceedance-frequency levels form 25 combined scenarios. Normalized historical recurrence weights are derived through similar-year intersections from 26 assigned historical years. In each scenario, 210 fixed combinations of renewable capacity and photovoltaic capacity ratio are evaluated using a medium- and short-term operational model solved by the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). A two-level decision method identifies the highest-scoring configuration in each scenario and then aggregates configuration scores across all scenarios using recurrence weights. Application to the clean-energy base in the middle reaches of the Yalong River Basin shows that inflow dominates operational-performance variation by affecting hydropower availability and the generation-plan level. Wind–photovoltaic resource conditions alter the balance between renewable output and flexible regulation, whereas the photovoltaic capacity ratio changes joint-output stability and the regulation required from cascade hydropower and pumped storage. Increasing renewable capacity raises transmitted energy, but excessive expansion increases curtailment and load-loss risks. The scenario-dependent highest-scoring configurations span 9000–12000 MW and photovoltaic capacity ratios of 35 %–55 %. Cross-scenario weighting identifies 9000 MW and a 40 % photovoltaic capacity ratio as the probability-weighted optimal configuration under the adopted settings. The framework links representative resource conditions, system operation, and capacity decisions for hydro-dominated renewable-energy planning.

title: Time-interleaved multistage heat pipe-assisted adsorptive dehumidification for stable and high-efficiency supply air control
abstract: This study proposes a multistage heat pipe-assisted adsorptive dehumidifier (HP-AD) designed to address the inherent limitations of conventional desiccant systems, such as excessive supply air temperature rise and high regeneration energy requirements. A fundamental deficiency in single-module HP-ADs is the occurrence of high-amplitude, sawtooth wave-like fluctuations in the supply air’s hydrothermal states. These instabilities are intrinsically tied to the adsorption/desorption kinetics of the adsorbent coupled with the discrete 180° rotation cycles of the module, which collectively compromise the consistency of indoor air quality. To mitigate these fluctuations, a multistage architecture comprising five adsorbent-coated fin-heat pipe modules was developed and experimentally validated. Central to this system is a time-interleaved operational sequence, where each module rotates 180° based on a predefined phase-shift interval to achieve quasi-steady-state dehumidification. To maximize thermal effectiveness via the thermosyphon effect, the heat pipes were oriented parallel to the gravitational vector, enabling the latent heat of the working fluid to passively recover adsorption heat and facilitate water vapor desorption in the regeneration section. Experimental results demonstrate that the five-stage configuration significantly stabilizes the outlet conditions, achieving a 59.5% reduction in temperature variation and a 91.5% decrease in humidity fluctuation compared to a single-module baseline. Furthermore, the moisture removal rate and coefficient of performance improved by 2.9 and 2.5 times, respectively, due to superior thermal utilization. These findings validate the proposed system as a high-performance, high-efficiency, and robust prototype for advanced ventilation applications requiring high-precision indoor air quality control.

Cost-as-signal: A chemically grounded framework for detecting stress in global precursor-material systems

Thermodynamically Consistent Feature Representation for Machine Learning-Based HHV Prediction of Municipal Solid Waste
Corrosion-Induced Perforation Failure in Shale Gas Gathering Pipeline Systems: Mechanisms, Accelerating Factors, and Protection Strategies
