Projected changes in global soil organic carbon stocks and their vulnerability to drought
abstract: Projected changes in global soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks under intensifying drought remain incompletely characterized, limiting assessments of terrestrial carbon vulnerability under climate change. We combined bias-corrected climate drivers with a skill- and independence-weighted ensemble of seven CMIP6 Earth system models. We then used standardized drought indices, multiscale partial-Spearman analyses, and land-cover comparisons to examine historical and projected changes in SOC stocks and heterotrophic respiration (R h ) fluxes, which represent complementary stock and respiratory-flux indicators. Under SSP5-8.5, the multi-model weighted mean projected a small decrease in late-century SOC relative to the 1985–2014 baseline (−0.26%), whereas changes among the seven individual models ranged from −4.68% to +3.32%, with five models projecting increases. In contrast, R h increased in all seven models, and the weighted-ensemble mean for 2070–2099 was 43.54% higher than the historical baseline. Projected SOC decreases in the weighted ensemble were concentrated in parts of the Northern Hemisphere mid- and high latitudes, whereas changes across lower-latitude and subtropical regions were spatially heterogeneous. At the global scale, SSMI showed the largest selected association magnitude with SOC, whereas the selected association magnitudes for Rh were generally similar for SPEI and SSMI. Across the 1–120-month candidate range, the selected accumulation scales varied across grid cells and drought indices. We interpret these values as descriptive summaries of the accumulation windows associated with the largest retained partial-Spearman coefficients. These association results are based on MMEM-derived drought indices paired with MMWM SOC and R h products, and their model dependence remains unquantified. The analysis maps scenario- and region-dependent patterns of drought-associated SOC vulnerability. Differences in CMIP6 soil‑carbon structure and among benchmark products limit quantitative interpretation.

title: Mapping European land-use driven carbon losses and gains: How scenarios, indicators, and methods shape outcomes
Monitoring and evaluating the just transition: Reflections on a of for Scotland, with lessons for beyond
Balancing Productivity, Ecology, and Social Well‐Being: Insights From Three Decades of Farmland Transformation in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Balancing food security, social equity, and ecological sustainability remains a persistent challenge in global agricultural systems. While economic and ecological aspects of land‐use transitions have been extensively studied, the long‐term dynamics of social functions and their interactions with other functions are less understood. This study investigates the decadal spatiotemporal patterns, functional relationships, and spatial association factors of farmland multifunctionality in China's major grain‐producing regions in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. A multidimensional indicator system was developed to capture economic, social, and ecological functions across 185 prefecture‐level cities, and a CRITIC‐entropy hybrid weighting method was applied to construct multifunctionality indices. Correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction was used to examine trade‐offs and synergies, and the GeoDetector model was employed to identify the explanatory power of factor stratification and factor interactions. The results reveal a paradoxical trajectory across the four benchmark years: while economic and ecological functions improved substantially, the social function declined. Functional relationships were reconfigured, with economic‐ecological interactions changing from conflict to synergy, whereas social‐ecological interactions changed from synergy to trade‐off. Natural conditions were weakly associated with spatial heterogeneity, market and demographic variables exhibited stronger associations before 2010, and policy‐related variables, especially farmland protection policy indicators, showed the strongest statistical associations thereafter. These findings provide one of the most comprehensive large‐scale and long‐term assessments of farmland multifunctionality transitions in China's grain regions. They highlight the importance of institutional arrangements in explaining spatial variation in trade‐offs and synergies, and underscore the need for integrated governance strategies that simultaneously promote productivity, ecological integrity, and rural social well‐being.

title: Economies of Scale to Consumption in Collective Households
abstract: ABSTRACT Browning et al. (2013) model collective‐household economies of scale in goods consumption by having each good be partly shared, instead of each good being public or private. We modify their model to achieve simple point identification and estimation of the economies of scale of consumption of each good, and we provide a new index of household level economies of scale. Our model has a linear form, permits households of varying composition, including children, and accommodates unobserved heterogeneity in both preferences and in the economies of scale of each good. We provide estimates using Canadian Surveys of Household Spending data.

title: Financing Risk in Infrastructure FDI : A Property Rights Perspective
abstract: Abstract Property rights theory (PRT) focuses on how allocation of residual control rights of ownership resolves incentive problems from incomplete contracts. However, when asset ownership is efficient for a transacting party, PRT ignores financial resource constraints preventing the party from purchasing it. We include creditors, who provide financial resources but are exposed to agency conflicts with equity‐owners, in property rights analysis. Multinational enterprises (MNEs) reduce agency conflict with creditors through contractual covenants and collateral. Yet contracts are incomplete. Under incomplete contracts, how do MNEs mitigate financing risk, the risk that supply of capital from creditors is delayed or entirely unavailable? We distinguish between incomplete contracts arising from weak property rights institutions and weak contracting institutions. We theorize that allocation of specified control rights through operating and maintenance (O&M) contracts to MNE‐owners mitigates financing risk in countries with weak property rights institutions because MNE‐owners possess high‐powered incentives to exert requisite effort to adapt operations to unexpected contingencies. In contrast, such allocation of O&M contracts to MNE‐owners increases financing risk in countries with weak contracting institutions because such allocation increases agency conflict between MNE‐owners and creditors. Empirical analyses of 363 project‐financed investments in 52 countries worth US$1.53 trillion over 1990–2018 support our theory.

title: Guiding Attention for Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation: How Strategic Leaders Translate Ethical Values
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on sustainable leadership recognizes the importance of leaders' values but says less about how these values gain organizational awareness. Drawing on the attention‐based view of the firm, this study examines how strategic leaders translate ethical values into organizational attention and under what conditions this process supports sustainability‐oriented innovation. We conduct a comparative multiple‐case study of six organizations in France, based on 92 interviews across hierarchical levels, site visits, and documentary evidence. The analysis identifies three configurations. Where formal attentional structures are weak, innovation projects temporarily bridge leaders and employees around shared values. Where leaders provide “air coverage,” ethical commitments guide strategic boundaries but remain partly decoupled from operational routines. Where attention is structurally distributed, ethical and business priorities are tightly coupled across organizational levels. These findings show that values do not automatically translate into action: Their organizational effects depend on perceived authenticity, communication channels, and attentional structures. The study extends sustainable leadership research by specifying the conditions of value enactment and extends the attention‐based view by revealing the normative foundations of attention distribution.

title: Can Beauty Save the World? A Multimethod Analysis of Regulatory Focus Appeals in Climate Change Advertising
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates how organizations can strategically design climate change advertising to foster greater consumer involvement by comparing the effectiveness of promotion‐ and prevention‐focused advertising appeals. Using a sequential explanatory mixed‐methods design, a facial coding experiment revealed that promotion appeals reduced sadness, which in turn positively influenced attitudes toward the ad and increased climate change involvement. A follow‐up qualitative study with communication managers provides practical insights into how these findings can inform the design of climate change advertising campaigns. By identifying the affective mechanism through which promotion‐focused appeals enhance climate change involvement, this study advances research on green advertising and climate change advertising and offers evidence‐based guidance for organizations seeking to design advertising campaigns that more effectively involve consumers with climate change. As organizations increasingly rely on green advertising to support sustainability initiatives, understanding how to design communications that motivate meaningful climate action remains a critical challenge for both researchers and practitioners.

title: From ESG to Biodiversity: Decoupling and Its Asymmetries as a Source of Biodiversity Risk
abstract: ABSTRACT While environmental, social and governance (ESG) research has extensively documented the risks stemming from disclosure and performance gaps, the growing demand for biodiversity reporting raises concerns that analogous inconsistencies may amplify corporations' exposure to biodiversity risk. Using a sample of 917 firm‐year observations from 2015 to 2023, this study examines whether biodiversity decoupling, the divergence between biodiversity disclosure and performance, is associated with corporations' exposure to biodiversity risk. Drawing on the legitimacy theory, we find that higher levels of biodiversity decoupling are associated with increased biodiversity risk. However, when distinguishing between the types of decoupling, we observe no significant association for positive decoupling, whereas negative decoupling is associated with lower biodiversity risk, suggesting that disclosure‐performance gaps operate differently in the context of biodiversity. We further show that environmental audit moderates the relationship between biodiversity decoupling and biodiversity risk by attenuating the association of positive biodiversity decoupling and the risk‐reduction association of negative biodiversity decoupling. Overall, our findings offer timely insights for corporations seeking to manage legitimacy pressures, for investors aiming to understand the drivers of biodiversity risk and for policymakers wishing to develop more robust biodiversity reporting standards.

title: Balancing risk and opportunity: Digital transformation, cybersecurity investments, and export performance in low-tech firms
Navigating the paradox: Empowerment and power dynamics in international social entrepreneurship
Business Model Bundles: Implications for Innovation in the Circular Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT Business model (BM) innovation is essential to the transition towards a circular economy, yet customers often resist circular BMs. This study investigates how manufacturers can innovate BMs for circularity in ways that increase customer acceptance. Drawing on a multiple‐case study of four manufacturers offering 21 product‐service system BMs, we introduce a new concept, the business model bundle: a strategic offering that packages multiple BMs within one contract and gives customers flexibility to move between them over time. We identify three defining characteristics: the combination of different BMs, contractual flexibility, and temporal transition. We theorize the BM bundle as a new form of BM innovation that creates, delivers, and captures value through the configuration of existing BMs rather than the invention of new ones. Our evidence indicates that the flexibility offered by BM bundles can reduce customers' initial commitment and make previously resisted circular BMs more acceptable. However, bundles may lead towards either greater or lesser circularity and therefore require deliberate design. The study extends innovation management and BM research by introducing the BM bundle that could open a new avenue in the field of BM innovation, and by identifying flexibility as a mechanism linking BM bundles to firm‐perceived customer acceptance.

Central Bank Economic Transparency and Managerial Learning
abstract: Abstract Central banks increasingly disclose their private information regarding the economy’s current and future state (CBET). Consistent with CBET shifting investors’ collection and pricing of aggregate-level (where managers do not have an information advantage) toward firm-level (where managers do have an information advantage) information, we find that CBET reduces managers’ learning from stock price. The results are (1) pronounced when firms do not provide guidance and when noise trading in firms’ stock is low, and (2) robust to using the 2013–2014 amendments to the Bank of England’s Inflation Report as an exogenous shock. Additional evidence suggests that CBET lowers investment efficiency. (JEL E22, E52, M41)

title: Directing the Labor Market: Shared Directors and Employee Flows
abstract: Abstract Using résumé data on over 20 million U.S. workers, we find that the flow of employees between a pair of firms sharply drops by about 20% during periods in which the firms share a board director. This relationship is stronger in settings where firms have greater potential gains from limiting worker mobility and is most pronounced for higher-skilled employees. Moreover, we find more connected firms have lower rates of internal promotion and no improvements in employee satisfaction. The evidence is consistent with shared directors serving as a mechanism for labor market coordination. (JEL G34, G38, J42, J62, J08, K21, K31, M50)

title: Chronologically consistent large language models
The decline of branch banking
Macroeconomic Implications of Executive Pay Caps,
abstract: I study the introduction of statutory caps on executive pay ratios (pay caps) in a span-of-control economy with heterogeneous managerial talent. Managers hire fewer workers than they would in the absence of pay caps, and the marginal product of labour is not equalized among firms. The ability of the marginal manager declines. Inequality between managers and workers, and among managers, declines, but inequality among workers increases. Quantitatively, overall inequality decreases substantially, especially via a reduction in top income shares, but the GDP losses are also significant. In addition, the redistribution favours the “middle” deciles between 50 and 90, rather than the bottom 50% of the income distribution. Future work will build on this “first pass” to analyse the effect of pay caps in economies distorted by monopsony power, non-pecuniary benefits of control, and managerial rent extraction.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Topology-free constructions of a universal type space as coherent belief hierarchies
The carbon reduction effects of new infrastructure construction: Evidence from local government special bonds in China
The fast and the studious? Ramadan observance and student performance
abstract: Abstract We examine how religious observance affects educational performance by studying the years in which Ramadan overlapped with the national end-of-secondary-school exams in the Netherlands. Using administrative microdata and a difference-in-differences design, we find that students who are most likely to fast obtain lower exam scores and are more likely to fail to graduate. As expected given the structure of the Dutch exam system, the increase in failure risk is concentrated among students near the pass threshold. Effects are larger in more religiously segregated schools. For longer-term outcomes, we document a substantially higher likelihood of dropping out among students aged 18 and older, who are legally permitted to leave school and therefore at risk of doing so. Finally, analyses of exam timing suggest that modest adjustments—such as avoiding scheduling two exams on the same day during Ramadan—may help reduce the disadvantages experienced by observant students.

title: Is bitcoin a hedge against central banking? Evidence from AI-driven monetary policy expectations
journal_name: Journal of International Money and Finance

title: How confirmation bias makes persuaders more honest
abstract: We study a Bayesian persuasion game in which a decision maker (DM) incurs psychological costs from belief-disconfirming information and chooses whether to engage with the sender’s experiment. We model preference-based confirmation bias as psychological discomfort from exposure to signals that conflict with the DM’s prior beliefs. Whenever persuasion is feasible, the sender must commit to a strictly more informative experiment than in the Kamenica–Gentzkow (2011) benchmark. This increases the DM’s “actual” welfare, defined as material welfare excluding the psychological cost term, when confirmation bias is moderate, while persuasion fails when the bias exceeds a threshold and the DM disengages. We then introduce processing-based confirmation bias, modeled as systematic misperception of signals. In isolation, it does not change equilibrium behavior or the DM’s “actual” welfare, but when combined with preference-based bias it strengthens the disciplining effect for the DM. A dynamic extension shows that future engagement concerns further increase the sender’s incentive to provide informative signals.

title: Selection and screening in cyber insurance markets
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how information frictions shape demand, screening, and contract design in the U.S. cyber insurance market. I develop a framework in which firms sort into coverage based on latent cyber risk while insurers screen using coarse signals and manage residual exposure more through coverage quantities than through price. Using proprietary broker data, I document three findings consistent with this mechanism. First, higher‐risk firms are more likely to enter the brokered market and apply for coverage. Second, conditional on application, insurer acceptance is more closely related to a survey‐based score than to external risk measures that better capture realized incidents. Third, among issued policies, differences in assessed risk are reflected more in limits and adjusted coverage than in price. The results show that cyber insurance capacity is constrained not only by aggregate supply, but by how coarse risk classification generates residual adverse selection that insurers manage through contract design.

title: What can we gain from pooling VAR and local projection impulse response functions?
N-LAS-IAM: Climate change in a balance-of-payments framework
abstract: Climate change is becoming a macro-financial development problem for peripheral economies, yet integrated assessment models remain poorly equipped to analyse climate vulnerability in externally constrained developing countries. Existing heterodox models are mostly closed or global, while balance-of-payments-constrained growth models treat climate in reduced form and incompletely formalise the financial channel. This paper introduces the N-LAS-IAM, a recursive framework coupling a Thirlwall–Hussain growth core with endogenous green structural change, capital flows under financial fragility, sovereign risk, and a climate module mapping global emissions into damages that feed back into profitability and sovereign fragility. Green structural change is endogenised through logistic diffusion equations governing trade income elasticities as functions of green R&D and the real exchange rate. The model is explored via Monte Carlo experiments in which damage intensity and climate-to-risk transmission vary while emissions, policy, and structural-change parameters remain fixed. Three results emerge. First, higher damage produces a more fragile debt regime with elevated spreads, tighter financing, and prolonged deleveraging. Second, damages widen the elasticity gap between exports and imports, slowing green upgrading and locking the economy into lower-sophistication trade patterns. Third, the damage-to-fragility relationship is nonlinear: below a threshold the economy absorbs shocks, but above it a self-reinforcing regime emerges where lower productivity, higher spreads, weaker inflows, and structural regression feed on one another. These findings suggest that physical damages erode policy capabilities by raising external finance costs when green investment is most needed, and that early mitigation may yield convex macroeconomic returns for peripheral economies under balance-of-payments constraints.

title: Know its worth? Factors affecting the social acceptability of water reuse: A mixed methods planned behavior model
abstract: Due to strong demographic pressure, rapid urban development, and climate change, water demand is increasing while usable freshwater supplies are being depleted. The reuse of treated wastewater (RTWW) is one of the avenues currently being explored to ensure the quantitative and qualitative security of the water supply. The interests for social acceptability emerged with risk management approaches and the subsequent debates on the role of technical progress, the implementation of major development projects, and their consequences for the environment between the late 1970s and early 1980s. The purpose of this article is to identify the factors that influence the building of RTWW acceptability. This study was carried out in southern France. It combines a quantitative survey on behavior related to engaging in RTWW, based on Ajzen's theory of planned behavior, with a qualitative socioeconomic study aimed at understanding representations and beliefs regarding RTWW. The findings show that a lack of knowledge about RTWW and the implementation of only a few RTWW projects result in a normative gap and a perceived lack of control. In addition, trust in managers and public authorities, the quality of treatments, as well as risks perceptions – particularly those relating to health – significantly influence intentions to engage in RTWW. Lastly, several factors such as emotions, types of uses, and environmental awareness play an underlying role by helping build perceptions of water reuse, trust in relevant stakeholders, and more accurate perceptions of risks.

title: Assessing the conditional calibration of interval forecasts using decompositions of the interval score
High-dimensional portfolio optimization with weight constraints: Forecasting models utilizing GARCH-EVT, R-vine copula, and SCAD penalty
Random satisficing model: Characterization and (generic) identification
abstract: Satisficing choice is a well-known decision-making rule. However, as the literature shows, its predictive power is limited because identifying the underlying primitives is difficult. We consider a random satisficing model (RSM) where the decision maker is endowed with a preference, a random threshold, and a random search order. We characterize RSM with two axioms that use the concept of “virtual satisficing sets” introduced in the paper. We also show that the underlying preference can be generically identified when the distribution of search orders has full support and is known to the analyst. Further, we consider a possible generalization of the result when the analyst does not have full knowledge of the distribution of search orders, and when the stochastic search orders do not necessarily have full support.

title: Valuing local water quality in Ontario using revealed preference data
abstract: Abstract Improving water quality is an important goal for policymakers, yet understanding the economic benefits people receive from changes in water quality is challenging because many of the benefits are non‐market in nature. We use spatially explicit lake Secchi disk depth measures and information on over 320,000 property sales to provide the most extensive revealed preference value estimates of water clarity improvements in Canada. We find that a 10% increase in water clarity (as measured by Secchi disk depth) appreciates nearby property values by 0.56%. We do not find evidence for higher price premiums for properties located within 0–250 m of a lake compared to 250–500 m. The findings remain consistent when employing property fixed‐effect models and a series of alternative model specifications. A 10% improvement in lake water clarity in southern Ontario is estimated to yield a total benefit of $2 billion across properties with an aggregate property value of $359 billion, translating to an average benefit of $151 per household. The increase in property values could provide $31 million in additional annual municipal tax revenue to fund water quality improvement initiatives.
journal_name: Canadian Journal of Agricultural Economics/Revue canadienne d'agroeconomie

title: What Are the Impacts of Certificate‐of‐Need Laws? A Review of the Evidence
abstract: This study reviews the literature on the impacts of Certificate-of-Need (CON) laws on outcomes related to hospitals. CON laws require the approval of states' health planning agencies for health care providers to engage in regulated actions such as opening or expanding facilities or purchasing equipment. Economic theory suggests that barriers to entry should reduce competition, leading to higher prices, greater per-firm quantity but lower market quantity, and larger net revenues for incumbent providers. However, defenders of CON laws argue that they ensure high quality standards for new entrants, while also offsetting distortions that disadvantage hospitals and put some at risk of closure. The preponderance of available evidence points toward CON laws restricting entry of new competitors, which in turn increases the number of procedures per hospital. At the same time, CON laws also appear to inhibit hospital expansion, and there is little evidence of increased prices or higher hospital profitability. Studies on hospital efficiency and quality of care for procedures performed exclusively at hospitals mostly point to null or negative effects, but evidence on quality is more mixed for services that can be provided outside of hospitals. With that said, there is a need for new research that utilizes the latest tools for identifying causal effects and better accounts for the wide variation in CON laws across states.

title: Symbolic Incentives Can Affect the Frequency of Blood and Plasma Donations: Evidence From 12 Years of Donors' Behavior
abstract: We investigate how donors respond to symbolic incentives, specifically medals, tied to donation intensity and duration. To this aim, we employ panel data encompassing the entire population of blood and plasma donors affiliated with the primary donor association (AVIS) in Tuscany, Italy, covering the period from 2008 to 2019. The structure of the award scheme adopted by AVIS enables us to examine the impact of two distinct characteristics of the symbolic incentives: the assignment as either private or public and the criterion of assignment based exclusively on the number of donations (donation-only) or, under less demanding donation requirements, also on the years of membership (donation-and-membership). After controlling for time-constant unobservable individual traits that may influence the level and the evolution of performance over a donor's career, we find that (i) these symbolic awards do not affect behavior before their obtainment, (ii) receiving an award through the donation-and-membership criterion leads to a subsequent increase in donation frequency, and (iii) receiving an award through the donation-only criterion, regardless of whether it is announced publicly or privately, does not boost donors' performance. These findings suggest that symbolic awards are effective when bestowed upon less accomplished donors by making their attainment not solely contingent on performance but also on membership, and are related to community identification and self-image concerns rather than status-seeking behavior.

title: Convergence to collusion in algorithmic pricing
abstract: Artificial intelligence algorithms are increasingly used by firms to set prices. Previous research shows that they can learn to collude, but how quickly and reliably they can do so has remained an open question. I study average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms that set continuous prices in the workhorse environment of this literature: a repeated Bertrand duopoly with symmetric firms, deterministic logit demand, and constant marginal costs, where agents observe only market prices and their own profits. The algorithms can converge to a collusive outcome within 50,000 periods, and in 36% of simulations learned punishments make one-period deviations unprofitable, so that high prices are mutual best responses. Successful simulations show cooperative behaviour supported by reward-punishment schemes that discourage deviations. When high prices are not supported by punishments, profitable deviations are typically on the order of hundredths of a percent.

title: Dynamics and determinants of exporter survival: A machine learning approach
The voting behavior of women-led mutual funds
Information design in cheap talk
abstract: Abstract An uninformed sender publicly commits to an informative experiment about an uncertain state, privately observes its outcome, and sends a cheap talk message to a receiver. We provide an algorithm valid for arbitrary state-dependent preferences that will determine the sender’s optimal experiment and his equilibrium payoff under a binary state space. We provide conditions for informative information transmission to occur or to fail. These conditions depend more on marginal incentives—how payoffs vary with the state—than on the alignment of the sender’s and the receiver’s rankings over actions within a state. The algorithm can be easily modified to study the canonical cheap talk game with a perfectly informed sender.

title: Do Commercial Property Taxes Affect Business Microlocation Decisions?

Money Creation for Crypto Space: Stablecoins or Central Bank Digital Currencies?
abstract: Stablecoins are the current go-to digital money to settle transactions on the blockchain. We explore the implications of introducing competing tokenized public digital monies (i.e., tokenized central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)). When they pay a moderate interest rate and guarantee users’ anonymity, tokenized CBDCs crowd out stablecoins. However, when they pay a high interest rate and have low anonymity features, stablecoin issuers could use tokenized CBDCs as collateral, promoting the creation of stablecoins. We identify conditions under which introducing a CBDC to compete with stablecoins in the crypto sector would be socially optimal. This paper was accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: Support from Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) [Grant 100018 219835].

title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
abstract: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04789 .

title: How should companies use empathetic robots to drive consumer engagement, and under what conditions?
journal_name: International Journal of Research in Marketing

title: Assessment of the Relationship Between Circular Supply Chain Management Practices and Sustainable Performance: A Meta‐Analysis of Empirical Evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT Given the growing economic, social, and environmental challenges, sustainable performance (SUSP) offers firms a viable pathway to overcome them and gain long‐term, meaningful business value. Several mechanisms, including the circular supply chain management (CSCM), are proposed to firms to achieve SUSP. However, some empirical findings have challenged this, prompting scholarly debate about the actual direction and strength of the relationship between CSCM and SUSP, thereby leaving prospective firms in a state of strategic ambiguity. To clarify the relationship, 55 empirical studies comprising over 15,000 observations and 109 effect sizes are synthesized through a psychometric, mixed‐model random‐effects meta‐analysis. The results show a positive and significant relationship, with the effect strongest in economic performance, followed by environmental performance, and weakest in social performance. A significant effect is established in most CSCM practices with SUSP dimensions. Economy type, firm size, sector, and innovation are established as significant moderators of the relationship. Findings guide managers on the CSCM practices to prioritize and inform policymakers on the contextual conditions under which the CSCM‐SUSP relationship is strongest. It advances the supply chain management (SCM) theories by clarifying the contingent and multidimensional performance effects of CSCM and resolving inconsistencies in prior findings.

title: Confronting Biodiversity Risk: Its Role in Shaping Corporate External Financing Choice
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how biodiversity risk shapes corporate financing decisions. We propose a Financing Hierarchy Distortion framework, arguing that biodiversity risk amplifies information asymmetry and legitimacy costs, thereby pushing firms toward debt‐heavy adjustments. To empirically test this, we introduce a novel firm‐level Biodiversity Risk ( Brisk ) measure derived from textual analysis of corporate disclosures and link it to objective ecological data via Biological Diversity Endowment ( BDE ). Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2009 to 2023 and excluding those in financial and real estate sectors and with ST designations, we find that higher biodiversity risk increases reliance on both formal and informal debt, particularly short‐term debt. These findings are robust to quasi‐causal identifications using difference‐in‐differences and instrumental variable strategies. Mechanism and heterogeneity analyses further corroborate the proposed framework and show that this distortion is more pronounced among firms in biodiversity‐dependent industries and those facing stronger institutional pressures. These adjustments, however, impose tangible economic costs, raising debt financing costs and depressing returns on assets. Overall, our findings highlight the unintended financial consequences of biodiversity risk, with policy implications for biodiversity disclosure standards, biodiversity‐linked financing instruments and the development of alternative credit channels to strengthen firm resilience under escalating ecological pressure.

title: Self-enhancement or self-protection? How artificial intelligence awareness shapes taking charge behavior
abstract: Purpose Drawing on self-enhancement and self-protection theory, this study aims to examine how artificial intelligence awareness (AIA) shapes hotel employees’ taking charge behavior (TCB), as well as the mediating effects of self-enhancement motivation (SEM) and self-protection motivation (SPM) and the moderating role of locus of control (LOC). Design/methodology/approach Using two-wave survey data from 428 hotel employees and their direct supervisors in China, hierarchical regression and bootstrapping procedures were used for data analysis. Findings AIA had a positive indirect effect on TCB through SEM and a negative indirect effect through SPM. LOC positively moderates the relationship between AIA and SEM and negatively moderates the relationship between AIA and SPM. Moreover, LOC significantly moderates the indirect effects of AIA on TCB via SEM and SPM. Practical implications Hotel managers should address employees’ motivational responses to AIA by enhancing SEM and reducing SPM through tracking artificial intelligence (AI) capability development and alleviating social comparison pressure in AI use. They should also tailor support to employees’ LOC and strengthen internal control beliefs. Originality/value By revealing two motivational mechanisms and highlighting the boundary role of LOC, this study extends research on employees’ TCB in the context of AI-driven technological change.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Perception of artificial intelligence and intrinsic work motivation: evidence from Vietnam
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how sales staff’s perceptions of AI (i.e. perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) drive their intrinsic work motivation through AI use experience (AUE) and how internal training (IT) moderates this process within tourism and hospitality business. Design/methodology/approach Rooted in the technology acceptance model (TAM), flow theory and self-determination theory (SDT), this study used exploratory sequential mixed-method design. Scale purification (EFA) and scale validation (CFA) were conducted using SPSS and AMOS and hypothesis testing results were validated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results revealed that PU and PEOU positively influence AI-specific intrinsic work motivation (AI-IWM) indirectly, through the mediating role of AUE. Furthermore, IT positively moderates the relationships between perception of AI and AUE, which ultimately improves AI-IWM. Practical implications The findings offer valuable insight into service and hospitality management sectors aiming to enhance work motivation among sales staff through AI. Given the significant influence of intrinsic motivation among sales staff in tourism and hospitality businesses, organization with a focus on AI adoption at workplace must be mindful of negative influence of AI on employees’ work motivation and outcome. Originality/value This study enriched the understanding of the motivations underlying the perception of AI and intrinsic work motivation by integrating insights from the TAM, SDT and flow theory. This study provided valuable implication for research and practices in the service business sector.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Consumption value in GenAI travel photography: a mixed-methods study from an affordance–constraint perspective
abstract: Purpose This study develops an affordance–constraint–value framework to explain how GenAI travel photography shapes consumption value and behavioral intentions. It aims to examine how perceived affordances and constraints relate to functional, emotional and social value, and how these value dimensions influence continuance and sharing intentions. Design/methodology/approach A three-phase mixed-methods design was used. Phase 1 applied topic modeling to 40,543 user-generated posts. Phase 2 surveyed 485 GenAI travel photography users and tested the structural model with PLS-SEM. Phase 3 used fsQCA to identify affordance–constraint configurations associated with high consumption value. Findings Phase 1 showed that public discourse centered on enabling conditions, value evaluations and behavioral tendencies. Phase 2 indicated that trialability, aesthetic creation and self-congruence were central to value formation, and that all three value dimensions increased continuance and sharing intentions. Phase 3 showed that high-value outcomes appeared through multiple sufficient configurations, with low AI hallucination risk recurring across solutions. Originality/value This study contributes to digital tourism and destination visual marketing by conceptualizing GenAI travel photography as generated self-in-place consumption. Integrating technology affordances and constraints theory with the theory of consumption value offers a more balanced explanation of how value is created, qualified and suppressed. Methodologically, it combines big-data exploration, net-effect testing and configurational analysis to explain value formation and its behavioral consequences.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Visualizing myself there: affordances of GenAI travel selfies for engagement and visit intention
abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) travel selfies have emerged as a novel pre-trip tourism touchpoint, yet their role in shaping user responses remains underexplored. Drawing on three-phase affordance actualization theory, this study aims to examine how GenAI travel selfie affordances are associated with user engagement and visit intention. Design/methodology/approach A three-study mixed-methods design was used, combining 32 photo-elicitation interviews, a survey of 526 users analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of affordance configurations. Findings Three affordances were identified: visual creation, generative controllability and self-presentation. All three were positively associated with cognitive, affective and behavioral engagement, except for one nonsignificant path. User engagement was positively associated with visit intention. The fsQCA results further indicated that high engagement can be associated with multiple affordance configurations. Practical implications GenAI travel selfies can serve as a soft, user-driven promotional touchpoint for destinations and hospitality brands. Designers and marketers could consider identity-relevant design, controllable and reliable generative functions and visually appealing outputs to encourage engagement and stimulate early-stage destination interest. Originality/value The research is among the early empirical studies of GenAI travel selfies in tourism. It extends affordance-based research to a visual, identity-centered GenAI context and combines net-effect and configurational evidence to explain how these affordances are linked to user engagement and visit intention.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Generativity and corrosion during scaling: How firms balance core and adjacent ecosystems to enable growth
abstract: There is rising theoretical and practical interest in entrepreneurial scaling beyond traditional linear growth models. Recent scholarship highlights ecosystem management as a promising alternative to understand scaling, but it remains unclear how firms can use ecosystem strategies for scaling up, particularly after hitting growth plateaus. Through an in-depth case study of a Brazilian logistics firm based on rich empirical material consisting of 53 interviews and supported by internal documents, this paper investigates how entrepreneurial firms use adjacent ecosystem strategies to overcome growth plateaus and sustain scaling. We introduce the concepts of generativity and corrosion to explain this phenomenon. Our findings reveal that overcoming growth plateaus by scaling through adjacent ecosystems is a dual process: firms must promote generativity by using core assets to create novel value in adjacent markets, while simultaneously preventing corrosion by protecting the mature core from resource competition and misaligned interests. This research provides a nuanced framework demonstrating that successful scaling requires balancing different ecosystem maturities and orchestrating cross-ecosystem synergies.

title: Beyond psychology and environment explanations: a linguistic microfoundation approach to entrepreneurs’ anxiety
abstract: We offer a novel theoretical account of why entrepreneurs experience anxiety and how entrepreneurs cope with anxiety. We integrate insights from linguistic theories into entrepreneurship literature to propose that entrepreneurs’ linguistic architecture—particularly the vocabulary their language provides for identifying and describing emotions (i.e., its emotion lexicon)—is an essential linguistic microfoundation that systematically shapes how entrepreneurs process and experience anxiety. As moderators, we examine how bilingualism and entrepreneurial experience can systematically alter how entrepreneurs’ linguistic architecture influences their anxiety. Our final sample was 1,251 entrepreneurs speaking 14 different languages, supplemented by an experimental study with 202 bilingual entrepreneurs in Hong Kong. We find that entrepreneurs with a richer vocabulary for identifying and describing emotions (i.e., a richer emotion lexicon) heighten anxiety due to more precise and vivid emotional processing, and bilingualism weakens, yet prior entrepreneurial experience strengthens the positive effect of emotion lexicon on anxiety.

title: CSR focus under competitive pressure: The role of national institutions
abstract: How does competitive pressure shape CSR strategy, and does this relationship vary across national institutional contexts? We challenge the prevailing binary framing that competitive pressure either promotes or suppresses CSR by arguing that competition reshapes how firms configure their CSR portfolios, not merely how much they engage. We introduce CSR focus strategy: a firm's selective emphasis on specific CSR dimensions while deliberately de-emphasizing others, allowing simultaneous differentiation and cost-economization through CSR under some conditions. Employing multilevel linear modeling (MLM) on a global dataset of 41 countries comprising 2294 firms from 2002 to 2020, we demonstrate that competitive intensity drives adoption of CSR focus strategy. Critically, this effect is contingent on national market-supporting institutions and firm size, where CSR focus strategies are most pronounced in institutionally weaker environments characterized by limited property rights protection and among smaller firms with limited stakeholder relational capital and opportunities. Further analyses reveal two subtypes, namely CSR excellence and CSR distinction , reflecting different portfolio configurations under competition. By establishing that institutional context shapes firms' CSR portfolio configuration under competition, our study advances international business research and reconciles opposing theoretical positions in the competition-CSR debate. Collectively, these findings extend the emerging portfolio-based view of CSR into the cross-country competitive domain.

title: The Bamboo Ceiling in the UK: Ethnicity–Gender Intersectionality, Risk Tolerance, and Leadership Attainment
abstract: ABSTRACT In the UK, Asians are often perceived as the “model minority” who face few hardships due to their strong educational performance and economic success. We question this perception by uncovering a “Bamboo Ceiling” in leadership attainment for certain Asian subgroups in the UK. Whereas many researchers and practitioners treat Asians as a monolith, we recognize heterogeneity among Asian subgroups and focus on comparing ethnic Chinese (the largest East Asian group) and ethnic Indians (the largest South Asian group). In Study 1, we analyzed CEOs and CFOs of the Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE) companies—the largest publicly listed companies in the UK—over a 14‐year period (2011–2024). There were virtually no ethnic Chinese CEOs or CFOs, whereas the representation of ethnic Indians in these positions did not differ significantly from that of Whites. In Study 2, we analyzed a large, nationwide dataset from the UK Biobank ( N = 322,734) to further investigate the moderating role of gender and the mediating role of risk tolerance. While ethnic Chinese overall experienced a Bamboo Ceiling (thus confirming Study 1's results), this main effect was moderated by gender: Ethnic Chinese men were significantly less likely than ethnic Indian and White men to attain leadership positions, a pattern partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance; by contrast, ethnic Chinese, Indian, and White women did not differ significantly and were each disadvantaged relative to their male counterparts. These effects were robust across survey‐based and polygenic measures of risk tolerance. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing among Asian subgroups and examining how ethnicity and gender intersect in leadership attainment.

title: Firm-specific trade policy effect uncertainty and the bullwhip effect
abstract: Purpose In an era of increasingly volatile trade policies, firms confront heightened uncertainty in demand forecasting and production planning, raising the potential for amplification of the bullwhip effect (BWE). Drawing on the BWE literature and on regulatory focus theory, which distinguishes between a promotion focus oriented toward gains and a prevention focus oriented toward loss avoidance, this paper investigates how firm-specific trade policy effect uncertainty (TPEU) influences the BWE, and how managerial regulatory focus moderates this effect. Design/methodology/approach Based on a sample of 37,017 firm-year observations from 4,104 publicly listed Chinese firms between 2002 and 2022, we employ ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings We find that TPEU significantly amplifies the BWE. This effect is exacerbated in firms led by promotion-focused top management teams (TMTs) and attenuated in firms led by prevention-focused TMTs. Mechanism analyses reveal that TPEU affects the BWE primarily through firms' operational adjustments on both the demand and production, as well as through broader supply chain restructuring. These results are robust to a series of empirical strategies designed to address potential endogeneity concerns. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on publicly listed Chinese firms and relies partly on textual measures derived from corporate disclosures. Accordingly, the findings may not fully generalize to firms operating in other institutional and trade policy environments, and the measures may partly reflect managerial disclosure choices. Future research could test and extend the proposed relationships through cross-country comparisons, alternative measures of trade policy effect uncertainty and managerial regulatory focus, and more granular operational data. Practical implications The findings suggest that firms should treat TPEU as an important source of operational instability. Managers should strengthen demand forecasting and policy monitoring, avoid excessive ordering and inventory adjustments, and manage customer and supplier restructuring carefully. Firms should also consider how TMT regulatory focus shapes operational responses to uncertainty and balance opportunity-seeking with risk-avoidance in supply chain decision-making. Social implications The study shows that trade policy uncertainty can generate operational consequences that extend beyond individual firms by amplifying demand and production variability and disrupting customer and supplier relationships. Such amplification can propagate through interconnected supply chains, potentially weakening overall supply chain stability during periods of trade policy change. The findings therefore highlight the broader social and economic value of improving firms’ ability to absorb policy-related uncertainty, maintain stable supply chain relationships and avoid unnecessary operational overreaction, thereby supporting more resilient supply chains in an increasingly uncertain global trade environment. Originality/value We contribute to the emerging literature on the intersection of operations and supply chain management and trade policy uncertainty by documenting the operational consequences of trade policy-induced uncertainty, and by underscoring the critical role of managerial regulatory focus in shaping operational responses to TPEU.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: External Governance Shocks and Legitimacy Repair Through CSR
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines how firms adjust their corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance when product market competitors experience forced chief executive officer (CEO) turnover. Specifically, this study investigates whether peer CEO dismissals, as governance shocks signaling intensified board monitoring, trigger strategic CSR responses among rival firms. Research Findings/Insights Using US firm‐year observations from 2003 to 2020, this research documents that peer dismissals significantly increase firms' CSR performance, with effects concentrated in the social dimension rather than the environmental or governance dimensions. The positive relationship is stronger for firms with greater analyst coverage and for firms operating in more competitive markets, indicating that external scrutiny and competitive pressure strengthen strategic CSR adoption. Value‐creation tests demonstrate that CSR engagement in response to peer dismissals is associated with improved subsequent accounting performance, particularly in the social dimension. Theoretical/Academic Implications The findings support legitimacy theory over agency theory in explaining CSR motivations under governance pressure. This research demonstrates that CSR serves as an active legitimacy‐building mechanism rather than being constrained by governance discipline when firms face institutional pressures from peer governance failures. This research enriches the peer spillover literature by moving the focus from passive information transfer to active legitimacy management and extends executive turnover research by identifying CSR as a strategic response channel to external governance shocks. Practitioner/Policy Implications Boards and executives should recognize that peer governance failures create reputational risks requiring strategic stakeholder engagement. The evidence suggests that CSR practices can effectively mitigate legitimacy threats following industry‐wide governance shocks. Policymakers should recognize that governance failures in one firm create industry‐wide legitimacy threats that extend beyond the affected company and that the information environment plays a critical role in shaping how these threats spread across product markets.

title: Correction: Rethinking the Rules: A Two-Sample Study of Ethical Climate and Employee Outcomes

Impact of organizational goals, leadership styles, and organizational culture on employee outcomes in the Korean public sector
abstract: This study examines how organizational goals, leadership styles, and organizational culture influence employee outcomes in the Korean public sector. Using Structural Equation Modelling, data from 6,170 public servants were analysed. Organizational goals positively influenced commitment and performance efforts. Transactional leadership positively affected organizational culture and commitment but negatively affected performance efforts, whereas visionary leadership showed positive effects across all three outcomes. Organizational culture enhanced commitment and performance efforts, while organizational commitment positively influenced performance efforts and perceived organizational performance. Performance efforts also enhanced perceived organizational performance. These findings highlight how goals, leadership, and collaborative culture jointly shape employee and organizational outcomes.

Macro-level geospatial determinants of E-bike crash risk: town-level analysis
abstract: Electric bicycles have become a dominant mode of transportation in many Chinese cities, including Guangzhou, raising growing concerns about traffic safety resulting in fatalities and injuries among riders. This study performs a macro-level geospatial analysis to explore the spatial variability of factors influencing town-level counts of fatal and injury (FI) and property damage only (PDO) e-bike crashes across 170 towns in Guangzhou, which in this study represent spatial patterns in crash risk at the town level. One year of e-bike crashes and traffic violation data, integrated with environmental and infrastructural variables, such as population density, road network characteristics, land use diversity, and public facility densities, was used to examine spatial associations with FI and PDO crash counts. Spatial autocorrelation and Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) analysis revealed significant clustering, with 64 towns (37.6%) identified as high-risk hotspots. To explore spatial heterogeneity in predictor associations, three models were applied: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR), and Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR). Within this exploratory Gaussian comparison, MGWR yielded the lowest AICc and highest adjusted R 2 ; however, most predictors exhibited near-global, spatially stationary associations, with localized variation observed only for selected predictors. Count-data diagnostics confirmed substantial overdispersion; therefore, geographically weighted negative binomial regression with a global dispersion parameter (GWNBRg) was applied, yielding deviance pseudo-R 2 values of 0.356 for FI and 0.251 for PDO crashes. Positive Gaussian associations for population density, traffic violations, and intersection density were not consistently corroborated by the negative binomial analyses. By contrast, higher school and healthcare facility densities were negatively associated with FI crashes in the global log-transformed negative binomial analysis (p = 0.014 and 0.027) and received greater nominal local GWNBRg support (29.4% and 17.1% of towns, respectively). These associations are observational and noncausal. These exploratory findings provide a preliminary data-driven basis for evidence-informed e-bike safety planning while highlighting that most predictors exhibit spatially stationary associations across towns.

title: Beyond Legal Recognition: Parental Acceptance and Couple-Level Minority Stress on Same-Sex Couples’ Well-Being in Chinese Societies
abstract: Abstract Previous studies in the Global North suggest that same-sex marriage brings positive impacts on the well-being of lesbian, gay, bisexual, queer, and plus (LGBQ+) individuals. Parental acceptance is challenging yet important for LGBQ+ individuals, especially in Chinese societies, which strongly emphasize harmony and heteronormative family relationships. This paper examines the association between the legal recognition of same-sex couple relationships and one’s individual and relational well-being, and how it is mediated by parental acceptance and couple-level minority stress. We surveyed 812 LGBQ+ respondents in committed same-sex relationships in two Chinese-majority societies, Taiwan (with legal recognition of same-sex couple relationships) and Hong Kong (without such policy). We found that Taiwan respondents reported higher levels of parental acceptance and a lower level of couple-level stigma and discrimination than their counterparts in Hong Kong. While Taiwan respondents reported better relational well-being, there was no significant difference in individual well-being between the two societies. Experience of couple-level stigma and discrimination was associated with higher levels of depression. We argue that parental acceptance explains much of the significant variation in relationship satisfaction, beyond living in societies with or without legal recognition of same-sex couple relationships. As such, we underscore the importance of parental acceptance for LGBQ+ individuals in their relationship with their same-sex partners in Chinese societies. Furthermore, as same-sex couples continue to encounter couple-level minority stress and challenges in gaining parental acceptance, there is a need for mental health and social services to provide targeted support to enhance their well-being.

title: Union Strength, Collective Bargaining, and Strike Activity: Insights From Chile's 2017 Labor Reform
abstract: ABSTRACT We study the causal impact of Chile's 2017 labor reform—which banned the replacement of striking workers and restricted unilateral extension of collective benefits—on strike activity, wages, and employment. Using administrative data on all regulated collective negotiations from 2008 to 2024 in a difference‐in‐differences framework that exploits pre‐reform variation in union density, we find no increase in strike incidence and modest decreases in strike voting and actual stoppages among more unionized firms. Effects on wages are negligible; effects on employment are positive but display pre‐reform trends. The pattern is consistent with the joint cost model and with the institutional‐context literature.
