Cybersecurity Disclosure Mandates and Cross‐Domain Compliance Spillovers
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether cybersecurity disclosure mandates generate compliance spillovers beyond their intended regulatory domain. Exploiting the staggered adoption of US state breach notification laws (BNLs), we find that mandatory breach disclosure reduces firms’ federal regulatory violations in non‐cyber domains by more than 5% in the first year after adoption. The effect is transitory, dissipating in subsequent years, but extends across several major regulatory domains. Cross‐sectional analyses show that the reduction is stronger among firms with greater organizational capacity and more effective internal controls. The findings are robust to a broad set of identification and sensitivity tests. Overall, the evidence suggests that cybersecurity disclosure mandates can operate as organizational governance shocks, inducing cross‐domain compliance spillovers when firms have stronger preexisting compliance infrastructure.

title: Disclosure Quality, Litigation Risk, and Regulatory Arbitrage in SPACs
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates regulatory arbitrage in going public via SPACs and its implications for disclosure quality and litigation risk. We find that, compared to fundamentally matched IPO peers, SPACs exploit regulatory gaps, resulting in less informative, more optimistic, and overconfident disclosures. These compromised disclosures are associated with a higher likelihood of securities litigation, particularly within the first year post‐merger. Importantly, the elevated risk arises from disclosure practices rather than the SPAC method itself. Our findings provide early benchmarks for evaluating recent reforms and underscore the importance of consistent oversight in investor protection.

title: Would a larger population increase long-run incomes?
Dynamic Effects of Population Aging on Natural Interest Rates
Dependent development at the energy transition: placing lithium imaginaries in Neoliberal and Contentious Peru
abstract: We examine lithium and development imaginaries in mining-dependent Peru, asking: What are these imaginaries? What narratives underpin them? Who articulates and shares them, and from where? What forms of state (in)action are envisioned in relation to them? The case study elucidates how alternative “imagined futures” coexist within a natural resource–dependent economy. The ruling national elites in Lima have a neoliberal imagination, treating lithium like any other mineral resource in the country. In contrast, professional elites in the mineral-rich but peripheral region of Puno adopt a resource nationalist view, advocating for direct state involvement in lithium industrialization and the transformation of the domestic energy system, shaped by beliefs on Bolivia’s developmental pathway. Among rural community leaders as well as political and social leaders in the districts near lithium and uranium deposits, however, the prevailing idea is that of a social license. In this view, each community has the capacity to negotiate development terms with mining companies independently. In the broader imagination at the resource periphery of a peripheral national economy, the state is perceived primarily as a minimalist governmental actor, necessary only to oversee and ensure the enforcement of mine-community agreements and to provide basic infrastructure. Thus, elites at the political center and communities near expected resource developments converge in their immediate pursuit of rents promised by resource commodification. In the dominant discourses, environmental concerns are often subordinated to economic development goals.

title: Governing Indigenous territories: trust, moral economy, and the legitimation of Indigenous territorial authority in the Honduran Moskitia
abstract: Formalizing Indigenous land rights is critical for environmental justice and sustainable development. Yet legal recognition often creates new territorial governing bodies tasked with managing collective lands, whose legitimacy cannot be assumed. This study examines how trust in Indigenous territorial authorities is built, contested, and withdrawn following the formalization of collective land rights in the Honduran Moskitia. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and household interviews in three villages across diverse socio-ecological settings, the study analyzes how residents assess their territorial authorities. The analysis treats trust as multidimensional and relational. The study examines different forms of trust—dispositional, rational, affinitive, and procedural—to identify the rationales that drive assessments of authority in each village. These rationales are interpreted through the lens of a Miskitu moral economy, framing trust assessments in terms of what residents expect of a territorial authority to be considered legitimate. A moral economy lens contributes analytically to a multidimensional trust framework by explaining why certain forms of trust feel more salient when evaluating authority performance and how they interact with one another. The central finding is that the socio-spatial configuration of land conflicts shapes which evaluative dimensions of trust become most salient. A multidimensional and relational trust analysis contributes a more granular understanding of this process: it shows how different forms of trust interact and shift through everyday encounters with authority, identifying the specific points at which legitimacy is strengthened, strained, or quietly lost.

title: Is Europe a laggard? Comparing the EU and the US using an interdisciplinary well-being framework
abstract: Well-being is increasingly recognized as a more meaningful measure of societal progress than economic output, yet most international comparisons continue to emphasize economic indicators. This focus has reinforced the perception that Europe is lagging behind the United States, with the productivity gap shaping the European Commission’s recent competitiveness agenda. Here, we compare European and American development from 1990–2023 using an interdisciplinary well-being framework that integrates five scientific schools of thought. We find that while the US increasingly outperformed the EU on productivity and income, the EU caught up in terms of various well-being indicators, including life satisfaction and education, while increasingly outperforming the US in life expectancy and safety. Europe also exhibits more equitable well-being outcomes and achieves them at lower environmental cost. However, in both regions, the conditions underpinning future well-being are under increasing pressure. These results challenge the dominance of economic metrics in evaluating progress and emphasize the need for inclusive development strategies that place sustainable well-being at their core.

title: Queueing with deadlines: Characterizing two transfer rules

Complex to compete? The role of global value chains and relatedness density in driving the economic complexity of EU regions
Pursuing post-neoliberal alternatives during the global governance interregnum: the case of Africa’s new oil producers
abstract: Does the twenty-first century ‘interregnum’ in global governance offer developing countries more space to pursue post-neoliberal alternatives? We address this question by investigating how new oil producers in the global South have negotiated international efforts to promote the ‘Norwegian Model’ of oil governance, which separates out policy, regulatory, and commercial functions. Comparative case-study analysis across three countries in Africa reveals a mixed picture. In most instances, adopting the Norwegian Model reduced rather than enhanced the capacity of new producers to govern oil, not least as newly fragmented oil sectors helped fuel inter-elite factionalism. On the space for pursuing post-neoliberal alternatives, most international actors have been unwilling to support the resource nationalist ambitions of ruling coalitions to either strengthen their own national oil companies or empower regulatory authorities to oversee international oil companies. Only where countries had already invested in state capacity to govern oil before the onset of neoliberal governance modalities have they been able to both improve their oil governance capacities and enact post-neoliberal alternatives. Deploying a critical political-economy framework, this study emphasizes the difficulties that global South countries face in navigating the current global governance interregnum but also identifies a path forward for those with specific histories of state-building.

title: Risk and Social Preferences: Theory and Evidence on Support for Redistribution and Environmental Protection
On the empirical relevance of the exchange rate as a shock absorber at the zero lower bound
Green Versus Sustainable Loans: The Impact on Firms' ESG Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies the development of a firm's Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance following the issuance of “green loans” earmarked for green projects versus “sustainable loans” benchmarked by ESG criteria. Firms issuing green loans improve environmental performance, particularly by reducing emissions, but experience declines in social performance, suggesting a trade‐off between environmental and social objectives. In contrast, sustainable loans are associated with broader ESG improvements, enhancing environmental and governance outcomes without a comparable social decline. Overall, loan design shapes corporate sustainability behaviour: green loans generate targeted environmental gains, whereas sustainable loans foster more balanced and holistic ESG performance improvements.

title: Macro‐Economic Uncertainty and Business Cycle Asymmetry
abstract: Abstract We propose a modified unobserved‐component model to investigate the link between macro‐economic uncertainty and business cycle asymmetry of the U.S. economy. The degree of skewness of shocks is assumed to vary with macro‐economic uncertainty. We develop an efficient Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. Our estimates suggest that high macro‐economic uncertainty tends to be associated with large and negative shocks to the cyclical (but not the trend) component. Quantitatively, a one‐standard‐deviation increase (decrease) in uncertainty results in an expected output change of −0.15 (0.10) percentage points. Low quantiles of the growth distribution, that is, growth‐at‐risk, are particularly susceptible to changes in uncertainty.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: Courts and chains: The real effects of judicial independence on supply chain stability
Next job: Matera. How tourism and spotlight shape the local labour market
The welfare effects of input price discrimination under endogenous horizontal differentiation
How ventures maintain stakeholder support amidst operational legitimacy threats
abstract: Abstract Research Summary We explore how ventures mitigate operational legitimacy threats— threats that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition . Through an inductive study of four ventures working to deliver their promised products following successful crowdfunding campaigns, we reveal a process of three rhetorical practices that ventures can use to maintain stakeholder support: humanizing the venture , normalizing setbacks and resolutions , and revising pragmatic claims . The first two practices contribute to the formation of dispositional legitimacy buffers that allow the third practice to be effective in mitigating fallout from exposed operational legitimacy threats. We conclude by offering contributions to the cultural entrepreneurship literature and to research on venture–stakeholder communication. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurs must often determine whether to disclose operational issues to stakeholders. On one hand, entrepreneurs may resolve these operational issues without stakeholders ever knowing of their occurrence. On the other hand, such issues could balloon to negatively impact whether a venture can deliver its promised offering. We identify three rhetorical practices, two of which entrepreneurs can utilize before an operational issue even occurs, to generate favorable judgments with stakeholders and increase the likelihood that their ventures will be able to maintain support if an operational issue becomes exposed.

title: Tax-Related Key Audit Matters and Changes in Multinational Income Shifting
The Effect of Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income Tax on U.S. Multinational Companies’ Cross-Border Tangible Investments
Personalization, Engagement, and Content Quality on Social Media: An Evaluation of Reddit’s News Feed
abstract: Digital platforms increasingly curate their content through personalized algorithmic feeds. Platforms have an incentive to promote content that increases the predicted engagement of each user to lift advertising revenues. This paper studies how ranking content to maximize engagement affects the credibility of news content with which users engage. In addition, I evaluate how the ranking algorithm itself can be designed to promote engagement with high-credibility content. Using data from the Reddit politics community, I exploit a novel discontinuity in the ranking algorithm to identify the causal effect of a post’s rank on the number of comments it receives. I use this discontinuity to identify a model of user comment decisions and estimate the credibility of news content that users engage with under a personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm. The personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm exacerbates differences in the credibility of news content with which users engage. I then evaluate a credibility-aware algorithm that explicitly promotes credible news publishers and find the platform can substantially increase the share of engagement with high-credibility publishers for a small reduction in total engagement. These findings suggest algorithmic interventions can be a useful tool for managers to balance engagement quantity and content quality. This paper was accepted by Hemant Bhargava, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06298 .

title: Using Representation Learning and Website Text to Identify Competitor Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to identify competitors using company websites to map competitive relationships among public and private firms. We apply representation learning techniques to create embeddings of companies based on website content, emphasizing information about industry-specific products and services. By placing all firms, public and private, within the same embedding space, we construct a peer competitor network that supports analysis of company interactions and market evolution. We label this new approach and set of network competitors as the website text-based network industry classification (WTNIC). We evaluate the quality of the network using multiple ground truth datasets and benchmarks and show that it offers a robust alternative for understanding competition at scale. Despite using noisy website data, WTNIC matches or outperforms prior approaches that rely on curated data. We demonstrate the value of WTNIC through a case study examining how competition from China affects the public and private peers of a focal firm, highlighting the importance of placing both public and private companies within the same embedding space. Funding: This work was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants 1561068 and 1937153], the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth College, the USC Marshall Institute for Outlier Research in Business (iORB), and the Smith School of Business at the University of Maryland. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06516 .

title: From Live to Recording: Consumer Demand and Response to Price Across the Livestreaming Lifecycle
abstract: Using data from a knowledge-sharing platform that sells recorded versions of paid livestreams, this paper finds that demand is surprisingly more price sensitive before the event than after, which is explained partly by consumer self-selection and the lower quality uncertainty once the livestream ends.

title: Macroeconomic implications of accounting standards
Does Gender Matter? Gender Signals in a UK Equity Crowdfunding Experiment
abstract: Abstract While research shows that women entrepreneurs often struggle to secure funding from traditional loan institutions, crowdfunding offers a unique channel to bypass traditional loan gatekeepers and directly access funds from the public. This study explores whether the gender of the entrepreneur sends a signal to a funder, specifically, whether gender homophily affects the organisational attractiveness of a business venture. Additionally, we explore if there are any effects of the organization type and equity return. Using an online survey experiment with UK participants ( n = 4510), via Prolific, we manipulated the gender of the entrepreneur (woman vs. man), the organization type (healthcare vs. fintech) and the equity return (5% vs. 10%) for a hypothetical business venture. Our findings may help explain the mixed results of extant research on gender and entrepreneurship. We found that the organization type, equity returns and experience of funders play a role in the extent to which funders find an organization attractive and willingness to support a business venture. Specifically, our findings show that healthcare ventures were more attractive to women, while men were more attracted to greater equity returns. As a scholarly contribution, we suggest that gender value homophily may partly explain the nuanced findings.

title: From Uncertainty to Risk: How Firms Respond in Circular Economy Transitions
abstract: ABSTRACT The transition to a circular economy exposes firms to multiple sources of uncertainty, yet existing research largely treats these challenges as barriers rather than drivers of firm behavior. This paper develops a conceptual understanding of how uncertainty is translated into risk and how this shapes firm responses in circular economy contexts. It proposes that firms translate uncertainty into perceived risk through identifiable organizational processes, and this translation varies systematically with firms' prior experience and resource flexibility in CE ‐related activity rather than being inferred only from firms' eventual responses. Building on this perspective, the paper extends the behavioral theory of the firm by showing that in circular economy settings, risk perception is shaped across networks of interdependent firms rather than within a single firm, and that anticipated and realized risk can push firms in opposite directions. It further specifies when perceived risk leads to defensive versus proactive firm responses, based on firm experience and resource flexibility. By positioning risk as a central mechanism linking uncertainty to firm behavior, the paper offers an integrated explanation of circular economy transitions with theoretical, managerial, and policy implications.

title: How Does Green Human Resource Management Shape Organizational Sustainable Performance? A Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how green human resource management (GHRM) shapes organizational sustainable performance (OSP) is increasingly important for aligning human resource practices with organizations' environmental, social, and economic sustainability goals. This study systematically reviews how GHRM shapes OSP by integrating performance analysis with an in‐depth synthesis based on the theory, context, characteristics, and methodology (TCCM) framework. Following the SPAR‐4‐SLR procedure, 391 articles from Web of Science and Scopus published between 2012 and April 2026 were analyzed for research performance, whereas a subset of 104 articles published in A*, A, and B journals according to the ABDC list was selected from this dataset for detailed content analysis. The findings show a sharp increase in publications since 2016 and reveal that the field is dominated by the Ability‐Motivation‐Opportunity framework, resource‐based view, social cognitive theory, and social learning theory. Empirical research remains concentrated in the hospitality, manufacturing, and service sectors and relies heavily on quantitative, cross‐sectional survey designs. The review also identifies several important gaps, including limited multi‐theoretical integration, insufficient attention to high‐emission and underexplored sectors, overreliance on subjective performance measures, limited use of longitudinal and mixed‐method designs, and inadequate examination of the dark side of GHRM. By integrating these insights into a TCCM‐informed multilevel framework, this study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which GHRM may shape OSP while offering a focused agenda for future research.

title: Mobilizing Dynamic‐Capability Microfoundations for Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation: The Role of Innovation Champions
abstract: ABSTRACT Organizations face growing pressure to respond to environmental and social challenges, yet research has not sufficiently explained how organizational actors mobilise dynamic‐capability microfoundations across the development of sustainability‐oriented innovations. Drawing on 68 semistructured interviews conducted between March and November 2024 across 18 EU and UK marine firms, this qualitative study examines how innovation champions and related actors support sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring. The analysis identifies an interconnected process: market exposure and network relationships support sensing sustainability‐oriented opportunities; perceived product–capability fit shapes whether those opportunities progress to seizing; and managerial mobilization, cross‐functional problem‐solving, and relationship coordination support reconfiguration. Rather than treating every influential manager as an innovation champion, the study distinguishes championing activities—persistent advocacy, boundary spanning, resource mobilization, and coordination—from formal organizational positions. The study contributes by explaining how actor‐level mechanisms connect successive dynamic‐capability stages in a sustainability‐oriented innovation context. Product–capability fit is presented as an emerging transition mechanism that requires further testing rather than as an entirely novel construct.

title: Mapping Non‐Linear ESG Trajectories in OECD Countries: A Topological Entropy Approach
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the evolution of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance across 38 OECD countries between 2010 and 2024 using a longitudinal and multi‐dimensional analytical framework. Moving beyond static ESG benchmarking approaches, it investigates how sustainability trajectories evolve under changing institutional, economic and governance conditions. The findings reveal that ESG transitions across advanced economies are neither linear nor uniformly convergent. Instead, countries follow differentiated sustainability pathways characterised by persistent trade‐offs across ESG dimensions. In particular, improvements in governance and social performance do not necessarily coincide with stronger environmental outcomes, highlighting the complexity of balancing competing sustainability priorities under conditions of uncertainty and external shocks. By integrating Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), Hierarchical Ascending Classification (HAC) and Topological Local Entropy Clustering (TLEC), the analysis provides a dynamic perspective on ESG evolution across OECD countries. The findings contribute to the sustainability strategy literature by emphasising the importance of adaptive and context‐sensitive governance frameworks for managing sustainability transitions. Practical implications are offered for policymakers, firms and investors seeking to strengthen long‐term ESG resilience and sustainability integration strategies.

title: The Aesthetic Paradox: How Visual Aesthetic Quality Shapes Digital Engagement on Social Media
abstract: Visual aesthetic quality (VAQ) is one of the most salient image characteristics of social media advertising, yet its nuanced effect on digital engagement remains underexplored. Building on existing research on the “beauty premium” and the “ugliness premium,” this research posits that the effect of VAQ follows a U-shaped pattern. Accordingly, a multi-study framework is proposed to verify both correlational and causal relationships. Study 1 quantifies VAQ of 11,559 post images leveraging the enhancer for aesthetics-oriented transformers (EAT) model, achieving an accuracy of 90.56%. Study 2 explores the correlation between VAQ and digital engagement via econometric analysis. Results reveal a U-shaped effect: both low and high VAQ lead to higher digital engagement than middle VAQ. This effect is more pronounced for posts with informational (vs. emotional) advertising appeals. Study 3 examines the causality with stimulus sampling and a randomized experiment, corroborating the findings of Study 2. Study 3 also uncovers the underlying mechanisms of the U-shaped effect: high VAQ enhances digital engagement primarily through perceived attractiveness, whereas low VAQ operates through perceived credibility. These findings refine the “beauty is always good” view into a nuanced U-shaped relationship and demonstrate how deep learning facilitates large-scale image analysis in social media.

title: From in-company to industry platforms: A process model of B2B platform transformation
Knowing when to quit: experience, binding financial constraints, and withdrawal from new venture creation
abstract: Abstract Why do people quit the startup process before a business is formed? We treat withdrawal from new venture creation as a test of Evans and Jovanovic’s (1989) model of liquidity constraints at the pre-entry margin. In the model, constraints bind when desired capital deployment exceeds what personal finances can support. We test three predictions with Entrepreneurship in the Population (EPOP) Survey data from 2023 to 2025, comparing 3980 responses from continuing nascent entrepreneurs with 6903 responses from people who considered or pursued a business and then stopped. Experienced founders report deploying more than twice the startup capital of novices. The association between pre-existing financial constraints and stopping is stronger for experienced founders. The experience gap in stopping odds is large at one financial constraint, marginal at two, and no longer detectable at three. A further implication, that funding-rationed seekers stop at higher rates, is directionally positive but not robust across years. The results are consistent with liquidity constraints binding at the pre-entry margin and help reconcile weak wealth-entry relationships with evidence that constraints matter.

The Role of Auditors’ Technology Readiness in IT Specialist Hour Allocation under Budget Pressure
