Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.

title: The Financial Premium
abstract: ABSTRACT We show that bonds issued by financial firms have higher spreads than bonds issued by industrial firms with the same rating and maturity, a difference that we refer to as the financial premium. Over the period 1987 to 2020, in the United States, this premium is 43 basis points on average, with the premium higher for lower ratings, higher during financial crises, and increasing in bond beta. We derive a model that explains the financial premium: banks hold diversified portfolios of nonfinancial debt, and bank debt therefore reflects more systematic risk than nonfinancial debt.

title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
abstract: ABSTRACT I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

title: Terrorism and Altruistic Giving: Evidence from Child Sponsorship
Mobile internet connectivity and household wealth in the Philippines
Heterogeneous patience, population growth, and wealth accumulation
abstract: Abstract We study a neoclassical growth model with population growth and heterogeneous agents. The model can be interpreted as either a Ramsey model with heterogeneous discounting and entry of new agents with zero endowments or an OLG model with infinitely-lived agents with different discount factors. We prove that, in the unique stationary equilibrium, agents other than the most patient may hold capital. Introducing public debt, a labor income tax, or a capital subsidy allows more agent types to save, reducing inequality among agents with different discount factors while increasing inequality among agents with the same discount factor entered in different periods.

title: Massive Open Online Courses and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from Colombia
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of MOOC certificates on labor market outcomes using a Coursera initiative that offered free certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although eligibility for free certificates was randomized, course completion rates were low-only 6.2% of eligible participants completed at least one course-so we rely on an event-study design to estimate the effects of receiving a certificate. The results show that MOOC certificates increases formal employment by about 5 percentage points, with larger impacts among participants who were not employed at baseline and those from low-income households, and no clear differences by gender. These gains are concentrated in employment at larger firms and in economic sectors aligned with the course content. Overall, while MOOCs have the potential to improve employment outcomes, additional interventions appear necessary to increase course completion rates.

title: Correction to: You Cannot Force Me Into Caregiving: Paternity Leave and the Child Penalty
Gambling for Re-election
abstract: Abstract We show that gambling-style behaviour is important in politics: politicians ‛gamble for re-election‚ in the context of a political leader selection. We exploit unique access to leaked information on MPs' individual decisions in the 2021 leadership election of Germany's centre-right parties. MPs are more likely to vote for a riskier candidate when facing lower re-election chances. These results match the predictions derived from our model of rational risk-taking. Gambling for re-election shows that MPs trade off leaders' expected quality against their riskiness. It provides a new explanation for intra-party dissent, and rationalises why parties may choose low quality leaders.

title: Remembering Cornelia Staritz: contributions to global production network and crisis research agendas
An extended energy system model for renewable energy expansion planning: The net energy perspective
Measuring efficiency and abatement costs in waste-to-energy: A nonparametric shadow pricing approach
Environmental regulatory risk
Growth-indexed bonds and debt distribution: Too little, too costly?
When women take all: Direct election and female leadership
Perceptions of own social class and local affluence: Effects on preferences for redistribution
(Most) everyone is above average: Optimism bias and insurance nonparticipation
abstract: Abstract We examine health insurance nonparticipation using a behavioral framework that integrates optimism bias with institutional safety nets. In our model, optimistic consumers underestimate their probability of health shocks. We show that nonparticipation—even under subsidized premiums—is rationalized by the interaction between optimism and an implicit medical bankruptcy floor that limits financial downside for low‐wealth households. Testing these predictions with data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, we create a proxy for optimism bias: the wedge between subjective health reports and objective clinical benchmarks. Consistent with theory, both lower income and higher optimism significantly depress insurance enrollment, with the behavioral friction concentrated among lower‐income households. Finally, because optimism bias positively predicts ex‐post healthcare expenditures across multiple care channels, our results are more consistent with a cognitive bias than private information.

title: Ethics, economics, and environmental stewardship: Religious moral frameworks as constraints for rational policy choice
Political Stressors and Birth Outcomes
abstract: Abstract We study political shocks as in-utero stressors, specifically the unexpected result of the 2016 U.S. presidential election. We investigate this shock using an innovative linkage: Colorado voter registrations and birth certificates, matched by sex, year, and name. While we do not find an effect on birth outcomes, we do find increased stress-related behaviors in pregnancy for Democrats and reduced prenatal care adequacy for Democrats and Independents, relative to Republicans. This adds new evidence on the effects of two-sided stressors, uses a novel data linkage, and expands the new economics area of politics as a determinant of health.

title: The Good Daughter?
abstract: Abstract We study the impact of Federal alcohol Prohibition in 1919 on workers in the alcohol industry and their families, using newly linked census records following spouses, sons, and daughters 1910-1940. Through 1930, affected men were less likely to work and worked in lower-skilled jobs when employed. By 1940, they were more likely to be employed, suggesting delayed retirement. Daughters of these workers were more likely to stay home, delay marriage, and work, even 20 years later. Sons were unaffected short-run. Those with sisters completed more schooling and earned more by 1940, suggesting daughters, not sons, served as the family’s safety net.

title: Bayesian p(h)ooling: Optimal pooling structure in quadratic Bayesian persuasion
Capital‐Labour Substitution in Macroeconomics: A Survey of Mechanisms, Dynamics and Policy Insights
abstract: ABSTRACT Macroeconomic conclusions often hinge on a single, hard‐to‐pin‐down parameter: the elasticity of substitution between capital and labour, σ . This survey synthesises theory and evidence on how results change once we move beyond the Cobb–Douglas benchmark (). We show how shapes factor income shares and productivity responses to capital deepening and technological change; how it alters transition dynamics; how it steers the direction of technological change; and how, by scaling factor‐demand elasticities, it amplifies taxation and misallocation effects. In labour‐market and matching frameworks, conditions how productivity and capital‐deepening shocks translate into wages and unemployment. Finally, affects equilibrium (in)determinacy and the scope for sunspots, bifurcations, and complex dynamics, depending on adjustment margins (such as variable capital utilization), externalities, financial constraints and policy feedback rules. By integrating classical insights with recent developments, this survey offers a coherent guide to macroeconomic mechanisms and public policy design.

title: The limits of issue ownership by international organisations: ideological demarcation and policy collaboration in global trade governance
abstract: How do international organizations (IOs) establish expert authority in crowded policy fields? This article investigates how IOs in global trade governance engage in boundary work to establish and maintain jurisdictional authority. Theoretically, we build on recent work that distinguishes between ‘frontstage’ performances and ‘backstage’ cooperation with research mapping the ideological topography of IOs. We argue that IOs can establish expert authority in a crowded global trade landscape, not by claiming exclusive ownership over key issues, but through the practice of ideological demarcation in flagship communications. Importantly, this practice takes place alongside policy collaboration in the day-to-day operations of trade-related IOs working on similar issues over time. We further demonstrate that intra-IO bureaucratic tensions can render cross-organizational collaboration more functional than internal coordination, as divisions can form epistemic and professional alliances across IO boundaries. Empirically, we focus on the relationship between the World Trade Organization and United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, combining automated content analysis and discourse analysis of flagship reports with elite interviews. This article thus enriches our understanding of how IOs engage in boundary politics and complements broader debates on how IOs establish authority, engage in self-legitimation, and navigate inter-institutional conflict, redundancy, and decay.

title: The winding road toward a wholesale digital euro: geoeconomics and bureaucratic politics
abstract: Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) have become a prominent topic in International Political Economy (IPE). Of particular interest are wholesale CBDCs, given their implications for payment infrastructures, both domestic and cross-border. The European Union (EU), one of the ‘great (financial) powers’, has been working on the development of a wholesale digital CBDC, yet progress has been uneven, characterized by sudden accelerations followed by periods of stasis. What accounts for this winding road toward the wholesale digital euro? Theoretically, we combine two approaches that are rarely deployed in tandem: geoeconomics and bureaucratic politics. Empirically, we show that a geoeconomic rationale, particularly concerns about the vulnerability of critical financial infrastructures in Europe and the desire to strengthen the international role of the euro, helps explain the drive toward a wholesale digital euro. At the same time, bureaucratic politics, understood as competing models sponsored by the main EU national central banks, accounts for the ECB’s cautious approach. In doing so, the paper contributes to the literatures on the weaponisation of finance, the geoeconomics of money, as well as the role of central banks as simultaneously geoeconomic and bureaucratic actors.

title: Income redistribution, preventive care, and longevity
Order of Entry and Market Performance in the Global Smartphone Industry
Adaptive Importance Sampling Estimation of an Open Economy Model With Fiscal Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT We propose and estimate an open economy general equilibrium model that includes international trade between Canada and the United States. We estimate our model using a new adaptive methodology based on the mixture of student's by Importance Sampling weighted Expectation–Maximisation (MitISEM). Our findings for the Canadian economy indicate that an increase in productive spending initially worsens the trade balance, whereas unproductive spending leads to a more persistent improvement through the contraction in private demand. We also show that the domestic real exchange rate appreciates on impact after both productive and unproductive government spending shocks, although the response is sharper and less persistent following a productive expenditure shock. Our structural framework uncovers highly asymmetric spillovers from the United States to Canada, successfully resolving the international transmission puzzle highlighted by Justiniano and Preston [12]. Finally, we conduct counterfactual exercises that consider alternative trade‐elasticity assumptions and a policy experiment involving a sizeable increase in US trade barriers.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Energy‐Related Uncertainty and Corporate Financialization
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the link between energy uncertainty and corporate financialization using data from 545 nonfinancial listed firms in Vietnam over 2007–2024. We find that higher energy uncertainty is associated with higher financial asset holdings. Mechanism analysis supports both real options and precautionary motives, as firms tend to delay real investment and shift toward liquid financial assets, particularly under conditions of tighter financial constraints. The effect is weaker for state‐owned enterprises but stronger in energy‐intensive industries and during economic downturns. Overall, the results suggest that energy uncertainty is associated with lower real investment and greater precautionary financialization, highlighting the importance of stabilizing energy markets.

title: Measuring differences of opinion: axiomatic foundations, utility representation, and truthtelling
Going Green: How Bank ESG Preferences Shape Corporate Green and Low-Carbon Technological Innovation
journal_name: Research in International Business and Finance

title: Government Report ESG Emphasis and Firms’ ESG Disclosure
journal_name: Research in International Business and Finance

title: The Power of Identity Pause: Perimenopause and the Embodiment Process
abstract: A growing volume of identity scholarship has started to challenge the Cartesian separation of body and mind, highlighting the importance of embodiment. While such research is enlightening, studies do not provide in-depth understanding of how some workers, but not others, are able to develop embodied identities (i.e., identities that are bonded with and bounded by their physical body). In particular, little is known about how this embodiment process occurs—or fails to do so—when changes within a worker’s body threaten their idealized identities (who they want and believe they should be). We examine this puzzle through an inductive study of perimenopause, which is a naturally occurring physiological transition experienced by most women. Unlike studies that have emphasized the importance of remedial identity or body work, our findings point to the criticality of an identity pause, which involves taking respite from striving to enact idealized identities. We illuminate how an identity pause gives workers the space to develop somatic attunement: the capacity to connect with, listen to, and respect their changing bodies. In so doing, our study calls attention to distinctive mechanisms that help develop embodied identities, advancing research on the body–identity nexus, embodiment, and women and work.

title: Transaction Hazards Through Ideological Filters: How CEO Political Ideology Influences Vertical Integration Decisions
abstract: Why do firms facing similar transaction environments adopt different boundary structures? Transaction cost theory (TCT) predicts governance choices based on transaction hazards, but persistent heterogeneity in vertical integration suggests that such efficiency-based explanations are incomplete. We examine whether CEO political ideology is associated with systematic variation in firm boundary decisions. Drawing on research on political ideology and strategic leadership, we argue that ideological orientations shape how executives evaluate and prioritize governance trade-offs. Using a panel of 1,198 U.S. public firms from 2001 to 2020 and a firm fixed-effects design exploiting CEO successions, we find that firms led by more conservative CEOs exhibit higher levels of vertical integration. This relationship weakens when asset specificity is high and when industries are more concentrated but is not amplified by demand volatility. Our findings suggest that firm boundaries reflect not only transaction conditions but also systematic differences in executive decision-making.

title: Populism and sustainable marketing practices: Insights from consumer-packaged goods manufacturers’ new product launches
abstract: Abstract While sustainable marketing practices have traditionally been grounded in stakeholder capitalism, the rise of anti-climate-action populism presents new challenges to firms’ sustainable strategies. Drawing on resource dependence theory, this study argues that anti-climate-action populism prompts firms to reduce sustainable marketing practices, specifically the use of environmentally friendly packaging in new product launches. However, we propose that subnational formal and informal institutions, such as economic freedom and cultural tightness, attenuate this effect. To test these hypotheses, we employ a quasi-natural experimental design, using the announcement of the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement to analyze its impact on sustainable marketing practices, based on a global sample of product launches by consumer-packaged goods manufacturers. Our difference-in-differences analysis supports these hypotheses. This study advances the understanding of the dynamic relationship between populism and subnational institutions, highlighting how different institutional pillars shape firms’ sustainable marketing strategies.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: From trade-off to paradox: a configurational theorizing and “quantum” approach to the resilience–sustainability tension in global sourcing
abstract: Abstract Global sourcing is increasingly caught between two persistent pressures: to be sustainable and resilient. While this relationship is often framed as a trade-off, we draw on paradox theory to conceptualize it as a persistent paradox, especially for MNEs coordinating complex supplier networks. Most paradox research addresses either how tensions are embedded in organizational systems or how they are socially constructed by managers, but rarely both. Drawing on the "quantum" approach to paradox, we bridge these ontological and epistemological perspectives, arguing that the resilience–sustainability tension is rooted in the structure of global sourcing systems and made salient through how managers interpret and combine sourcing decisions. Following a configurational roadmap of three stages—scoping, linking, and naming—we theorize five systemic sourcing factors (location choice, supplier redundancy, inventory buffer, green certification, and the sustainability premium) and examine how they are evaluated by 72 Italian procurement managers through a factorial survey, a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and interviews. Managers favor coherent bundles over standalone levers, combining certification-based sustainability assurance alongside resilience-oriented levers such as proximity, redundancy, and buffers. We conceptualize three archetypal sourcing logics— integrator , resilience-first , and cost-only —offering managers a practical vocabulary for framing and legitimating sourcing choices when both pressures collide.

title: From Text to Beta: Macroeconomic Disclosures and Firm-Level Systematic Risk
Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation for Ad Measurement
abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates of advertising incrementality but are difficult to scale. We propose Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation (PIE), which reframes ad measurement as a campaign-level prediction problem. PIE uses a sample of RCTs to learn a mapping from campaign features to causal effects, then applies it to campaigns not run as RCTs. Because the RCTs identify the causal effects, PIE can incorporate post-determined features—campaign-level aggregates such as test-group outcomes, exposure rates, and last-click conversions, computed after campaign completion. These metrics reflect the consumer behaviors that generate treatment effects, so they carry predictive information about incrementality, even though they would be invalid controls in a causal model. Using 2,226 Meta ad experiments, PIE achieves an out-of-sample [Formula: see text] for incremental conversions per dollar, compared with [Formula: see text] for industry-standard seven-day last-click attribution. In a decision-making framework, PIE disagrees with RCT-based decisions in only 8%–12% of campaigns, compared with 12%–20% for last-click attribution. We conclude that PIE can help scale causal measurement from a limited number of RCTs to a large set of nonexperimental campaigns. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01108 .

title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
abstract: Predictive AI models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict, but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge.

title: Dominant Deceptions: How Future-Oriented Narratives Transform into Deception
Repatterning Interactions in Remote Work Environments: Bolstering Psychological Safety Through Mutually Humanizing Self-Disclosure
From Scarce Resources to Resourcing Spirals: A Theory of Mindful Resourcing
The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
abstract: We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
abstract: ABSTRACT When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Textual analysis reveals that calls feature cautious, litigious language for both upward and downward revisions, whereas conference and A/I day communications remain optimistic. In line with these framing differences, calls are associated with amplified reaction to negative news and are followed by more favorable earnings surprises, suggestive of effective expectation management, whereas conferences and A/I days are associated with muted reactions and reduced analyst dispersion and are followed by less favorable surprises. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

title: Diagnosing Image-Ad Success: An Interpretable and Scalable Framework for Liking, Sharing, and Memorability
journal_name: International Journal of Research in Marketing

title: China's Initial Public Offering Peer‐based Valuation: Market versus Regulatory Pricing Regimes
abstract: Abstract In 2014, China's initial public offering (IPO) valuation regime shifted from market‐based pricing to a regulatory system with a de facto 23× P/E ratio cap. This institutional change provides a compelling setting to examine how institutional constraints affect valuation efficiency and information transmission. Using a sample of IPOs and hand‐collected peer firms, we document that regulated IPOs are systematically undervalued by 42–56.9% relative to their peers. Their valuations negatively predict post‐IPO returns, while market‐priced IPOs exhibit no such pattern. A low‐minus‐high price‐to‐value strategy yields annualized abnormal returns of 15.6% for IPOs under regulatory pricing, with no comparable profits under market pricing. These effects appear to operate through two interconnected channels: corporate competitiveness and stock price informativeness. Rather than reflecting costly signalling, constrained valuation serves as an information revelation mechanism of firm quality. Our findings provide novel evidence on how institutional frictions shape information transmission beyond conventional signalling incentives.

title: Navigating the Digital Capital Paradox: Whether and How It Impacts Export Intensity
abstract: Abstract Established firms are making substantial investments in digital capital (DC) – that is, capitalized software and systems – to enhance exports, yet they often face perplexing, even negative returns. We argue that this tension reflects an inherent resource–liability paradox, where DC acts simultaneously as a strategic resource and an operational liability. Drawing on paradox theory, we examine a framework that specifies how dynamic capability and external institutional frictions shape the outcomes of this persistent tension. Using longitudinal data of Chinese listed firms, we find that the unmanaged paradox manifests as a significant negative impact on export intensity. We theorize and demonstrate that a strong firm‐level digital orientation (DO) enables firms to reconcile the tension and reverse the negative effect. Informal institutional distance exacerbates the core paradox, while formal distance does not, highlighting the primacy of implicit, cognitive frictions over explicit, regulatory costs. Our study enriches the export literature and paradox theory by identifying DO as a higher level dynamic capability and advancing understanding of contextual intensification by disentangling the distinct roles of formal and informal institutional distances. Hence, realizing DC's international value depends not on the investment itself, but on the firm's ability to manage these internal contradictions within challenging institutional contexts.

title: Employee Perceptions of Organizational Sustainability: A Systematic Review and Integrative Multilevel Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT Employee perceptions are central to whether organizational sustainability initiatives become embedded in workplace practice or remain symbolic. This study reviews 123 peer‐reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2024 to clarify how employees interpret organizational sustainability and how these interpretations are associated with workplace outcomes. The findings show that perceptions are linked to individual values and capabilities, leadership signals, green HRM practices, sustainability communication, perceived authenticity, and wider stakeholder pressures. Favorable perceptions are associated with engagement, pro‐environmental behavior, creativity, and organizational citizenship for the environment, whereas perceived greenwashing or corporate hypocrisy is associated with weaker trust and commitment. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory, the Resource‐Based View, and Signaling Theory, the study proposes an association‐based multilevel framework that positions employee perceptions as the interpretive link between sustainability drivers and individual, organizational, and external outcomes.

title: Beyond Linear Paths: Configurations of Networks, Knowledge, and Dynamic Capabilities for Sustainable MSMEs
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite extensive research on entrepreneurial business networks (EBNs), knowledge management (KM), and dynamic capabilities (DC), three questions remain theoretically underdeveloped and empirically unexplored in resource‐constrained MSMEs. These concern the integrative mechanisms through which EBN and KM jointly cultivate DC, the differential mediation logic of DC across sustainability outcome types, and the configurational pathways through which these constructs collectively produce sustainability outcomes. Using PLS‐SEM and fsQCA on data from 316 manufacturing MSMEs in Uttar Pradesh, India, this study finds that DC fully mediates the effects of EBN and KM on sustainable competitiveness (SComP), whereas sustainable performance (SP) retains direct network and knowledge effects, reflecting its operational proximity to resource inputs. The necessity analysis confirms no single condition is individually necessary for high SP, and fsQCA reveals nine equifinal configurations, showing that high SP is achievable through multiple strategic routes. These findings offer actionable insights for managers and policymakers in emerging‐economy contexts.

title: Idiosyncratic influences of hotel occupancy on energy consumption: Moderating effects of service style, hotel size, and hotel class
Human resource intervention studies: Prevalence, challenges, and opportunities
The AI entrepreneurial actor: Towards a theoretical framework for artificial intelligence as entrepreneurial actor
abstract: Classical theory assumes upon a human entrepreneur who bears uncertainty, exercises alertness and recognises opportunity. We examine what becomes of that assumption when artificial intelligence (AI) performs these issues. Defining AI as agentic systems built on large foundation models, we analyse how far such systems manifest core entrepreneurial attributes and where they reach fundamental limits. We propose the AI Entrepreneurial Agency Framework (AEAF), a four-level model organised along two conceptually independent dimensions: the autonomy of AI judgment and the degree of Knightian uncertainty in the task environment. Three falsifiable propositions theorise the redistribution of uncertainty and accountability, the intentionality boundary on opportunity framing and alertness, and the cognitive-computational re-conception of the individual–opportunity nexus. Incorporating Bayesian entrepreneurship, we specify where AI accelerates experimentation and where it cannot. A structured review of fourteen studies positions the AEAF as an integrated platform for this frontier, with implications for theory, strategy and AI governance.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: Strategic framework for digital marketing localization: advancing the standardization-adaptation debate in international marketing strategy
abstract: Purpose This conceptual paper responds to the evolving needs of international marketing strategy (IMS) by proposing a theoretically grounded Digital Marketing Localization Framework (DMLF). The framework revisits the standardization versus adaptation debate, emphasizing its relevance in digitally mediated environments. Design/methodology/approach A structured literature review was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar (1983–mid-2025) pertaining to IMS frameworks, digital platforms, cross-cultural behavior and decision-making models. Several peer-reviewed articles and book chapters were included, while studies limited to traditional media or the B2B context were excluded. This synthesis incorporates key classical debates regarding IMS, and advances in digital ecosystems, personalization and cultural engagement. Drawing on an interdisciplinary approach that blends theoretical constructs from interrelated fields, this paper develops a structured, multi-dimensional decision-making framework. Findings The study highlights the importance of integrating cultural sensitivity, platform-specific dynamics and algorithmic personalization into IMS theory. It addresses gaps in pre-digital frameworks by offering actionable insights for navigating the complexities introduced by digital platforms and cross-border data governance. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual study, the framework requires empirical validation through future research. Our paper outlines testable propositions and methodologies to evaluate the effectiveness of DMLF across diverse markets. Future researchers need to focus on examining the unresolved tensions between; AI-driven efficiency and culturally embedded authenticity, automation compared to cultural sensitivity, standardization logic compared to adaptive learning, algorithmic optimization compared to managerial judgment and their impact on local decision-making. Practical implications The DMLF provides actionable guidance for marketing executives to balance global coherence with local relevance. It enables organizations to systematically evaluate digital localization options, ensuring decisions are guided by contextual insights rather than intuition. Originality/value This research contributes to IMS by adapting foundational debates to the complexities of digital globalization. It offers a comprehensive framework tailored to internet-enabled international operations and proposes an agenda for empirical research that aligns with IMS’s broader shift toward analytical rigor and theoretical innovation.

title: Employees’ voluntary disclosure about business outlook and labour hiring efficiency
How High‐Tech Firms Achieve Organizational Resilience Using Dynamic Capabilities and Different Types of Innovations in VUCA Environments
abstract: ABSTRACT High‐tech firms must achieve organizational resilience (OR) to remain viable in volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) environments. Although specific dynamic capabilities (DCs), particularly integrative and reconfiguring capabilities, allow such firms to integrate and complement resource/capability gaps and align resources to maintain evolutionary fitness and develop different types of innovations to become resilient, how they leverage both to achieve OR in VUCA environments remains unexplored to date. This study uses a multiple‐case study approach to explore how high‐tech firms achieve OR by leveraging integrative and reconfiguring capabilities and different types of innovations in VUCA environments. This study finds that high‐tech firms focus on market dynamics, adaptive management innovations, and efficiency‐driven management and process innovations to become resilient. They develop these innovations using proactive and time‐oriented, support activities‐focused, and technology‐driven reconfiguring capabilities, respectively. Additionally, they use ambidexterity‐focused integrative capability to develop supply chain adaptive product innovations and extended technology leveraging market innovations to become resilient. The deployment of complementarity‐oriented integrative capability is found useful in building existing technology leveraging market innovations that underlie firm resilience. This study contributes to the innovation management literature by offering a granular, comprehensive strategic understanding that incorporates both foundations (DCs) and key drivers (innovations) to achieve OR in VUCA environments. It provides managers with nuanced insights for use in developing overarching R&D and innovation strategies by effectively allocating and renewing resources using feature‐specific integrative and reconfiguring capabilities to develop diversified, distinctive types of innovations that provide firms with resilience to support operational continuity in VUCA environments.

title: Reaffirming the validity of unobtrusive personality measures: A comment on Harms et al. (2025) and guidance for the field
abstract: Abstract As unobtrusive measures of CEO personality have become more common in organizational research, questions about their validity have grown. Harms et al., Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology, (2025) 98, e70052 recently formalized some of these concerns in a meta‐analysis, citing higher average intercorrelations and weaker associations with firm performance relative to survey‐based measures as evidence of their lack of validity. We argue that these criticisms are overstated, reflecting both a misunderstanding of what unobtrusive measures capture and limitations in the authors' assumptions and meta‐analytic approach. Whereas self‐report surveys capture executives' self‐concepts, existing unobtrusive measures typically assess externally observed or expressed personality. We suggest that relatively higher average intercorrelations are theoretically expected when assessments reflect stylized expressions of CEOs' observed tendencies, and we provide evidence that unobtrusive measures can meaningfully distinguish between traits. We further argue that, given what they represent and their application in large firms, unobtrusive measures likely relate differently to outcomes shaped by external audiences as compared to aggregate financial outcomes. Consistent with this logic, we show substantive differences in the relationships between unobtrusive measures of CEO personality and market performance compared to accounting performance. Our study reaffirms the validity of unobtrusive personality measures and offers guidance for their appropriate evaluation, interpretation and continued refinement.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: The moralization paradox at work: How Supervisor's moral framing depletes subordinates' self‐regulatory resources and suppresses proactive problem prevention
abstract: Abstract Integrating moral and ethical considerations into work is often presumed to yield a wide range of beneficial outcomes. Yet these benefits may not be unconditional, as prevailing scholarship has largely overlooked the potential costs associated with self‐regulatory resource depletion and diminished self‐initiated behaviours that are critical for averting future work disruptions. Drawing on ego depletion theory, we theorize that supervisor's work moralization can inadvertently hinder subordinates' proactive problem prevention by elevating their experiences of ego depletion. Furthermore, we posit that subordinates' reflective moral attentiveness intensifies this relationship, such that highly reflective individuals are more susceptible to the depleting effects of supervisor's work moralization, which in turn exacerbates the reduction in their proactive problem prevention. To test these propositions, we conducted two complementary empirical studies: Study 1, an experience sampling investigation, and Study 2, a vignette‐based laboratory experiment. Across both studies, the findings robustly supported our hypotheses. This research advances the literature by challenging the predominantly positive narrative of work moralization, illuminating its paradoxical potential to undermine subordinates' proactive behaviours, and providing novel theoretical insight into the boundary conditions and self‐regulatory mechanisms shaping the consequences of moral framing in the workplace.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: The scientist–practitioner divide revisited: From bridging a gap to navigating the layers of a knowledge ecosystem
abstract: Abstract Discussions about the scientist–practitioner divide have shaped industrial, work and organizational psychology (IWOP), including landmark publications in this journal ( Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology 74 , 2001, 391–411; Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology 79 , 2006, 173–178). Yet, this dyadic metaphor may no longer reflect the complexity of the IWOP knowledge landscape. Drawing on the principles of the divide metaphor, we argue for reconceptualizing IWOP as a knowledge ecosystem, namely a dynamic, multilayered environment in which diverse actors create, translate, contest and apply scientific evidence. We highlight how end‐users extend beyond practitioners to include policymakers, regulators, courts, unions, educators and workers. We further distinguish between end‐users and end‐beneficiaries to illuminate how IWOP knowledge can generate uneven consequences for different recipients. We argue that an ecosystem metaphor enables a more complete and ethically grounded understanding of IWOP knowledge. Finally, we examine how structural forces, such as the prestige trap, can influence what knowledge is produced, rewarded and legitimized.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: Artificial intelligence in sales (2017-early 2026): field consolidation and the rise of human-AI collaboration
AI Companions and Loneliness: Conceptualizing and Operationalizing Synthetic Mindfulness and Exploring Its Role in Alleviating Loneliness
abstract: ABSTRACT The rise of AI companions has sparked interest in their potential to alleviate the growing social problem of loneliness, yet evidence of their effectiveness remains unsettled. Drawing on social surrogacy theory with a theories‐in‐use approach, this research introduces synthetic mindfulness, defined as consumers' judgment of an AI companion's capacity to maintain an attentive presence, engage in a non‐judgmental way, and respond with sensitive attunement to their needs. We argue that these judgments shape whether consumers experience AI companions as capable of reducing their loneliness. Across one qualitative and four quantitative studies, we develop and validate a three‐dimensional measure of synthetic mindfulness. Our final study demonstrates that higher judgments of synthetic mindfulness reduce loneliness via consumers' strengthened sense of belonging and self‐esteem. This research advances understanding of how AI companions can effectively address loneliness and provides a conceptual foundation for examining synthetic mindfulness in human–AI relationships.

title: Power Distance Beliefs and Luxury Brand Communication: Cross‐Cultural Differences in the Effects of Exclusivity and Heritage
abstract: ABSTRACT Luxury brands communicate symbolic value through a variety of brand signals, among which exclusivity and heritage represent two most prominent yet conceptually distinctive luxury signals. However, little is known about whether consumers respond equally favorably to these alternative luxury brand signaling strategies. This research examines how luxury brand signaling strategies (exclusivity vs. heritage) interact with consumers' [power distance beliefs (PDB) to influence consumer responses. In three online and one field studies, we operationalized PDB through multiple approaches, including experimental manipulations, measurement of chronic individual differences, and a country‐level proxy designed to capture variation in average PDB across national contexts. The findings reveal that low‐PDB consumers show more favorable responses (click‐through rate, incentive‐compatible choice, purchase intention, and willingness to pay a premium) for heritage signals, whereas high‐PDB consumers respond more favorably to exclusivity signals. Moreover, this interactive effect occurs through serial mediation of recognition benefits and brand attachment. This research contributes to international marketing and cross‐cultural branding literature by highlighting how tailoring luxury brand communications to cultural contexts can enhance engagement and commercial outcomes across diverse markets.

title: Love It, Hate It, Can't Quit It: Mapping the Duality of Social Media Use
abstract: ABSTRACT Social media use (SMU) is increasingly central to consumer–brand engagement; however, consumers routinely describe it as both a source of connection and utility and a driver of loss of control and diminished well‐being. This research advances an integrative duality framework that reconciles perceived value and behavioral addiction through a dialectical mechanism in which consumers cycle through value (thesis), experienced costs (antithesis), and imperfect syntheses, such as boundary setting, platform switching, and abstinence attempts. Using a three‐study, multi‐method design, we show convergent evidence that net‐benefit models do not fully capture SMU outcomes: mixed emotions and ambivalent evaluations frequently co‐occur within the same accounts and persist across contexts, including discourse about quitting. Theoretically, the study amends net‐benefit accounts of engagement by specifying a dialectical mechanism, perceived value (thesis), experienced cost (antithesis), and imperfect synthesis, that explains why consumer ambivalence toward platforms persists instead of resolving. The framework's originality lies in treating ambivalence as a structural property of platform engagement.

title: Platform-Based Servitization: Reconciling Competing Growth Logics for Industrial Firms
abstract: Servitization and platformization represent distinct logics through which industrial firms pursue growth. Servitization increases value through close customer integration, whereas platformization drives growth through ecosystem orchestration and scalability. These logics involve an inherent tension between relational depth and scalable flexibility, which the service literature has yet to resolve. This study draws on a systematic cross-field review of 129 articles spanning service, marketing, management, and information systems to theoretically ground platform-based servitization. We contribute to servitization by explaining how four configurational archetypes—product–service, customer solution, innovation, and transaction platforms—drive growth through platform-based servitization. Through a series of propositions, we explain how the cumulative layering of these configurations supports reinforcing and transformative pathways to growth, while data network effects emerge as a central growth mechanism, and combinatorial governance helps manage tensions between competing growth logics. We also contribute to platform scholarship by highlighting relational depth with customers and service partners as a critical condition shaping B2B platform transitions. For managers, our framework provides a strategic roadmap for leveraging platforms to move from digitalized product–service offerings to scalable platform growth. Finally, our findings open a research agenda for service scholars to further explore platform-based servitization.

title: Fixation or exploration? A state-dependent dual decoder approach to attribute-aware session-based recommendations
Personnel Psychology's 40 Questions Series: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Organizations
abstract: ABSTRACT This article presents a curated set of 40 questions on diversity, equity, and inclusion in organizations (DEI) to address myths and misperceptions about its role in Industrial/Organizational (I/O) Psychology and Management research and practice. We crowdsourced questions from our professional networks and organized the responses into themes including foundations of DEI, the business case, DEI effectiveness, DEI resistance, legal interpretations, DEI pullback, measurement, and programs and vehicles. Though the review is not entirely comprehensive, the aim is to utilize the most up‐to‐date literature to answer many of the most pressing questions about DEI.

title: The unintended effect of monetary incentives on shirking in manufacturer–reseller relationships
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how temporal changes in manufacturer monetary incentives influence reseller behavior within manufacturer–reseller relationships. We theorize, using agency theory, and examine empirically how the manufacturer's incentive changes have complex and unintended effects on the reseller's shirking, ultimately shaping the manufacturer's economic performance. Design/methodology/approach We test our hypotheses on the effect of incentives using data from two successive surveys of exporting manufacturers in partnerships with foreign resellers, together with archival sources. Findings We observe a U-shaped relationship of monetary-incentive changes with shirking. The results reveal that when monetary incentives are decreasing (left-side of the U), their effect on reseller shirking is negative, but when they are increasing (right-side of the U), they can have a positive effect on shirking. The U-shaped relationship steepens when import market GDP growth is high. Practical implications Manufacturer managers should scrutinize and even resist reseller requests to increase monetary incentives because in most cases, the intended positive act of boosting incentives leads to an unintended increase in reseller shirking and a reduction in manufacturer performance. Originality/value We adopt a novel approach that examines intertemporal changes in monetary incentives within manufacturer–reseller relationships. Our findings add to modern thinking on agency theory, which views the level of convergence between the principal's and the agent's economic interests as a dynamic process shaped by wider considerations pertaining to relationship status.

title: Exclusion Experiences of Highly Qualified Migrants: From Overt Discrimination to Subtle Microaggressions
abstract: Abstract We conducted a qualitative interview study exploring the exclusion experiences of 130 highly qualified migrants in Germany and made a surprising discovery: Contrary to dominant narratives, our interviewees report only minimal instances of overt discrimination. At the same time, our data reveal the prevalence of subtler forms of exclusion, which recent research conceptualizes as microaggressions. Thus, our study underscores that the absence of overt discrimination does not equate to an inclusive environment. Next to revealing the relevance of microaggressions, we show how migrants experience them, why their experiences can differ, and how they react to them. Particularly, we find that the negative experience of microaggressions can be related to an undermined sense of belonging, entitlement, and inclusion in majority country and working contexts. We further disclose that the following dimensions affect migrants’ experiences of microaggressions: context, (first or second) generation, (non-)recognizability of foreign background, and cultural identity. By highlighting that microaggressions are crucial for understanding exclusion of highly qualified migrants and providing detailed information around experiences and reactions, this paper integrates and contributes to two growing discourses relevant to business ethics research: migration as well as diversity, equity, and inclusion. Based on our analysis, we further propose solutions that are pertinent for managers, employing organizations and societies at large in their efforts to create inclusive environments for migrants.

title: Extreme Temperatures and the Cost of Public Debt: Evidence from China
abstract: Climate risk is priced by investors in the municipal bond market and is reflected in government financing costs that need to be identified. Based on theoretical analysis, this paper matches project-level data on local government special bonds (LGSBs) issued by Chinese local governments between 2018 and 2021 with city-level meteorological data to empirically evaluate the impact of extreme temperatures on issuance spreads for these bonds. The empirical results show that extreme high temperatures increase the spreads of LGSBs. The mechanism is that extreme heat weakens expected project return prospects and decreases government fund revenues. This paper reveals the climate risk factors implicit in the price formation of local government bonds in China, highlighting the importance of incorporating climate risks into fiscal decision-making frameworks.

title: Combining digital and green technologies in regions: How to close the gap with respect to the frontier?
abstract: This paper focuses on the combination of green and digital technologies at the regional level. Using patent data, we put forward an original measurement of the regional speed of green-digital (i.e. twin) combination: the temporal distance between the time at which a combination is realised for the first time in the frontier region and the time at which this same combination is accomplished in the focal region. We proceed by investigating the drivers and the technological impact related to this speed. We find that the speed of combination is enhanced by dealing with broad and diverse twin technologies. The speed at which the gap is closed, also crucially depends on the interdependencies between green and digital domains, captured by the overlap in their knowledge bases. Counterintuitively, the longer the combination paths, the faster the region combines green and digital technologies. This finding is then rationalised further looking at the policy and network characteristics. Finally, we find that the earlier the combination happens, the greater is likely to be the impact on subsequent inventions, but only for granted patents. Overall, these results are discussed in terms of policy recommendations, given the high attention placed by policymakers on the twin transition.

title: A Public Philosophy for Public Administration in Times of Democratic Crisis
abstract: ABSTRACT Public administration is at the center of the global democratic crisis. Meeting this challenge requires more than managerial and analytic competence—it requires a public philosophy grounded in the first principles of democratic ethos. We offer such a philosophy, drawing on four seminal thinkers whose concepts reflect the conditions public administrators face in times of democratic crisis. Judith Shklar's liberalism of fear establishes a negative obligation to refuse cruelty and resist its institutionalization. Alasdair MacIntyre's internal goods of practice create a positive obligation to cultivate virtue and protect the integrity of administrative practice. Isaiah Berlin's agony of choice obligates administrators to acknowledge irreducible value conflicts and their consequential impact on democratic life. Hannah Arendt's enlarged mentality provides a framework for thinking across perspectives so that judgment under conflict becomes democratically defensible. Together, these concepts form a public philosophy for public administration with practical significance for administrative judgment, organizational culture, and institutional courage.

title: Is Public Sector a Better Place for Moms to Work? Exploring Sector Difference in Child Penalties on Women
abstract: ABSTRACT With commonly stabler and more flexible working environment, is public sector a better place for moms to work? Theorizing child penalties from sector difference perspective, we argue that childbirth may cause less gender gaps in unemployment and earnings but greater gender disparities in working time commitments in the public sector since job stability and family‐friendliness may form gender norms that depreciate women's work in the public sector. We test our hypotheses by employing event study designs using data from China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022). We found that women public employees experienced smaller child penalties in unemployment and earnings while greater child penalties in working hours than private counterparts, which can be explained by greater family responsibilities and spousal depreciation of women's jobs after childbirth. This paper advances theories of gender equity in public administration by proposing distinct child penalties in the public sector that challenges conventional beliefs.

title: From Public to Private Governance, and Back—Eco‐Modulation as De‐Privatization in Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
abstract: ABSTRACT The European Union is advancing circular economy policies, aimed at reducing the environmental impacts of products across their life‐cycles. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) exemplifies this strategy. It privatizes the end‐of‐life management of products to their producers, seeking thereby to incentivize the producer to design environmentally more sustainable products. However, EPR has failed to deliver significant improvements in product design. This article examines the EU's attempts to strengthen eco‐design in EPR through ‘eco‐modulation’. Applying the theory of competence‐and‐control, the article argues that the introduction of eco‐modulation will destabilize the public‐private balance in EPR, shifting EPR back from private towards public governance. This de‐privatization is expected to refine EPR's role within the EU's policy mix. Our findings thus offer insights for the development of EPR‐related circular economy policies, while also contributing to theories of privatization.

title: Within‐Sector Job Mobility and Worker Outcomes in England's Adult Social Care Sector
abstract: ABSTRACT England's adult social care sector faces persistently high staff turnover. This article examines the effects of individual‐level within‐sector job mobility on hourly pay and working hours and identifies the employer types and contractual arrangements that attract such mobility. Using an event‐study difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, we show that job mobility increases hourly pay by 4.5% in the first year, rising to 6.1% after 5 years. Instrumental variable analyses either corroborate the DiD estimates or show higher impacts. Mobility also raises weekly working hours and reduces the likelihood of 0‐h contracts by around 7.0 percentage points. Employer‐specific wage premia account for nearly half of observed pay gains, whereas worker–employer match effects play little role. Workers predominantly move to higher paying employers—particularly local authorities and community‐based services—into fixed‐hours contracts and out of direct care roles. Moves into 0‐h contracts result in modest pay losses. Men experience larger pay gains from mobility than women.

title: Decentralization as an anticorruption strategy: does revenue autonomy make a difference?
abstract: This study investigates how revenue autonomy is associated with documented municipal corruption risk, distinguishing between own-source tax and non-tax revenues. Drawing on public administration theories of decentralization, it adopts a meso-level analysis of Italian medium-to-large municipalities and relies on an event-based indicator derived from legally mandated anticorruption reports. The empirical strategy combines dynamic correlated random-effects logit, dynamic random-effects probit, and fixed-effects logit models, complemented by sensitivity analyses simulating under-reporting scenarios. Results indicate that higher levels of both tax and non-tax revenue autonomy are negatively associated with documented corruption risk. Tax autonomy shows stronger associations where political competition is higher, whereas the non-tax revenue pattern is more consistent with a service-based responsiveness logic. These findings, observed in the Italian municipal context, suggest that revenue autonomy is not a uniform anticorruption safeguard but an institutional feature whose relevance depends on revenue composition, accountability conditions, municipal capacity, and reporting practices.

Facial Asymmetry and Sexuality in Women
abstract: People perceive more symmetrical individuals as more attractive; therefore, facial symmetry has been linked to mate selection. Being perceived as more attractive could also increase women's indirect reproductive benefits that would follow from pronounced sexuality and enhanced mating. Sexuality can be examined either as long-term, through sociosexual orientation, or through current sexual activity and desire. This study explored the relationship between facial asymmetry and female sexuality, while taking into account a relationship status and, due to the potential differences in facial asymmetry between female from rural and urban areas, the place of residence. Long-term sexuality was measured with the three subscales of the Sociosexual Orientation Inventory (SOI-R): Behavior, Attitude, and Desire. Current sexual activity and desire were assessed with questions about their frequency and intensity (based on the Female Sexual Function Index). Simple correlations revealed a weak, negative association between facial asymmetry and the number of sexual partners in the last year (ρ = - .23, 95% CI [- 0.45, 0.01], p = .047), SOI Attitude (ρ = - .25, 95% CI [- 0.44, - 0.03], p = .031), and sexual desire (ρ = - .21, 95% CI [- 0.43, - 0,00], p = .082). However, these effects were no longer significant after including place of residence as a confounder (.42 < p < .91). These results highlight the importance of external conditions when investigating correlates of facial asymmetry.

title: Problematic Pornography Use Among Swedish Adolescents: Characteristics and Clinical Implications
abstract: Abstract Problematic pornography use (PPU) is the most common manifestation of compulsive sexual behavior disorder (CSBD). Many adults seeking help for CSBD report onset during adolescence, yet there is limited knowledge of PPU in adolescents and its predisposing factors. This study investigated the prevalence of self-perceived PPU among Swedish adolescents and explored associated factors as well as pornography use patterns. In this cross-sectional study, data were collected from a representative sample of 3106 Swedish third-year senior high school students. Information on sociodemographic background, pornography use, sexual behaviors, health, and experiences of abuse was collected. PPU was based on self-reported difficulties in refraining from or stopping pornography use. Gender-stratified descriptive statistics and logistic regression analyses were used to examine relationships between groups and variables. PPU was reported by 10.4% of respondents, with a higher prevalence among boys (18.8%) compared to girls (3.9%). It was associated with increased time spent on pornography and higher exposure to violent or other concerning sexual content. Compared to the reference group, adolescents with PPU exhibited higher rates of abusive experiences, mental health issues, risky behaviors, and nonsuicidal self-injury. Gender-specific patterns emerged. PPU is a significant issue among Swedish adolescents, particularly boys. Addressing concerns related to pornography use, underlying vulnerabilities and gender-specific factors is crucial to prevent the progression of PPU into adulthood and in treatment efforts.
