title: Monetary policy and mergers and acquisitions
Measuring Measurement Error
abstract: Abstract We collect 2,848 instrumental variable (IV) regressions from 391 papers published in top economics and finance journals and show that estimated IV coefficients are often much larger than their OLS counterparts, even when theory suggests they should be smaller. We derive meta-regression estimators that distinguish measurement error bias from omitted variable bias and simultaneity bias; applying our estimators to a set of 1,040 comparable regressions from 139 papers, we find that measurement error shrinks reported coefficients by about two to four times. Measurement error remains quantitatively important even after accounting for weak instruments, publication bias, instrument invalidity, and heterogeneous treatment effects. Our results suggest that measurement error is a severe, pervasive, and understated source of bias in economics and finance.

title: Foreign exchange intervention in dollarized economies: A quantitative evaluation
Generalizing the Pareto principle with endogenous populations
Simulating competitive collocation strategies with deep reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a simulation model based on deep reinforcement learning to study competitive collocation strategies of two internationalizing firms. Drawing on the strategic interaction and competitive collocation literature in IB, we explore the factors determining the performance-optimizing degree of collocation in market-seeking internationalization for a duopoly in product markets. Our simulation suggests that a high degree of collocation between the two firms is optimal in many circumstances. Whereas mid-to-high levels of collocation are driven by low competitive intensity, low entry barriers, low home-market size, and high market-size variation, complete collocation emerges under high competitive intensity, low first-mover advantage, and smaller home-market size. High entry barriers, combined with low variation in market size and strong liabilities of foreignness, drive the opposite case of complete mutual avoidance. A key takeaway from the simulation is a focus on the competing firm in global expansion: in many cases, it becomes key to limit the rival’s growth options and to enter key markets before access becomes more restricted. We discuss the possibilities of using computer-simulation-based approaches to theorizing on internationalization.

title: CEO Ideologically (In)Congruent Activism and Investor Reactions: An Attribution of CEO Intentions Perspective
abstract: Abstract The phenomenon of chief executive officers (CEOs) taking activism stances on contested sociopolitical issues is increasing, yet it remains unclear how observing investors discern CEO intentions behind activism engagements, thereby shaping their judgments and subsequent reactions. By relaxing the assumption that CEO activism is an unabashed expression of personal beliefs, we propose the concept of CEO ideologically (in)congruent activism and develop a framework wherein investors may attribute CEO intentions underlying incongruent (versus congruent) activism engagements as more organization‐driven (versus self‐driven) interest pursuits, thereby leading to more positive investor evaluations and reactions. Furthermore, we argue that the positive effect of CEO ideologically incongruent activism on investor reactions will be amplified when the CEO owns a higher level of stock ownership but weakened when the firm receives a greater corporate social responsibility (CSR) rating. We corroborate our propositions using a sample of CEO activism events for S&P 500 firms from 2012 to 2021. Our findings demonstrate the heterogeneity and critical influence of CEO intentions behind activism engagements and shed light on how investors integrate multi‐informational cues when evaluating and reacting to managerial incongruent behaviours.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

title: EXPRESS: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

title: Competition and Diversity in Generative AI
abstract: Recent evidence, both in the laboratory and in the wild, suggests that the use of generative artificial intelligence reduces the diversity of content produced. As generative AI penetrates more markets and reaches widespread adoption, should we still expect to see content homogenization? Our work begins with a simple observation: content producers do not act in isolation. Instead, they compete with one another (e.g., for customers or attention). We explore the impact competition has on both content diversity and overall social welfare when producers use generative AI. Through a formal game-theoretic model, we show that competitive markets select for diverse AI models, mitigating monoculture. We further show that a generative AI model that performs well in isolation (i.e., according to a benchmark) may fail to provide value in a competitive market. Our results highlight the importance of evaluating generative AI models across the breadth of their output distributions, particularly when they will be deployed in competitive environments. We validate our theoretical results with a series of experiments involving generative text and image models. Overall, our results suggest that homogenization due to generative AI is unlikely to persist under strong competition. This paper was accepted by Itai Ashlagi, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02761 .

title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors acknowledge funding from the University of Konstanz for Study 2, Harvard University Pershing Square Foundation for Human Research, and Harvard Business School. The funders had no role in data collection and analysis, the decision to publish, or preparation of this manuscript. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03600 .

title: Customer air quality perceptions: conceptualization, scale development, and validation
Measuring Organizational Constructs in Large-Scale Text: An interpretive framework combining topic modeling and BERT
abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

title: Media Review: Homebound: Caste, Muslim Identity, and the Organizational Politics of Stigmatized Lives
Media Review: The Ocean between Utopias and Dystopias
Media Review: The Objects That Count Us
Media Review: Moving From Robust Identities to Ontological Differences in Organization Theory?
The Good Idea Dilemma
Who Qualifies to Assure? The Professional and Managerial Capture of Sustainability Assurance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how the qualification of assurors in sustainability and environmental reporting assurance (SERA) is constructed and why it remains fiercely contested. Drawing on actor–network theory (ANT) and qualitative evidence from regulators, NGOs, assurors and reporting companies in India, we conceptualise ‘qualification’ as a ‘boundary object’ flexible enough for competing actors to invoke, yet too ambiguous to secure substantive credibility. Assurance standards do not license practitioners, a function ordinarily undertaken by regulators and professional bodies. Nevertheless, ISAE 3000 (Revised) requires the engagement partner to possess ‘sufficient competence in the underlying subject matter’ and requires practitioners who are not professional accountants to identify the equivalent professional requirements under which they operate. Our analysis examines what becomes of these competence requirements when no external mechanism consistently verifies the claims made. The findings reveal that assurance standards require competence but rely substantially on practitioners to identify and disclose the professional requirements governing their work, without themselves providing an external licensing or verification mechanism. This ambiguity enables professional and managerial actors to privilege reputational legitimacy over the transparent demonstration of expertise, potentially reducing assurance to a symbolic exercise rather than a mechanism of substantive accountability. The study contributes to the SERA literature by reframing qualification as a fragile, networked achievement rather than a fixed credential. It highlights the need for transparent, dialogic and enforceable mechanisms through which competence claims can be demonstrated, scrutinised and sustained, thereby safeguarding independence, rigorous materiality assessments and stakeholder trust. These findings offer theoretical and practical insights for standard setters and policy makers seeking to mitigate greenwashing and strengthen the integrity of sustainability assurance.

title: Biodiversity Action Planning Within a Global Agricultural Supply Chain
abstract: ABSTRACT Agriculture is a primary driver of biodiversity loss through habitat conversion and degradation. Companies are increasingly being asked to investigate, disclose, and act on their biodiversity impacts by both regulatory policies and voluntary commitments. Yet companies lack practical guidance for identifying actions that mitigate negative externalities and improve natural systems on commodified lands and throughout their supply chains. We collaborated with an international food and beverage company sourcing from 120 regions around the world to develop a generalizable opportunity mapping framework based on cost‐effectiveness. We used publicly available datasets, a decision‐theoretic prioritization framework, and included both quantitative and qualitative insights. Our intent is to demonstrate how opportunity mapping and prioritization can integrate biodiversity into a company's decisions or nature strategies. Our approach helps companies see where and how their activities may contribute to pressures on biodiversity. We then help companies operationalize those insights into sourcing policies, regional investment, and engagement strategies across supply chains.

title: Beyond Disclosure: Sustainable Finance Regulation and the Pricing of ESG Performance in Mature Capital Markets
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether and under what conditions Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance becomes financially meaningful in mature capital markets. Using a longitudinal transatlantic panel of large firms listed in the EURO STOXX 50 and S&P 100 over the period 2015–2024, we analyse the within‐firm association between lagged ESG performance, market valuation, and accounting profitability. We further examine whether this relationship changes around the 2018 EU Action Plan on Financing Sustainable Growth and the 2021 implementation of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation, and whether ESG controversies moderate the financial relevance of ESG performance. Firm and year fixed‐effect models show that improvements in ESG performance are positively but only weakly associated with Tobin's Q , whereas no systematic relationship emerges with accounting profitability. Policy interaction models and a dynamic event study provide no evidence of a discrete strengthening of the ESG–valuation relationship for EU‐domiciled firms relative to US‐domiciled firms following the selected regulatory milestones. ESG controversies are directionally associated with weaker ESG value relevance, although the evidence is more pronounced for profitability than for market valuation. Moreover, the Environmental, Social, and Governance pillars are not statistically distinguishable from one another. Among large and highly visible firms, sustainable finance regulation may operate as institutional codification and credibility infrastructure rather than as an abrupt valuation shock, although the evidence is equally consistent with limited statistical power and with measurement error in a domicile‐based indicator of regulatory exposure. The results highlight the conditional and statistically fragile nature of ESG value relevance and should be generalized cautiously beyond institutionally mature capital markets.

title: Research on the mechanism of linking time pressure to career growth among hotel employees
abstract: Research overlooks how and why identical cognitive appraisals of time pressure translate into divergent coping behaviors. Drawing upon the cognitive appraisal theory of stress, this study investigates the mechanisms linking time pressure to the career growth of frontline hotel employees. Utilizing a three-wave time-lagged design, we collected survey data from 323 frontline hotel employees in China and analyzed it using PLS-SEM via SmartPLS 4.0. The results reveal that challenge appraisal and hindrance appraisal play differentiated mediating roles between time pressure and career growth, with job crafting serving as a crucial behavioral bridge in the transformation from stress appraisal to career growth. Furthermore, achievement motivation significantly moderates this transformation from stress appraisal to job crafting behavior. This study provides empirical evidence for the hospitality industry to implement differentiated stress management and employee development interventions.

title: How much greenery matters: effects on visual attention, guest perceptions and brand outcomes
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how varying levels of indoor greenery capture visual attention and affect guest perceptions and brand outcomes. It also examines the mediating roles of fascination and perceived aesthetic quality in linking greenery to brand outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-design experiment exposed participants to two virtual hotel lobbies: a control with no greenery and one of three greenery conditions (low: 2% coverage, medium: 16% or high: 30%). Eye tracking captured gaze behavior during exposure, while post-exposure surveys measured fascination, aesthetic quality, brand love and willingness to pay more. Findings Indoor greenery attracted greater visual attention than the no-greenery condition, as indicated by generally higher fixation counts and longer dwell times. Even low greenery enhanced fascination, aesthetic quality, brand love and willingness to pay more, with medium and high conditions producing progressively stronger effects. Fascination and aesthetic quality increased brand love, which subsequently strengthened willingness to pay more. Practical implications The findings highlight the strategic value of indoor greenery as a visually salient hospitality servicescape feature that enhances guest perceptions and supports brand outcomes. Furthermore, this study suggests that indoor greenery can serve as a strategic brand-signaling cue that helps align guest perceptions with desired market positioning. Originality/value By combining eye tracking and self-reported measures across four experimental conditions, this study provides objective evidence of greenery’s visual salience and identifies the perceptual pathways linking it to brand outcomes.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: International scaling of social innovations through digitalization: A 3D framework
abstract: Social enterprises that embed social innovations (SIs) play a critical role in advancing the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), representing an estimated US$12 trillion market opportunity. Yet, how SIs internationalize in the presence of institutional voids remains underexplored in international business research. Using a history-to-theory and history-in-theory approach, this study examines how dynamic capabilities and digitalization enable the international scaling of SIs. We find that international diffusion depends on capabilities such as boundary spanning, international sensing, legitimacy building, business diplomacy, and market shaping. Digitalization accelerates scaling, contingent on factors including timing, resources, intellectual property ownership, purpose, and technology scope. Our findings also suggest that traditional internationalization metrics—such as exports, FDI, subsidiaries, and foreign sales—do not adequately capture SI internationalization. Instead, internationalization is reflected in the cross-border diffusion of innovations and social impact, alongside the ability to attract international funding, partnerships, talent, and legitimacy while balancing social impact with financial sustainability.

title: The SME network dilemma: Capability building versus capability erosion
abstract: Cluster membership is widely expected to make small firms innovative. Often it does not. We locate the explanation inside the firm rather than in its network position. Integrating the dynamic capabilities and attention-based views, we argue that an SME’s external ties matter less for the resources they carry than for what they do to the routines that process those resources—building them in one case, eroding them in the other. Evidence from a four-informant survey of 186 SMEs in government-led Chinese industrial clusters is consistent with this account. Business ties are associated with higher innovativeness indirectly, through stronger absorptive capacity and firm agility. Political ties, once their substantial overlap with business ties is held constant, run in the opposite direction: they are associated with weaker agility, and their negative association with absorptive capacity falls short of conventional significance. Neither tie type retains a detectable direct association with innovativeness: network position appears to matter through the internal routines that convert it. We name this second pathway capability erosion, a decay that we attribute not to overuse or historical lock-in but to the systematic diversion of scarce managerial attention, and we offer it as one explanation for why so many SMEs remain innovation laggards in resource-rich clusters.

title: The yin and yang in the angel market: Angel group gender diversity and investment performance
Bouncing, believing and building: Resilient coping, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, perceived venture performance, and state fragility
abstract: Using data from 19,593 entrepreneurs across 37 countries, we examine whether the associations among resilient coping, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, and perceived venture performance vary across levels of state fragility. The results show that the conditional indirect effect of resilience on perceived venture performance through entrepreneurial self-efficacy is stronger in non-fragile contexts than in the most fragile contexts represented by the Iraqi and Nigerian samples. In the most fragile context, resilience is more directly associated with perceived venture performance, while the association between resilience and entrepreneurial self-efficacy becomes stronger under moderate fragility before weakening under extreme fragility. This exploratory pattern is consistent with the possibility that resilience may serve multiple functions across contextual conditions, while primarily supporting capability building in more stable environments and serving a more direct, maintenance-oriented role under extreme fragility. The findings point to the importance of context-sensitive approaches to entrepreneurial support and capability development.

title: How strong event systems influence organizational features in multinational enterprises: the case of global mobility during COVID
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Critical accountants in the face of ecological crises: towards a more-than-human critical resilience
abstract: This study investigates the identity work of critical accountants in the face of ecological crises, drawing on 28 semi-structured interviews and an autoethnographic account. Identity work encompasses the mental and physical practices critical accountants employ to sustain their identity in adequacy with their community of scholars. The findings show that critical accountants exhibit a variety of resilience mechanisms but rely heavily on collective practices, challenging previous accounts that focus on individual strategies. The study nevertheless shows that these collectives do not include their non-human relatives. The article argues that this disconnect might explain a relative disengagement from critical environmental accounting research, while attenuating the negative effects of ecological crises on critical accountants' well-being. Based on these findings, the article proposes adopting “more-than-human critical resilience,” which refers to the land-based and ethical collective practices developed by humans and non-humans to resist the neoliberal capture of society.

title: Do textual attributes of management commentary matter for analyst coverage and information quality: evidence from the United Kingdom
abstract: Purpose This study examines whether the readability of management commentary is associated with analysts' coverage and the precision of analysts' information sets. It further investigates whether analysts' experience, access to resources and forecast boldness moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Using 5,117 firm-year observations from 974 UK-listed firms, we employ ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models to examine the association between management commentary readability and analyst outcomes. To address potential endogeneity concerns and assess the robustness of our findings, we conduct additional analyses using entropy balancing, the Heckman (1979) two-stage procedure, omitted variable bias analysis, instrumental variable estimation and alternative measures of readability. Findings We find that firms with less readable management commentary have greater analyst coverage and higher precision of analysts' information sets. Decomposing total information precision into public and private components, we find that lower readability is positively associated with both public and private information precision. These findings are consistent with lower readability increasing the value of analysts' information-processing and information-production activities and suggest that analysts respond to less readable commentary by both processing publicly available information and acquiring additional private information. We further show that analyst experience and forecast boldness strengthen the positive association between lower readability and both analyst coverage and information precision. In contrast, analysts' access to resources strengthens the association between lower readability and analyst coverage but does not significantly moderate the association with information precision. Additional analysis indicates that the component of textual complexity attributable to observable business complexity is positively associated with analyst coverage and with total and public information precision, but not with private information precision. Research limitations/implications The findings have implications for regulators, standard setters, firms and investors by highlighting the need to distinguish unnecessary complexity from textual complexity arising from economically relevant information. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on narrative disclosures readability and analyst behaviour by highlighting analysts' information-provider role and demonstrating that the association between management commentary readability and analyst outcomes varies with analysts' attributes, particularly their experience and forecast boldness.

title: The upside of Mess: conceptualising (dis)order as a dynamic family resource
abstract: This study examines how domestic (dis)order emerges as shifting states shaped by everyday socio-material interactions. Drawing on assemblage theory and photo-elicitation interviews with 22 households, we show how (dis)order develops through dynamic relations among family members, objects, spaces, and temporal rhythms. We identify three assemblage capacities—transient, functional, and conducive—that shape how disorder materialises and is understood, along with three corresponding management strategies: restoring, tolerating, and concealing. Beyond the home, these capacities extend assemblage theory by providing a transferable framework for theorising how assemblages generate distinct emergent states across consumer and marketplace contexts. Reconceptualising (dis)order as an emergent assemblage property rather than an individual shortcoming, the study reveals conditions under which mess serves as a productive resource supporting household flow, functional efficiency, and relational harmony. The study also offers practical implications for flexible storage design, functional mess zone identification, and organisation solutions that support family wellbeing.

title: The Effect of Smile Cues on Food Calorie Perception: The Moderating Role of Dietary Restraint
abstract: ABSTRACT Consumers are becoming increasingly attentive to healthy eating and the caloric content of their food. However, when judging a food's calories, they often lack sufficient knowledge or objective information and therefore rely on marketplace cues to make subjective evaluations. Although smile cues are widely used in food marketing, little is known about how consumers' dietary restraint shapes the calorie‐related inferences they draw from such cues. Across five studies, we show that, for foods that are inherently indulgent or can meaningfully be construed in indulgence‐related terms, smile cues increase perceived indulgence, which in turn leads to higher calorie perceptions more strongly when dietary restraint is higher or situationally activated. Extending the focal calorie perception process to downstream behaviors, we further show that consumers were less likely to choose foods with a smile cue when dietary restraint is activated than not. These findings contribute to the literature on food calorie judgment, smile, and dietary restraint.

title: Smiling in influencer marketing: how smiles shape authenticity and consumer engagement
abstract: Purpose Many influencer marketing campaigns feature smiling influencers. However, whether smiling is always beneficial, and under which circumstances it might not be, remains underexplored. This paper aims to examine how an influencer’s smile (vs no smile) affects consumer engagement with influencer posts. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a field study and several online experiments. In the field study, they analyzed 802 influencer campaigns with a total of over 125 million consumer interactions (i.e. liking and commenting). In the experiments, participants viewed influencer posts featuring commonly promoted products such as headphones (nStudy2 = 192, nStudy4 = 231), sunglasses (nStudy3 = 304) and protein bars (nStudy5 = 236, nSupplemental = 247). Findings The authors show that a smile (vs no smile) in influencer posts can backfire. Smiling can lead to lower engagement by reducing perceived authenticity. However, this negative effect is contingent upon influencer type (micro vs macro) and sponsorship presence (sponsored vs. non-sponsored). Research limitations/implications While Instagram was the authors’ focus, smile effects may be different on other platforms. Although they focused on engagement, other marketing outcomes may exhibit different patterns. Finally, other contextual factors may influence whether smiling backfires or not. Practical implications Marketers and influencers should carefully consider the use of smiles when endorsing products on social media. While smiling may enhance engagement for micro influencers, it can have the opposite effect for macro influencers. However, for macro influencers, smiling may still boost engagement when the product recommendation is not sponsored. Originality/value In revealing a negative effect of smiling in influencer posts, along with an underlying mechanism and boundary conditions, the authors’ study advances the influencer marketing literature. The authors show that a smile can increase engagement and purchase likelihood for some influencer types and campaigns, while it can decrease it for others. Thus, they provide a nuanced picture of the importance of smiling in influencer marketing on social media.

title: Can leisure travel help combat loneliness in later life?
Leading by example: how major customers shape suppliers' implementation of process-based rights
abstract: Purpose Drawing from research on dependence and embeddedness in supplier-major customer relationships, this study examines the implementation level of process-based rights (PBR) – including freedom of association, workforce diversity, and fair and non-discriminatory treatment of workers – within supplier-major customer dyads. The study also empirically investigates how customers' transactional governance and relationship history with suppliers interplay in suppliers' PBR implementation. Design/methodology/approach Using 482 unique supplier-major customer dyads over 14 years (2010–2024), we performed hierarchical analysis to estimate the direct and interaction effects of customers' PBR implementation, transactional governance, and relationship history on their suppliers' PBR implementation. Findings Our results show that major customers exert a significant influence on suppliers' PBR implementation. Furthermore, transactional governance and a long relationship history work in synergistic ways only when the customer itself demonstrates average to high levels of PBR, but not when customer PBR implementation levels are low. Originality/value As one of the first studies to explore PBR within supplier-major customer dyads, our findings underscore the important role of customers in leading the implementation of labor standards, rather than as an enforcer of labor standards, in motivating supplier compliance.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Big Data Development and Corporate Environmental Strategy: Evidence from Green Innovation Engagement
Who Gains from creative destruction? Evidence from high-quality entrepreneurship in the United States
abstract: The question of who gains from high-quality entrepreneurship is crucial to understanding whether investments in innovative startup firms produce socially beneficial outcomes. Although entrepreneurship is widely viewed as a central driver of economic growth, recent research has raised concerns that it may also exacerbate inequality and other undesirable social outcomes. We bring new evidence to this debate by analyzing the impact of entrepreneurship on a variety of local economic outcomes, including income inequality, average incomes, and income mobility, using IRS and U.S. Census Bureau microdata. We find that entrepreneurship indeed increases income inequality, although this effect fades in the years after firm founding. While entrepreneurship produces statistically significant income gains across the distribution, the economic magnitude of these effects varies dramatically, with benefits concentrated among top earners. We also find that entrepreneurship can serve as a mobility tool for less well-off individuals, increasing their probability of rising to the top of the income distribution. These income and mobility gains, however, are uneven across demographic groups.

title: Routinized Deference: Predictive Screening and Bureaucratic Capacity in Child Protective Services
abstract: Abstract Predictive algorithms are increasingly used to support frontline decision-making in public administration, but evidence remains limited on how they affect bureaucratic capacity. This study examines county-level adoption of predictive screening tools in U.S. Child Protective Services using NCANDS data (2010–2023) and a stacked difference-in-differences design. Leveraging staggered adoption, I find no change in the total number of investigations opened and a sizable decline (about 15%) in the share of investigations that are substantiated. These results are inconsistent with operational capacity gains and more consistent with misclassification that erodes analytical capacity. These findings are consistent with a mechanism of routinized deference: under workload and accountability pressures, algorithmic recommendations can become procedurally defensible defaults. Overall, this study argues that predictive screening is not capacity-enhancing by default, as routinized deference can undermine the professional judgment central to bureaucratic work.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Unpacking the causal complexity of collaborative effectiveness in urban marginalized community regeneration: a fuzzy-set configurational analysis
abstract: This study examines the causal conditions shaping collaborative effectiveness in the regeneration of marginalized urban communities. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis of 22 Chinese cases, it identifies facilitative leadership as a necessary condition for achieving high collaborative effectiveness and weak institutionalization as a necessary condition for low effectiveness. The sufficiency analysis reveals three distinct pathways to effective collaboration and three to ineffective collaboration. The findings show that collaborative effectiveness depends on context-specific configurations of resource support, institutionalization, governance structure, and facilitative leadership. No single condition is sufficient in isolation; rather, effectiveness emerges through complementarity, functional equivalence, and asymmetric substitutability among conditions. The study contributes to a more context-sensitive and configurational understanding of collaborative governance.

title: Mapping empathy in policy work: how public servants understand and use it
Representative Bureaucracy in Private Philanthropy: Testing Discretion and Racial Representation in Community Foundation Grantmaking
abstract: As public service delivery increasingly involves non-governmental actors, public administration theory needs to examine how its core frameworks operate beyond traditional bureaucracies. This study extends representative bureaucracy theory to private philanthropy, an increasingly crucial actor in local public service delivery, by testing whether racial representation in leadership corresponds with equitable grantmaking outcomes. Analyzing longitudinal data from 912 U.S. community foundations between 2012 and 2016, this study finds that racial representation in foundation leadership corresponds with increased grantmaking to organizations serving communities of color when leadership retains sufficient discretion, but that this relationship weakens as donor control rises, particularly through donor advised funds. These patterns are consistent with representative bureaucracy theory's emphasis on discretion as a key mechanism linking passive and active representation. These findings advance theoretical understanding by illuminating the interplay between representation and discretion within private philanthropy, while carrying implications for equitable resource distribution as public services increasingly involve non-governmental actors.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Severity at the Gates: Or Why Prevention is the Aim of Reproductive Genetic Carrier Screening
abstract: Reproductive autonomy is usually described as the aim of publicly funded reproductive genetic carrier screening. I argue that this misdescribes the practice. These programs do not include conditions because any information might support choice. They include them because severity sets the scope. The aim of these programs, therefore, is prevention: not preventing the birth of particular persons, but offering a preventive response to the serious suffering associated with some severe inherited conditions. Reproductive autonomy, however, is the legitimate means by which a liberal program may pursue that aim, through information, counseling and voluntary decision making. That pursuit must satisfy what I call a liberal proviso, so that prevention does not become pressure, stigma or eugenic state steering. Naming prevention also enriches the disability critique. It makes both inclusion and exclusion morally visible and warranting justification, since both express judgments about which forms of suffering warrant collective response.

title: Missed opportunities: lessons from Haitian AIDS patients and their relevance today
Authors’ Response: Quasi-experiments rely on design choices: a reflection on Renson and Westreich’s “What makes a study design quasi-experimental?”
Navigating GenAI in the workplace: skills transformation & tension
abstract: By automating the content creation process, Generative AI is reshaping creative work, but its impact on knowledge workers remains underexplored, which this study seeks to examine. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 knowledge workers, this study examines what is being transformed in the workplace and how these shifts are being perceived by the knowledge workers who use GenAI. Using Social Shaping of Technology (SST) as a conceptual lens to understand the interaction between technology and knowledge workers, the study finds that participants perceived GenAI as an efficient tool that provides cognitive relief and enhances productivity during times of resource constraint. Tensions also arose around authenticity, creativity, a sense of fulfillment, and the perception of effort. The adoption of GenAI has created downstream labor and demand for new skills as it shifts knowledge workers’ roles away from creator to editor/fact-checker while creating tension as participants balance their desire for efficiency with fears of diminished creativity and domain knowledge, skills atrophy, and threats to content ownership.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Estimating Changes in Small Area Life Expectancy Disparities in Philadelphia
abstract: There is substantial geographic variation in life expectancy (LE). The COVID-19 pandemic caused a mortality crisis, but it is unclear how small-area variations in LE changed during the pandemic. We estimated gender-specific LE by census tract in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (2017–2019 and 2020–2022), and compared disparities in LE at birth before and during the pandemic. To account for small counts, we employed a Bayesian Poisson model borrowing strength from neighboring census tracts by using conditional autoregressive priors, and from known age-specific mortality patterns by using an adaptation of the TOPALS (tool for projecting age patterns using linear splines) method. We then summarized LE and computed total and income-based disparities in LE by period. The median [10th–90th percentile] change in LE during the pandemic was −2.10 [−5.39 to 0.40] and −1.37 [−3.23 to 0.39] years for men and women, respectively. Declines were concentrated in the same areas that had lower LE at baseline. We found widening disparities due to a steeper decline in LE in lower-income areas during the pandemic. Our study leveraged Bayesian models to produce reliable local-level estimates in small areas, highlighting the disparate impacts that the pandemic had on population health.

title: Developing the Universal Child Abuse Screening Tool (U-CAST) for Epic: A Qualitative Analysis of Expert Working Groups
abstract: Child abuse and maltreatment remain major public health concerns in the United States. Early identification is challenging, particularly for clinicians without specialized pediatric training, and disparities in detection raise concerns about bias. Universal screening integrated into electronic health records (EHRs) may improve detection and equity. To develop an evidence-based, user-friendly, and broadly applicable universal child abuse screening tool (U-CAST) for integration into the EPIC Foundation System. A qualitative study engaged nine expert working groups comprising 17 specialists in child abuse pediatrics, pediatric trauma surgery, general pediatrics, and pediatric emergency medicine. Between February and April 2022, groups met virtually to discuss screening content, clinical decision support, workflow integration, and implementation considerations. Meeting transcripts were analyzed using inductive coding and thematic analysis. Five themes emerged: (1) the importance of universal screening; (2) essential tool components; (3) appropriate clinical settings; (4) actionable follow-up protocols for positive screens; and (5) local program evaluation. Preliminary implementation data demonstrated successful integration, high screening completion rates, and encouraging performance in identifying children with suspected physical abuse. U-CAST was developed through a multi-disciplinary expert process and designed for integration into Epic workflows. Preliminary findings support its feasibility and clinical utility.

title: Reliability and quality of YouTube exercise videos for people living with lung cancer: a cross-sectional content analysis
Rethinking Multilevel Governance. By ArthurBenz. Cheltenham, UK: Edward Elgar Publishing, 2024. 208 pp. ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐530628‐2
Social-media engagement in municipalities: a citizen perspective
abstract: This article focuses on citizen engagement through social media. While prior research has addressed engagement from an administration-centred viewpoint, this study prefers a citizen perspective, interpreted with the Uses and Gratifications Theory. We administered a survey through Facebook pages of the largest cities in Quebec and boroughs of Montreal. Results show that informative content is more likely to increase engagement. The publication of good news and timely responses by municipalities also seem to foster engagement, while elements such as media richness seem less relevant. Our findings highlight several implications for public administrations seeking to promote a citizen-centred approach.

title: Dynamic start-up and operating window analysis of an ammonia-fueled SOFC system with flexible cracking ratio operation
A GPU-accelerated multi-physics coupling framework based on the lattice boltzmann method for performance analysis of utility-scale photovoltaic power plants
An interpretable aging prediction model for Ni-rich all-solid-state batteries informed by mechanistic modeling
abstract: Ni-rich all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are promising candidates for next-generation energy storage technology, while they suffer from much more severe capacity fading than lithium-ion batteries with liquid electrolyte, severely compromising their practical application and commercialization. Accurate degradation prediction is required to improve the operational stability of Ni-rich ASSBs. A novel degradation prediction framework for NCA (LiNi 0.8 Co 0.16 Al 0.03 , Nickel content: 80%) cathode ASSBs is proposed based on a mechanism model combined with deep neural network in this study. This study first constructs a three-dimensional physical model of ASSBs with NCA cathodes. On the basis of experimental observations, three cathode capacity degradation processes, namely interfacial side reactions, interfacial delamination and particle cracking, are parameterized. Subsequently, the CNN-LSTM hybrid framework is constructed for model training, and a multi-level prediction module is further embedded into the architecture to leverage the advantage of physical model in capturing battery internal characteristics, e.g., the Li concentration as an additional feature. Validated by simulation data, the proposed model possesses the high prediction accuracy in estimating NCA-based ASSBs degradation. Comparative analyses are carried out against the prediction model without concentration correction to further verify the rationality of the proposed prediction framework, indicating that concentration correction substantially enhances the prediction accuracy under small-sample scenarios. The three-dimensional mechanism model-neural network fusion framework proposed in this work verifies that neural networks embedded with physical prior information such as lithium-ion concentration exhibit stronger learning capacity. Even under limited data conditions, the framework can accurately predict capacity degradation of ASSBs with NCA cathodes. This study provides theoretical references for performance prediction and battery management of NCA-based ASSBs.

title: Assessing behavior-conditioned building flexibility potential across building types for photovoltaic accommodation
abstract: Building flexibility is increasingly recognized as an important demand-side resource for renewable energy integration, yet its characterization in real buildings remains challenging because flexibility is strongly conditioned by operational behavior and is difficult to quantify without detailed system information. This study proposes a behavior-informed framework to assess behavior-conditioned flexibility potential across building types using historical operation data, and further examines its potential implications for photovoltaic (PV) accommodation under building-cluster scenarios. Using 15-min measured electricity data from multiple types of public buildings in Hangzhou, China, the framework first establishes baseline load behavior through quantile-based modeling, then identifies feasible operating ranges from historically comparable operating conditions, and finally estimates behavior-conditioned flexibility potential in terms of both instantaneous adjustable power and duration-based adjustable energy. XGBoost-SHAP analysis is further employed to interpret the statistical associations between input features and the estimated flexibility indicators, and an aggregated analysis is conducted to evaluate the value of flexibility potential for PV accommodation under different curtailment constraints. For the studied public-building dataset, the estimated flexibility potential shows clear heterogeneity across building types. Load level, hour of day, outdoor temperature, and daily load characteristics show the largest contributions to the model predictions, suggesting that the estimated flexibility potential is closely associated with energy-consuming behavior. At the cluster level, the results further reveal that high flexibility does not necessarily translate into high PV accommodation potential. Under a 15% curtailment threshold, the average PV capacity factor of the realistic mixed-building aggregation scenario increased from 0.288 to 0.369 in the flexibility-enhanced scenario, corresponding to an absolute increase of 0.08 and a relative improvement of 27.9%. Across different aggregation capacity levels, the relative improvement in PV accommodation ranged from 23% to 30%. These results indicate that the cluster-level value of flexibility depends strongly on the temporal match between flexible load patterns and PV generation. This study provides a scalable data-driven approach for characterizing building flexibility from historical operational data and offers new insights into the potential contribution of behavior-conditioned flexibility to renewable energy integration and building-cluster planning under specified scenarios.

title: Estimation of aggregate flexibility regions for distributed flexible resources using limited information
abstract: Distributed flexible resources (DFRs) can support power-system operation only if aggregators can report their flexibility regions as operating conditions change. Existing aggregation methods generally require detailed device-level states, which may be unavailable, as well as repeated online optimization. This paper proposes a limited-information physics-informed neural network (PINN) for estimating aggregate flexibility regions of DFRs. Its inputs are low-dimensional operating-condition descriptors, and its output is a feasibility-oriented representative polyhedral region conditioned on those descriptors. Physical feasibility and boundary tightness are embedded through support- and projection-based errors and differentiable active-hyperplane residuals, enabling training without precomputed ground-truth flexibility-region labels. The proposed pretraining, full-network training, and loss-weight scheduling scheme prioritizes physical feasibility while retaining boundary tightness. Case studies show that the estimated regions vary predictably with operating conditions and achieve a favorable balance between physical implementability and economic performance relative to alternative aggregation models. Across the operational tests, 96.25% of PINN dispatch trajectories had zero relative disaggregation error, and the maximum error was 4.72%. Dispatch costs remained comparable to those of the full-information inner approximation. Once trained, the estimator requires neither complete device-level information nor an online optimization solver. The proposed framework therefore lowers the deployment barrier for condition-dependent flexibility estimation in practical distributed-resource aggregation.

title: Hydrogen integration for sustainable aviation propulsion: Evaluating recirculation efficiency in PEMFC systems
Shaping street rhythms: Spatial context and the temporal patterns of pedestrian activity
Solar PV as a buffer against energy security risks during geopolitical shocks: The case of Pakistan during the 2026 US–Iran war
abstract: The 2026 US–Iran war disrupted global energy markets, particularly in economies dependent on imported fossil fuels. Pakistan, given its geographic proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and high reliance on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), was expected to face severe stress in its electricity sector. However, a comparison of key energy-sector indicators before and during the conflict, benchmarked against the 2022 Russia–Ukraine energy-price shock, suggests that the impact on Pakistan’s electricity sector was comparatively moderate relative to the 2022 energy-price shock, despite the severity of the external shock. The evidence indicates that the rapid expansion of distributed solar played an important role by reducing reliance on imported fuels and weakening the transmission of international fuel-price volatility into domestic electricity markets. These findings reveal that distributed renewable energy can serve not only as a pathway to decarbonization but also as a strategic instrument for strengthening energy security and resilience to geopolitical shocks in an increasingly volatile global energy landscape.

title: From data-driven prediction to closed-loop intelligent bioconversion: A framework for artificial intelligence in organic solid waste treatment
abstract: Organic solid waste (OSW) bioconversion has become a key strategy for converting biodegradable wastes into renewable energy, stabilized products, and recoverable nutrients. However, aerobic composting and anaerobic digestion are inherently dynamic and heterogeneous biological processes, where substrate variability, microbial succession, mass transfer, process instability, and greenhouse gas emissions complicate reliable operation. Current AI applications span methane-yield and compost-maturity prediction, soft sensing, process optimization, digital twins, and simulation-based control modeling. Nevertheless, most existing applications remain confined to prediction, optimization, or advisory functions and lack direct integration with on-site physical feedback. In this critical review, we systematically evaluate the current capability distribution and deployment maturity of AI-enabled OSW bioconversion, while distinguishing demonstrated implementations from a proposed pathway toward closed-loop operational intelligence. Among 85 direct AI/model implementation studies, 38 primarily addressed prediction, diagnosis, or soft sensing, 36 addressed optimization or advisory decision support, and 11 addressed simulation-based control modeling; none demonstrated supervisory/semi-autonomous or fully closed-loop operation on physical OSW-bioconversion equipment. Particular attention is paid to process-state representation, mechanism-informed interpretation, sensing infrastructure, predictive and optimization models, deployment maturity, and the persistent gap between model outputs and implementable control actions. We further propose a normative cyber–physical framework that integrates multi-source sensing, state reconstruction, world modeling, decision optimization, actuation, and feedback updating. This review reframes AI in OSW bioconversion as an engineering tool for carbon mitigation, nutrient recovery, and circular waste infrastructure rather than only a means of improving prediction accuracy.

title: Synergistic decomplexation and electrosorption for sustainable copper recovery from photovoltaic wastewater: An integrated O3/SPC-MCDI process
Molecular Size Mediates Sunlight Effects on the Biodegradation of Aquatic Dissolved Organic Matter: Insights from the Reservoir Wetland and Incubation Experiment
abstract: Abstract Dissolved organic matter (DOM) in aquatic ecosystems is crucial to climate, water quality, and water sanitation. However, little is known about how photochemical and biological processes interact to regulate the cycling of DOM in water environments. Here, we investigate the photobiochemical processing of different molecular weight (MW) fractions of aquatic DOM by incubating them with microbes in the dark and light/dark cycling environments via microcosm experiments. Light exposure has distinct effects on the medium (MMW; 1–20 kDa) and low (LMW; <1 kDa) MW fractions and can enrich photoautotrophic bacteria and taxa that could benefit the utilization of aromatic compounds. The decay of the MMW fraction displays the highest light sensitivity, with light increasing the net depletion of tannin- and condensed aromatic-like molecules and production of labile substrates (e.g., protein-like) from photoautotrophic bacteria. In contrast, the net decomposition of the LMW fraction is the least promoted by light exposure, as light induces the net production of complex aromatic molecules that are more persistent. Our findings provide new insights into the photobiochemical and molecular mechanisms underlying the ecological impacts of aquatic DOM and their relevance for wider processes.

title: Selective Oxidation of Sulfoxide to Sulfone in Chloride/Peroxymonosulfate Systems: Reassessing a Diagnostic Probe for High-Valent Metal-Oxo Identification
abstract: Abstract The selective oxidation of sulfoxides to sulfones, particularly using methyl phenyl sulfoxide (PMSO), has been widely adopted for over a decade as a diagnostic method for high-valent metal-oxo (HVMO) species in advanced oxidation processes (AOPs). Here, we demonstrate that this transformation proceeds efficiently via non-HVMO pathways in metal-free systems, challenging the probe’s specificity. Using the chloride/peroxymonosulfate (Cl−/PMS) system as a model, PMSO is converted to methyl phenyl sulfone (PMSO2) with high selectivity (83.5%−98.7%) across pH 3.5−11. Kinetic, isotopic, and computational analyses reveal a pH-dependent mechanistic switch for the high-yield transformation of PMSO to PMSO2. Under acidic conditions, Cl2/HOCl generated from the two-electron oxidation of Cl− by HSO5− through nucleophilic addition mediate oxygen-atom transfer from water via a chlorosulfonium cation intermediate, with Cl2 dominating PMSO selective oxidation (kapp = 1.58 × 106 M−1 s−1; 47.91 M−1 s−1 for HOCl). Under alkaline conditions, nucleophilic attack by SO52− formed via PMS hydrolysis becomes predominant (16.38 M−1 s−1). The reaction kinetics are linearly dependent on Cl− concentration, and similar selective oxidation is observed in other metal-free AOPs (e.g., base/PMS, HCO3−/PMS, and Cl−/peracetic acid). Our findings necessitate reassessing the sulfoxide probe’s specificity for HVMO identification in PMS-based systems containing chloride or alkalinity, and underscore the imperative for rigorous mechanistic validation in water treatment.

title: Perspectives and Mitigation Methods for Underappreciated Amine Escape from CO2 Desorption
abstract: Abstract Amine-based CO2 capture is increasingly limited by amine escape and aerosol emissions that drive solvent loss and secondary pollution. Research has focused on the absorber, leaving the desorption section─where intensive CO2 release, water-vapor entrainment, and rapid cooling coincide─overlooked as an escape source. Here, we combine molecular dynamics simulations with bench-scale experiments to resolve the mechanism and control of amine escape during CO2 desorption. Counter to absorber-side expectations, a CO2-rich atmosphere suppresses rather than promotes aerosol nucleation: elevated CO2 competitively disrupts the H2O–H2O hydrogen-bond network stabilizing water-centered nuclei, with stable clusters essentially absent at 75 vol % CO2. New aerosol formation is thus favored near the low-CO2 reboiler outlet, while cooling in the upper column grows preexisting aerosols. Measurements revealed an 82% decrease in the total amine concentration along the column, consistent with the descending rich solvent acting as an important amine sink, while preexisting aerosols continued to grow in the upper section. Guided by this mechanism, a combined mitigation strategy is proposed: a low-volatility solvent formulation lowered aerosol by 66% relative to MEA, increasing the rich-solvent CO2 loading offered a favorable trade-off, and upstream scrubbing–condensation captured residual species. Together, these measures reduced amine escape by over 99% (to <1.4 ppm) while increasing CO2 product purity. By reframing the desorber as a key emission unit, these results support strategies for reducing desorber-side amine and aerosol emissions.

title: Halogenated Nucleosides: Highly Toxic Biogenic Disinfection Byproducts Prevalent in Drinking Water
abstract: Abstract Five decades of research on disinfection byproducts (DBPs) reveals only the tip of the iceberg, with humus as their primary precursor. Here, we identified 15 halogenated nucleosides (HNSs) as new DBPs originating from biological materials in drinking water. A nationwide survey across China revealed that their individual detection frequencies ranged from 87% to 100%, with the maximum concentration reaching 141 ng/L. Two quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models were developed based on the cytotoxicity and genotoxicity data, with dipole moment (μ) and sum of the degree of valence (SVDe) as key cytotoxicity descriptors, and molar refractivity (R) together with number of H-bond donors (NHD) for genotoxicity. Integrated concentration and toxicity data revealed that halogenated (deoxy)cytidines and halogenated (deoxy)adenosines warrant priority regulatory consideration. The concentrations of HNSs were positively correlated with both pH (r = 0.6, P = 0.0005) and residual chlorine (r = 0.5, P = 0.0095) of drinking water samples, which may be related to local precipitation, temperature, and economic development. This study expands the scope of DBP research beyond humus-derived DBPs to biomolecule-derived ones.

title: Unveiling Whole Water Neurotoxicity through Sensitive Electrophysiological Functional Profiling: Beyond Conventional Morphological Metrics
abstract: Abstract Neuroactive contaminants typically coexist as complex mixtures in aquatic ecosystems, exerting deleterious effects through combined exposures. However, current assessment approaches based on morphological endpoints (e.g., neurite outgrowth) lack sufficient sensitivity to capture functional neurotoxicity of these mixtures. To address this gap, this study establishes in vitro functional neurotoxicity testing (iFNT), an ultrasensitive bioassay leveraging high-density microelectrode arrays to profile cortical network electrophysiology. Validated using reference toxicants, their mixture, and whole water samples, iFNT achieves 5- to 500-fold higher sensitivity than the neurite outgrowth assay. This heightened sensitivity enables clearer discrimination of functional phenotypes for both individual compounds at environmentally relevant concentrations (10–8 M) and whole water samples without preconcentration, providing a powerful tool for evaluating real-world neurotoxic risks. Alarmingly, conventional monitoring indicators exhibited a pronounced mismatch with iFNT profiles across wastewater treatment stages, demonstrating that seemingly acceptable routine readings masked the persistence of latent neurotoxicity. This study challenges morphology-based paradigms, revealing that accurate whole water risk assessment necessitates integrating functional biological endpoints into future monitoring frameworks.

title: Bromine Monoxide Radical Likely Dominates Dimethylsulfide Oxidation before the Springtime Onset of Arctic Ice Melt
abstract: Abstract To understand the atmospheric fate of dimethylsulfide (DMS) during the Arctic spring-to-summer transition, we measured volatile methylated sulfur (VMS) species, including DMS and DMS-derived oxidation products, dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), and dimethylsulfone (DMSO2), in the Fram Strait during May and June of 2023. Elevated DMSO contributions to VMS accompany depleted O3, high surface albedo, and air temperatures < 0 °C in air masses influenced by snow-covered sea-ice regions, suggesting that BrO•-initiated oxidation dominated DMS loss prior to the onset of sea-ice melt. In GEOS-Chem simulations, BrO• is the dominant oxidant for DMS, but modeled BrO• concentrations from sea-salt debromination alone are too low to replicate observed O3, DMSO, and DMSO2, suggesting a missing source of reactive bromine from sunlit saline snow. BrO•-initiated oxidation reduces the DMS lifetime and oxidizes DMS through methanesulfinic acid (MSIA) more quickly in the gas phase and in higher yields compared to •OH-initiated oxidation alone. Once melt onset begins and snowpack-driven halogen activation shuts off, •OH oxidation likely dominates Arctic DMS oxidation. Our observations highlight the seasonal variability of halogen oxidation impacting sulfur species in the Arctic marine region, which are likely to change as the sea-ice extent decreases and the melt season in the Arctic lengthens.

title: Atmospheric Removal of Nitrous Oxide: Approaches and Feasibility
abstract: Abstract Nitrous oxide (N2O) is the third-largest contributor to anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing and the dominant anthropogenic ozone-depleting emission. While mitigation can flatten emissions, there is no clear pathway to eliminate residual emissions from agriculture and other diffuse sources, a key challenge for climate stabilization. The potential role of atmospheric removal has not been holistically assessed, yet N2O’s high potency and long atmospheric lifetime indicate the potential for a durable climate benefit. This review synthesizes emerging approaches for atmospheric N2O removal, organized by reaction mechanism (thermal destruction and thermocatalysis, photolysis, gas-phase radical reactions, photocatalysis, and biological reduction) and deployment format (closed versus open system). Each is evaluated for technical efficacy, climate viability, environmental and social viability, and economic plausibility using lower-bound cost models. No approach yet satisfies all four: gas-phase radical reactors are precluded by their kinetics, thermocatalytic and photocatalytic reactors require ten- to hundred-fold performance gains, and open-system approaches have the lowest cost floors but face the greatest measurement and governance challenges. These results identify the performance thresholds and broader constraints that govern feasibility across pathways, providing a foundation for a research agenda and for assessing the role of N2O removal alongside emissions mitigation.

title: Toward Rational Design of Low-Salt-Rejection Reverse Osmosis for Minimal and Zero Liquid Discharge
abstract: Abstract Low-salt-rejection reverse osmosis (LSRRO) has emerged as a promising technology for concentrating high-salinity brines in minimal- and zero-liquid-discharge (MLD/ZLD) applications. However, rational LSRRO design remains hindered by uncertainties about how existing modeling frameworks should be interpreted and applied. In this Perspective, we critically examine the limitations of process modeling and module-scale analysis in LSRRO design. Conventional process models can yield misleading predictions for spiral-wound LSRRO modules because the stagewise concentration cutoff embedded in these models is based on the cumulative permeate composition rather than the local permeate conditions that govern water transport. Experimental results and local transport calculations show that the brine concentration in spiral-wound LSRRO stages is not constrained by a fixed thermodynamic concentration cutoff. Nevertheless, standalone process models remain inherently limited in assessing practical feasibility because they do not resolve kinetic constraints, such as declining water flux along the module. Module-scale analysis is therefore essential for linking local transport behavior to practical design metrics, including membrane area requirements, productivity, and achievable brine concentration. However, its predictive accuracy is constrained because transport parameters derived from conventional local transport models vary with salinity, which challenges their use as constants across the module. This Perspective therefore highlights the need for condition-dependent and experimentally validated local transport descriptions to enable rational LSRRO design for future MLD/ZLD applications.

title: Dynamic Nature of Soil Iron Minerals: Recent Advances Using Iron Isotope Tracers and Mössbauer Spectroscopy
abstract: Abstract Iron plays a central role in defining the redox and surface chemical environment of soils and sediments, by mediating the behavior of nutrients, pollutants, and carbon compounds. However, the mechanisms that drive dynamic changes in Fe speciation and mineral composition can be difficult to trace. Over three decades, technical advances in spectroscopy and theoretical modeling techniques have revealed detailed mechanisms of Fe mineral recrystallization and transformation. Here, we provide a perspective on the application of iron isotopic tracers to the development of atomic-scale mechanistic understanding of Fe mineral dynamics. We review key milestones in the advancement of 57Fe tracers coupled with 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy and draw links between the understanding of Fe dynamics with 57Fe tracers and biogeochemical cycling of other elements in soils and sediments. Iron isotopes are increasingly used in Fe biogeochemistry research, and our analysis will point out unique opportunities offered by 57Fe tracers to unravel important questions in soil biogeochemistry today.

title: Sex-Specific Associations of Gestational OPE Exposure with Offspring Digit Ratio: A Birth Cohort Study
abstract: Abstract The effect of prenatal organophosphate esters (OPEs) exposure on offspring reproductive development and the potential role of the placenta remain unclear. We investigated the associations of prenatal OPE exposure with the second-to-fourth digit ratio (2D:4D) and the mediating role of placental DNA methylation (DNAm) levels of PPAR pathway genes. Maternal urine OPE metabolites at 12–16 gestational weeks were measured. Placental DNAm levels at birth and children’s 2D:4D at ages 4 and 6 years were assessed. Multiple linear regression, BKMR, and causal mediation analyses were applied. We observed associations between prenatal exposure to BBOEP, BEHP, DBP, and DPP and increased 2D:4D in boys, whereas DBP and DCP were associated with decreased 2D:4D in girls. BKMR identified alkyl-OPEs, particularly BBOEP, as the primary contributors in boys. Moreover, hypermethylation of RXRA, ACAA1, and ACADM was associated with decreased 2D:4D in all populations. In girls, the associations among higher OPE exposure, increased ACAA1 methylation, and lower 2D:4D suggested a potential mediation pathway, while the mediation effects were not statistically significant. These findings suggest sex-specific associations between prenatal OPE exposure and 2D:4D. The potential role of placental PPAR-related DNAm in these associations warrants further investigation.
