How does young children’s digital resilience operate within and across homes and communities? A thematic analysis of parents and early years educators’ experiences
abstract: This paper examines how young children aged 0–5 years build digital resilience within interconnected home and community contexts. While playing, exploring, and socialising are central to early experiential learning, little is known about how parents/carers and educators support children to recognise, manage, and recover from mistakes in connected environments. Conceptualising digital resilience as a socio-ecological construct, the paper draws on findings from the TYKES project to address this gap. Using a multi-method qualitative design, the study thematically analyses semi-structured interviews with parents/carers (n = 17) and early years educators (n = 5), alongside focus groups with educators across two settings (n = 8), conducted using purposive sampling over a ten-month period (May 2024–February 2025). The paper argues that digital resilience is a relational and context-dependent process that unfolds across nested home and community environments, rather than solely within individual children or discrete settings. It highlights the importance of social capital and everyday interactions in shaping children’s emerging capacities to navigate online challenges. The paper contributes to the literature by demonstrating how parents/carers and educators actively cultivate digital resilience as an emergent capability, embedded in socio-ecological relations. The findings point to the need for more holistic and coordinated support across education systems, policymakers, industry, and governments to enable young children to thrive on the Internet.

title: Effect heterogeneity of loneliness and social support on incident hypertension in older, normotensive populations
abstract: Abstract Although social isolation is known to impact those with cardiovascular disease, its relationship with incident hypertension is unclear. In this retrospective cohort study, we used data from the All of Us research program. Participants were enrolled between May 2017-April 2023, aged 50+ years, and had at least 60-days of EHR data pre-index date. We identified incident hypertension during follow-up. Those classified as hypertensive at or prior to the index date were excluded. We defined low social support and loneliness as binary variables. Using causal forests, we estimated treatment effects as unweighted and overlap-weighted risk differences (RD). A total of 24,720 participants with a median follow-up of 2.6 years were included. While loneliness and social support were not significantly associated with incident hypertension in the overall population, causal forests revealed meaningful effect heterogeneity, with socially isolated male (RD: 0.038, 95% CI 0.002 to 0.075; overlap-weighted RD: 0.027, 95% CI -0.005 to 0.059) and Gay or Lesbian participants (RD: 0.108, 95% CI 0.011 to 0.205; overlap-weighted RD: 0.11, 95% CI 0.008 to 0.211) experiencing a significantly elevated risk. This illustrates how machine learning, when embedded within epidemiologic frameworks, can detect subgroup vulnerability that other approaches may obscure, enabling targeting of limited resources.

title: Military-specific factors and incident melanoma diagnoses among active duty participants in the millennium cohort study, 2000 - 2021
abstract: Service members experience unique occupational hazards that may increase their risk for melanoma. This longitudinal study aimed to determine associations between deployment status, environmental exposures, and solar exposures and incident melanoma among active duty service members. Millennium Cohort Study survey data (2001-2021) were linked with deployment and military health care records (2000-2021). Adjusted Cox proportional hazards models estimated effects of exposures and covariates on incident melanoma. Risk of melanoma diagnosis by age (early vs late onset) and anatomical site (sun-protected vs sun-exposed skin) were also estimated. Among 115,512 service members, 184 were diagnosed with melanoma during the study period (61% were <40 years old and 77% diagnosed on sun-protected skin). Melanoma risk by demographics was consistent with civilian studies. Among this military population, those who deployed (adjusted hazard ratio [AHR] 0.55 [95% CI 0.40, 0.75]) had reduced melanoma risk. Conversely, those who self-reported being exposed to occupational hazards (AHR 1.43 [95% CI 1.05, 1.95]) had elevated melanoma risk. Findings were consistent with the “healthy deployer effect,” while self-reported occupational hazards were associated with an increased risk of melanoma. Results may be informative for understanding melanoma etiology, risk counseling, and screening.

title: The authors reply to ‘consistency and positivity are valuable for causal education and communication’ by lee Kennedy-Shaffer
Turning the Lens on Sexual Perpetration: Predictors of Acknowledging Sexual Perpetration
abstract: Factors related to sexual perpetration acknowledgment are virtually unstudied, leaving a significant gap in the sexual violence literature. The current study explored (1) perpetration frequency and tactics and (2) acceptance of myths about sexual aggression (AMASA) as potential predictors of acknowledgment. In addition, post-traumatic stress and depressive symptoms were examined as possible correlates of perpetration acknowledgment. A secondary aim of this study was to provide descriptive data for the proportion of people who have sexually perpetrated and who also endorse being victimized (i.e. victim-perpetrator overlap in adulthood) as well as rates of perpetration acknowledgment in this sample. The data used were from a larger study of 1,177 participants recruited from Prolific, a university research pool, and snowball methods using a cross-sectional design. Of the 722 eligible participants, 305 (42.2%) endorsed perpetration and 302 (99.0%) of those endorsed victim-perpetrator overlap. Our results revealed positive associations between frequency and acknowledgment. Further, there were significant differences between the tactic used and acknowledgment. Finally, group differences based on acknowledgment were found when examining AMASA and psychological distress. The current study addressed critical gaps in the literature by examining factors related to perpetration acknowledgment, providing insights that can guide future research, develop theory, and inform interventions.

title: Social Media Use and Openness to “Sugar Relationships”: Cultural Tightness–Looseness as a Moderator Across 22 Countries
abstract: Abstract Social media use has been widely linked to sexual attitudes, yet it remains unclear whether its association with openness to sugar relationships is uniform across countries or contingent on country-level normative contexts. In the present study, we examined whether country-level cultural tightness–looseness moderated the relationship between social media use and openness to sugar relationships across 22 countries. Openness to sugar relationships was conceptualized as a manifestation of a broader orientation toward sexual–economic exchange. Using data from 22,292 adult women drawn from a large cross-national dataset, we tested this framework with Bayesian multilevel modeling. Measurement invariance of the openness construct was assessed, and alignment procedures were applied to address cross-country non-invariance prior to analysis. Cultural tightness–looseness was modeled as a country-level moderator of the individual-level association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships, while age was included as a control variable. Results revealed a positive association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships. In addition, this association was modestly stronger in countries characterized by lower normative constraint, suggesting that country-level norm strength may shape the attitudinal relevance of digital exposure. Models including this interaction outperformed alternative specifications that incorporated a range of theoretically plausible country-level covariates, including indicators of digital infrastructure, socioeconomic structure, and internet freedom. Although the interaction effect size was modest, the findings suggest that the attitudinal correlates of social media use vary systematically across countries and highlight the importance of country-level normative contexts in research on sexual–economic openness.

title: Benefits and Harms of Adult Videos: A Sex Difference Social Representations Analysis Among Young Adults in Japan
abstract: Pornhub Insights (2025) reported that Japan ranked 11th worldwide in total traffic, indicating widespread use of adult videos (AV). Existing research has primarily focused on AV-related harms from expert and Western perspectives. Few studies examine how Japanese young adults perceive these effects, particularly the benefits that sustain use, and sex differences remain underexplored. This study investigated the core social representations of AV benefits and harms and how they differ by sex. Data were collected from 251 Japanese participants, of whom 137 (54.6%) were male, with a mean age of 20.71 years. Most participants (81.3%) reported using AV, and most identified as heterosexual students. Data were analyzed using prototypical analysis to identify elements with high consensus. Five key observations emerged: (1) Both genders see “satisfaction,” “pleasure,” and “crime prevention” as key benefits of AV. (2) Sex differences appeared in describing benefits, with men mentioning “sex education” and women mentioning “stress relief.” (3) Both genders identified “incorrect knowledge” as a primary representation of AV-related harms. (4) Male respondents cited “addiction” as a harm, whereas female respondents were more likely to reference “encouraging sexual crime.” (5) More words or phrases were used to describe AV benefits than harms. These findings may inform targeted interventions and policy discussions.

title: From atomic structure to catalytic function: Morphology engineering of MXene for Electrocatalytic energy conversion
Static reconfiguration techniques for PV under the corn canopy with deep reinforcement learning
abstract: Valve integrated photovoltaic (PV) systems deployed in agricultural environments are prone to power mismatch caused by shading from maize canopies. To mitigate this issue, a static reconfiguration strategy based on shadow informed deep reinforcement learning is proposed. The method collects physically consistent irradiance information under maize canopy shading and constructs a deep reinforcement learning framework in which the average power loss rate is used as the optimization objective. This framework enables offline optimization of photovoltaic cell array layouts. The results demonstrate that the array configuration discovered by the proposed framework, which learns current mismatch mechanisms and applies a global trade off strategy, achieves an average maximum output power of 1.401 W. This performance significantly exceeds that of the conventional total cross-tied topology, which produces 1.057 W, and the Sudoku-based (SDK) method, which achieves 1.103 W. The corresponding relative improvements are 32.6% and 27.0%, respectively. In addition, the static reconfiguration matrix designed using this approach achieves an average maximum power loss rate of 42.31%. This study provides a new reference for the static reconfiguration of micro-photovoltaic arrays under shading conditions and confirms the effectiveness of physics guided, data driven optimization for reliable photovoltaic system design in complex natural environments.

title: Optimizing biochar quality and economics across feedstocks and pyrolysis temperatures in a 50,000 t/year carbonization demonstration
abstract: Biomass carbonization plays a critical role in industrial fuel substitution and efficient carbon sequestration, yet commercial-scale evidence linking biochar quality and economic performance based on actual operating data remains limited. Herein, based on an established biomass carbonization demonstration with an annual processing capacity of 50,000 t/year, 8 typical biomass feedstocks sourced within the collection radius (800 km) of the demonstration were selected as raw materials. Focusing on pyrolysis temperature, which is the key parameter governing biochar production, the quality and economic viability of biochar produced under the demonstration were systematically evaluated. Actual production data and economic parameters were analyzed using techno-economic assessment, correlation analysis, Random Forest prediction, Shapley interpretation, and Pareto optimization. At 500 °C, the fixed carbon contents and higher heating values of the 8 biochars ranged from 52.17% to 80.49% and from 5225 to 7525 kcal/kg, respectively. Only wood chips and bamboo chips exceeded 75% fixed carbon, reaching 75.85% and 80.49%, with corresponding higher heating values of 7373 and 7525 kcal/kg. The mixed biomass production line, using rice husk, sunflower seed shells, leafy firewood, pine branches, and green mountain wood, achieved the best economic performance, with an IRR of 8.19% and an NPV of 22.44 million Chinese yuan (CNY); in contrast, the bamboo-chip and wood-powder lines had negative NPVs and IRRs below the 2.5% discount rate. Pearson analysis linked Ash content, Volatiles matter content and temperature to heating value ( r = 0.77, 0.80, 0.31) and cost ( r = −0.55, 0.65, 0.38). Machine-learning-based Pareto optimization predicted an optimal trade-off for pine branches pyrolyzed at 375–425 °C, yielding 6821.60–6830.35 kcal/kg at 861.63–862.35 CNY. This work has developed an optimization strategy for industrial applications through experimental evaluation and machine learning feedback based on actual demonstration, thereby providing the theoretical foundation for the design and control of biochar production.

title: A relational retrofitting void in the private rented sector: the Brighton and Hove ‘loop’
When do hydrogen technology patents improve ecological performance? Cross-country evidence on mediation and threshold effects in the load capacity factor
abstract: This paper asks whether hydrogen technology patents improve ecological performance, and under what conditions. Using a balanced panel of 48 countries over 2000–2024 and a multidimensional patent value index, we estimate two-way fixed effects models for the load capacity factor (LCF), the ratio of biocapacity to the ecological footprint. We find that hydrogen patent value is positively associated with the LCF, with a level-dependent magnitude: a one-standard-deviation increase in transformed patent value is associated with an LCF 4.2% higher for an economy at ecological balance and 6.3% higher for one in ecological deficit. This gain comes mainly from a smaller ecological footprint and only marginally from greater biocapacity. The result holds under a shift-share instrument, heteroskedasticity-based identification, weak-instrument-robust inference, plausible-exogeneity analysis and dynamic panel estimation. Turning to mechanisms, a joint parallel-mediation model attributes 6.8% of the total effect to technical human capital and 7.2% to hydrogen production subsidy policy. The association is positive in both fossil-dependence groups, without a robust difference between them, but significant only in below-median-income economies. Panel threshold estimates show that it strengthens once institutional quality exceeds approximately 0.31 on a 0–1 index, turns from negative to positive once internet penetration passes about 92%, and becomes positive and statistically significant once a country operates three or more carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) facilities. For policy, hydrogen innovation is better assessed alongside absorptive capacity, digital infrastructure and operational carbon-management capacity than as a standalone environmental instrument.

title: Lithium resource supply structure evolution and low-carbon transition pathways in China's lithium-ion battery industry: A dynamic material flow analysis and scenario assessment
Life cycle assessment of hydroponic container farm use in U.S. urban food system transitions
Advancing Environmental Justice Research within and beyond Science and Engineering
abstract: Abstract Scientists and engineers have historically approached questions of environmental justice (EJ) differently from social scientists and humanists, from how they formulate problem scope to how they propose solutions. While scientists and engineers have assessed distributional injustices extensively, there are opportunities for deeper interdisciplinary collaboration with other EJ schools of thought. In this Perspective, we first present an EJ schematic for a science and engineering audience, where we trace epistemologies within EJ schools to show how EJ scholars conceptualize knowledge, how this relates to their methods, and how they present and publish work. We survey the EJ literature─mainly work related to the United States─across disciplines to determine major tensions within EJ and between EJ, science, and engineering scholarship. We also discuss possibilities for enabling interdisciplinary collaboration for scientists and engineers working on EJ-related questions by analyzing epistemological compatibilities. Next, we highlight opportunities to facilitate collaboration through an illustrative interdisciplinary case study. We conclude with takeaways for scientists and engineers moving forward, alongside some of the challenges accompanying interdisciplinary EJ research.

title: Coupling 18F Radiotracer Imaging with Synchrotron Fe Speciation to Resolve Biogeochemical Dynamics in PHC-Contaminated Soils
abstract: Abstract In petroleum hydrocarbon (PHC)-contaminated subsoils, iron bioavailability often is believed to constrain the degradation of PHC contaminants, but spatially resolved evidence linking microbial activity with Fe transformations is scarce. Here, we bridge this gap by integrating phosphor imaging using positron-emitting radiotracer [18F]fluorobenzene─a high-fidelity surrogate for benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, and xylene (BTEX)─with synchrotron-based X-ray spectroscopy. This multimodal approach allows for targeted mineralogical fingerprinting, guided by direct visualization of microbial activity within PHC-contaminated soils. Bulk X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) showed little contrast, but microspectroscopy analysis revealed diffuse Fe at active zones and discrete Fe grains in inactive matrices, a pattern consistent with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II) and porewater transport before reprecipitation/reoxidation. Zones of high microbial activity were enriched in reactive phases (ferrihydrite, siderite, and green rust) comprising 27–71% of total Fe, whereas inactive matrices sequestered Fe mainly in Ca–Fe silicates with less than 25% reactive Fe. The recurring presence of green rust and vivianite aligns with phosphate-associated early-stage products under long-term tripolyphosphate biostimulation. We conclude that hydrocarbon degradation co-occurs spatially with Fe(III) bioreduction to mobile Fe(II), lateral transport in porewater, and phosphate-associated reoxidation/reprecipitation, processes that bulk methods often obscure but microscale mapping reveals. These insights support potential comanaging Fe and P amendments and targeted delivery of amendments to enhance PHC bioremediation in cold, calcareous soils.

title: Purple Phototrophic Bacteria as a Novel Platform for Coenzyme Q10 Production from CO2, Syngas, and Sulfur Waste Byproducts
abstract: Abstract The efficient conversion of CO2 and industrial waste streams into value-added products remains a critical challenge for sustainable microbial processes. Here, we present the first systematic demonstration of purple phototrophic bacteria (PPB) as platforms for the autotrophic valorization of CO2 and industrial off-gases or sulfur byproducts into valuable metabolites. Genome-guided screening combined with experimental validation identified strains capable of coupling photoautotrophic growth with the production of CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments. Among them, Rhodospirillum rubrum DSM 467 and DSM 107 exhibited the highest performance, maintaining stable CO2 and H2 consumption under semicontinuous operation and accumulating up to 9.6 ± 0.2 mgCoQ10 gbiomass–1 under CO2/ H2 conditions, comparable to engineered production systems. In addition, R. rubrum DSM 467 efficiently oxidized CO from syngas via the water–gas shift reaction, displaying hierarchical substrate utilization driven by energetic constraints. In contrast, Marichromatium purpuratum simultaneously oxidized H2 and thiosulfate (S2O32–), enabling parallel electron input into the photosynthetic electron transport chain and enhanced growth. Overall, these results establish PPB as robust and metabolically flexible biocatalysts for converting CO2 and industrial waste streams into high-value chemicals with direct applications in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries.

title: Unveiling the Hidden Load: High Flux and Deposition Dynamics of Atmospheric Microplastics in the North China Plain
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric microplastics (MPs) play an important role in the transport of MPs across diverse environmental media, yet their annual deposition dynamics across heterogeneous urban–cropland regions remain poorly understood. We conducted a one-year field campaign at three contrasting sites in the North China Plain (NCP): Beijing (BJ, urban), Tianjin (TJ, industrial/coastal), and Handan (HD, agricultural). Atmospheric bulk-deposition samples were characterized for particle deposition rates, size, morphology, and polymer composition, with observations evaluated using meteorological and land-cover information. Deposition rates were significantly higher in BJ than in TJ (p < 0.05) and HD (p < 0.001). Median (interquartile range) deposition rates were 34640 (18703–90472), 14367 (6000–25810), and 6990 (3903–11790) items m–2 d–1 in BJ, TJ, and HD, respectively. Small particles (20–50 μm) dominated particle abundance (80.7%), whereas fragments dominated particle morphology (90.4%). Backward trajectories indicated seasonal differences in potential air-mass transport pathways. Integrating particle mass estimates with land-cover data yielded order-of-magnitude estimates of annual atmospheric MP inputs of approximately 6 Gg to urban areas and 17 Gg to cropland in the northern NCP. These results reveal pronounced spatiotemporal variability in atmospheric MP deposition and highlight the dominance of small MP fragments across urban and cropland ecosystems.

Coupled Dynamics and Energy Capture of Oscillating Water Column and Point Absorber Arrays on a Shared Floating Platform
abstract: Array deployment is a promising route for the large-scale utilization of wave energy, and hybrid systems combining oscillating water columns with point absorber buoys may enable energy capture over a wider frequency range. However, their capture characteristics when integrated on a shared floating platform remain insufficiently understood. This study investigates the coupled dynamics and capture characteristics of such a configuration using a time-domain model based on linear potential flow theory. Specifically, platform motion modifies the capture spectra of both converters. For the configuration considered here, platform heave plays the dominant role. The resulting spectra exhibit a short-period capture peak associated with the characteristic response of the converters, a long-period capture peak associated with platform heave resonance, and an intermediate trough caused by nearly in-phase motion between the converters and the platform. Near the platform heave resonance, the responses of the two converter types partially overlap, and the coupled system exhibits negative coupling, with its total captured power below the sum of the two standalone systems. Outside this region, their distinct frequency responses provide spectral complementarity, mitigating the capture trough and broadening the effective capture range. Additional irregular-wave simulations show that the resonance-related negative coupling and frequency complementarity identified under regular waves remain evident under broadband excitation. These results demonstrate how shared-platform dynamics govern both negative coupling and spectral complementarity between different wave energy converters.

Optimising resource management in data-scarce environments: A modelling approach for Greater Cairo
abstract: Pressing environmental challenges present significant obstacles to cities’ sustainable development and underscore the need for effective resource management. However, resource management studies often overlook or oversimplify the spatial and social dimensions of resource use, limiting their ability to target interventions to specific population groups and integrate them into urban planning. Addressing this requires disaggregated data that capture spatial variation and interdependencies between socio-economic factors and resource consumption. Yet such data are often scarce in Global South contexts, where data limitations frequently hinder meaningful resource management research. This research develops a hybrid multi-scale analysis framework that integrates Spatial Microsimulation, Multi-Scale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR), and Geodemographic Classification to help researchers address data limitations and generate policy-relevant insights. The framework offers three contributions: methodological, empirical, and policy translation. The research provides the first systematic, household-level analysis of food-water-energy consumption patterns across Greater Cairo. Spatial microsimulation creates robust synthetic household datasets by integrating multiple surveys, while MGWR reveals spatially varying drivers of consumption. The geodemographic classification delivers the first empirically grounded typology of Greater Cairo households based on demographic, socio-economic, and consumption characteristics. Lastly, the applied probability-based allocation of clusters to neighbourhoods offers an indicative tool for exploring differentiated tariff structures and area-specific demand management, validated through expert workshops. By addressing Greater Cairo’s data limitations, the framework offers a replicable approach for other cities facing similar constraints, supporting the transition to evidence-based, spatially differentiated resource management in the Global South.

title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
abstract: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

title: Cognitive ability, risk preferences and errors
abstract: Abstract In this paper we examine the link between cognitive ability, risk preferences and the errors that people make. We build a unique dataset that contains almost 260,000 decisions made under risk in a variety of tasks by approximately 13,000 individuals, with each person having completed a test designed explicitly to measure their cognitive ability. Our analysis suggests that intelligence has (1) no impact on risk preferences and (2) a robust link to errors. Our results have implications for the development of theories that seek to explain the impact of cognitive ability on decision making.

Biased by sustainability? How cognitive biases shape procurement decisions under information equivocality
abstract: Purpose Climate change introduces new informational asymmetries across supply chains, increasing managers' need to process sustainability-related information in procurement decisions. Such information is equivocal, making its interpretation challenging and increasing decision-makers’ susceptibility to cognitive biases. Building on organizational information-processing theory and behavioral decision-making research, this study examines how cognitive biases shape procurement decisions involving sustainability information. Design/methodology/approach We developed hypotheses on cognitive biases emerging from three characteristics of sustainability information: structural properties (risky choice framing, attribute framing, numeracy and anchoring), inferential dynamics (halo effect) and social influences (herd effect). We tested these hypotheses through between-subject vignette-based experiments depicting individual, one-shot procurement decisions. The experiments were conducted in person with 475 participants, including managers and students. Findings We found that sustainability-oriented procurement decisions are vulnerable to cognitive biases. In particular, biases induced by the structural properties of information produced the strongest effects across both managers and students, followed by distortions emerging from inferential dynamics. In contrast, socially driven distortions emerged only among students, suggesting that professional experience mitigates reliance on peer behavior. Originality/value This study extends organizational information-processing theory-based sustainable supply chain management research by demonstrating that individual-level cognitive biases shape the interpretation of sustainability information. In doing so, we characterize the interpretation stage as being sensitive to information architecture, inferential reasoning and, under conditions of social influence, the professional experience of the decision-maker. Finally, we provide guidance for designing sustainability information and procurement decision processes that reduce susceptibility to cognitive biases.

Direct Evidence for Carbon Monoxide-to-Dioxin Conversion via Fly-Ash-Catalyzed Sequential Reactions in Incineration Flue Gas
abstract: Abstract The formation of polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) in industrial thermal processes is traditionally attributed to solid carbon precursors via de novo synthesis. Carbon monoxide (CO), despite serving as an operational indicator of incomplete combustion, has not been directly implicated as a molecular carbon source for dioxin generation. Here, we provide definitive experimental and mechanistic evidence that CO can be catalytically converted into dioxins and dioxin-like compounds through a sequential reaction network mediated by fly ash. Using fixed-bed reactors packed with real fly ash, we isolate CO, H2O, and HCl as minimal reactants to reconstruct flue-gas chemistry. Transition metal species (Cu, Fe) in fly ash catalyze CO conversion via a coupled water–gas shift and Fischer–Tropsch-type process, generating a wide spectrum of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons. Concurrently, fly ash mediates HCl oxidation to active Cl2, enabling chlorination of these intermediates into chlorobenzenes and chlorophenols, which subsequently evolve into polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs), and ultimately PCDD/Fs. Notably, Cl4–8DD/F congeners account for >90% of the formed PCDD/Fs, consistent with de novo synthesis signatures. This work establishes a new mechanistic paradigm for dioxin generation and highlights CO emission control as a critical lever for mitigating toxic pollutant generation.

abstract: The biogeochemical coupling of silicon (Si) and carbon (C) in floodplain lakes has been increasingly disrupted by human activities, yet the mechanisms and trajectories of this decoupling remain poorly constrained. Here we present well-dated sediment records of biogenic silica (BSi) and associated geochemical proxies spanning the past century from three sub-lakes of Poyang Lake to fill this knowledge gap. Despite divergent BSi-content trajectories shaped by the contrasting hydrological settings among these sub-lakes, BSi/TOC mass ratios consistently reveal a systematic transition from coupled Si-C cycling toward decoupling. This transition intensified following dam construction in the 1950s-1960s and the acceleration of anthropogenic nutrient loading from the 1980s onward. Random forest modeling further reveals that following damming and eutrophication, catchment erosion and nutrient enrichment ranked as the strongest positive and negative predictors of BSi/TOC variation, respectively, with these associations strengthening as hydrological connectivity to the main lake declined. Furthermore, the decreased BSi/TOC ratios during the decoupling phase indicate possible silicon limitation and are consistent with increased inputs of non-siliceous algae. Because dam-driven silica retention and nutrient enrichment co-occur in many regulated rivers and lakes elsewhere, the risk of Si-C decoupling merits evaluation well beyond Poyang Lake, with implications for freshwater carbon sink assessments.

abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)

Matching Function Equilibria with Partial Assignment: Existence, Uniqueness and Estimation
abstract: We argue that models coming from a variety of fields, such as matching models and discrete choice models among others, share a common structure that we call matching function equilibria with partial assignment. This structure includes an aggregate matching function and a system of nonlinear equations. We provide a proof of existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium and propose an efficient algorithm to compute it. For a subclass of matching models, we also develop a new parameter-free approach for constructing the counterfactual matching equilibrium. It has the advantage of not requiring parametric estimation when computing counterfactuals. We use our procedure to analyze the impact of the elimination of the Social Security Student Benefit Program in 1982 on the marriage market in the United States. We estimate several candidate models from our general class of matching functions and select the best fitting model using information based criterion.

Crime and Prices:Thefts of expensive precious metals from cars
abstract: Whether economic incentives matter for crime is studied in a novel way, from expensive precious metal thefts by thieves stealing catalytic converters from cars. Sharp and sizable variations in the prices of precious metals embedded in converters are combined with newly assembled U.S. crime data. Precipitously fast increases in precious metal prices generated a sizeable rise in auto-part thefts, while subsequent price declines and policy responses quickly reversed this pattern. The resulting boom-and-bust dynamics provide clean evidence that prices affect crime, and for these crimes that local resale infrastructure and target availability shape both the magnitude of this effect and the effectiveness of policy response.

Concentration and convergence: Regional productivity in Türkiye, 1950–2020
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a comprehensive long‐run analysis of regional productivity convergence in Türkiye using a novel dataset combining newly compiled employment estimates with recent output estimates. The seven‐decade analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence driven by labour reallocation away from agriculture alongside within‐industry convergence. A distinctive pattern emerges: aggregate economic concentration proceeded together with productivity convergence, with distinct regional clusters forming. Furthermore, shift‐share decomposition shows industry‐mix effects persistently explain significant regional productivity variation, reflecting sustained agriculture‐other sectors productivity differences, with western regions enjoying both favourable sectoral composition and regional competitiveness advantages. From a policy perspective, agricultural productivity improvements offer significant potential for reducing regional disparities.

The Effect of Red Scare Propaganda on U.S. Public Opinion: Evidence from the Newspapers of William Randolph Hearst
abstract: Could anti-redistributive sentiment have long-run roots in Red Scare-era propaganda? In the 1930s and 40s, the media mogul William Randolph Hearst espoused vehement anti-communist rhetoric in his newspapers. Fears of socialism went head-to-head with FDR’s New Deal, the first wide-scale federal spending program. Using variation in newspaper penetration across U.S. counties, I show that an increase of 10 percentage points in Hearst circulation per capita decreased support for FDR by 2.1 percentage points. I also show evidence that these effects are long run, decreasing support for public healthcare and welfare programs through the late twentieth century.

title: Borrowed plumes: the gender gap in claiming credit for teamwork
The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

title: The incidence and distributional effects of electric vehicle subsidies in China
Identifying the impact of exposure to armed conflict on individual preferences and field behavior: Evidence from Turkish draft Veterans
abstract: Building on a population-level natural experiment, this study identifies the causal impact of exposure to armed conflict in a combatant role on risk, ambiguity and time preferences and related field behaviors for the average adult male randomly picked from the target population. Our setting allows us to analyze the difference in preferences without confoundment by community-level effects of conflict. Those exposed exhibit higher risk tolerance, ambiguity neutrality, patience and time consistency. We also find exposure leads to an increase in entrepreneurial activity but has no significant effect on risky health behaviors, and that elevated agency partially accounts for these shifts. Taken together, these patterns indicate that combat exposure alters preferences in ways that are not inherently positive or negative for economic welfare; what matters is how such preferences are expressed. Our results suggest agency as one potential channel through which exposure shapes this expression, making it more constructive than maladaptive in this setting.

title: Financialization of Bitcoin: Spot ETFs and Futures Pricing Efficiency
abstract: Does Bitcoin behave like a currency asset and is it becoming more integrated into financial markets? To answer this, we investigate whether financialization can be identified in the futures market around the introduction of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) using Markov switching models, Fama–French regression tests and structural break analysis. We conduct an event-based analysis of the implicit yield [r*]—an interest rate equivalent measure that includes the convenience yield and risk premiums specific to Bitcoin. Using data from December 11, 2017, to March 14, 2025, we study regulatory regime shifts around the launch of both futures and spot-based ETFs. We observe that ETFs impact volatility, information efficiency and institutional participation. While theory suggests that such instruments should improve market efficiency and reduce speculative frictions, our findings challenge this view. Our results, using Fama’s regression tests, showed weak forecasting power. This suggests an element of market inefficiency as well as that Bitcoin futures market prices are currently driven largely by speculative flows. That said, certain evidence shows that the introduction of ETFs marks the early stages of financialization.

title: Globalised but divided: European corporations and the EU’s geoeconomic turn against China
Corporate Tax Changes and Credit Costs
abstract: Abstract We examine changes in the state corporate tax rate across the U.S. and their implications on the pricing and quantity of loans. We find that the cost of credit decreases by approximately 10 basis points following a tax cut. When we account for the magnitude of tax changes, a one‐percentage‐point tax cut (hike) is associated with a 10.5 (9.2) basis‐point decrease (increase) in loan spreads. Our findings mainly originate from the demand side: large firms are able to mitigate the effects of tax increases, while less profitable firms experience larger reductions in borrowing costs following tax cuts. The effect on the equilibrium loan amount is statistically and economically insignificant, consistent with a weak supply effect and an inelastic loan supply curve.

title: Behavioral signals and credit pricing: Evidence from credit cards
The Economics of Data Unions: Optimal Data Sharing and Coordination
abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07249 .

title: How scents shape product color choices
journal_name: International Journal of Research in Marketing

title: Recomposing Management Education Under Climate Crisis: Towards a Composting Heuristic for Epistemic Change
abstract: Abstract Management learning and education (MLE) is increasingly critiqued for its reliance on anthropocentric and profit‐maximization paradigms, which fail to adequately address the escalating ecological and climate crises. In this article, we call for an epistemic shift in MLE by introducing the metaphor of composting as a lens for collective reflexive critique. We propose a composting heuristic inspired by the social practices of managing organic matter—landfill, industrial composting and community composting—to help MLE educators critically examine the epistemic foundations, limitations and possibilities that shape their teaching and learning practices. This metaphorical framework highlights an epistemic transition towards a multispecies and regenerative pedagogical paradigm, grounded in relational ontology, care and embodied practice. We argue that engaging with the metaphor of composting—and reflecting critically on one's positioning within the landfill‐industrial‐community composting heuristic—can catalyse a collective endeavour to drive epistemic change in MLE in response to the urgent demands of climate and ecological breakdown.

title: EXPRESS: Interactive Blind Lead-In Ads and Purchase Conversion: The Roles of Completion and Creative Design Features
abstract: Interactive display advertising increasingly employs delayed product disclosure in multi-stage formats, yet little is known about how they affect purchase behavior when exposure to the reveal depends on users’ interaction. This article studies interactive blind lead-in (BLI) ads with a randomized field experiment: over 109,000 customers of a book retailer were assigned to a BLI ad with delayed reveal or a static ad with immediate disclosure. The experiment identifies a boundary condition on the transfer of prior interactivity findings to user-controlled delayed-reveal advertising: assignment to the BLI format does not increase average purchase conversion, as interactivity’s positive mechanisms need not produce a conversion gain when most exposures end before the reveal. Using random assignment as an instrument, completing the BLI sequence increases long-term purchase conversion among compliers (a 46.6% lift; 437 completions per incremental purchase), indicating that delayed-reveal interactivity is effective only when users meaningfully interact with the ad. Completion varies across ads consistent with a Cost-of-Progress framework: early informational cues predict higher completion, late-stage textual and visual complexity predicts lower completion, and social cues predict higher completion when placed before the final stage. A supplementary study shows that the downstream impact of BLI interaction depends on overall hedonic experience.

title: Forward‐Looking ESG Relevance and Corporate Performance: Evidence From Credit Ratings
abstract: ABSTRACT How does the relevance of ESG issues relate to firm performance, and does ESG relevance moderate the relationship between ESG engagement and firm financial outcomes? Using a novel indicator introduced by Fitch Ratings, we provide new empirical evidence to answer these questions. The forward‐looking indicator measures the relevance of ESG issues to firms' credit ratings. It captures firms' financial sensitivity to ESG‐related issues from a credit‐rating perspective. Utilising a sample of 663 firms from 55 countries, we examine the relationship between ESG relevance, its subcategories and firm performance. We find that environmental relevance has a significant negative association with firm performance. The results are economically meaningful as a one‐standard‐deviation increase in the environmental relevance score associated with decreases in Tobin's Q and return on assets ( ROA ) by 5.7% and 11.9%, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate how ESG relevance interacts with ESG performance in explaining firm performance. We find that environmental relevance significantly weakens the positive association between environmental performance and firm financial performance. The association between ESG relevance and firm performance is primarily concentrated in environmental relevance, while the moderating effect is concentrated in Tobin's Q . The findings remain broadly robust to instrumental variable regressions, propensity score matching and alternative measures of firm performance. Further analysis of the disaggregated components of environmental relevance indicates that the negative association is primarily concentrated in the relevance of greenhouse gas emissions. Our findings provide important insights into why ESG relevance matters for investors and firm performance, an issue that is often neglected in the literature.

title: Silent Strategies: CEO Populism, Supply Chain Opacity, and Biodiversity Disclosure
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether CEO populist rhetoric is associated with corporate biodiversity disclosure and whether supply‐chain opacity conditions this relationship. Using an unbalanced panel of 1828 nonfinancial listed firms from 12 European countries over 2014–2022, the analysis comprises 15,842 firm‐year observations in the baseline estimation. Firm fixed effects, two‐stage least squares, and two‐step system GMM models are used to account for unobserved heterogeneity, potential endogeneity, and dynamic persistence. The findings show that CEO populist rhetoric is negatively associated with biodiversity disclosure and positively associated with supply‐chain opacity, indicating that stronger populist rhetoric coincides with less visible, specific, and verifiable publicly reported upstream supply‐chain information. The moderation analysis provides qualified evidence that lagged supply‐chain opacity strengthens the negative association between CEO populism and biodiversity disclosure, suggesting that executive rhetoric is more strongly related to lower nature‐related transparency when upstream information is less visible and verifiable. These findings extend the understanding of biodiversity disclosure beyond a predominantly technical reporting perspective by showing that nature‐related transparency is associated with both executive rhetorical framing and the informational conditions surrounding upstream supply chains. Integrating upper echelons theory with stakeholder and institutional perspectives, the study explains how CEO rhetoric may shape the interpretation of external accountability demands while supply‐chain opacity affects the informational conditions under which such interpretations are reflected in disclosure. The study contributes to research on executive communication, sustainability governance, biodiversity reporting, and the credibility of corporate environmental disclosure.

title: When Eco‐Innovation Backfires: Governance Thresholds That Reverse Green Business Strategy in Sub‐Saharan Africa
abstract: ABSTRACT Sub‐Saharan Africa is attracting an increasing share of international climate finance, yet whether eco‐innovation consistently translates into environmental improvements remains unclear and highly variable across the region. This study examines the effect of eco‐innovation on carbon intensity and identifies the governance and infrastructural conditions under which its environmental benefits materialise. Using a balanced panel of 32 Sub‐Saharan African countries from 2002 to 2024, the study employs two‐way fixed‐effects estimation with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, Hansen threshold regression, interaction models and two‐stage least squares estimation to address cross‐sectional dependence, nonlinearity and endogeneity. The results show that eco‐innovation reduces carbon intensity on average, but its effectiveness is highly governance‐dependent. Although eco‐innovation lowers carbon intensity in West and Southern Africa, it is associated with higher carbon intensity in East and Central Africa, revealing an eco‐innovation paradox. Threshold analysis identifies a critical governance breakpoint at a Worldwide Governance Indicator score of −0.35, below which eco‐innovation increases carbon intensity and above which its environmental effect becomes negative. Approximately 42% of country‐year observations fall below this threshold. The findings further show that digital infrastructure strengthens the environmental benefits of eco‐innovation, whereas renewable energy consistently reduces carbon intensity irrespective of governance quality. The study advances the eco‐innovation literature by identifying a measurable institutional threshold that explains heterogeneous environmental outcomes and provides a practical governance benchmark for firms, policymakers and development finance institutions seeking to maximise the environmental returns to green investment in Sub‐Saharan Africa.

title: Does Corporate Water Performance Matter to Investors?
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates whether corporate water performance matters to investors, using water consumption, withdrawals, and discharge as three proxies of performance. Based on a sample of 2141 US firm‐year observations with available water data in the CDP annual surveys over 2014–2019, we find that poor corporate water performance is consistently associated with lower market value. This valuation penalty is weaker among firms that voluntarily disclose their water performance data to the CDP, but stronger among firms with a dedicated CSR committee on the board. Our results are robust to potential endogeneity issues. Overall, our findings suggest that investors reward sound water management and penalize weak practices more heavily when governance structures raise expectations for environmental stewardship. The study offers policy‐relevant insights by highlighting the financial benefits of transparent water reporting and contributes to the emerging literature by showing that water stewardship is a value‐relevant corporate strategy.

title: The Influence of Voluntary Environmental Disclosure on the Environmental Impact of Waste Reduction Activities
abstract: ABSTRACT Using the Attention Based View (ABV) as a theoretical framework, this study investigates the moderating influence of firm voluntary environmental disclosure on the effectiveness of waste avoidance and waste management to improve two environmental metrics that have received differing levels of attention: carbon emissions and water usage. Employing a panel fixed effects estimation strategy, the results provide two key findings: (1) differing effectiveness of waste reduction strategies to reduce environmental harm and (2) voluntary disclosure moderates the effectiveness of waste reduction strategies to reduce environmental harm, though not always beneficially. Voluntary disclosure improves the environmental benefit of waste avoidance while attenuating that of waste management. Moreover, the moderating influence is more pronounced for water usage, showing that concerns receiving less external attention may benefit more from internal changes in managerial attention.

title: Corporate Governance and Sustainability Disclosure in Environmentally and Socially Sensitive Industries
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how corporate governance relates to environmental and social sustainability disclosure in environmentally and socially sensitive industries and whether these relationships differ from low‐impact industries. Drawing on stakeholder–agency and resource dependence theories, we analyze 3276 firm‐year observations from 503 European Union‐listed firms during 2011–2021 using OLS, instrumental‐variable, and two‐step system‐GMM estimations. Board size and gender diversity are positively associated with both disclosure dimensions. Board independence is positively associated with social disclosure, whereas CEO duality is negatively associated with social disclosure. Supplementary analysis of 6097 observations from 965 firms shows that most relationships between governance and disclosure do not differ significantly by industry sensitivity. However, CEO duality has a significantly more negative association with social disclosure in sensitive industries than in low‐impact industries. These findings identify industry sensitivity as a selective boundary condition and underscore the need to distinguish environmental from social disclosure when evaluating board effectiveness.

title: From Smart Waste Management to Environmental Performance: The Mediating Roles of Blockchain Transparency and Corporate Image in the Textile Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital investment in smart waste management does not automatically translate into environmental performance (EP) gains, and this technology–performance gap is acute in the textile and apparel (T&A) industry, the world's second most polluting sector. Drawing on the resource‐based view, institutional theory, the technology acceptance model, the technology–organization–environment framework, and technological determinism as a rival baseline, this study tests whether smart waste management system (SWMS) adoption improves EP directly, and whether blockchain technology (BCT) and corporate image (CI) mediate this relationship, with environmental management system (EMS) as a moderator. Survey data from 294 T&A professionals in Bangladesh were analyzed using PLS‐SEM (SmartPLS 4) across eight hypothesized paths. SWMS shows no significant direct effect on EP; instead, the SWMS–EP relationship is fully mediated through a serial BCT–CI pathway, and this pathway is strengthened by EMS. The findings indicate that technology adoption alone is insufficient for environmental gains without complementary reputational and governance mechanisms, offering both a theoretical refinement of technology–performance models and practical guidance for green business strategy and circular economy activation in global apparel supply chains.

title: Who Benefits from Climate Investment? Gendered Employment Quality and Asymmetric Effects in the Green Transition
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate investment is widely expected to generate a “double dividend” by improving environmental sustainability while promoting inclusive development. However, its labor market consequences remain insufficiently understood. Using panel data from 28 OECD and European economies over the 2001–2023 period, this study examines how climate investment affects employment quality and gender inequality. The findings reveal a significant asymmetry: Climate investment substantially reduces female vulnerable employment, while its effect on male vulnerable employment is statistically insignificant. The resulting change in the female–male gap is therefore driven by improved female employment outcomes rather than deterioration in male outcomes. Mechanism analysis indicates that these effects operate through structural shifts toward service‐oriented sectors and improvements in female human capital. The effects are more pronounced in lower‐income, labor‐market‐flexible, and highly digitalized economies. These findings suggest that climate investment does not generate uniformly inclusive outcomes, but instead reshapes employment quality through gender‐differentiated access to emerging economic opportunities during the green transition.

title: Foreign knowledge spillovers and new product development speed in boundary-spanning teams: A sufficiency–necessity perspective on digital interoperability and collaborative conflict resolution capabilities
Understanding the spillover effect of personal AI use on service innovation: the role of psychological capital and conscientiousness
abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.
