title: Culturally Inherited Language Negativity and Management Forecasts
Mapping Digital Platforms and Their Infrastructural Foundations for Biodiversity: A Bibliometric Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Biodiversity loss is increasingly recognized as a grand challenge requiring new forms of innovation, coordination, and knowledge integration across organizational and institutional boundaries. While digital technologies have substantially advanced how biodiversity is monitored, measured, and managed, less is known about how digital platforms and their underlying infrastructures can support innovation processes aimed at biodiversity protection and regeneration. This paper offers a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research connecting digital platforms, their infrastructural foundations, and biodiversity, based on a dataset of 528 scientific publications. Using co‐citation and keyword co‐occurrence analyses, the study maps the intellectual structure and evolution of this emerging field and identifies five promising research frontiers: platform governance for collective action, biodiversity data infrastructures, innovation for biodiversity, digital platforms as innovation intermediaries, and the orchestration of scalable nature‐based solutions. Building on these findings, the paper develops an integrative framework explaining how platform design and governance shape organizational coordination, knowledge integration, and innovation mechanisms, ultimately influencing biodiversity outcomes. The findings reveal that existing research remains largely technology‐driven, with a strong emphasis on monitoring and biodiversity data generation, while questions related to platform governance, ecosystem orchestration, and biodiversity valorization remain comparatively underdeveloped. By repositioning digital platforms as organizational infrastructures for biodiversity‐oriented innovation, rather than merely technological tools for ecological monitoring, this study contributes to the literature on digital innovation, platform ecosystems, and R&D management, while outlining a future research agenda for designing innovation ecosystems capable of supporting biodiversity‐positive transformation.

title: Matching for impact: a dyadic process model of mentor–venture alignment in entrepreneurial support organizations
abstract: Business incubators and accelerators (BIAs) play a central role in regional entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing mentoring to support new venture development, yet mentoring outcomes vary considerably. While prior research documents mentoring benefits, limited attention has been paid to how mentors and ventures are matched or how these processes shape outcomes. This study conceptualizes mentor–venture matching as a dyadic, co-constructed process and examines how alignment between mentors and ventures shapes the formation and evolution mentoring relationships and their outcomes. Drawing on a multi-stage qualitative research design involving interviews with program managers, twenty mentors, and twenty-one new ventures across twelve Belgian BIAs, as well as follow-up interviews with ventures, the study identifies distinct yet complementary selection criteria on both sides of the dyad. Mentors evaluate ventures based on experiential alignment, deep-level personal characteristics, and venture-specific attributes, whereas ventures assess mentors based on expertise, interpersonal qualities, and value alignment. The findings show that alignment across these dimensions is associated with different mentoring outcomes, ranging from short-term problem solving to access to networks, investment opportunities, and long-term professional collaborations. This study develops a process model explaining how early-stage matching conditions shape the depth, durability, and strategic value of mentoring relationships over time. By linking matching processes to differentiated outcomes, the study advances a dyadic perspective on entrepreneurial mentoring and contributes to research on entrepreneurial ecosystems by demonstrating how BIAs act as intermediaries shaping how mentoring relationships influence access to resources within entrepreneurial ecosystems.

title: Adapting to extreme heat: how corporate responses enhance customer stability
abstract: Purpose This paper examines the impact of extreme heat risk on corporate customer stability in the Chinese market. Design/methodology/approach Using a comprehensive dataset from 2012 to 2023, we find that greater exposure to city-level extreme heat risk incentive firms to adopt adaptive adjustments, thereby enhancing customer stability. Findings This effect is mainly achieved through three channels, including optimizing human capital, advancing digital transformation and strengthening supply chain finance. Cross-sectional heterogeneity test reveals that the impact is more pronounced in firms with lower labor intensity, fewer high-skilled employees and limited trade credit access. These findings provide novel evidence on how firms transform climate-related risks into opportunities to strengthen resilience, and offer important implications for corporate adaptation strategies and policy support in the context of global climate change. Originality/value Our research makes several contributions in three major aspects. First and foremost, our findings extend the literature on the economic consequences of extreme heat; furthermore, our research enriches the literature on the determinants of customer stability; last but not least, by examining the mechanism linking extreme heat risks at firm locations to customer stability, our study extends organizational adaptation theory to the context of climate risk and supply chains, enriching the theoretical framework on how climate factors influence corporate supply chain networks.

title: Covered interest rate parity in the presence of time-varying transaction costs: an application of the fractional integration approach
abstract: Purpose We demonstrate that fractional integration offers an improved framework for assessing the reliability of the covered interest rate parity condition compared with traditional unit root tests. Specifically, in the presence of transaction costs, the parity condition will tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds, making the process fractionally integrated at that bound which renders traditional unit root tests unsuitable. Given the widespread adoption of parity conditions in practice, in areas such as risk management and foreign exchange rate forecasting, an approach which permits an assessment of the reliability of these models, particularly for volatile markets such as emerging markets, is crucial. Design/methodology/approach We propose a threshold autoregression framework that more effectively identifies near-unit-root behaviour and improves market classification relative to conventional approaches. The analysis uses data from the industrialized markets of Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, New Zealand and Singapore, as well as the emerging markets of India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, with the USA serving as the reference market. Findings Our results show that shocks to covered interest rate parity are asymmetric and that the parity conditions tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds. Originality/value The fractional integration approach is well established in the econometric literature, though we are the first to apply this in this context. In relation to the international finance literature on tests of parity, recent attention has been almost exclusively on the causes of parity deviations than on assessing the reliability of the condition as an exchange rate forecasting instrument.

title: Explainable medical artificial intelligence: The impact of agent and explanation types on health persuasion
I deserve better: beauty work increases consumer preference for advanced products
abstract: Consumers often engage in beauty work to improve their physical appearance. Prior research has largely focused on how such efforts shape others’ perceptions and inferences about the focal individual. However, little is known about its impact on consumers’ self-perception, particularly how these shifts influence subsequent product preferences. This research demonstrates that beauty work increases consumers’ preference for advanced products by heightening their perceived deservingness. Specifically, after engaging in beauty work, consumers are more likely to choose products featuring premium packaging, upgraded hardware, advanced services, and superior auxiliary functions. This effect occurs because beauty work uniquely generates a sense of “I deserve better”, a mechanism not observed in a general self-improvement activity. Additionally, we identify three boundary conditions: the effect dissipates (1) when beauty work does not produce visible appearance enhancement, (2) among entity theorists, and (3) when consumers make choices for others. Together, this research contributes to the literature on beauty work and offers practical implications for promoting advanced products.

title: Why some countries lead and others lag: The political economy of promoting battery electric vehicles
abstract: This study examines how macro-socioeconomic and institutional factors shape government policy orientations toward battery electric vehicle (BEV) promotion within the broader context of technological transitions. Using a political economy lens, we identify eight key factors — car industry, car infrastructure, car culture, oil and gas industry, energy sector, income per capita, air pollution and health, and environmental awareness — through an extensive literature review and a Delphi-based case study of Australia. A structured descriptive synthesis across 12 diverse countries indicates that BEV policy promotion is weak where multiple high-impact factors, such as a resistant auto industry, powerful oil and gas interests, and an entrenched car culture, converge unfavourably. Conversely, where environmental consciousness, pollution concerns, supportive infrastructure, and industrial ambitions align, as in Denmark, China, and Germany, pro-BEV policies are more robust. The study contributes to the analysis of low-carbon technological transitions by developing a diagnostic framework for assessing how differing macro-socioeconomic and institutional conditions relate to BEV policy orientations. Composite scores range from −10 to +21 across the sample, with 5 countries classified as supportive, 3 as ambivalent, and 4 as constraining; for example, Denmark exhibits strongly supportive conditions, while South Africa reflects strongly constraining structural factors. This offers a pragmatic tool for policymakers to assess national contexts and for researchers to interpret transition pathways, highlighting how both formal structures and informal political dynamics—such as lobbying, legacy industry influence, and cultural attitudes—shape the trajectory of sustainable mobility.

title: Investigating pro-environmental policy effectiveness from a consumer perspective
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the consumers’ perceived policy effectiveness to advance understanding of how environmental policies are evaluated across policy attributes, levels of attributes and contexts from a consumer perspective. Design/methodology/approach Three choice-based conjoint experiments were conducted to assess consumers’ perceived policy effectiveness for environmental policies varying in policy attributes (informational, economic and regulatory), levels of attributes (facilitating, constraining or absent) and contexts (plant-based food, electric vehicles and sustainably sourced clothing). Data were collected from student and general population samples. Conditional multinomial logit (cMNL) models were used to estimate the effects of policy attributes and attribute levels on choices of the most effective policy. Findings This research shows that consumers consistently perceive facilitating policies as more effective than constraining policies across different policy attributes (informational, economic and regulatory) and contexts (plant-based food, electric vehicles and sustainably sourced clothing). Findings highlight a fundamental misalignment between consumer-perceived and empirically assessed policy effectiveness. Research limitations/implications This study draws on Australian samples, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other cultural and institutional contexts. Future studies should examine whether this study’s findings can be extended to other cultural settings or conduct comparative research across countries with different cultural values. Practical implications The research advises policymakers and social marketers to avoid equating policy preference with perceived policy effectiveness. The findings help policymakers in identifying which policies are likely to face public resistance and where policy design or communication may be needed to better align public perceptions with empirical effectiveness. Originality/value The findings contribute to the policy and consumer behavior literature by establishing perceived policy effectiveness as a distinct construct worthy of investigation in its own right and by demonstrating that it is jointly shaped by policy attributes, levels of those attributes and contexts.

title: Rethinking human–AI agency in tourism and hospitality: A framework for the agentic AI era
Resolving the “privacy paradox” in digital tourism: A decision process lens
abstract: In digital tourism, travelers frequently disclose personal data despite expressing privacy concerns (i.e. “privacy paradox”). Although mandatory consent explains some disclosure, tourists retain meaningful choice across many encounters. Existing research offers limited insight into how tourists actually navigate these decisions. Drawing on narrative interviews with forty experienced Chinese digital tourists analyzed via the Gioia methodology, this study reconstructs disclosure as a process and identifies five qualitatively distinct decision modes—risk-benefit analysis, anchoring-adjustment, habitual, peer-influenced, and social norms-driven. These modes are linked through two experiential trajectories, analytically reconstructed from participants’ retrospective accounts: a self-centered path from deliberate analysis toward habitual automation, and an other-centered path from peer mimicry toward normative internalization. Both outcomes arise from accumulated disclosure decisions, but only one constitutes privacy cynicism. The paradox is thus mechanistically plural, reframing privacy theory and platform design in tourism.

title: Extreme environmental distance and global sustainability engagement: Evidence from the United Nations Global Compact
Giving Beyond Borders: Antibribery Enforcement and Philanthropic Giving Overseas
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study investigates why and how US multinational enterprises (MNEs) engage in philanthropic giving to foreign countries, exploring whether enforcement actions under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) influence such giving behavior. Research Findings/Insights Using FCPA enforcement actions as reputational and enforcement shocks, we find that while firms directly implicated in violations (focal firms) do not alter their foreign philanthropic giving, peer MNEs operating in the same host countries significantly increase their donations. This increase is consistent with peer firms using philanthropy strategically to mitigate reputational spillovers, manage heightened enforcement risk, and build reputational capital. We establish these findings using a stacked difference‐in‐differences design. Theoretical/Academic Implications The study advances the literature on corporate philanthropy by identifying cross‐border enforcement shocks and peer effects as key determinants of international corporate philanthropy. We further contribute to research on nonmarket strategies by demonstrating that philanthropy can serve as a strategic response to regulatory and reputational risks. Practitioner/Policy Implications Our findings suggest that antibribery enforcement can influence corporate social behavior beyond focal firms, prompting philanthropic responses among peer MNEs operating in the same host country. Policymakers and regulators should consider these spillover effects when designing enforcement strategies. Likewise, corporate practitioners should recognize international philanthropy as a strategic tool for managing global compliance and legitimacy.

title: Employee Communication and Silence: The Role of Managers' Voice Solicitation
abstract: ABSTRACT The aim of this study is to explore employee communication as a distinctive Human Resources (HR) practice and its relationship to employee silence. Building on signalling theory and drawing on a nationally representative sample of 1200 respondents from the UK workforce, our findings reveal that effective employee communication is negatively related to employee silence via the mediating role of managerial voice solicitation. Our study makes significant contributions to the theory of Human Resource Management. Specifically, we depart from studies exploring bundles of HR practices to focus on employee communication as a distinctively important HR practice. In addition, our findings shed light on the existence of a signalling chain, highlighting the important role managers can play in dampening employee silence and its negative workplace repercussions. Furthermore, in contrast to previous work focusing on structural factors promoting employee silence, our study turns the spotlight on ways to alleviate it. Given the harmful effects of employee silence on both employees and organisations, our study offers actionable insights into how such a behaviour can be diminished in the workplace.

title: The Prestige Catalyst: How CEO Awards Accelerate Corporate Green Transformation Through Institutional Channels
Regularized Government Accounting Supervision and Suppliers’ Cash Holdings: Evidence from Supply Chain Spillover Effects
abstract: This article takes the reform pilot of strengthening accounting supervision carried out by the Ministry of Finance in selected provinces and municipalities at the end of 2020 as a quasi‑natural experiment, and adopts the difference‑in‑differences method to investigate the supply chain spillover effect of regularized government accounting supervision on the cash holding level of supplier firms. The study finds that when midstream firms are located in regions with the accounting supervision reform pilot, the cash holding level of their supplier firms decreases significantly. Mechanism tests show that regularized government accounting supervision functions mainly through two channels, namely reducing supply chain risks faced by suppliers and increasing the supply of trade credit. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the above effect is more pronounced among supplier firms that are state‑owned enterprises, have high customer concentration, and belong to high‑tech industries. This research expands the research boundary of the economic consequences of government accounting supervision, reveals the microeconomic effects of external regulatory institutions transmitted through supply chain relationships, and provides empirical evidence for improving China’s accounting supervision system and enhancing the financial resilience of supply chains.

title: When Executives Double as Board Secretaries: A barrier to corporate green innovation?
Industrial policy in times of market power
abstract: We explore the effects of different industrial policies in a macroeconomic agent-based model calibrated to reproduce the decline in US business dynamism over the last half-century. R&D subsidies to innovators raise GDP growth but exacerbate the trend toward rising market power, while financial subsidies to adopters and standard capital-replacement schemes have negligible aggregate effects. A meaningful reversal of market power emerges only when innovation support is paired with adoption-oriented measures that relax the knowledge constraints of small adopters, e.g. the establishment of a National Competence Center providing technology transfer and knowledge upgrading. The effectiveness of each policy is dependent on the underlying technological regime: the growth–dynamism trade-off is sharpest in science-based regimes and attenuated in scale-intensive and supplier-dominated ones.

title: Follow the Money: The State and the Architecture of Union Funding
abstract: ABSTRACT Trade unions need money to sustain the staff, infrastructure and activities on which all forms of union power depend, yet the financial dimensions of unions and their power have been largely overlooked in the comparative study of industrial relations. This article addresses the gap by using unions’ financial means as a revealing lens for understanding the role of the state in shaping union power. The comparison distinguished two ideal‐typical logics of state action behind union funding. Under indirect action, the state enables unions to convert membership into income, producing a tight coupling between union funds and organisational power. Under direct action, the state channels funds to unions on the basis of their recognised societal roles, decoupling income from membership. Systematised during the early decades of the twentieth century, these two action paths present fundamental transformations through liberalisation, leading to the financialisation and politicisation of union funding. By analysing the structures and changes in unions’ financial sustainability, this framework reveals the state's constitutive role in shaping and transforming union power.

title: Nudging citizens to use chatbots: an information and default option approach
abstract: Governments are increasingly adopting chatbots to reduce administrative burdens and improve service quality, yet citizens’ willingness to use them remains limited. Drawing on nudge theory, this study examines how information framing and default options influence citizens’ willingness to use chatbots in public services. Using a survey experiment in China, the results show that participants exposed to a loss frame were more willing to use chatbots than those exposed to a gain frame. The default option alone did not significantly affect willingness. However, the interaction between information framing and default settings was significant. Specifically, the positive effect of loss-framed information on citizens’ willingness to use chatbots was stronger when a default option was presented, suggesting that defaults amplify the effect of loss framing. Overall, the study offers practical insights into designing strategies to promote chatbot adoption in public services.

title: What Is a Terminal Disease? Hidden Expansion of Medically Assisted Death in the United States
abstract: Medically assisted death (MAD) in the United States is legally restricted to adults with a terminal disease. When these laws were debated and adopted, the term “terminal disease” was used by lawmakers and the public with a common sense understanding: an incurable disease that would inevitably cause death in the near term, regardless of treatment. Since then, published case reports, government correspondence, annual report data, and professional discussions indicate that some clinicians now apply the terminal disease criterion to cases where death is expected primarily because the person refuses or cannot access food, water, or standard medical care. This constitutes a de facto expansion of MAD eligibility, likely enabled by excessive clinician discretion and weak state oversight, with significant implications for the legal, ethical, and democratic foundations of terminal illness-based MAD regimes.

title: Cohort Profile Update: The Spanish Longitudinal Study on Ageing and Health (Edad con Salud)
Differences in SARS-CoV-2 rapid diagnostic testing usage by COVID-19 vaccination status can bias vaccine effectiveness estimates against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection from a test-negative design
Data-driven exploration of occupations and lung cancer risks using regularized regression models
Beyond health: loneliness and productivity growth across countries
abstract: Abstract Objectives: Loneliness is an established risk factor for poor health, yet its macroeconomic consequences remain unclear. We examined whether country-level loneliness is associated with productivity and long-run productivity growth. Methods: We combined 2023 Gallup World Poll data (145,072 respondents from 105 countries) with productivity measures from the Penn World Table. Country-level loneliness prevalence was based on respondents who reported feeling lonely for much of the previous day. Ordinary least squares models estimated associations between loneliness and total factor productivity (TFP), TFP growth, and related outcomes, adjusting for income, age, health problems, urbanization, and region fixed effects. Results: Loneliness was not associated with contemporaneous TFP levels but was consistently linked to lower long-run TFP growth. A one-standard-deviation increase in loneliness was associated with a 0.48-percentage-point lower annual TFP growth rate (0.37 standard deviations). These associations were robust across alternative growth periods. Loneliness showed weak evidence of greater TFP growth volatility but was not associated with human capital, physical capital, or aggregate output growth. Conclusions: Countries with higher loneliness exhibit slower long-run productivity growth but not lower productivity levels. Public Health Implications: Reducing loneliness may improve population health while potentially supporting economic resilience and productivity.

title: Is segregation bad for your heart?: a natural experiment for residential racial segregation exposure during childhood and cardiovascular disease risk
abstract: Abstract Background: Residential racial segregation is hypothesized to cause inequities in cardiovascular disease. Yet existing work is largely associational and has rarely tested longitudinal effects of childhood segregation on later CVD. Here, we leverage quasi-random urban planning decisions in Northern US cities prior to the Great Migration as an instrument for segregation as Black families moved North, providing a natural experiment. Methods: We followed Ananat’s work showing railroad track configurations serve as an instrument for segregation at the metropolitan area level. We linked Ananat’s data to the birthplaces of participants in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (1968-1994, n=829 Black & 1,262 White), following them through 2023. Race-stratified accelerated failure time models used an instrumental variables design and cluster bootstrapping, progressively adjusting for other railroad features, socioeconomic status, and birth year. Results: Estimates suggest childhood residential segregation causally delays the onset of CVD or hypertension for White people but speeds it up for Black people, though confidence intervals and instrument strength varied across model specifications. Non-instrumented models directly adjusting for confounders yielded strongly attenuated results in the same direction. Conclusion: Segregation is likely a cause of Black-White CVD inequities, not just a correlate. Causal designs across the life course are needed.

title: The French Paradox 2, a remake for Norway ?
Driver-initiated takeover in highway tunnels: effects of non-driving-related tasks on driving workload and takeover risk
Authorization environments for climate policy: a public value–based typology across countries
Understanding the influence of education and training on policy analytical capacity development
Differences in reporting child abuse by mothers and young adults
abstract: Background Measuring violence against children (VAC) requires understanding competing sources of bias, with evidence suggesting caregivers underreport abuse. Objective This study examined differences in reported child abuse by respondent using longitudinal data and identified factors influencing maternal reporting. Participants and settings Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), we analyzed mothers' cumulative prospective reports of physical and psychological abuse experienced by their children, alongside young adults' retrospective self-reports. Methods Difference between prevalence of abuse by respondents was estimated using McNemar's test for paired proportions. Concordance between respondents was assessed using Cohen's kappa and Prevalence-Adjusted Bias-Adjusted Kappa (PABAK). Multivariable logistic regressions identified maternal characteristics associated with reporting. Results Physical and psychological child prevalence was 6.23% (95% CI 5.51–7.02), and 11.77% (95% CI 10.80–12.81) among young adults, with significant differences by respondent ( p < 0.05). Mothers reported higher prevalence of psychological abuse and lower physical abuse than young adults. Cohen's kappa was 0.11 and 0.16 for physical and psychological abuse. PABAK showed higher agreement: 0.82 and 0.63. Mothers had lower odds of reporting physical or psychological abuse when the child was a female, 0.69 (95% CI 0.51–0.93). Conclusion While reports from mothers and children showed limited concordance, there was no consistent evidence that mothers systematically underreported abuse when identical questions were used. However, mothers' reporting varied by the child's sex and maternal characteristics. This work underscores the importance of considering identity and social norms in VAC measurement, by triangulating data from multiple respondents to improve accuracy in prevalence estimates.

title: Surveillance Path Dependence: Technological and Institutional Lock-In of Digital Surveillance Infrastructures in China
abstract: Digital surveillance infrastructures are widely critiqued for their use-side problems of access, privacy, and discrimination, but meaningful intervention requires understanding how these infrastructures are developed and stabilized in the first place. This paper examines China’s health code systems (HCSs) as a revelatory case of path dependence in the development of digital surveillance infrastructures. Drawing on news, first-hand interviews, and fieldwork, we trace how local governments chose to embed contact-tracing systems within the pre-existing digital ecosystems of Alipay and WeChat, primarily at the local level. Such choices persisted despite the central government’s openly cautious stance toward private tech giants and its subsequent attempts to develop independent alternatives. We describe this trajectory as surveillance path dependence, in which the convergence of pre-existing technological foundations, tight temporal pressure, and institutional incentives within a fragmented authoritarian institutional context locked new applications into established digital surveillance paths. This study suggests that mitigating the adverse societal impacts of large-scale digital surveillance requires intervening directly in the foundational design and institutional deployment of digital ecosystems rather than at the level of use-side effects.

title: We have come a long way, but…..not far enough
Assessing physical activity using Fitbit trackers and the association with quality of life among newly diagnosed patients with hematologic cancer
On the Presumption of Linearity in Behavioral Media Effects Research
How to Talk with the Academic Community about Contested Knowledge: A Confrontational-Reflexive Interview Model
abstract: Interviewing academics about contested knowledge presents significant methodological challenges, as the interview situation often activates “official” professional repertoires that conceal ambivalence and the active construction of epistemic boundaries. To address these limitations, the authors propose and evaluate the confrontational-reflexive interview model (CRIM), a research design aimed at systematically eliciting reflexivity and analyzing boundary-work in situ . The model treats the interview not as a neutral information extraction tool but as a structured sequence of meaning-making occasions. Stage 1 establishes a baseline narrative in expert interviews and focus groups, which is subsequently disrupted by a standardized “confrontation stimulus”—a scholarly text explicitly challenging the dominant disciplinary consensus—forcing participants to negotiate their position against a credible internal critique. Stage 2, conducted approximately one month later via asynchronous written correspondence, introduces temporal distance to test the stability and revisability of these accounts outside the immediate pressure of the face-to-face interaction. Drawing on a study of political scientists’ discourse on conspiracy theories, the authors demonstrate that although standard interviewer probes often fail to unsettle “official” narratives, the combination of a third-party textual confrontation and delayed reflection successfully reveals the specific conditions under which experts reproduce, repair, or redraw the boundaries of legitimate knowledge. The authors argue that CRIM contributes to sociological methodology by offering a replicable framework for observing expertise as a contingent, interactional performance.

title: Better together? Exploring factors of effectiveness and efficiency of mandatory intermunicipal cooperation
Coordinating data centre microgrids and mobile power sources for distribution network resilience: A data-driven distributionally robust optimisation approach
Climate-reliable power systems via stochastic programming with scenarios generated with a posteriori time aggregation
Economic and emissions analysis of natural gas power with high-efficiency CO2 capture
Renewable power-to-heat for low-rank coal upgrading: a 4E analysis of an electrified pyrolysis polygeneration system
Techno-economic perspective on emerging cryogenic and non-cryogenic boil-off hydrogen compression systems
Mechanism-dependent antagonism of auxiliary information in substation-level load disaggregation for distribution network planning
Characterizing the inter-temporal flexibility region of multi-source district heating systems for power system support
Energy cascade utilization in SOFC-GT hybrids: the approach to ultra-high efficiency and multi-generation
Synthesis of ammonia and its application in the sustainable steel process: A review
Fintech, climate shocks, and agricultural land use transition: Evidence from farmers in China
Social comparison feedback and residential electricity conservation: Field experimental evidence from Mexico
The rise and fall of Northvolt: From sustainability to battery geopolitics and industrial failure in the European Nordics
abstract: Northvolt was one of Europe's most ambitious electric vehicle battery manufacturers and recyclers. The Group aimed to produce low-carbon and recycled lithium-ion batteries in the gigafactory Northvolt Ett located in Skellefteå, northern Sweden. Its rapid development and abrupt collapse in a seemingly favourable policy context provide a critical entry point into the political economy of Europe's decarbonisation and reindustrialisation agenda. Based on an interdisciplinary single-case study, this article reconstructs Northvolt's trajectory at multiple territorial and governance levels (across municipal, Swedish, Nordic, and European policy levels). It draws on a qualitative research framework combining documentary analysis, field visits in Sweden, and seventeen semi-structured interviews with a multi-level sample (workers, industrial actors, researchers, trade union representatives and policymakers). We show that Northvolt's arrival was embedded in a broader shift in transition governance, from sustainability-oriented goals towards geopolitical and supply-security concerns. Yet, this reframing lacked corresponding transformation of public intervention instruments, leaving limited public capacities for strategic coordination and crisis response. This article analyses how this policy architecture helped Northvolt to build financial credibility, but simultaneously failed to address the project's systemic vulnerabilities. Two potential drivers of the failure at Northvolt Ett are examined in depth: offtake-related constraints and operational misalignments. Overall, the article brings an empirical analysis of the collapse of a European battery champion to the literature on the political economy of the energy transition.

title: Electrochemical energy storage beyond steady state: Real world automotive dynamics as a missing dimension in battery science
Resilience in the circular economy: Perspectives for better alignment
abstract: This perspective article addresses the role of systemic resilience in circular economy (CE) debates. It underlines resilience as an important feature and proposes ways of how CE metrics and decision-making could be better aligned.

title: Exploring the effects of food consumption transition and yield enhancement on cultivated land requirements in China
Heavy-Duty Diesel Vehicle Deterioration: Impact of Vehicle Age and Emission Control Technology on NO x Emissions
abstract: Abstract This study examines the effect of aging and deterioration on NOx emissions from heavy-duty diesel trucks (HDDTs) with different emission control technologies, including Engine Control only, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). In-use tailpipe emissions were measured from 12,023 HDDTs from 13 roadside measurement campaigns conducted in California and Utah between 2008 and 2024. Vehicle registration records and the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) engine certification database were used to identify engine NOx control technology. At younger ages, SCR-equipped HDDTs generally emitted significantly less NOx than non-SCR-equipped HDDTs. However, after several years of aging, NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs were comparable to or exceeded those from non-SCR-equipped HDDTs across locations, engine manufacturers, and engine model years. Although cumulative lifetime emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs remained lower than non-SCR HDDTs, the reduction in lifetime NOx emissions was substantially smaller than estimated by EPA’s MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES). MOVES predicts an 80% reduction in lifetime NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs, whereas our estimate is approximately 32%. These findings may indicate that the long-term benefits of SCR for reducing HDDT NOx emissions are smaller than expected and highlight the need for continued emissions monitoring of in-use HDDTs.

title: Chasing Bubbles: Toward a Standardized Approach for Quantifying Methane Ebullition Using Bubble Traps in Streams and Rivers
abstract: Abstract Ebullition transports large quantities of the potent greenhouse gas methane (CH4) from stream sediments into the atmosphere. However, the use of different sampling designs complicates comparisons of CH4 emissions estimates between studies. Here, we present the first systematic review of sampling designs used in the past for assessing fluvial CH4 ebullition rates. In addition, we conducted field experiments to estimate the optimal number of bubble traps and the length of the sampling period, and to assess uncertainties in determining CH4 content in the emitted bubbles. Our results demonstrate considerable spatial variability in bubble fluxes (0–4.8 L m–2 d–1) and CH4 content in the bubbles (0.01–67%), necessitating a larger number of bubble traps than typically deployed in streams. Using fewer traps leads to greater deviations in CH4 ebullition estimates than shorter deployment times. Therefore, the robust sampling design should account for strong small-scale heterogeneity in streams through an adequate number of bubble traps and link bubble fluxes to trap-specific gas content. It should also consider the risk of CH4 concentration decreases in accumulated bubbles over a few days, primarily due to redissolution, followed by oxidation and leakage.

title: Post-Regulation of Nitrogen Configurations in Nitrogen-Doped Carbon Electrodes for Enhanced Capacitive Deionization
abstract: Abstract Nitrogen doping is widely used to enhance the electrochemical performance of carbon materials, yet its effectiveness is often limited by electrochemically inactive or inaccessible nitrogen configurations. Here, we develop a coupling-agent-mediated amidation strategy to postregulate nitrogen-doped carbon, selectively enriching amino nitrogen while tailoring the distribution of pyridinic, pyrrolic, and graphitic nitrogen. The introduced −NH2 groups elevate the surface charge density, which is favorable for ion adsorption and diffusion. Density functional theory calculations, together with electrochemical kinetic analyses, reveal that edge-type nitrogen, particularly the lone electron pairs on amino nitrogen, can strongly interact with salt ions, resulting in effective electrical-double-layer compression and shortened ion diffusion distance. Consequently, the optimized electrode achieves a specific adsorption capacity of 70.3 mgNaCl g–1 and a time-averaged adsorption rate of 2.3 mgNaCl g–1 min–1 in 1000 mg L–1 NaCl solution at a cell voltage of 1.6 V. Its electrosorption behavior toward monovalent and divalent cations is also systematically evaluated in synthetic brines and actual industrial recirculating cooling water. This study provides a facile, powerful strategy to rationally design carbon electrodes for high-performance electrochemical ion storage and separation applications.

title: River Plastic Retention and Export across Europe
abstract: Abstract Rivers play a central role in the global distribution of plastic pollution. Despite recent research showing that the majority of plastic is not transported to the sea, most plastic transport models have not explicitly included plastic retention in rivers. We propose a new model to quantify micro- and macroplastic retention on land and in rivers, and export toward the sea. Of the 3.55 Mt year–1 of plastics emitted to the environment, only 0.1% of microplastics and 0.5% of macroplastics are exported from the river outlet. This results in 16.8 (15.7–35.1) kt year–1 of microplastic and 3.2 (1.4–12.1) kt year–1 macroplastic export. Rivers store plastic, retaining 68.3 (156.5–350.1) kt year–1 of microplastics (5.3%) and 84.6 (37.2–320.5) kt year–1 of macroplastics (2.5%), while the greatest proportion of plastic remains on land. Although large basin size and high plastic emission to land characterize high absolute micro- and macroplastic retention and export, large basin size is a weaker predictor for high plastic retention and export per capita. By aggregating ranks for plastic export and retention, we provide a new and comprehensive outlook on the most polluting rivers of Europe. This work provides crucial baseline estimates for plastic pollution in light of missing plastic reduction quotas to guide future prioritization and assessment of mitigation actions.

title: Phage-Based Biofilm Control in Engineered Water Environments
abstract: Abstract Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.

title: Multi-Scale Multi-Indicator Assessment of Material Recovery Pathways: The Case of the United States Flat Glass Sector
abstract: Abstract Material recovery and circularity analysis offers critical insights for understanding future scenarios and informing strategic decisions toward resource use. However, existing approaches often lack the granularity and breadth needed to capture supply chain dynamics and economy-wide impacts simultaneously. We introduce a novel quantitative framework─Supply Chain Operations Research through Physical Input-Output (SCORPIO)─that addresses this gap by enabling multi-scale assessment of material recovery strategies across both supply chain and macroeconomic levels. To demonstrate SCORPIO’s capabilities, we apply it to flat glass flows in the United States, examining waste valorization practices, including open- and closed-loop recycling. By assessing economic, workforce, and environmental indicators, SCORPIO reveals the potential outcomes and trade-offs of different waste valorization solutions in a holistic manner. Results show that both open-loop and closed-loop recycling of glass from utility solar and commercial buildings have the potential for positive economic impacts at the supply chain and economy level. However, the effect on environmental impacts was less certain, with open-loop recycling generally performing better than closed-loop pathways. This case study illustrates how the SCORPIO framework can support stakeholders navigating the transition toward increased material recovery, offering a methodological foundation applicable to other material systems facing environmental and resource challenges.

title: Monitoring Advanced Hydration Station (AHS) Water Quality in Flint, MI, School Buildings: Field Grab Sampling and Filter-Based Lead Assessment
abstract: Abstract School drinking water lead exposure remains a public health concern. In addition, time-variant lead concentrations pose challenges to monitoring practices. This study evaluates the lead (and, for some experiments, bacterial) removal performance of advanced hydration stations (AHS) with membrane filters, activated carbon block filters, and LED UV disinfection in Flint, Michigan. Laboratory challenge testing and more than 400 grab samples were collected from influent and effluent water from over 70 field-deployed AHS units during three sampling campaigns in 2022 and 2023. Our study confirmed that AHS units effectively removed lead. The median influent lead concentrations ranged from 6 to 14 μg/L, with 53% of samples exceeding 10 μg/L. Lead levels in effluent water were almost all below the detection limit (98% of samples). Effluent bacteria concentrations monitored during the first field sampling campaign in 2022 were all below detection, and removal during challenge testing were >2.6 log reduction. A subset of filters (n = 21) from those harvested in July 2022 were acid-extracted to assess the total accumulation of lead. This information, along with the cumulative volume of water processed, was used to calculate a volume-averaged lead concentration that represents avoided lead exposure and identifies potential hot spots of lead release to prioritize remediation activities. The outcomes of this monitoring campaign demonstrate the effectiveness of the AHS units at removing lead and bacteria, and the importance of using filter-based monitoring to inform AHS maintenance and identify upstream sources of lead.

title: Convergent Biogenic Magnetite Formation from Diverse Iron (Oxyhydr)oxide Precursors Drives Cr(VI) Reduction via an Environmental Battery Mechanism
abstract: Abstract Iron (oxyhydr)oxides mediate electron flux across coupled biogeochemical cycles in anoxic environments, yet whether their biogenic transformation feeds back to reshape interfacial electron transfer efficiency remains unresolved. Here, five structurally distinct iron (oxyhydr)oxide precursors (ferrihydrite, goethite, magnetite, wüstite, and hematite) were exposed to anaerobic sulfur-oxidizing bioreactors under Cr(VI) stress, and their transformation trajectories were tracked using synchrotron EXAFS spectroscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, DFT calculations, and metagenomic profiling. Mineral bioavailability decreased in the order ferrihydrite > goethite > magnetite > wüstite > hematite, a hierarchy governed by lattice iron-leaching energetics quantified via DFT (Efev from −8.96 eV for ferrihydrite to 5.76 eV for hematite). Despite this wide disparity in precursor lability, all biotransformation trajectories converged on magnetite as the thermodynamically stable end point. In the ferrihydrite system, biogenic magnetite reached 60% of the final solid phase and operated as an in situ “environmental battery” (storing and releasing electrons through reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) lattice cycling), lowering interfacial charge transfer resistance and producing a 4.77-fold higher pseudo-first-order Cr(VI) reduction rate constant than the mineral-free biotic control (C-S). Metagenomic analysis revealed mineral-specific restructuring of the microbial community toward a tightly coupled sulfur–iron redox network. These results reframe precursor mineralogy from a determinant of intrinsic reactivity to a kinetic regulator of biogenic electron-buffer formation, providing a mechanistic basis for mineral-informed bioremediation design.

title: From Bench-Scale Experiments to Technical Scale-Up: Rethinking Sorption Research for the Removal of Trace Organic Contaminants from Water
abstract: Abstract Drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater systems are increasingly challenged by trace organic contaminants (TrOCs), including PFAS, pharmaceuticals, pesticides, and other persistent and highly mobile contaminants that occur at ultralow concentrations in complex water matrices. Sorption-based treatment processes remain central to TrOC removal because they can concentrate dilute contaminants without generating potentially toxic transformation products. However, much of the current sorption literature remains disconnected from the needs of performance prediction and technical scale-up. Equilibrium and kinetic parameters are often derived under simplified laboratory conditions, using empirically fitted models, elevated contaminant concentrations, and/or nonrepresentative water matrices, limiting their physical interpretability and transferability across treatment scenarios. This review critically examines three interconnected areas governing the engineering relevance of sorption data: thermodynamic principles governing sorption equilibria, mechanistic interpretation of sorption kinetics, and the evaluation and transition of novel sorbents to scaled treatment systems. By identifying limitations in prevailing experimental practices and aligning equilibrium characterization, kinetic modeling, and sorbent evaluation with application-relevant conditions, this review provides a framework for generating mechanistically grounded sorption data to support material selection and translate laboratory-derived sorption data into process design parameters for pilot- and full-scale TrOC treatment systems.

title: No Significant Elimination of Perfluoroctanesulfonate and Other Common Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances by Adult Fathead Minnows, Pimephales promelas
abstract: Abstract Bioaccumulation dynamics of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) remain poorly understood, and kinetic-based information is lacking across environmental gradients, particularly for Cyprinidae, the largest and most diverse fish family. We examined the influences of pH (6.5, 7.5) and salinity (0.3 g/L, 3.0 g/L) on uptake and elimination kinetics of 19 PFAS, which were selected at low concentrations not eliciting standardized adverse outcomes, in the common Cyprinidae, Pimephales promelas. These PFAS consisted of short- and long-chain perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonates (PFSAs), a sulfonamide, and fluorotelomer sulfonates. Water, whole-body tissue, and plasma were collected over time, and samples were analyzed via liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Rapid uptake was observed in tissue, reaching pseudo-steady-state conditions within 24–96 h of exposure initiation; uptake rates increased with chain length but were not influenced (p > 0.05) by pH or salinity. During four separate experiments, no significant (p > 0.05) elimination was observed for PFDA, PFDoDA, PFTeDA, total PFOS, PFOSA, and 8:2 FTSA. Kinetic-based bioaccumulation factors (BAFs) increased with chain length for PFCAs and PFSAs, and exceedances of BAF cutoff values were identified. No significant (p > 0.05) elimination of these PFAS indicates that Cyprinidae should be considered during future bioaccumulation studies.

title: Economic Potential of Nuclear Power in the Transportation Sector: Analysis of E-Fuels as An Alternative Fuel for Total Cost of Ownership and Vehicle Emissions
abstract: Abstract Advanced nuclear reactors could expand U.S. nuclear energy beyond electricity generation into transportation by supplying heat and power for hydrogen and synthetic hydrocarbon fuel production. We evaluated nuclear-enabled hydrogen for fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and nuclear-derived electro-fuels (e-fuels) for internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) and hybrid vehicles across selected light-, medium-, and heavy-duty classes. Economic performance was assessed using total cost of ownership (TCO), and environmental performance was evaluated using life-cycle emissions. We then estimated carbon abatement costs for alternative fuel/vehicle pathways relative to conventional gasoline and diesel systems. Our findings indicate that conventional ICEVs fueled by gasoline or diesel generally remain the lowest-cost options in 2035. For small sport utility vehicles (SUVs), however, hybrid vehicles using nuclear-based e-fuels and battery electric vehicles (BEVs) with home charging increase TCO modestly relative to gasoline vehicles, while e-fuels achieve the lowest emissions among the alternatives. In long-haul trucking, hydrogen and e-fuels show potential, with marginal TCO increases relative to conventional systems and relatively low abatement costs. Although hydrogen and e-fuels produced with advanced nuclear reactors remain relatively expensive, continued advances in reactors, electrolysis, and fuel synthesis, together with scale economies, could improve competitiveness, diversify transportation fuel options, and reduce emissions.

title: Evaluating Emergency Emission Controls During an Unprecedented Regional Haze Event Using Causal Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Emergency emission controls are widely implemented to mitigate severe haze, yet their effectiveness is difficult to disentangle from meteorological variability and concurrent changes in activities. Here, we develop a three-step evaluation approach integrating air quality meteorological normalization, augmented synthetic control, and machine-learning prediction to causally quantify intervention-attributable changes in local emission strength and ambient pollutant concentrations. Applied to Shijiazhuang’s unprecedented 45-day “Sharp Sword to Cut Haze” campaign in 2016, the approach revealed that local emission strengths of PM2.5, PM10, SO2, NO2, and CO were reduced by 4.3%, 4.8%, 15.8%, 5.8%, and 15.3%, respectively. Corresponding concentrations fell by 42.1 (14.8%), 47.4 (12.4%), 13.8 (16.6%), 15.8 (15.5%) μg·m–3, and 0.9 mg·m–3 (19.6%). Observation-based PM2.5 source apportionment results independently supported these estimates: contributions from vehicle emissions, steelmaking, and coal combustion were 4.1%, 11.0%, and 21.7% lower, respectively, than during the corresponding period in 2017. Despite stringent controls, PM2.5 averaged 243.2 μg·m–3 during the intervention period. Thus, stringent local controls substantially reduced emissions, but regional transport and unfavorable meteorology partly offset the resulting air quality benefits, highlighting the need for coordinated regional mitigation.

Digital economy-driven resilience enhancement in the global food supply chain
abstract: The global food system is undergoing significant changes due to the digital economy, but the specific impact of this on the resilience of the food supply chain remains unclear. This study examines the impact of the digital economy on the resilience of food supply chains in 106 countries between 2013 and 2023. The findings show that although the digital economy is growing internationally, its development is still unequal, especially in terms of digital market and digital governance. Food trade networks are becoming more interconnected; trade in plant-based foods is more geographically diverse, while trade in animal-based foods is more closely linked. Resilience patterns reveal significant disparities, with high-income countries continuing to have a distinct edge. For animal-based food supply chains, digital technology is the main source of resilience (35.6% of total feature importance); for plant-based food supply chains, on the other hand, GDP is the most important factor (54.2%). The degree to which different digital economy factors affect resilience is determined by threshold effects. Critical levels usually fall between 36 and 74 on the digital economy index, depending on the food type and digital dimension. These results highlight the necessity of category-specific approaches to help create more resilient and sustainable global food supply chains.

title: Predictive energy management for hybrid amphibious vehicles integrating operating condition recognition and condition-matched speed prediction
abstract: The substantial differences between land and water operating conditions, abrupt power-demand variations, and multi-objective optimization conflicts pose significant challenges to real-time energy management for hybrid amphibious vehicles. This study proposes a coordinated predictive energy management strategy integrating online operating-condition recognition and speed prediction to improve power response, fuel economy, and battery safety. A switchable hybrid powertrain operates in series mode on land and parallel mode on water. Representative operating conditions are identified offline using kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) and K-means++ clustering, and the resulting labels are used to train a long short-term memory (LSTM) network for online recognition. A dual-path condition-dependent adaptation mechanism is established: discrete condition labels select the corresponding condition-matched variational mode decomposition–radial basis function (VMD-RBF) speed predictors, while continuous distances to cluster centers adaptively adjust the power-response and fuel-economy weights of the predictive equivalent consumption minimization strategy (ECMS). Real-vehicle tests show that the proposed strategy reduces the mean 0–100 km/h acceleration time on land by 14.9% compared with the conventional predictive strategy, avoids the engine-overload shutdown observed in six of ten rule-based tests, and reduces the mean 0–60 km/h acceleration time on water by 9.2% compared with the rule-based strategy. The proposed framework provides an effective approach for coordinated energy management across amphibious operating domains.

A mechanistic-data fusion framework for lifetime prediction of PEMFCs under cross-temperature condition
abstract: The performance degradation of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) has always been a key issue restricting their large-scale commercial application. As PEMFCs are increasingly used in heavy-duty vehicles, the demanding load conditions widen the operating temperature range of stack and lead to cross-temperature operation conditions. Under these conditions, the degradation behavior of PEMFCs becomes highly nonlinear, posing significant challenges to the accuracy of existing lifetime prediction models. Therefore, this study conducts cross-temperature durability experiments and proposes a mechanistic-data fusion framework named Freq-PEANet (Frequency-based Period-wise & Exogenous-Endogenous Association Network). It hierarchically couples a Frequency Filter Block and a Times Block to capture nonlinear degradation dynamics by jointly modeling the global trend and multi-period temporal variations. A Cross-Attention Block is further introduced to fuse recovery features derived from distribution of relaxation times (DRT) analysis and operating variables as exogenous inputs for assisting the endogenous target. This block assigns time-varying weights to exogenous variables at each time step, improving information utilization of exogenous variable. Compared with best-performing benchmark models, the proposed framework reduces the root-mean-square error by 26.74% on the static dataset and by a significantly higher 42.73% on the cross-temperature dataset. This method provides a new interpretable framework to predict PEMFC lifetime under cross-temperature conditions.

Application of Organic Superabsorbent Cellulosic Polymers ( OSCPs ) and Cyanobacteria on Reduction of Aeolian Losses
abstract: ABSTRACT Establishing biocrusts on sandy surfaces in harsh desert environments presents significant challenges due to extreme ecological conditions. To address these challenges, this study examined the effects of two organic superabsorbent cellulosic polymers (OSCPs)—carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and guar gum (GUA)—on the establishment of cyanobacterial crusts on aeolian sands, specifically using a consortium of Nostoc sp. and Microcoleus vaginatus . The optimal concentrations of GUA and CMC for maximum cyanobacterial growth were determined through preliminary optimization assays. The resulting suspensions, combining OSCPs and cyanobacteria, were applied to sandy substrates. After 60 days of inoculation, the cyanobacterial crusts were analyzed for exopolysaccharide (EPS) accumulation, chlorophyll a content, physical and chemical properties, shear strength, and compressive strength. Additionally, wind tunnel tests were conducted to measure aeolian mass flux under the different treatments. Results indicated that the cyanobacteria + CMC treatment outperformed all others, increasing chlorophyll a by 114% and EPS production by 108% to 280% depending on the EPS fraction. This treatment also enhanced organic carbon and nitrogen accumulation, crust thickness (~21 mm), shear strength (51.39 kPa), and available water capacity (+110%). Furthermore, it raised the wind erosion threshold velocity from 11.5 to 19.7 m s −1 , reducing aeolian mass flux by over 98% at wind speeds up to 19.7 m s −1 . In contrast, GUA alone resulted in the lowest compressive strength and mass flux rates. These findings suggest that combining cyanobacteria with OSCPs, particularly CMC, is an effective strategy for promoting biocrust formation and mitigating soil erosion in arid environments.

How Peer Working Hours Shape Individual Preferences: Experimental Evidence From Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how colleagues' working hours influence individual working hours preferences. We conducted a representative survey experiment among German employees in 2024, in which participants received randomized information about colleagues' working hours. We combine the survey experiment with quantitative and LLM‐based text analysis of an open‐ended question. Colleagues' hours causally influence stated preferences, yet respondents' explanations focus on personal reasons. This shows that social factors influence working time preferences alongside the individual considerations that respondents most frequently identify. Our findings highlight the importance of collective action for working‐time policy and reveal methodological considerations for studying labor supply preferences.

Trihalomethane Exposure, Seminal Plasma Metabolomics, and Semen Quality in Healthy Men: A Meet-in-the-Middle Approach
abstract: Abstract Exposure to trihalomethanes (THMs) has been linked to reduced human semen quality, but the critical windows of vulnerability and underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We therefore measured untargeted seminal plasma metabolomics to identify metabolic biomarkers and biological pathways linking blood THM concentrations to repeated measurements of semen quality (4146 measurements over a 3 month follow-up period) among 762 healthy Chinese men. We found inverse associations between blood THM concentrations (i.e., chloroform, bromodichloromethane, and chlorinated THMs) and semen volume and total sperm count (all P values <0.05), which were most pronounced for exposure measured 70–90 days prior to semen collection (corresponding to the early stage of spermatogenesis). Metabolome-wide association analyses identified 90 metabolites that were simultaneously associated with blood THM concentrations and sperm-quality parameters. Mediation analyses further revealed that 44 metabolites, enriched in the pathways of unsaturated fatty acid biosynthesis, steroid hormone biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, linoleic acid metabolism, pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis, and β-alanine metabolism, mediated a considerable proportion (8.1–41.3%) of the inverse relationships between THM exposure and semen quality. Our results suggest that THM exposure during the early stage of spermatogenesis is associated with reduced human semen quality, potentially driven by perturbations in lipid metabolism, steroid hormone synthesis, and antioxidant-related metabolisms.

title: Linking Protist-Bacteria Trophic Interactions to Organic Matter Chemodiversity: Insights from a Coal Mine Ecological Restoration Chronosequence
abstract: Abstract Restoring soil biota and dissolved organic matter (DOM) is essential for sustainable ecological restoration of coal mine sites. Protists, as key microbial predators, are recognized as regulators of multiple belowground processes, yet their roles in shaping DOM during ecological restoration remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated a field-scale coal mine ecological restoration chronosequence using vegetation surveys, ultrahigh-resolution Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR-MS), and high-throughput Illumina sequencing. Restoration increased plant diversity, coverage, and aboveground biomass, which are key resources for soil organic matter inputs. Soil DOM shifted toward more thermodynamically stable compounds, with enhanced chemodiversity during the restoration process. Protistan diversity, particularly of phagotrophic taxa, increased with restoration age, potentially exerting top-down control that increased bacterial diversity but suppressed fungal diversity. Co-occurrence network analysis and random forest modeling revealed that plant biomass was positively linked with phagotrophic diversity, which might influence DOM composition through direct transformation of organic matter (OM) or indirect regulation of bacterial transformation of OM, contributing to the accumulation of recalcitrant molecules with high stability. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized trophic cascade linking protists to DOM chemodiversity at the molecular level, highlighting the importance of integrating protistan regulation into soil ecological restoration strategies for mine sites.

title: Winter and Summer Differences in Oxylipin Responses to Ambient Particles: Roles of Sizes and Constituents
abstract: Abstract Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) has been associated with increased mortality risk, but whether it is more harmful on colder or warmer days is unclear. Here, we investigate seasonal variations in PM2.5 mass, sizes, constituents, and their association with oxylipin changes in humans. In a panel study of 123 adults in Beijing, we measured 27 PM2.5 metrics and five circulating lipoxygenase-derived oxylipins (i.e., leukotriene B4 [LTB4], 5-, 8-, 12-, and 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid [HETE]) across winter and summer. PM2.5 exposure was associated with peak oxylipin increases at lag 0–1 days. Across particle size fractions and constituents, oxylipin increases ranged from 3.3% to 114.2%, with the most robust associations for ultrafine particles, accumulation mode particles, organic carbon, and chloride. Furthermore, an exposure-response relationship between UFP and oxylipins was observed only in summer. An IQR increase in UFP was associated with oxylipin changes of 12.9–97.7% in summer and −7.7 to 18.8% in winter. Conversely, oxylipin increases associated with accumulation mode particles and organic carbon were greater in winter. These findings suggest that the sizes and constituents of PM2.5 may partially explain the seasonal difference in the health effect of PM2.5 exposure, helping identify components associated with stronger biomarker responses in specific seasons.

title: Root-applied taurine reduces grain cadmium and improves rice yield by decreasing Cd transport and increasing Cd retention in roots
Dormant and green-up season mowing maximizes productivity-derived vegetation carbon input potential in coastal wetlands
abstract: Managing coastal Phragmites australis wetlands through seasonal mowing can alter belowground C input potential and soil CO 2 and CH 4 fluxes. However, how mowing timing affects vegetation structure and belowground C input potential across phenological stages remains poorly resolved. To address this management gap, we conducted a long-term randomized-block experiment in the Yellow River Delta, comparing an unmown control (CK) with annual mowing at green-up (March, 3M), peak growth (July, 7M), and dormancy (December, 12M). We quantified vegetation structure and production, estimated belowground net primary productivity (BNPP) using ingrowth cores, operationally estimated heterotrophic respiration ( R h ) using root exclusion and derived autotrophic respiration ( R a ) as the difference between total soil respiration and R h , measured soil CH 4 flux, and conducted scenario-based regional scaling of BNPP-derived belowground C input potential using the remotely mapped P. australis area. BNPP-derived belowground C input potential was greatest under December mowing, intermediate under March mowing, and lowest under July mowing. Targeted regressions showed positive associations of shallow coarse-root biomass with R a and shallow fine-root biomass with R h , whereas plant height was negatively associated with soil CH 4 flux. Under the full-coverage scenario, additional regional BNPP-derived belowground C input potential reached 0.170 ± 0.018, 0.100 ± 0.036, and 0.043 ± 0.017 Tg C yr −1 under 12M, 3M, and 7M, respectively. December mowing therefore produced the largest BNPP-derived belowground C input potential among the tested timings, whereas March mowing showed an intermediate response. Scenario-scaled C input potential should not be interpreted as realized ecosystem C sequestration or net climate benefit.

title: Plant-derived high-C:P amendments enhance legacy phosphorus utilization in phosphorus-enriched greenhouse soil via stoichiometric regulation and microbial functional coupling
abstract: Long-term intensive fertilization has accumulated large legacy phosphorus (P) pools in greenhouse vegetable soils, while substituting chemical fertilizers with livestock manure may exacerbate soil P loading. We evaluated pakchoi growth and legacy P utilization in an acidified, P-enriched greenhouse soil, comparing an unfertilized, unamended control (CK) with equal-carbon inputs of low-C:P, high-P chicken manure (OF) and high-C:P, low-P plant-derived amendments: alkali lignin (AL), straw (ST), and alkali-lignin-modified straw (AST). Compared with the OF, shoot dry weight was 47.0% and 12.4% higher under ST and AST, respectively, while shoot P uptake increased by 80.2% and 76.8%. OF produced an apparent P surplus, whereas ST and AST generated negative apparent P balances, indicating current-season amendment P inputs could not offset shoot P removal and supporting enhanced legacy P utilization without further accumulation of available or labile inorganic P. Plant-derived amendments increased soil C:P and pH, generally enhanced C- and N-acquiring enzyme activities, and reduced ecoenzymatic vector angles, alleviating relative microbial P-acquisition limitation. Metagenomic and random forest analyses showed that enhanced P acquisition was not primarily linked to a single P-cycling process, but more closely associated with resource stoichiometry and soluble N status, alongside coordinated restructuring of microbial C degradation, N transformation, and P-cycling functions. Overall, AL most strongly ameliorated acidity but elicited weak plant responses; ST produced the strongest biomass response, while AST maintained comparably high P acquisition and markedly improved soil pH. These high-C:P amendments provide a low-P alternative to high-P manure inputs, offering a strategy for reduced-P management and legacy P utilization.

title: Honeycomb monolith-based multichannel reactor for methane bioconversion into ectoine
abstract: A novel gas-liquid multichannel bioreactor based on cordierite honeycomb monoliths was engineered and operated under internal gas and liquid recirculation for methane bioconversion into ectoine. The assessment of the volumetric gas-liquid mass transfer coefficients for O 2 ( k L a O 2 ) in this novel bioreactor showed values up to 1472.7 ± 111.6 h −1 , representing an increase of one order of magnitude over conventional bubble column reactors. Bubble measurements were consistent with a flow regime compatible with Taylor-flow operation, suggesting that liquid-film renewal was likely a major contributor to mass-transfer enhancement. During diluted-methane bioconversion into ectoine, stable operation at relatively high gas and liquid recirculation rates was achieved after gradual enrichment of the halotolerant mixed methanotrophic culture, potentially because of the associated hydrodynamic shear stress. After inoculum adaptation, methane bioconversion efficiencies and capacities of up to 72.9% and 45 g m 3 h −1 , with an ectoine concentration of 32.1 mg gVSS −1 , were achieved when operating with a gas residence time of 30 min, and gas and liquid recirculation of 40 L min −1 and 25 L min −1 , respectively (corresponding to a k L a O 2 of 679.5 ± 57.3 h −1 ). Process performance was supported by a well-adapted inoculum dominated by Methylophaga , Methylonatrum and Methylotuvimicrobium , which accumulated 44% of the relative abundances. Monoliths as microchannels in high gas-liquid mass transfer reactors represent a promising platform for methane valorisation, but further optimisation of operational parameters is required to intensify ectoine production from methane.

Spatial prediction of coastal groundwater nitrate using combined feature selection and explainable machine learning
abstract: Groundwater nitrate contamination is an important issue affecting groundwater quality and safety. Accurate prediction of groundwater nitrate concentrations and identification of key influencing factors are of great significance for groundwater pollution prevention and water resource management. Taking the lower reaches of the Huangshui River as the study area, 452 groundwater samples collected in July 2023 were used to predict groundwater NO 3 − -N concentrations by integrating Spearman correlation analysis, self-organizing map (SOM)-Boruta feature selection, Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), RF-XGBoost stacking modeling, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and geographic information system (GIS)-based spatial mapping. The dataset was divided into 361 training samples and 91 independent test samples, and model robustness was further assessed through cross-validation and 1000 repeated resampling runs. The SOM-Boruta method selected eight key variables: TDS, SO 4 2− , TH, Cl − , NH 3 -N, COD, F − and pH. All three models showed good predictive ability, with the RF-XGBoost stacking model yielding the most favorable test-set performance (R 2 = 0.881, RMSE = 13.266 mg/L, MAE = 9.284 mg/L).SHAP analysis identified TDS as the predictor with the highest contribution to model predictions across the three models. GIS-based RF-XGBoost prediction showed groundwater NO 3 − -N concentrations ranging from 5.31 to 59.83 mg/L, with higher values in the north, lower values in the south and transitional values in the central area. These findings support groundwater nitrate spatial identification, water quality assessment and regional groundwater resource protection.

title: Spatial differentiation and urban environmental associations of avian co-occurrence network roles: Evidence from Guangzhou, China
