Insight into the urine progression and DOM transformation mechanism for sustainable nitrogen-water synergistic recovery in space stations
abstract: Urine represents a critical water resource for closing the water and nitrogen loop in life support systems during manned space exploration. This work focuses on the impacts of pretreatment agents on urine progression and dissolved organic matter (DOM) transformation during long-term storage, with a perspective towards technology innovation for nitrogen-water synergistic recovery from urine in space. Urea hydrolysis, driven by microbial activity, was identified as the primary driver of urine variation, initiating rapid changes within 8 h of storage. The time point of significant DOM variation was prior to urea hydrolysis, and fresh humic-like substance from recent biological activity, which were dominated the variations of DOM. Meanwhile, the increasing NH 4 + -N and pH can resulted in precipitation, such as MgNH 4 PO 4 , which showed potential risks to the urine transport and treatment devices. Both H 2 SO 4 and CrO 3 showed excellent urine stabilization performance with urea hydrolysis rates of 0.10∼0.17 within 336 h. However, there have divergent DOM transformation pathways and sediment components: H 2 SO 4 influenced the fresh DOM by microbial inhibition through acidic environment, and uric acid and CaSO 4 were the main sediments; CrO 3 could enhance the degradation of protein-like substances by strong oxidation, and generate Cr-containing dense sediments. Therefore, the selection criteria for technologies and pretreatment agents on urine recovery are proposed, which encourage the integration of membrane separation and biosynthesis. This work reveals the dynamic variation and the mechanism of pretreatment agents during urine storage, which offers the basis for innovation in urine recovery for deep space exploration.

title: A sensitivity-informed correlation-based framework for detecting runoff pollutant hotspots in grazed catchments: Implications for precision cattle grazing to improve water quality
abstract: Cattle grazing is a known source of water pollution. Identifying areas within grazinglands where cattle activity contributes most to downstream water quality impairment is important for effective management. This study presents a framework to detect these runoff pollutant hotspots. The framework is based on Pearson correlation coefficients between cattle presence across the catchment and water quality at the outlet. Cattle locations were recorded at 5–60 min time intervals using Virtual Fencing (VF) technology in three experimental catchments located in north-central Oklahoma, USA, two under rotational grazing and one continuously grazed. Escherichia coli (E. coli) , total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN), and total phosphorus (TP) were measured during runoff events between March 2022, and June 2024. The spatial and temporal scales at which runoff quality was most affected by cattle presence were determined through a sensitivity analysis of grid cell size (GCS), time interval ( Δ T ) between consecutive cattle Global Positioning System (GPS) records, and pollutant half-life (HL) representing manure decay. The strongest grid cell-scale correlations between water quality parameters and cattle presence ranged from 0.48 to 0.83 for E. coli , 0.70 to 0.86 for TKN, and 0.67 to 0.90 for TP. These hotspots were detected using grid cell sizes ranging from 70 m × 70 m to 100 m × 100 m, and half-life values ranging from 3 to 12 days for E. coli , 3–23 days for TKN, and 3–20 days for TP. Compared to the continuously grazed catchment, hotspots in rotationally grazed, VF-managed catchments with cattle exclusion from riparian buffers were fewer, diffused, and located away from streams. Significant positive spatial autocorrelation was observed in five hotspot maps. Hotspot identification was influenced by pollutant persistence and grazing management, with rotational grazing showing fewer and more diffuse hotspots than continuous grazing.
